Cross-platform with unified output.

- [x wifi](/mod/wifi.md): WiFi tool with multiple modes:- "x wifi" (default = sum): interface hardware info + all available networks table- "x wifi info": WiFi adapter hardware info (card type, MAC, firmware, PHY modes)- "x wifi stat": compact table of all available networks (current + scanned),  current network marked with *, like "x disk stat"- "x wifi scan": scan nearby networks with SAVED column showing known networks- "x wifi connect": connect to a WiFi network- "x wifi enable/disable": turn WiFi on/off- "x wifi prefer": manage saved/preferred networksCross-platform (macOS/Linux/Windows) with TTY color support.
- [x usb](/mod/usb.md): USB tool with three modes:- "x usb" (default = sum): detailed device info + compact device table- "x usb info": detailed USB device info in key:value format  (name, vendor, serial, speed, product ID, vendor ID, device version, location)- "x usb ls": compact device table (DEVICE, VENDOR, SPEED, SERIAL)Cross-platform (macOS/Linux) with TTY color support.Speed shows human-readable labels: 12M (USB 1.1), 480M (USB 2.0),5G (USB 3.0), 10G (USB 3.1/3.2).
- [x display](/mod/display.md): Display tool with four modes:- "x display" (default = sum): detailed display info + compact display table- "x display info": detailed display properties in key:value format  (name, type, resolution, refresh rate, connection, serial, product/vendor ID)- "x display ls": compact table (DISPLAY, TYPE, RESOLUTION, REFRESH, CONNECTION)- "x display stat": real-time display status (brightness)Cross-platform (macOS/Linux/Windows) with TTY color support.Data sources:  macOS — system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType (text + JSON)  Linux — xrandr (with /sys/class/drm fallback)  Windows — wmic Win32_DesktopMonitor

# X-CMD

> X-CMD is a POSIX shell toolkit: 333+ modules, 500+ portable packages, 1200+ software installation recipes.

## 1. Installation & Setup

### Installation

**Quick install (Linux/macOS/BSD/Windows WSL/GitBash, bash/zsh):**
- curl: `eval "$(curl https://get.x-cmd.com)"`
- wget: `eval "$(wget -O- https://get.x-cmd.com)"`

**Non-POSIX shells (Fish, Elvish, Nushell, xonsh, tcsh):**
- Fish docs: https://x-cmd.com/start/fish.md
- Elvish docs: https://x-cmd.com/start/elvish.md
- Nushell docs: https://x-cmd.com/start/nushell.md
- xonsh docs: https://x-cmd.com/start/xonsh.md
- tcsh docs: https://x-cmd.com/start/tcsh.md

**System package managers:**
- Homebrew: `brew install x-cmd`, then run `x-cmd` to activate
- AUR: `sudo yay -S x-cmd`, then run `x-cmd` to activate

**Windows PowerShell:**
- PowerShell docs: https://x-cmd.com/start/powershell.md

**Docker containers (minimal environments without curl/wget):**
- From host: `x docker run -x -it <container>` or `x docker setup <container>`

**Verify installation**: check `~/.x-cmd.root/X` and `~/.x-cmd.root/bin/x-cmd` exist.
**Update**: `x upgrade` or re-run the install script.
**Uninstall**: `x uninstall self`

### Loading & Fallback

1.  **Load**: Before using `x` commands, run:
    ```sh
    [ -f ~/.x-cmd.root/X ] || eval "$(curl https://get.x-cmd.com)"
    . ~/.x-cmd.root/X
    ```
2.  **Fallback**: If `x` is not available (non-persistent shell session), use standalone command `x-cmd <module> [args]` (located at `~/.x-cmd.root/bin/x-cmd`, no shell function loading required).
3.  **Final Fallback**: If `x-cmd` is also not found, use absolute path: `~/.x-cmd.root/bin/x-cmd <module> [args]`

## 2. AI Usage Rules

- **Tool Availability**: `x <tool>` (e.g., `x jq`, `x python`) auto-detects whether the tool is installed; if missing, silently installs a portable version. Use when you need to ensure a tool is available.
- **Enhanced Modules**: Some modules provide enhanced functionality and behave differently from native commands (e.g., `x docker` ≠ `docker`, provides metadata extraction and status monitoring). Run `x <module> --help` before use.
- **Structured Output**: `x` modules output TSV, JSON, or `key: value` formats in pipe mode. Prefer `--json` flag when available.
- **No TTY Constraint**: DO NOT run interactive/TUI app commands in AI environments.

## 3. X-CMD Architecture

### Module Types

X-CMD functionality is organized as logical modules in two categories:

1. **Command Enhancement Wrappers**: `x id`, `x uname`, `x df`, `x docker`, etc. enhance native system commands.
   - TTY mode: Interactive TUI or colored structured output for human reading.
   - Pipe mode: Structured data output (TSV or JSON) for program/AI parsing.
   - Note: Enhanced modules (e.g., `x docker`) behave differently from native commands — not drop-in replacements.

2. **Shell Function Modules**: `x str` (string manipulation), `x tldr` (documentation browser), `x ccal` (Chinese calendar), etc. provide functionality not available natively.

### Smart Detection (e.g., `x jq`)

- System already has jq installed → uses the existing version directly.
- System has no jq → automatically downloads a portable version via `x snap jq` and runs it.
- For AI: just call `x jq` uniformly — no need to worry about whether the tool is pre-installed.

### Package System (`x env`)

X-CMD manages a portable package system with static/dynamic linked packages, no root privileges required, no impact on system environment.

Three usage modes:
- `x env use jq`: Global install to user environment — `jq` command available after loading x-cmd.
- `x env try jq`: Temporary install — only available in current shell session, not retained after exit.
- `x snap jq`: On-demand download and direct execution — no environment variable changes.

Other commands: `x env ls` (view installed), `x env ll` (view all available packages), `x env unuse <pkg>` (uninstall), `x env gc` (reclaim space).

Full package list: `x env ll` or https://x-cmd.com/pkg.md

### Software Installation (`x install`)

Different systems use different package managers with different naming and syntax (apt, dnf, brew, scoop, etc.), and some software can only be installed via `curl | sh`. `x install` abstracts all these differences behind a unified alias:

- `x install docker`, `x install git` — one command, auto-selects the best install path for the current system.
- Covers 1200+ commonly used software installation recipes.

Full install recipes: `x install ll` or https://x-cmd.com/install.md

## 4. Help System

Explore usage autonomously via three levels:
1. `x --help` — View all available modules.
2. `x <module> --help` — View module functions and subcommands.
3. `x <module> <subcommand> --help` — Get TLDR examples for a specific subcommand.

## 5. Common Modules Quick Reference

> Run `x <module> --help` for details.
> All modules: `x --help` or https://x-cmd.com/mod.md
> All packages: `x env ll` or https://x-cmd.com/pkg.md

- **Data Processing**:
  - `x jq`, `x yq` — JSON/YAML/TOML processing.
  - `x csv` — Query and convert CSV/TSV data.
  - `x str` — String manipulation (Base64, URL encoding/decoding, regex replace, random string).
  - `x sed`, `x sd`, `x grep`, `x rg` — Stream editing and high-performance search.
- **System & Network**:
  - `x id`, `x df`, `x free`, `x ps`, `x stat`, `x hash` — System status and file fingerprinting (structured output in pipe mode).
  - `x ip`, `x dns`, `x ping`, `x curl`, `x ssh` — Network diagnostics, geolocation, and connection management.
- **Messaging**:
  - `x feishu`, `x dingtalk`, `x telegram`, `x discord` — Bot notification sending.
- **Runtime Environments**:
  - `x python`, `x node`, `x go`, `x bun`, `x java`, `x deno` — Runtime environment configuration.
- **DevOps & Container**:
  - `x docker` — Enhanced Docker management (note: behavior differs from native `docker`).
  - `x gh`, `x gl`, `x git` — CLI wrappers for code hosting platforms.
- **Cloud Script Repository (`x hub`)**:
  - `x hub login` — Login/register an account (AI can run this command directly to log in).
  - `x hub file put/get/ls/cat` — Cloud file upload, download, list, view.
  - `x hub file share <cloud_path>` — Create a share link for a cloud file, supports `--expires` to set expiration.
  - `x hub file share zip <cloud_zip_path>` — Unzip a cloud zip and generate a multi-file site share link, can be used to host static websites (zip must contain index.html), supports `--entry` to specify the entry file.
  - `x hub file share ls` / `x hub file share rm` — View and delete share links.
  - `x hub cc` — Cloud compilation of Go/Zig/Rust scripts.
  - `x hub rag ask/upload` — AI knowledge base search and document upload.
  - `x hub account/access/org` — Account, access control, and organization management.
- **Platform & Tools**:
  - `x mac` — macOS system info and battery; `x termux` — Android environment enhancement.
  - `x zuz` — Smart decompression (auto-detects format); `x gram`, `x writer` — AI workflow orchestration.
  - `x tldr`, `x man`, `x cht` — Fast command examples and cheat sheets.

## 6. AI Skills

X-CMD provides 200+ skills to enhance Agent context awareness:
- `x skill ll`: List all available skills or view all collected skills (https://x-cmd.com/ai.md).
- `x skill suggest`: Get recommendations based on the current directory (useful during project setup or tool selection).
- `x skill add <skill-id>`: Activate a specific skill.
- `x agent setup`: Install x-cmd prompts and skills into the current Agent.

## 7. Error Recovery

- If a command fails, run `x <module> --help` to verify correct usage.
- If a module is not found, run `x --help` to search available modules.
- If a package download times out, retry once or use `x install <pkg>` to try via system package manager.

## 8. Reference

- Official: https://x-cmd.com
- All Modules (333+): https://x-cmd.com/mod.md (or `x --help`)
- All Packages (500+): https://x-cmd.com/pkg.md (or `x env ll`)
- Collected AI Skills / MCP (140+): https://x-cmd.com/ai.md (or `x skill ll`)
- Collected software installation recipes (1200+): https://x-cmd.com/install.md (or `x install ll`)
- Local Docs: `x nihao --llmstxt`

# x abox

abox is a command-line tool for managing AI Agent Docker containers.

It provides the ability to quickly start, stop, and restart containers,

as well as interact with containers via tmux, ssh, exec, etc.

Suitable for local development and testing of AI programming agents (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode).


::: tip Quick Start:
1. Start container: `x abox start`
2. Connect to container and open tmux session named claude: `x abox tmux :claude`
3. Stop container: `x abox stop`
:::


## Examples

Start default container (no SSH)

```sh
x abox start
```

Start container with SSH (random password)

```sh
x abox start --pass - --port 2222
```

Start named container with SSH key

```sh
x abox start --key ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub --port 2222 -n mybox
```

Remove default container

```sh
x abox rm
```

List all abox containers

```sh
x abox ls
```

Connect to default container via tmux

```sh
x abox t
```

Start tmux session named 'claude' in container

```sh
x abox tmux :claude
```

Stop default container

```sh
x abox stop
```

Pause default container

```sh
x abox pause
```

Resume default container

```sh
x abox resume
```

Start interactive bash in default container

```sh
x abox cmdi bash
```

Clean up all abox containers and images

```sh
x abox clearall
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x abox start](/mod/abox/start.md) | Start a new abox container |
| [x abox stop](/mod/abox/stop.md) | Stop the specified abox container |
| [x abox restart](/mod/abox/restart.md) | Restart the specified abox container |
| [x abox pause](/mod/abox/pause.md) | Pause the specified abox container |
| [x abox resume](/mod/abox/resume.md) | Resume the specified abox container |
| [x abox rm](/mod/abox/rm.md) | Remove the specified abox container |
| [x abox ls](/mod/abox/ls.md) | List all abox containers |
| [x abox fz](/mod/abox/fz.md) | Interactively select abox containers using FZF |
| [x abox tmux](/mod/abox/tmux.md) | Connect to container via tmux |
| [x abox cmd](/mod/abox/cmd.md) | Execute command in container (non-interactive) |
| [x abox cmdi](/mod/abox/cmdi.md) | Execute command in container (interactive) |
| [x abox login](/mod/abox/login.md) | Login to container (start bash) |
| [x abox clearall](/mod/abox/clearall.md) | Stop and remove all abox containers and images |

# x advise

Through the advise jso, provide the current command suggestions (completion, help ...)


::: tip
In interactive terminal (zsh &gt; 5.0 or bash), Can use Tab to get completion information
:::

::: tip The `___X_CMD_ADVISE_DISABLE` variable being set to 1 will disable the advise command completion feature.
The `___X_CMD_ADVISE_WITHOUT_DESC` variable is set to 1 to control not displaying the description information during autocompletion

The `___X_CMD_LANG` variable can control the language displayed in autocompletion (zh or en)
:::

::: tip
When the `___X_CMD_ADVISE_ACTIVATION_ON_NON_POSIX_SHELL` variable is set to 1, setting up x-cmd in a NON-POSIX SHELL environment (elv, fish, nu, onsh, tcsh) triggers the activation of advise injection.
:::


## Examples

Example: view advise specification (AI quick start)

```sh
x advise spec
```

Example: check advise config syntax

```sh
x advise lint
```

Example: AI test advise completion effect

```sh
x advise aitest
```

Example: list loaded advise jso files

```sh
x advise ls
```

Example: view advise jso content for tldr

```sh
x advise cat tldr
```

Example: load completion config for a command

```sh
x advise init tldr tldr/advise.jso
```

Example: update all completion packages

```sh
x advise man update all
```

Example: use Carapace as external completion tool

```sh
x advise addon use carapace
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x advise ls](/mod/advise/ls.md) | Show all available advise jso file |
| [x advise rm](/mod/advise/rm.md) | Delete the specified advised jso file that has been loaded, empty will delete all by default |
| [x advise which](/mod/advise/which.md) | Returns the path corresponding to the loaded advise jso file |
| [x advise cat](/mod/advise/cat.md) | Displays the specified advise jso file. |
| [x advise init](/mod/advise/init.md) | Use the advise jso file to load command completion |
| [x advise addon](/mod/advise/addon.md) | Choose whether to use external tools for command completion |
| [x advise spec](/mod/advise/spec.md) | Show the advise spec documentation |
| [x advise man](/mod/advise/man.md) | Manage x-cmd/advise and bash/zsh-completion advise jso files |
| [x advise autoload](/mod/advise/autoload.md) | Manage the auto-load mode for x-cmd command completions |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x agent</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span>

Integrate x-cmd into Claude, Codex, Cursor, Kimi and other AI tools.



Two operation modes:
1. request - Single-shot quick calls for simple Q&A
2. job - Long-term task iteration with auto-planning and execution


::: tip
First-time users should run `x agent setup` for initialization, then `x agent --cfg zero_harness=claude` to set default AI tool
:::

::: tip Quick start:
1. `x agent request "Explain this code"` —— Single Q&A
2. `x agent run "Add unit tests"` —— Auto-iterate to completion
3. `x agent run ./agent.md "Fix the bug"` —— Run with predefined config
:::

::: tip Harness is the AI tool interface. Popular options:
- claude —— Claude Code (most capable, recommended)
- codex —— OpenAI Codex
- kimi-cli —— Kimi CLI
- gemini-cli —— Google Gemini
- opencode —— Open-source multi-model tool

Full list in `x agent --cfg` hint
:::

::: tip Job data is saved to `~/.x-cmd/data/agent/job/` by default, one directory per task (timestamp-named)
Use `--job-id` to reference the same task across commands, e.g.:



`x agent run --job-id mytask ./agent.md "do it"` then `x agent job status --job-id mytask`
:::

::: tip claude-code requires 2.1.41+ for `claude auth` subcommand
Upgrade: `x env use claude-code` or `npm install -g @anthropics/claude-code`
:::

::: tip `tdown` is short for `teardown` — it disassembles the agent setup.
It reverses what `setup` did: removes the x-cmd prompts and skill0 symlinks that `setup` installed.
:::


## Examples

Example: Initialize and select default AI tool

```sh
x agent init
```

Example: First-time AI tool setup

```sh
x agent setup
```

Example: Set Claude as default tool

```sh
x agent --cfg zero_harness=claude
```

Example: Single AI Q&A

```sh
x agent request "Explain this code"
```

Example: Create and execute long-term task

```sh
x agent run "Add unit tests"
```

Example: Run standardized task with config

```sh
x agent run ./agent.md "Fix the bug"
```

Example: Start interactive AI chat in a workspace

```sh
x agent chat --workspace ./myproject
```

Example: Check task status (YAML format)

```sh
x agent job status --job-id mytask --yml
```

Example: Parse Claude Code session log, extract per-turn cost & efficiency stats

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid>
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x agent init](/mod/agent/init.md) | Initialize agent config, interactively select and set default AI tool |
| [x agent setup](/mod/agent/setup.md) | One-click configure all mainstream AI tools, auto-install x-cmd prompts and skills |
| [x agent tdown](/mod/agent/tdown.md) | Tear down setup configuration, remove x-cmd prompts and skill0 symlinks |
| [x agent unify](/mod/agent/unify.md) | Merge scattered AI tool configs into unified ~/AGENTS.md |
| [x agent request](/mod/agent/request.md) | Single-shot AI invocation — send prompt, get response, exit immediately (non-interactive) |
| [x agent chat](/mod/agent/chat.md) | Launch interactive AI chat with session reuse and workspace binding |
| [x agent --cfg](/mod/agent/--cfg.md) | Persistent configuration (written to file, cross-shell sessions) |
| [x agent --cur](/mod/agent/--cur.md) | Temporary configuration (current shell only, not written to file) |
| [x agent run](/mod/agent/run.md) | [Shortcut alias] Equivalent to `x agent job run`, run task with predefined agent config |
| [x agent isready](/mod/agent/isready.md) | Check if agent has completed initialization |
| [x agent job](/mod/agent/job.md) | Manage long-term iterative tasks (create, execute, monitor, stop) |
| [x agent stat](/mod/agent/stat.md) | [Experimental] Extract per-turn cost & efficiency statistics from AI agent session logs |

# x aider

Aider is an open-source AI coding assistant developed by the Aider-AI team. Designed primarily for the command line or terminal, it enables seamless collaboration with large language models (LLMs) without the need for a complex graphical interface.

It supports popular models out of the box, including Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1, Chat V3, OpenAI o1, o3-mini, and GPT-4o, and can also connect to any local or API-compatible LLM. Aider automatically maps the code structure of your entire Git repository, allowing it to understand context across multiple files and make coherent edits.

With support for over 100 programming languages, Aider can automatically generate semantic Git commit messages and perform commits. It also supports voice-to-code input, embedding screenshots or web content, and automatic linting and testing—making it ideal for developers to achieve AI pair programming within their local workflow.

Project URL: https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider


::: tip Aider works best when run inside a Git repository.
Voice input feature requires additional voice dependencies to be installed.
:::


## Examples

Launch interactive pair-programming session in-terminal

```sh
x aider
```

## Usage

```sh
x aider
```

# x arp

This module is used to display the local system's ARP cache table, supporting three output formats: CSV, TSV, and TUI application.

The header information for TSV/CSV is: ip, mac, if, suspicious, scope, type

## Examples

This is equivalent to 'x arp --auto'.  In this mode, interactive mode is started if standard output is connected to a terminal (tty); otherwise, output is in TSV format.

```sh
x arp
```

Display all ARP tables, including entries in an incomplete state

```sh
x arp --all
```

Do not display the manufacturer or organization information associated with the MAC address

```sh
x arp --no-vendor
```

View ARP cache table in csv format

```sh
x arp --csv
```

View ARP cache table in tsv format

```sh
x arp --tsv
```

Check ARP cache table with the tui app

```sh
x arp --app
```

## Usage

```sh
x arp [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--all`, `-a` | Display all ARP cache tables, including entries in an incomplete state |
| `--no-vendor`, `-n` | Do not display the manufacturer or organization information associated with the MAC address |
| `--auto` | If the standard output is connected to a terminal (tty), it starts in interactive mode (`--app`); otherwise, it outputs in TSV format (`--tsv`). This is the default behavior for `x arp` |
| `--app` | Check ARP cache table with the tui app |
| `--tsv`, `-t` | Output in TSV format |
| `--csv`, `-c` | Output in CSV format |
| `--raw`, `-r` | Output in the raw data format |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x arp ls](/mod/arp/ls.md) | Retrieving the ARP table |

# x ascii

The ascii module is designed to handle tasks related to ASCII, such as looking up the ASCII code table, displaying characters, pictures, and artistic fireworks in ASCII artwork.

Except for the table subcommand implemented in shell/awk, the rest of the commands use pkg or npm to download and run on demand, for example, cfont and map use modules hosted on npm and download and run on demand with least privilege through deno.

## Examples

Example: View ASCII code table

```sh
x ascii table
```

Example: View ASCII codes for lowercase letters

```sh
x ascii table lower
```

Example: View ASCII code for Ctrl-A

```sh
x ascii table ^A
```

Example: View character for hex 0x41

```sh
x ascii table 0x41
```

Example: Convert 'x-cmd' to ASCII art

```sh
x ascii cfont x-cmd
```

Example: Create ASCII art with red-blue gradient

```sh
x ascii cfont x-cmd -g red,blue
```

Example: Center text with red background

```sh
x ascii cfont x-cmd -a center -b red
```

Example: Display ASCII firework animation demo 1

```sh
x ascii firework -d 1
```

Example: Draw ASCII line graph for 1-10

```sh
seq 1 10 | x ascii graph
```

Example: Display ASCII world map in terminal

```sh
x ascii map
```

Example: Convert image to ASCII art

```sh
x ascii imagec photo.jpg
```

Example: Render Mermaid diagram in terminal

```sh
x ascii mermaid
```

# x asdf

asdf is an extensible version manager supporting installations of various development language environments and software tools such as Ruby, Node.js, Elixir, and Erlang.


::: tip
The asdf ecosystem relies on git commands, so if git is missing from your environment, you may encounter failures when using asdf to install certain software.
:::

::: tip The asdf module now supports versions of asdf rewritten in Go (v0.16.0 and above).
Compared to the previous Bash-based implementation (such as v0.15.0 and earlier), the new version introduces significant structural changes.

Users are encouraged to read the official upgrade guide to ensure a smooth transition: https://asdf-vm.com/guide/upgrading-to-v0-16.html
:::


## Examples

Open the interactive app search software and proceed with the installation

```sh
x asdf
```

Install and use Node.js in the global environment

```sh
x asdf use nodejs
```

Uninstall the installed Node.js

```sh
x asdf unuse nodejs
```

Deactivate asdf，so that the software installed by asdf cannot be run directly

```sh
x asdf --deactivate
```

## Usage

```sh
x asdf [SUB_COMMAND] <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | extends `asdf` subcmd or options |

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x asdf --install](/mod/asdf/--install.md) | Install the specified version of asdf |
| [x asdf --uninstall](/mod/asdf/--uninstall.md) | Uninstall asdf and remove related data (the .asdf directory in the HOME directory). |
| [x asdf --activate](/mod/asdf/--activate.md) | Activate asdf, allowing globally installed software to run directly |
| [x asdf --deactivate](/mod/asdf/--deactivate.md) | With asdf deactivated, the newly launched shell won't automatically load asdf's environment variables, like PATH.  This means any software globally installed via asdf will be inaccessible. |
| [x asdf --upgrade](/mod/asdf/--upgrade.md) | Update Asdf to the latest version. |

| [x asdf unuse](/mod/asdf/unuse.md) | Uninstall the specified package and remove its plugin.(equivalent to plugin remove) |
| [x asdf ddgo](/mod/asdf/ddgo.md) | Search software related information fron offical github repo by using DuckDuckGo |
| [x asdf ddgoai](/mod/asdf/ddgoai.md) | Summarize content list about asdf software using DuckDuckGo and AI module |
| [x asdf --](/mod/asdf/--.md) | Run the asdf command directly |

# x assert

Test assertion tool for verifying test results.



Returns non-zero exit code on failure.

Project: https://github.com/x-bash/assert


::: tip Test Best Practices:
1. Use 'x assert -- [ test ]' for command success
2. Use 'x assert ! cmd' for expected failures
3. Quote variables: 'x assert === "$a" "$b"'
4. Negate with ^: 'x assert is-file ^nonexist'
5. Var leakage: 'x assert var save' → call function → 'x assert var cmp'
:::


## Examples

Test: verify command succeeds with return 0

```sh
x assert true [ 1 -eq 1 ]
```

Test: verify command fails with non-zero

```sh
x assert ! false
```

Test: ignore stderr, verify command succeeds

```sh
x assert exit-0 noisy_cmd
```

Test: batch verify multiple values are integers

```sh
x assert is-int 1 2 3 4 5
```

Test: batch verify multiple float numbers

```sh
x assert is-float 3.14 2.718 0.5
```

Test: batch verify multiple positive integers (&gt;0)

```sh
x assert is-positive 42 100 999
```

Test: batch verify multiple variables are set

```sh
x assert is-set HOME PATH USER
```

Test: batch verify multiple variables are unset (^negation)

```sh
x assert is-set ^UNDEFINED ^NOTSET ^EMPTY
```

Test: verify multiple values all equal (3+)

```sh
x assert === "$a" "$b" "$c" "$d"
```

Test: verify value is in multiple candidates

```sh
x assert == "$status" pending running completed failed
```

Test: complex regex match

```sh
x assert =~ "$str" "^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$"
```

Test: glob matches any of multiple patterns (4+)

```sh
x assert =- "$file" "*.yml" "*.yaml" "*.json" "*.toml"
```

Test: batch verify multiple files exist

```sh
x assert is-file /etc/passwd /etc/hosts /etc/resolv.conf
```

Test: batch verify multiple directories exist

```sh
x assert is-folder /tmp /var /home
```

Test: batch verify multiple files do NOT exist (^negation)

```sh
x assert is-file ^nonexist1 ^nonexist2 ^nonexist3
```

Test: verify stdout output (heredoc)

```sh
x assert stdout echo hi <<EOF
hi
EOF

```

Test: verify stdout output (pipe)

```sh
echo expected | x assert stdout cat
```

Test: verify stderr output

```sh
x assert stderr grep pattern file <<EOF
pattern
EOF

```

Test: verify custom exit code

```sh
x assert return-42 mycmd
```

Test: save variable snapshot

```sh
x assert var save
```

Test: compare snapshot (detect variable leakage)

```sh
x assert var cmp
```

Test: detect if function accidentally modifies global variables

```sh
myfunc() { local x=1; y=2; }
x assert var save
myfunc
x assert var cmp

```

Test: allow new my_func_result variable (+declare)

```sh
x assert var save
my_func
x assert var cmp +my_func_result

```

Test: allow count and status to change (:declare)

```sh
x assert var save
process_data
x assert var cmp :count :status

```

Test: verify command fails with specific exit code

```sh
x assert exit-42 false
```

Test: combine multiple assertions for complex validation

```sh
x assert is-file /etc/passwd /etc/hosts && x assert is-folder /tmp /var
```

## Usage

```sh
x assert [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--`, `true` | Expect command to succeed (return 0). Example: x assert -- [ -f file ] |

| [x assert var](/mod/assert/var.md) | Variable snapshot: save snapshot, cmp changes (+new/-removed/:changed), print snapshot |
| [x assert is-nonempty](/mod/assert/is-nonempty.md) | Expect file is non-empty (size &gt; 0) |

| [x assert is-float](/mod/assert/is-float.md) | Expect float(s) |

# x aur

`x aur` is an AUR helper tool designed for Arch Linux users. It combines with fzf to provide a smooth interactive UI, allowing users to intuitively filter and select packages.

Additionally, it offers features to view popular package rankings (top) and analyze package popularity (stat), helping users quickly locate high-quality and popular applications in the AUR.

## Examples

Interactively search and view package lists using fzf, equivalent to 'x aur fz'

```sh
x aur
```

View the details of the 'x-cmd' package

```sh
x aur info x-cmd
```

View the top 200 most popular applications in AUR

```sh
x aur top 200
```

List packages in TSV (Tab-Separated Values) format

```sh
x aur ls --csv
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x aur fz](/mod/aur/fz.md) | Interactively search and view package lists using fzf |
| [x aur info](/mod/aur/info.md) | View detailed information about a package |
| [x aur ls](/mod/aur/ls.md) | View package list |
| [x aur top](/mod/aur/top.md) | List the most popular packages (displays 1000 by default) |
| [x aur update](/mod/aur/update.md) | Update AUR package list |
| [x aur stat](/mod/aur/stat.md) | Analyze and display the distribution of AUR package popularity by intervals, including the most popular value and the number of packages within each interval |

# x bfind

Breadth-first search sharing prune rules with x find, shallow results first, ideal for incremental exploration


::: tip
Shares the same three-dimension prune model as x find: (1) hidden dirs, (2) project noise, (3) HOME platform dirs. See x find --help for details.
:::

::: tip
Default depth is 3. Use --depth to go deeper. For git projects, prefer git ls-files and git grep.
:::


## Examples

BFS search current directory (default 3 layers)

```sh
x bfind .
```

5-layer search

```sh
x bfind --depth 5 .
```

Show all results

```sh
x bfind --all .
```

Exclude vendor and target, find .go files

```sh
x bfind --prune vendor:target -- . -name "*.go"
```

HOME search, disable HOME prune

```sh
x bfind --no-homeprune ~
```

All three dimensions off, raw find (BFS mode)

```sh
x bfind --unhide-all --reset-prune --no-homeprune -- .
```

Convert DFS find output to BFS order

```sh
find . -name "*.go" | x bfind --dfs2bfs
```

Reorder x find results by depth

```sh
x find . -type f | x bfind --dfs2bfs
```

List grep-matched files shallow-first

```sh
grep -rl "TODO" . | x bfind --dfs2bfs
```

## Usage

```sh
x bfind [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--depth` |  | Set maximum depth (default 3) |
| `--unhide` |  | Exempt hidden dirs from prune (supports : separator) |
| `--prune` |  | Add prune targets (supports : separator) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--unhide-all` | Do not exclude any hidden directories |
| `--reset-prune` | Clear project noise list (hidden dir prune and HOME prune unaffected) |
| `--no-homeprune` | Disable automatic HOME directory prune |
| `--all` | Show all results (unlimited depth) |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Show active prune lists |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x bfind --dfs2bfs](/mod/bfind/--dfs2bfs.md) | Reorder DFS paths from stdin into BFS order |

# x brew

Enhanced Homebrew command wrapper for macOS and Linux package management.

Provides convenient subcommands for installing, listing packages,

managing mirrors, proxies, and analytics.

## Examples

Example: Select software to install using TUI application

```sh
x brew
```

Example: Install multiple packages with brew

```sh
x brew install curl wget git
```

Example: List all installed packages

```sh
x brew ls
```

Example: List all installable Homebrew casks

```sh
x brew lr --casks
```

Example: Set up Tsinghua Source for Homebrew

```sh
x brew mirror set tuna
```

Example: Disable brew analytics to minimize privacy risks

```sh
x brew analytics off
```
## Introduction



The brew module is dedicated to enhancing the Homebrew user experience on the command line. It provides additional useful features such as changing Homebrew download sources, setting up proxies, and viewing download data.



## Protect Privacy by Disabling Homebrew Analytics



By default, Homebrew [collects user usage data](https://docs.brew.sh/Analytics) (such as software installation, uninstallation, and update data) to better optimize the software installation and usage experience. We recommend that users disable this feature to protect their privacy.


```bash
x brew a off
```



## Enhanced Features


1. `x brew mirror` : Manages Homebrew mirror sources and helps users switch between various mirrors like Alibaba, Tsinghua, and USTC.
2. `x brew proxy` : Unlike mirror, proxy is used to set up Homebrew proxies. You can set a global proxy or a proxy effective only for the current Shell session.
3. `x brew analytics data` :
   - Retrieves software download data from Homebrew's official statistics via the [Homebrew Formulae](https://formulae.brew.sh/analytics/) website.
   - Data can be output in JSON or CSV format using `--json|--csv` parameters.
   - By default, it opens the x-cmd specific CSV app in TUI format, presenting the data in a table sorted by download volume in descending order.
4. `x brew` | `x brew analytics` : Alternatively, you can simply use `x brew` or `x brew analytics` to interactively select the applications to install and view download data through an interactive UI.

## Usage

```sh
x brew
```

# x btop

btop (https://github.com/aristocratos/btop) is a resource monitor that shows

usage and stats for processor, memory, disks, network and processes.

This module prioritizes using the local btop command. If it's not available,

it will download and run via pixi (Linux/macOS) without installation,

ensuring no impact on your environment. For Windows, it installs via scoop.



Key features for memory analysis:
- Preset 1: Process-focused view with detailed memory per process
- Interactive filtering: Filter processes by name or PID
- Sort by memory: Press 'm' to sort processes by memory usage
- Shortcut keys: 'p' / 'Shift+p' to cycle through 4 preset views
- Help panel: Press '?' for full keyboard shortcuts


::: tip 【btop Preset View Quick Switch】
btop provides 4 preset views, switchable via:


1. Launch with preset: x btop -p &lt;num&gt;

   -p 0: Default view (all resources)

   -p 1: Process-focused view (best for memory analysis)

   -p 2: CPU-focused view

   -p 3: Network-focused view


2. Runtime switching:
   - Press 'p': Next preset
   - Press 'Shift+p': Previous preset



【Memory Analysis Best Practices】


1. Launch with: x btop -p 1 (process-focused view)
2. Press 'm' to sort by memory usage
3. Filter by process name (e.g., 'chrome')
4. Press '?' for more shortcuts



Common shortcuts:

  m     - Sort by memory

  c     - Sort by CPU

  n     - Sort by process name

  /     - Search filter

  f     - Freeze updates

  ?     - Help panel

  q     - Quit
:::


## Examples

Launch btop to view real-time system resources

```sh
x btop
```

Launch with process-focused view (best for memory analysis)

```sh
x btop -p 1
```

Show btop help

```sh
x btop -- -h
```

Launch with CPU-focused preset

```sh
x btop -- --preset 2
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x btop --](/mod/btop/--.md) | Run the 'btop' command directly |

# x ccal

The ccal module is a terminal-based calendar tool designed for Chinese users.

It provides a clear view of both Gregorian and lunar calendars, including solar terms,

traditional Chinese holidays, sexagenary cycle (heavenly stems and earthly branches),

six-day cycle, and daily almanac guidance for auspicious and inauspicious activities.

Ideal for checking Chinese festivals or consulting the traditional calendar for daily planning.



AI Agent Ready:
- Structured output (YML/TSV/CSV) designed for AI parsing and tool integration
- Rich tiaoxiu (调休放假) data: holidays, make-up work days, weekend schedules
- Offline-first: bundled lunar calendar data, no external API calls needed
- Accurate lunar date conversion including leap months
- Full-year holiday planning support for schedule-aware agents


::: tip Output mode auto-detection:
- TTY (terminal): colorful table output
- Pipe/non-TTY: YML or TSV format output (AI parseable)

Use --yml&#124;--tsv&#124;--csv&#124;--tty to force specific format
:::


## Examples

Interactively view calendar (equivalent to 'x ccal fz')

```sh
x ccal
```

View calendar for May 9, 2026

```sh
x ccal info --yml 2026-05-09
```

View today's calendar

```sh
x ccal t
```

List month data for May 2026

```sh
x ccal ls --yml 2026-05
```

List year data for 2026

```sh
x ccal ls --yml 2026
```

View ±7 days around May 9, 2026

```sh
x ccal around --yml 2026-05-09
```

View upcoming holidays and weekends from May 2026

```sh
x ccal tiaoxiu --yml 2026-05-01
```

View next 30 days of holiday schedule

```sh
x ccal tiaoxiu -n 30
```

View 2026 full year holidays

```sh
x ccal tiaoxiu -n 365 2026-01
```

Show holidays and work days only, exclude plain weekend rest

```sh
x ccal tiaoxiu --hide-plain-rest -n 30
```

Interactively view solar terms, holidays, make-up work days for each month

```sh
x ccal fzm
```

## Usage

```sh
x ccal [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--cfg` | Configuration for weekday naming, auspicious/inauspicious display, etc |
| `--cur` | Current session default value management for ccal |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x ccal fz](/mod/ccal/fz.md) | Use fzf to provide an interactive calendar interface, allowing quick jumps to specific dates or holidays |
| [x ccal fzm](/mod/ccal/fzm.md) | Interactively view the solar terms, holidays, and make-up work days for each month |
| [x ccal fzy](/mod/ccal/fzy.md) | Interactively view the dates of traditional festivals, zodiac animals, and leap months for each year |
| [x ccal around](/mod/ccal/around.md) | View ±7 days around a specified date (15 days total), showing day-level calendar data.



Data provided: date, lunar_date, jianchu (值星), weekday, jieqi, xiuxi (休/工), yi (宜), ji (忌), holiday |
| [x ccal tiaoxiu](/mod/ccal/tiaoxiu.md) | View upcoming holidays, weekends, and make-up work days from a starting date.



Output fields: date, weekday, xiuxi (假/工/休), reason
- 假 = 假日 (holiday or holiday-adjacent weekend)
- 工 = 工作日 (make-up work day)
- 休 = 休息日 (regular weekend) |
| [x ccal info](/mod/ccal/info.md) | View detailed calendar information for a specified date, defaulting to the current day.



Fields provided: date, lunar_date, lunar_daycount, jianchu (值星), weekday,

bazi (干支), jieqi (节气), jieqi_next, holiday, xiuxi (休/工), yi (宜), ji (忌) |
| [x ccal ls](/mod/ccal/ls.md) | List calendar data in various formats (day/week/month/year view).



Data provided:
- Day/Month view: date, lunar_date, jianchu (值星), weekday, jieqi, xiuxi (休/工), yi (宜), ji (忌), holiday
- Month summary: year_month, jieqi_list, tiaoxiu_xiu (放假), tiaoxiu_gong (上班)
- Year view: year, xuanyuan, shengxiao, leap_months, chunjie, qingming, duanwu, zhongqiu |
| [x ccal update](/mod/ccal/update.md) | Update ccal resource data |

# x ccmd

Cache command execution results to avoid re-running time-consuming commands.

Supports cache expiration time (n[smhdw] format), automatic cache invalidation and updates.

Ideal for caching slow operations like curl, complex queries, etc.


::: tip **Default execution**: `x ccmd -- <command>` directly caches command output
**Time units**: s(second), m(minute), h(hour), d(day), w(week) - default 1d

**Example**: `x ccmd 1h -- curl https://api.example.com/data`



**Note**: The -- separator is required when using exec subcommand
:::


## Examples

Example: cache ls command result (default 1 day)

```sh
x ccmd -- ls -la
```

Example: cache HTTP request for 1 hour

```sh
x ccmd 1h -- curl https://httpbin.org/get
```

Example: cache IP geo query for 30 minutes

```sh
x ccmd 30m -- x ips geo 1.1.1.1
```

Example: view cache path for curl command

```sh
x ccmd which curl
```

Example: clear cache for curl command

```sh
x ccmd invalidate curl
```

Example: clear all caches

```sh
x ccmd clear
```

Example: use custom cache directory

```sh
x ccmd setup /tmp/my-cache
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x ccmd which](/mod/ccmd/which.md) | View cache file path for specified command |
| [x ccmd clear](/mod/ccmd/clear.md) | Clear all cache files |
| [x ccmd invalidate](/mod/ccmd/invalidate.md) | Invalidate specified command's cache, will regenerate on next run |
| [x ccmd setup](/mod/ccmd/setup.md) | Set custom cache directory (default uses system temp directory) |
| [x ccmd teardown](/mod/ccmd/teardown.md) | Clean up and remove custom cache directory setting |
| [x ccmd exec](/mod/ccmd/exec.md) | Execute command and cache result (default subcommand) |
| [x ccmd v1](/mod/ccmd/v1.md) | v1 API interface (internal use) |
| [x ccmd _x_cmd_advise_json](/mod/ccmd/_x_cmd_advise_json.md) | Generate advise JSON (internal use) |

# x cd

This module is an enhanced version of the `cd` command implemented using the Posix shell, awk, and find.


::: tip
The interactive environment has a default alias set as `alias c='x cd'`
:::


## Examples

Switch directories, which is equivalent to the `cd ~/.x-cmd.root` command

```sh
c ~/.x-cmd.root
```

Change directory to /bin, list directory contents, then return to the original directory.

```sh
c /bin ls
```

Switch back to the last directory, which is equivalent to the `cd -` command

```sh
c -
```

Open the interactive app to search for the historical path and jump to it, equivalent to the `c ,` command

```sh
c
```

Find matching paths from the history path based on keyword and jump to them

```sh
c ,[keyword]
```

Go back to the parent directory that matches the keyword

```sh
c -b [keyword]
```

Find and jump to the subdirectory that matches the keyword

```sh
c -f [keyword]
```

Using Path Aliases

```sh
c :<relm name>/src
```

List the configured path aliases

```sh
c -r ls
```

Run the `ls -lah` command within the specified directory (without changing the current directory).

```sh
c ~/.x-cmd.root ls -lah
```

Open the parent directory interactively and select to jump

```sh
c ...
```

The system supports path abbreviations. You can search for paths in the format `/u[word]/b[word]` and the system will redirect you accordingly.

```sh
c /u/b
```
## Introduction



The `x cd` is designed to enhance the `cd` command, making it an **upgraded version of the `cd` command**. Implemented using Posix shell and awk, it offers a more comfortable path-switching experience and powerful advanced features like quickly locating frequently used directories from history, setting path aliases for common directories, and more. It only depends on `grep` and `find`, allowing it to function fully even in minimal busybox environments.



:::info

Given the frequent use of `cd`, when x-cmd is loaded, an alias for `x cd` is set as `alias c='x cd'`, so users only need to type `c` instead of `x cd`.

:::



## Five Enhancements for Path Navigation



### 1. History Directories -- Frequently Used Directories


- In an interactive environment (not script execution), the `cd` module records your history directories and provides quick jump suggestions based on that.
- Simply running the `c` command opens an interactive history directory list, making it easy and convenient to select the directory to navigate to.
- The history directory list is stored locally, **only recording the last 500 unique directories** by default — in practice, 500 entries are more than sufficient for regular use (300 is actually enough for me). Having too many entries might negatively impact the interactive experience and speed.
- `c ,{keyword}` allows you to search for a directory containing `{keyword}` in your recent history. If only one directory is matched, it will jump to it immediately; if multiple directories are matched, the `cd` module will provide an interactive history directory list for you to choose from.



### 2. Relm -- Directory Aliases


- `c --relm set {alias} {directory}`: Allows users to set an alias for a specified directory for quick navigation.
- `c :{alias}`: Jumps to the directory associated with the alias. The `cd` module defines a directory with an alias as **relm**, allowing users to jump to the **relm** or subdirectories within it, e.g., `c :desk/src` jumps to the src directory within the current user's desktop.


- Based on system characteristics, the `cd` module already provides aliases for commonly used directories, such as:
  - `c :desk`: The current user's desktop directory;
  - `c :down`: The user's download directory;
  - `c :`: The directory where the shell loaded x-cmd — useful in terminal IDEs; for example, if you open a terminal in VS Code, it initializes at the project root directory, allowing you to quickly return to it with `c :`;
  - `c :git`: If the current directory is within a git-managed folder, it jumps to the root .git directory;
  - And many more, which users can view with the `c --relm` command.



### 3. Backward Navigation -- Backward


- `c -b [keyword]`: Used to navigate back to a parent directory. Similar to the `c ,{keyword}` command, but limits the jump range to all parent directories of the current directory, suitable for scenarios where the current directory path is long and hard to identify.
- `c ...`: A more interactive version of the `c -b` command, with the added feature of directory previews.
- `c .../{keyword}`: An alias for the `c -b [keyword]` command.



### 4. Experimental Features


1. **Forward Exploration**:
    - **Intended Scope**: All subdirectories within the current directory and its next two levels.
    - **Reason for Experimental Status**: This feature relies on `find`, which may cause lag in interactive use when dealing with many directory files. Therefore, the `maxdepth` for `find` is set to 3. Further optimizations will be made in future updates of the `cd` module.




2. **Abbreviation Exploration**:
    - **Concept**: You can use path abbreviations, such as `c /u/b`, `c /usr/b`, and `c /u/bin`, to jump to the `/usr/bin` directory.
    - **Process**: For the command `c /u/b`, if no `/u/b` path is found, the `cd` module will search for paths like `/u[word]/b[word]` (e.g., `/usr/bin`). If only one directory path is matched, it will jump to it immediately; if multiple paths are matched, the module will provide an interactive list for selection.


3. **Running Commands or Scripts in Specified Directories**:
    - **Concept**: Quickly run commands or scripts in a specified directory without changing the current directory.
    - Command format: `c {folder} [command]` or `c [option] [,|:][keyword] [command]`, for example:
      - `c ~/.x-cmd.root ls -lah`: Equivalent to the command `( cd "~/.x-cmd.root"; ls -lah)`.
      - `c :work vim .`: Conveniently helps you open a commonly used work directory with `vim`.



### 5. On Sorting History Directories: Using LRU Instead of LFU



In short, the `cd` module assumes history directories are frequently used and adopts the **LRU (Least Recently Used)** strategy, only recording when switching directories with `x cd` or `c` commands, and storing up to 500 records to generate directory suggestion lists.



Unlike `z` and `autojump`, the `cd` module does not use frequency (popularity) for sorting, relying only on recent usage for sorting. The main considerations are:
1. Design Philosophy:
    1. If multiple results are matched, users should refine the search criteria to filter the target result, rather than computing or guessing the final result.
    2. We believe presenting multiple results side by side, with order being unimportant, is not worse than sorting by "recency of use" instead of "frequency of use."
2. Performance Considerations:
    1. We **do not want to introduce too much computational complexity**; the `cd` module should **perform well in environments with limited computing power**.
    2. The current **LRU strategy requires very little computation**.
3. We are unsure whether to introduce more complex external file indexing (file dependencies) and design (additional bugs), and more importantly, this involves privacy concerns.
4. We are currently unable to clearly determine the final positioning of the `cd` module, nor whether introducing more advanced sorting strategies would be beneficial, so we prefer a simpler, more reliable implementation.



We believe that using history records, the LRU strategy, and interactive search should achieve satisfactory results. However, the x-cmd team will continue to carefully analyze actual usage scenarios and explore more user-friendly designs in the future.

## Usage

```sh
x cd [SUB_COMMAND] <#1>
```

| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Directory path |

# x claude

claude-code is a terminal-based AI programming agent developed by Anthropic.

Powered by Claude Opus or Sonnet models, it enables semantic codebase search, patch generation, command execution, and Git operations through natural language.

It supports sub-agent workflows for parallelized tasks and enhances developer productivity directly from the command line.

Project: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code


::: tip x-cmd provides multiple ways to run claude-code with third-party models:
- On-demand: Use commands like `x claude mm` (MiniMax), `x claude glm` (Zhipu), `x claude or` (OpenRouter) to fetch the API key from the corresponding module and run claude-code directly
- Global config: Use `x claude use glm` to write configuration to ~/.claude/settings.json, then running `claude` directly will use that model
- Project config: Use `x claude use --project glm` to write configuration to .claude/settings.local.json in the current project, affecting only that project
:::


## Examples

Use Claude Code

```sh
x claude
```

Launch the FZF app to interactively browse and manage local sessions

```sh
x claude sess
```

Remove Claude Code's automatic Co-Author signature from commits

```sh
x claude attribution rm
```

Set up the Claude Code statusline using the el theme (default)

```sh
x claude stl setup
```

Show token usage and costs for the last 7 days

```sh
x claude usage
```

Launch claude-code and connect to the DeepSeek V4 model.

```sh
x claude ds
```

Configure claude-code to use the MiniMax Coding Plan

```sh
x claude use minimax
```

Configure claude-code to use Xiaomi Token Plan

```sh
x claude use other "https://token-plan-cn.xiaomimimo.com/anthropic" MIMO_API_KEY mimo-v2.5-pro
```

x claude [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]

## Introduction



The coin module is a CoinCap CLI module encapsulated using Shell and AWK based on the CoinCap API by the x-cmd team. It aims to obtain real-time information from the CoinCap platform in a lightweight and efficient manner.



## Main Features
- As a module of x-cmd, the coin module provides complete out-of-the-box functionality and friendly command-line completion.
- The coin module follows the design philosophy of the x-cmd CLI in its command design, thus maintaining consistency with other x-cmd CLIs.
- Uses x-cmd's TUI system to provide a consistent and easy-to-use command-line interface.
- Combined with the jo module of x-cmd, the returned information is filtered and integrated, and then converted into a more readable presentation method to improve user experience.

## Usage

```sh
x coin
```

# x colr

The Color Finder is a tool for finding ANSI colors and their corresponding color codes. It supports both 256-color and RGB color systems.

## Examples

List the code for all the colors in the 256-color palette and their corresponding approximate colors

```sh
x colr
```

A color-coded chart displaying 8-color

```sh
x colr 8
```

Find colors that are similar to green

```sh
x colr ls green
```

Display approximate colors for red

```sh
x colr --red
```

Find colors that are similar to rgb(0128,0)

```sh
x colr 0,128,0
```

Find colors that are similar to #008000

```sh
x colr #008000
```

Output rainbow colors, with minimum RGB color value of 100, maximum RGB color value of 200, and color gamut interval of 50

```sh
x cowsay hello  | x colr rainbow --min 100 --max 200 --step 50
```

```sh
x colr [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

| `--red` | Display approximate colors for red, maroon, and pink |
| `--yellow` | Display approximate colors for yellow and orange |
| `--green` | Display approximate colors for green, azure, olive, and live |
| `--gray` | Display a Approximate color for gray |
| `--black` | Display approximate colors for gray and black |
| `--white` | Display approximate colors for gray and white |


## Sub Commands

# x column

awk re-implementation of GNU `column`, 100% compatible — align delimited text into a table, or arrange lines into side-by-side columns; auto reverse-video the title row on tty; table mode supports per-column color and per-N-row underline


::: tip
Use it like `column` directly: `x column -t -s : file` is GNU `column -t -s : file`, options first
:::

::: tip
`--tsv` is shorthand for `-t -s $'\t'`; `--csv` runs the input through `x tsv fromcsv` first then tabulates as TSV, with proper quoted-field handling
:::

::: tip
Default delimiter is whitespace, with consecutive runs collapsed (matches GNU column); pass -n to keep empty cells
:::

::: tip
Without -t, fill mode kicks in: each line is one entry, arranged in side-by-side columns within `-c <width>` (default: terminal width, 80 fallback); perfect for `ls | x column`
:::

::: tip
Coloring is tty-aware: the title row (row 1) gets wrapped in reverse video (`\033[7m...\033[0m`) when stdout is a terminal, plain bytes when piped — so `... | grep` stays clean
:::

::: tip
NO_COLOR=1 to disable, --color to force on, --no-color to force off
:::

::: tip
Pure shell + awk under the hood: parsing in lib/main, alignment and color in lib/awk/table.awk and lib/awk/fill.awk
:::

::: tip
Drop-in for environments that lack `column` (busybox containers, Alpine images, minimal rootfs): runs as long as dash + awk are available, no extra deps
:::


## Examples

Example: Tabulate the TSV form of /etc/passwd

```sh
x passwd --tsv | x column --tsv
```

Example: Tabulate epoch river output (auto-TSV when piped)

```sh
x epoch river | x column --tsv
```

Example: Tabulate CSV output (--csv handles quoted fields internally)

```sh
x csv file.csv | x column --csv
```

Example: Tabulate `ps` output (default whitespace, runs collapsed)

```sh
ps -eo pid,user,comm | x column -t
```

Scenario: Without -t: arrange `ls` output in side-by-side columns (fit terminal width)

```sh
ls | x column
```

Scenario: Force plain output (honours the NO_COLOR convention)

```sh
NO_COLOR=1 x column -t -s : file
```

Scenario: Force colors on, pipe to `less -R` for paging

```sh
x column -t -s : --color file | less -R
```

## Usage

```sh
x column [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-s` &lt;delim&gt; |  | Input delimiter; empty means whitespace (space / tab, runs collapsed) |
| `-o` &lt;sep&gt; |  | Output column separator, default two spaces |
| `-c` &lt;width&gt; |  | Output width (fill mode uses this to decide how many side-by-side columns; default — terminal width) |
| `--color-per-column` &lt;spec&gt; |  | Custom per-column colors as colon-separated ANSI SGR codes (table mode only); e.g. "31:32:34" = red/green/blue for columns 1/2/3 |
| `--underline-every` &lt;n&gt; |  | Underline every Nth line (table mode only); N=1 underlines every line |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `-t` | Table mode: split each line by -s and pad columns to the widest cell |
| `--tsv` | Tab-separated shorthand (equivalent to -t -s $'\\t'; `x epoch river` auto-outputs TSV when piped) |
| `--csv` | CSV shorthand — convert to TSV first (handles quoted fields), then tabulate as TSV (equivalent to `... | x tsv fromcsv | x column -t -s $'\t'`) |
| `-n` | Do not collapse runs of delimiters (only meaningful with whitespace input) |
| `--color` | Force ANSI colors on (table mode: title reverse + per-column cycle; fill mode: per-column cycle + first-row reverse; auto-on for tty, auto-off for pipes) |
| `--no-color` | Force ANSI colors off (also respects the NO_COLOR env var) |

# x cosmo

The cosmo suite of applications refers to software tools compiled with the Cosmopolitan C Library. Cosmopolitan, an open-source project developed by Justine Tunney, aims to compile C/C++ programs into universal binaries capable of running across multiple operating systems like Windows, Linux, and macOS, all without the need for virtual machines or interpreters.

For more information about the Cosmopolitan project, please visit https://justine.lol/cosmopolitan/


::: tip
"x cosmo &lt;bin&gt;" by default utilizes the APE loader (automatically downloaded upon first use) to execute the binary, equivalent to "x cosmo --aperun &lt;bin&gt;".
:::


## Examples

Interactive selection of program to use

```sh
x cosmo
```

Use cosmo's lua

```sh
x cosmo lua
```

Install lua to the specified directory

```sh
x cosmo -i lua <target directory>
```

Use TUI to select a directory from the list of directories in the current PATH variable and install `make` to that directory

```sh
x cosmo -i make
```
## introduce



The cosmo module is designed to help users quickly install and utilize binary files built with the [Cosmopolitan Libc](https://github.com/jart/cosmopolitan).



:::info

Cosmopolitan Libc makes C a build-once run-anywhere language, like Java, except it doesn't need an interpreter or virtual machine.

Instead, it reconfigures stock GCC and Clang to output a POSIX-approved polyglot format that runs natively on Linux + Mac + Windows + FreeBSD OpenBSD + NetBSD + BIOS with the best possible performance and the tiniest footprint imaginable.

It is created by a legendary programmer, [Justin Tunney](https://justine.lol/). Look on her works, yet Mighty, and Despair !

:::



This module uses the cosmo APE loader by default to run binary files:


- Avoids startup problems encountered when running cosmo binaries directly in environments such as WINE and WSL
- This method takes less time to start



In addition, the module also provides:


- Interactive UI: Enter x cosmo to list all cosmo binaries in an interactive list, helping users search more conveniently and reduce input errors.
- Global installation: Users can use the x cosmo -i command to install the binary to the /usr/bin directory without specifying a loader to execute.
- Module integration: Some x-cmd modules have integrated cosmo binaries. For example, user can use `x make` and `x qjs` to use make and qjs cosmo binary.

## Usage

```sh
x cosmo [SUB_COMMAND] <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | application name |
| `#2` | argument of the program |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x cosmo use](/mod/cosmo/use.md) | Install the tool into the current user's global environment |
| [x cosmo unuse](/mod/cosmo/unuse.md) | Cancel the use of the specified program in the global environment |
| [x cosmo --install](/mod/cosmo/--install.md) | Install the application to the specified directory |
| [x cosmo --ape](/mod/cosmo/--ape.md) | Use and Registration APE Loader |
| [x cosmo --run](/mod/cosmo/--run.md) | Run the specified application of the cosmo series |
| [x cosmo --add](/mod/cosmo/--add.md) | Install and deploy the specified application |
| [x cosmo --ll](/mod/cosmo/--ll.md) | List all available applications |
| [x cosmo --ls](/mod/cosmo/--ls.md) | List applications in interactive mode |
| [x cosmo --which](/mod/cosmo/--which.md) | Get the installation path of the specified application |
| [x cosmo --author](/mod/cosmo/--author.md) | View more information about the authors of Cosmopolitan |

# x cowrie

The cowrie module, built on Docker, provides a streamlined way to launch and manage cowrie, making it easy for users to set up and test their own honeypot environments.

Cowrie (https://github.com/cowrie/cowrie) is an open-source interactive honeypot project. It simulates a real SSH and Telnet service environment, allowing attackers to freely roam within the honeypot, recording all their actions for later analysis of their attack patterns and collection of malicious code.

## Examples

Create and run a cowrie container using the default configuration

```sh
x cowrie run
```

Create and start a Cowrie container named 'test'

```sh
x cowrie run --name test
```

Connect to the cowrie container running on port 2223 using ssh

```sh
x cowrie test
```

Show the running logs of the cowrie container

```sh
x cowrie log
```

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |

# x cpu

CPU tool with three modes:
- "x cpu" (default = sum): static info + real-time load, all in one view
- "x cpu info": static hardware info only (model, cache, ARM features, etc.)
- "x cpu stat": real-time CPU load only (overall + per-core usage)

Also supports endianness detection. Cross-platform with unified output.

## Examples

Example: Display full CPU overview (info + stat)

```sh
x cpu
```

Example: Show static CPU hardware info only

```sh
x cpu info
```

Example: Show basic CPU info

```sh
x cpu info --simple
```

Example: Show real-time CPU load only

```sh
x cpu stat
```

Example: Detect system endianness

```sh
x cpu endianness
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x cpu sum](/mod/cpu/sum.md) | First shows all static hardware fields, then appends real-time CPU load stats (same as running bare "x cpu") |
| [x cpu info](/mod/cpu/info.md) | Show static CPU hardware information only — no load stats. |
| [x cpu stat](/mod/cpu/stat.md) | Show real-time CPU load statistics only — no hardware info. |
| [x cpu endianness](/mod/cpu/endianness.md) | Detect system endianness (l for little, b for big) |

# x cron

Lightweight cron job scheduler with add, remove, list, and match testing.

Jobs are isolated by namespace with per-namespace timezone support.

Supports standard cron time format (min hour day month dow).

Each job is stored as a directory containing the cron pattern, cmd script,

and optional description.


::: tip Three-way comparison: cron = recurring scheduled task (cron mission with multiple jobs); bgjob = one-shot background task; worker = persistent background process (e.g. daemon).
See x bgjob --help for full comparison.
:::


## Examples

Example: Add a described job that runs every 5 minutes

```sh
x cron add --name myjob --desc "say hello" "*/5 * * * *" "echo hello"
```

Example: Add a one-time job

```sh
x cron add --once --name greeting "0 9 * * *" "echo good morning"
```

Example: List all jobs

```sh
x cron ls
```

Example: Remove a job

```sh
x cron rm myjob
```

Example: Test if current time matches a cron pattern

```sh
x cron match "*/5 * * * *"
```

Example: Test if a specific time matches a cron pattern

```sh
x cron match "*/5 * * * *" "30 8 16 4 4"
```

Example: Set scheduling timezone for the current namespace

```sh
x cron tz Asia/Shanghai
```

Example: Start the cron daemon

```sh
x cron service start
```

Example: Debug daemon for a namespace in foreground

```sh
x cron run --ns mynamespace
```

Example: Manually trigger a one-time job run

```sh
x cron runonce
```

Example: Execute a specific job directly for testing

```sh
x cron exec myjob
```

Example: View the latest execution details for a job

```sh
x cron history myjob
```

Example: View execution details for a specific timestamp

```sh
x cron history myjob 1715673705
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x cron add](/mod/cron/add.md) | Add a cron job |
| [x cron rm](/mod/cron/rm.md) | Remove a job by name |
| [x cron ls](/mod/cron/ls.md) | List all jobs in the current namespace (TSV: name pattern desc once last_start last_end last_status last_exit_code cmd) |
| [x cron match](/mod/cron/match.md) | Test if a time matches a cron pattern (uses current time by default) |
| [x cron tz](/mod/cron/tz.md) | Configure the timezone for job scheduling |
| [x cron run](/mod/cron/run.md) | Run the cron daemon in the foreground (loop, check and run matching jobs every minute) |
| [x cron runonce](/mod/cron/runonce.md) | Execute all jobs matching the current time once (no loop) |
| [x cron history](/mod/cron/history.md) | View execution details for a cron job (shows latest if timestamp omitted) |
| [x cron exec](/mod/cron/exec.md) | Execute a specific job's command directly (ignoring cron time match, for testing) |
| [x cron service](/mod/cron/service.md) | Manage the cron daemon |

# x cutt

print in tabular form using matrix data

## Examples

Select rows 1-3, column 2 from whitespace-separated data

```sh
printf "%s\n" "a1 a2 a3" "b1 b2 b3" "c1 c2 c3" | x cutt 1:3 2
```

The `x ascii` command outputs a TSV table to the pipe.  `x cutt --tab` selects rows 100-N and columns 1, 3, and 6-end.

```sh
x ascii | x cutt --tab 100:-10 1,3,6:
```

Specify colon as delimiter with -d, select column 2 from all rows

```sh
printf 'a1:b1:c1
a2:b2:c2
' | x cutt -d : : 2
```

Output the second column data of rows 1 to 3 in the matrix data

```sh
printf "%s\n" "a1 a2 a3" "b1 b2 b3" "c1 c2 c3" | x cutt 1:3 2

```

Output the second column data of rows 1 and 3 in the matrix data

```sh
printf "%s\n" "a1 a2 a3" "b1 b2 b3" "c1 c2 c3" | x cutt 1,3 2

```

Use --tab to force tab-separated output for TSV data

```sh
printf 'a1\tb1\tc1\na2\tb2\tc2\na3\tb3\tc3\n' | x cutt --tab : 1,3

```

Use --normal to ignore tab detection and force whitespace splitting with space-separated output

```sh
printf 'a1\tb1\tc1\na2\tb2\tc2\na3\tb3\tc3\n' | x cutt --normal : 1,3

```

Use -d to specify a custom colon delimiter

```sh
printf 'a1:b1:c1\na2:b2:c2\na3:b3:c3\n' | x cutt -d : : 2

```

## Usage

```sh
x cutt [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Row range [start:end].  Start and end are 1-based indices.  Use a single number for a single row.  A negative number indicates an offset from the end of the file (e.g., -1 is the last row, -2 is the second to last).  Ranges are inclusive. |
| `#2` | Column range [start:end]. Start and end are 1-based indices. Use a single number for a single column.  A negative number indicates an offset from the end of the line (e.g., -1 is the last column, -2 is the second to last). Ranges are inclusive. |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-d` |  | Specify the delimiter character or string used to separate columns in the input data.  If omitted, the command attempts to auto-detect the delimiter. |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--auto` | Default mode. Reads the first line of input; if it contains a tab character (\\t), both input and output field separators are set to tab. Otherwise falls back to AWK's default whitespace-based field splitting. |
| `--tab`, `--tsv` | Force tab as the field separator for both input and output. |
| `--normal` | Use AWK's default field separator. Fields are split by whitespace (spaces, tabs, etc.), and output fields are joined by a single space. No auto-detection is performed. |

# x cve

The CVE command-line interface, powered by x-cmd, fetches CVE indexes from x-cmd/cve via curl.


::: tip x cve                          # browse / fzf over every cached CVE (newest first)
- **The 4 commands you'll actually use:**
  ```sh
  x cve info CVE-2024-0001       # look up by id (or `x cve 2024-0001`)
  x cve detail CVE-2024-0001     # pull the FULL upstream record (affected, CWE, references, ADP)
  x shodan cve CVE-2024-0001     # enrich with Shodan: EPSS, KEV, exploits, vendor advisories
  ```

  See &lt;https://x-cmd.com/mod/cve&gt; and &lt;https://x-cmd.com/mod/shodan/cve&gt;.
- No API key, no sudo, no background services. `x cve` is a thin shell module backed by per-year xz-compressed TSVs published daily at `github.com/x-cmd/cve/releases/download/data/`.
- **`x shodan cve` is worth the extra hop** when you need to know "is this exploitable, who's affected, what's the patch" — Shodan aggregates EPSS, KEV listing, exploit writeups, and vendor advisories that the upstream CVE record itself doesn't carry.
- Cache hit on the second call onward — current year refreshes every 1 day, older years stay cached 180 days.
- Shorthands: `x cve 2026` is `x cve year --tsv 2026`; `x cve 2026-9999` is `x cve info CVE-2026-9999`; `x cve 2026-05` is `x cve year 2026 | grep CVE-2026-05`.
- For the full upstream record (affected products, CWE, references, timeline, ADP), use `x cve detail CVE-YYYY-NNNN`.
:::


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |

# x cwe

The CWE command-line interface, powered by x-cmd, fetches the MITRE CWE catalog via curl.


::: tip
- No API key needed. Data comes directly from the public MITRE CWE catalog.
- First call downloads `2000.csv.zip` (~640 KB) and caches it locally.
- Cached catalog rarely changes (30-day TTL); force a refresh with `x cwe update`.
- The catalog is large (969+ entries) — use `x cwe fz` for interactive browsing or `x cwe ls --tsv | grep <pattern>` to script.
- For the full upstream record (description, related weaknesses, mitigations, consequences, observed examples), use `x cwe info CWE-NNN`.
:::


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x cwe info](/mod/cwe/info.md) | Look up one or more CWE records by id (full description, related weaknesses, mitigations, consequences, etc.) |
| [x cwe ls](/mod/cwe/ls.md) | Stream every cached CWE row. TTY → fzf picker; pipe → TSV. Auto-refreshes if cache is stale (&gt;30 days). |
| [x cwe fz](/mod/cwe/fz.md) | Interactive fzf picker over every cached CWE |
| [x cwe update](/mod/cwe/update.md) | Refresh the local CWE cache from MITRE |
| [x cwe data](/mod/cwe/data.md) | Manage the local CWE cache; query its location, status, and base URL |
| [x cwe --](/mod/cwe/--.md) | `x cwe info` shortcut — treat bare arg as a CWE id |

# x date

Get current time, convert time formats, compute time differences


::: tip Default outputs current time in ISO format (equivalent to x date dump)
--&lt;fmt&gt; defaults to ISO when omitted; &lt;timestamp&gt; uses now when omitted

Supports seconds/milliseconds/decimal timestamps (1743038674 / 1743038674123 / 1743038674.123)
:::

::: tip
Developers could use timestamp_ for efficiency
:::


## Examples

Example: Output current time in ISO (default dump behavior)

```sh
x date dump
```

Example: String format suitable for filenames

```sh
x date dump --str
```

Example: UTC short ID

```sh
x date dump --vlid
```

Example: Convert timestamp to ISO (supports s/ms/decimal)

```sh
x date dump --iso 1743038674
```

Example: Custom strftime-style format output

```sh
x date dump --fmt '%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S'
```

Example: Get current timestamp (seconds)

```sh
x date timestamp
```

Example: Convert ISO time string to timestamp

```sh
x date timestamp '2026-03-27 12:00:00'
```

Example: Convert date string to timestamp

```sh
x date iso2ts '2026-03-27'
```

Example: Convert vlid short ID to timestamp

```sh
x date vlid2ts '260327_092434'
```

Example: Calculate days between two dates

```sh
x date diff '2026-01-01' '2026-03-27'
```

Example: Calculate distance from date to today

```sh
x date diff '2026-03-27'
```

Example: Compute difference between two epochs (seconds)

```sh
x date minus 1743038674 1743000000
```

Example: Show time difference in human-readable form

```sh
x date minus --human 1743038674 1743000000
```

Example: Compute difference in days

```sh
x date minus --day 1743038674 1743000000
```

Example: Subtract two date strings

```sh
x date minus --human '2025-03-27' '2025-03-26'
```

Example: Parse ISO time string to timestamp

```sh
x date parse '2026-03-27T09:24:34+0800'
```

Example: Parse time string with custom fmt

```sh
x date parse --fmt '%Y/%m/%d' '2026/03/27'
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x date dump](/mod/date/dump.md) | Format the current time or a timestamp; defaults to ISO when --&lt;fmt&gt; is omitted |
| [x date timestamp](/mod/date/timestamp.md) | Get current timestamp (seconds), or convert a time string to a timestamp (supports various ISO formats) |
| [x date timestamp_](/mod/date/timestamp_.md) | Get current timestamp into variable x_, or convert a time string to a timestamp (non-output form) |
| [x date iso2ts](/mod/date/iso2ts.md) | Convert an ISO format time string to a timestamp (seconds) |
| [x date vlid2ts](/mod/date/vlid2ts.md) | Convert a vlid format (YYMMDD_hhmmss) string to a timestamp (seconds) |
| [x date parse](/mod/date/parse.md) | Parse a formatted time string into an epoch timestamp (default fmt='%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z', falls back to system TZ when no offset is given) |
| [x date diff](/mod/date/diff.md) | Calculate days between two dates (single arg calculates distance to today) |
| [x date minus](/mod/date/minus.md) | Compute the difference between two times (output seconds, human-readable duration, or days); accepts epoch seconds or date strings; single arg computes distance to now |

# x dbnomics

DBnomics is one of the world's largest economic data aggregators, covering free data from IMF, World Bank, ECB, and more.

This module is x-cmd's lightweight CLI wrapper for the DBnomics Web API (v22).


::: tip No authentication required. All API requests are cached for 1 hour via x ccmd.
Docs: https://api.db.nomics.world/v22
:::

::: tip Recommended exploration path:
1. x dbnomics alias — check pre-defined aliases (us.cpi, bis.eur, etc.)
2. x dbnomics search &lt;keyword&gt; — full-text search datasets
3. x dbnomics provider — browse data providers
4. x dbnomics dataset &lt;provider&gt; — browse specific datasets
5. x dbnomics series &lt;provider&gt; &lt;dataset&gt; — list series
:::

::: tip How to find a full series ID:
1. x dbnomics provider — find provider_code (e.g. IMF, BIS)
2. x dbnomics dataset &lt;provider&gt; — find dataset_code (e.g. WEO:2024-10)
3. x dbnomics series &lt;provider&gt; &lt;dataset&gt; — find series_code

Full ID format: provider_code/dataset_code/series_code
:::

::: tip
The data subcommand only supports single series. Use align for multi-series aligned output.
:::

::: tip IMF WEO unit notes: persons = millions, us_dollars = billions, pcent_change = percent change.
DBnomics API does not provide magnitude info; refer to each data source's official docs.
:::

::: tip IMF WEO dynamic alias — imf.&lt;cc&gt;.&lt;suffix&gt;
Examples: imf.th.gdp (Thailand GDP), imf.kr.cpi (Korea CPI), imf.cn.gdp.growth (China GDP growth)

Country codes: x dbnomics code region2

Indicator suffixes: x dbnomics code weoseries
:::

::: tip IMF WEO economic group alias — imf.&lt;group&gt;.&lt;suffix&gt;
Examples: imf.eu.gdp (EU GDP), imf.g7.gdp.growth (G7 growth), imf.asean.ppp (ASEAN PPP)

Groups: eu (EU), euro (Euro area), g7, asean, world, advanced, emerging, latam, mideast, devasia, africa, deveur

Full list: x dbnomics code weoagg
:::

::: tip BIS exchange rate dynamic alias — bis.&lt;currency&gt; (monthly vs USD)
Examples: bis.eur (Euro), bis.cny (CNY), bis.jpy (JPY)

Currency codes: x dbnomics code currency
:::

::: tip BIS central bank rate dynamic alias — bis.rate.&lt;cc&gt; (monthly policy rate)
Examples: bis.rate.us (Fed), bis.rate.eu (ECB), bis.rate.jp (BOJ)

Country codes: x dbnomics code cbpol
:::

::: tip Pre-configured aliases (bls.cpi, fed.10y, wb.gold, etc.) managed by x dbnomics alias.
IDs without / match dynamic patterns first, then pre-configured alias table.
:::

::: tip gov.* indicators distinguish absolute vs ratio: gov.revenue is national currency, gov.revenue.gdp is % of GDP.
ppp.share is the country's share of world GDP (PPP basis).
:::


## Examples

Fetch China GDP growth rate (IMF WEO annual)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.cn.gdp.growth
```

Fetch US PPP GDP (purchasing power parity)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.us.ppp
```

Fetch US government debt (% GDP)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.us.gov.debt.gdp
```

Fetch US government revenue (% of GDP)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.us.gov.revenue.gdp
```

Fetch US core inflation (excl. food & energy)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.us.core.inflation
```

Fetch US output gap (% of potential GDP)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.us.output.gap
```

Fetch Japan employment (millions)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.jp.employment
```

Fetch Korea national savings (% GDP)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.kr.savings
```

Fetch Germany current account balance (% GDP)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.de.ca
```

Fetch China share of world GDP (PPP basis)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.cn.ppp.share
```

Fetch US GDP deflator

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.us.gdp.deflator
```

Fetch Japan government net debt (% GDP)

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.jp.gov.net.debt.gdp
```

Fetch EU GDP growth rate

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.eu.gdp.growth
```

Fetch G7 inflation rate

```sh
x dbnomics data imf.g7.inflation
```

Fetch US CPI (BLS monthly)

```sh
x dbnomics data bls.cpi
```

Fetch EUR/USD exchange rate

```sh
x dbnomics data bis.eur
```

Fetch US Fed policy rate

```sh
x dbnomics data bis.rate.us
```

Fetch gold price (WB annual)

```sh
x dbnomics data wb.gold
```

Compare US/Germany/Japan CPI (IMF WEO annual)

```sh
x dbnomics align imf.us.cpi imf.de.cpi imf.jp.cpi
```

Compare US fiscal revenue, expenditure, and net lending (% of GDP)

```sh
x dbnomics align imf.us.gov.revenue.gdp imf.us.gov.expenditure.gdp imf.us.gov.net.lending.gdp
```

Compare US Treasury yield curve

```sh
x dbnomics align fed.10y fed.2y fed.3m
```

Compare China/US/Japan PPP GDP (purchasing power parity)

```sh
x dbnomics align imf.cn.ppp imf.us.ppp imf.jp.ppp
```

List all pre-configured aliases

```sh
x dbnomics alias
```

List all IMF WEO indicator suffixes

```sh
x dbnomics code weoseries
```

# x df

Enhanced `df` command combining `df` and `mount` output.

Supports multiple output formats: TUI app, CSV, TSV, and raw.



Platform-specific columns:
- Linux/Windows: Filesystem, Type, Size, Used, Avail, Use%, Mounted_path, Mounted_attr
- macOS: Filesystem, Type, Size, Used, Avail, Capacity, iused, ifree, %iused, Mounted_path, Mounted_attr


::: tip Default behavior (--auto):
- TTY: Interactive TUI
- Piped: TSV format
:::


## Examples

Interactive view (TTY) or TSV output (piped)

```sh
x df
```

View disk usage with TUI app

```sh
x df --app
```

Output disk info in CSV format

```sh
x df --csv
```

Output disk info in TSV format

```sh
x df --tsv
```

Show sizes in pure numeric form (no unit conversion)

```sh
x df --numeric
```

## Usage

```sh
x df [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--auto` | Auto mode: TUI for TTY, TSV for pipe (default) |
| `--app` | Interactive TUI application |
| `--tsv`, `-t` | TSV format output |
| `--csv`, `-c` | CSV format output |
| `--raw`, `-r` | Raw format output |
| `--numeric`, `-n` | Numeric sizes without unit conversion |
