# x disk

Disk tool with device management and mount/unmount operations

Cross-platform with TTY color support and --tsv output for stat.

## Examples

Example: Display full disk overview (info + stat table)

```sh
x disk
```

Example: Show disk hardware info only

```sh
x disk info
```

Example: Show basic disk info

```sh
x disk info --simple
```

Example: Force cache refresh, re-fetch disk info

```sh
x disk info --fresh
```

Example: Show filesystem usage table

```sh
x disk stat
```

Example: TSV output (scripting friendly)

```sh
x disk stat --tsv
```

Example: List disks and partitions

```sh
x disk ls
```

Example: Eject all removable disks

```sh
x disk eject
```

Example: Eject a specific disk device

```sh
x disk eject /dev/disk3
```

Example: Mount device to mount point

```sh
x disk mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb
```

Example: Mount device with options

```sh
x disk mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/usb --options rw,noatime
```

Example: Unmount a mounted filesystem

```sh
x disk umount /mnt/usb
```

Example: Lazy unmount (even if busy)

```sh
x disk umount --lazy /mnt/usb
```

Example: Remount as read-only

```sh
x disk remount /mnt/usb ro
```

Example: Remount as read-write

```sh
x disk remount /mnt/usb rw
```

Example: List all available devices and mount status

```sh
x disk device ls
```

Example: Show detailed device info

```sh
x disk device info /dev/sdb
```

| [x disk info](/mod/disk/info.md) | Show static disk/volume hardware information only — no usage stats. |
| [x disk stat](/mod/disk/stat.md) | Show filesystem usage in compact table format, grouped by physical disk. |
| [x disk ls](/mod/disk/ls.md) | Show compact tabular listing of disks and partitions. |
| [x disk eject](/mod/disk/eject.md) | Eject removable media (USB drives, optical discs, etc.). |
| [x disk mount](/mod/disk/mount.md) | Mount a device to a mount point directory. |
| [x disk umount](/mod/disk/umount.md) | Unmount a mounted filesystem. |

| [x disk device](/mod/disk/device.md) | List or inspect available block devices. |

# x display

Display tool with four modes:
- "x display" (default = sum): detailed display info + compact display table
- "x display info": detailed display properties in key:value format

  (name, type, resolution, refresh rate, connection, serial, product/vendor ID)
- "x display ls": compact table (DISPLAY, TYPE, RESOLUTION, REFRESH, CONNECTION)
- "x display stat": real-time display status (brightness)

Cross-platform (macOS/Linux/Windows) with TTY color support.

Data sources:

  macOS — system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType (text + JSON)

  Linux — xrandr (with /sys/class/drm fallback)

  Windows — wmic Win32_DesktopMonitor

## Examples

Example: Display full display overview (info + ls table)

```sh
x display
```

Example: Show display details only

```sh
x display info
```

Example: Force cache refresh, re-fetch display info

```sh
x display info --fresh
```

Example: List displays in compact table

```sh
x display ls
```

Example: Show real-time brightness status

```sh
x display stat
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x display sum](/mod/display/sum.md) | Display full overview (equivalent to x display). |
| [x display info](/mod/display/info.md) | Show detailed display properties in key:value format. |
| [x display ls](/mod/display/ls.md) | Show compact display table. |
| [x display stat](/mod/display/stat.md) | Show real-time display status. |

# x dnf

dnf command enhancements

## Examples

Use the interactive app to search for all available packages

```sh
x dnf
```

Set the mirror source of dnf to Aliyun mirror

```sh
x dnf mirror set ali
```

List the available mirror source

```sh
x dnf mirror ls
```

Install curl using dnf

```sh
x dnf install curl
```

Set the proxy used for dnf

```sh
x dnf proxy use http://127.0.0.0:8888
```
## introduce



The goal of the dnf module is to enhance the user experience of using dnf on the command line. This is primarily manifested in the following aspects:


1. Interactive UI:
    - Provide system-supported interactive lists for installing software packages, aiding users in conveniently searching for packages and reducing input errors.
    - For selected packages, users can choose to install, reinstall, or view information, among other actions.
2. Mirror Source Replacement: Using the `dnf mirror` command enables swift replacement of suitable dnf mirror sources, streamlining the cumbersome configuration process and thereby enhancing the download speed of software packages. (Currently only supporting Fedora and CentOS, with plans to support more distributions in the future).
3. Proxy Usage: Offer the proxy command to afford users greater flexibility in managing dnf proxy settings.
4. For commands requiring root permissions, we have encapsulated them using the sudo module, omitting the need for the sudo prefix and ensuring all command formats conform to `x dnf {subcmd}`. Of course, non-root users still need to provide the sudo password when executing these commands.

## Usage

```sh
x dnf [SUB_COMMAND] <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | extends `dnf` subcmd or options |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x dnf fz](/mod/dnf/fz.md) | Using fzf as an interactive UI to select the applications you want to install |
| [x dnf install](/mod/dnf/install.md) | Install applications using dnf |
| [x dnf mirror](/mod/dnf/mirror.md) | Setting the dnf mirror for debian/ubuntu |
| [x dnf proxy](/mod/dnf/proxy.md) | Display or change the current proxy used for dnf |

# x dns

DNS (Domain Name System) configuration management utilities.

View current DNS settings, list available DNS servers,

and refresh DNS cache on the system.

## Examples

Example: Show current DNS configuration

```sh
x dns
```

Example: View detailed current DNS settings

```sh
x dns current
```

Example: List all available DNS servers

```sh
x dns ls
```

Example: List DNS servers in JSON format

```sh
x dns ls --json
```

Example: Pipe the list (auto-falls back to TSV when stdout is not a TTY)

```sh
x dns ls | cat
```

Example: Refresh DNS cache on the system

```sh
x dns refresh
```

Example: Reload DNS configuration (re-read config without changing it)

```sh
x dns reload
```

Example: Set system-wide DNS (default behavior; scutil / all interfaces / Linux 3-tier fallback)

```sh
x dns set 8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1
```

Example: Set DNS for a specific service / connection / interface

```sh
x dns set Wi-Fi 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4
```

Example: Write directly to /etc/resolv.conf (Linux only; containers, chroots)

```sh
x dns set --file 8.8.8.8
```

Example: Preview the commands without executing them

```sh
x dns set --dry-run 8.8.8.8
```

Example: Revert system-wide DNS to DHCP

```sh
x dns reset
```

Example: Revert a specific service / connection / interface to DHCP

```sh
x dns reset Wi-Fi
```

Example: Save current DNS state as 'home-router'

```sh
x dns backup home-router
```

Example: Restore DNS from the 'home-router' backup

```sh
x dns restore home-router
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x dns current](/mod/dns/current.md) | View the current DNS configuration information |
| [x dns ls](/mod/dns/ls.md) | List available DNS server addresses |
| [x dns refresh](/mod/dns/refresh.md) | Flush the DNS response cache |
| [x dns reload](/mod/dns/reload.md) | Reload the DNS configuration (make the service re-read config) |
| [x dns set](/mod/dns/set.md) | Set DNS servers (system-wide by default; per-target if a target is given) |
| [x dns reset](/mod/dns/reset.md) | Revert DNS to automatic / DHCP defaults (system-wide; per-target if a target is given) |
| [x dns backup](/mod/dns/backup.md) | Save current DNS state to a named backup |
| [x dns restore](/mod/dns/restore.md) | Restore DNS from a previous backup |

# x docker

A wrapper around native Docker commands powered by x-cmd, offering interactive UIs and shortcut commands to simplify container and image management for improved developer and DevOps workflows.


::: tip
The interactive environment has a default alias set as `alias xd='x docker'`
:::


## Examples

Pull the ubuntu image from ECR

```sh
x docker ecpull ubuntu
```

Start a new container and install x-cmd, but will not change the rc file, x-cmd is not started by default, you need to manually execute `x-cmd`

```sh
x docker run -x [OPTIONS] <IMAGE>
```

Install x-cmd in a running container, and execute the command, it will try to change the rc file

```sh
x docker exec -x [OPTIONS] <CONTAINER> <COMMAND>
```

Interactive Docker management interface powered by fzf, allowing quick access to containers and images

```sh
xd fz
```

Pull the alpine image from ECR

```sh
x docker ecpull alpine
```

Run typeinc to test your typing speed and accuracy

```sh
xd alp typeinc
```

Lookup ASN and routing information for bing.com

```sh
xd alp asn -n bing.com
```

Pipe ASCII output as YAML stream to yq running inside a container

```sh
x ascii --yml | xd alp yq
```

## Usage

```sh
x docker [SUB_COMMAND] <#n>
```

# x eget

Download and install pre-built binaries from GitHub/GitLab/Codeberg Releases (Inspired by zyedidia/eget); `x eget use <name>` installs to ~/.local/bin in one step, and for well-known projects a bare name (e.g. `x eget use jq`) is auto-completed to the source repo via the x install database; supports GHPROXY for accelerating GitHub downloads; on slow downloads, automatically reroutes through x-cmd's eget hosting (keeps it working in the China region).


::: tip
Pure shell reimplementation, 100% compatible with zyedidia/eget CLI (inactive). MIT License.
:::

::: tip
Recommended: `x eget use [owner/]<repo>` — downloads from the official Release and installs to ~/.local/bin (x-cmd automatically adds ~/.local/bin to PATH).
:::

::: tip Bare-name completion (e.g. `x eget use jq` → jqlang/jq) is powered by the x install database.
The database exists purely to map common project names to their source repos for convenience — it is **NOT a recommendation or security vetting** of the projects themselves. Judge trustworthiness before installing.

See https://x-cmd.com/install, or run `x i` for interactive browsing.

If you are the project author and want your project included in the database, see https://x-cmd.com/install/submit.
:::

::: tip Multi-forge support: GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg. Use short names gh:/gl:/cb: to specify.
e.g., x eget gl:owner/repo downloads from GitLab. Gitee not supported (requires login).
:::

::: tip
x eget downloads directly from the author's repo — all versions available on demand. x pkg is x-cmd's curated stable channel, only shipping vetted releases.
:::

::: tip
Developers package and publish to releases following naming conventions, users download instantly with x eget and run instantly with x eget snap.
:::

::: tip When a download hits speed issues (notably in the China region), x-cmd automatically reroutes through
its eget hosting to finish the download — a feature, not a config, with nothing to set up, so `x eget`

just works on any network. The switch reason is named in the log (e.g., `stalled (connection too slow)`);

disable with --no-mirror.
:::

::: tip Whether you use your own ghproxy or x-cmd's eget hosting above, only the asset download is rerouted —
api.github.com always stays direct. GitHub downloads are SHA-256 verified by default, with the digest

fetched straight from api.github.com and never through any hosting, so the checksum stays trustworthy and

can verify the hosted asset, guaranteeing download integrity and security. GitLab / Codeberg release APIs

have no digest field, so those links skip verification silently; use --no-verify to disable.
:::

::: tip How rate limits are avoided on api.github.com (60 req/hr unauthenticated). Token chain: `EGET_GITHUB_TOKEN` → `GITHUB_TOKEN`
→ `GH_TOKEN` → `gh auth token` — users with a configured `gh` CLI get the 5000/hr authenticated quota automatically, no env var

to export. If no token is available (or auth still rate-limits), we fall back to scraping the GitHub releases page HTML

(`expanded_assets/<tag>`) for asset links — that path is barely throttled. In practice you almost never hit a limit.

In CI / compliance scenarios, set `EGET_NO_GH_AUTH_TOKEN=1` to disable the `gh auth token` auto-lookup — only explicit

env vars are honored.
:::

::: info Env `___X_CMD_GHPROXY_ENDPOINT`: route slow GitHub downloads through a proxy. Applies only to github.com asset downloads — api.github.com and other forges (gitlab / codeberg) are unaffected.
Two endpoint shapes are auto-detected:
  - prefix:  `___X_CMD_GHPROXY_ENDPOINT="https://your-proxy.example.com"`         =&gt; https://your-proxy.example.com/https://github.com/...
  - replace: `___X_CMD_GHPROXY_ENDPOINT="https://your-proxy.example.com/github.com"` =&gt; https://your-proxy.example.com/github.com/...

Trailing slashes are normalized. Once set, both `x eget` and `x eget snap` are affected; download log prints `Using GHPROXY: ...`.
:::


## Examples

Install to ~/.local/bin (recommended)

```sh
x eget use fzf
```

Remove a use-installed binary

```sh
x eget unuse fzf
```

Download and run instantly, no PATH install (like npx)

```sh
x eget snap fzf -- --version
```

Browse all eget-installable packages indexed by x install (~800+)

```sh
x eget ls
```

List all releases of a repo

```sh
x eget ls fzf
```

Original eget: download default binary to current directory

```sh
x eget BurntSushi/ripgrep
```

Original eget: download to a specific directory

```sh
x eget --to ~/.local/bin BurntSushi/ripgrep
```

Original eget: download a specific version

```sh
x eget --tag v2.42.1 cli/cli
```

Original eget: cross-platform download

```sh
x eget --system linux/amd64 cli/cli
```

Original eget: download via URL

```sh
x eget https://github.com/x-cmd-build/rumdl/releases/tag/0.1.25
```

Original eget: download from GitLab using short name

```sh
x eget gl:owner/repo
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x eget download](/mod/eget/download.md) | Download and install binary — the default behavior; the subcmd can be omitted (`x eget <repo>`) |
| [x eget snap](/mod/eget/snap.md) | Download and run instantly without PATH install; like npx |
| [x eget use](/mod/eget/use.md) | Install binary to ~/.local/bin |
| [x eget unuse](/mod/eget/unuse.md) | Remove a use-installed binary |

# x elv

elvish is a new shell written in Go, suitable for users who want to perform complex data manipulation and interaction in the command line.

This module mainly provides support for calling the x-cmd toolset on elvish; and adds functions such as searching the official website ( elv.sh ) , using without installation, and generating elvish commands with LLM.

## Examples

Introducing the x-cmd toolkit (including x command, c command, @gpt, comma command, etc.) to the elvish environment.

```sh
x elv --setup
```

Search the elv.sh website for content related to "alias" and display the search results in an interactive table format.

```sh
x elv : alias
```

Start elvish. If elvish is not already installed locally, it will be automatically installed and used through the x-cmd pkg system (this process will not affect your environment variables or dependencies).

```sh
x elv
```

## Usage

```sh
x elv [SUB_COMMAND] <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | extends `elvish` subcmd or options |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x elv setup](#x-elv-setup) | Inject the x-cmd toolset into the elvish environment, by default it is all. |
| [x elv ddgo](#x-elv-ddgo) | Search the elv.sh website for the specified content |


### x elv setup

Inject the x-cmd toolset into the elvish environment, by default it is all.


- **Sub Commands**:


| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x elv setup all](#x-elv-setup-all) | (Default) Introduce the x-cmd toolset into the elvish environment with one click (introduce the a.elv and x.elv files in the lib directory) and modify the $HOME/.config/elvish/rc.elv file to introduce the x-cmd toolset. |
| [x elv setup mod](#x-elv-setup-mod) | Only inject the enhanced module of x-cmd into the elvish environment (introduce the a.elv and x.elv files in the lib directory), but do not automatically introduce it in rc.elv (only introduce the a.elv and x.elv files in the lib directory). |
| [x elv setup rc](#x-elv-setup-rc) | Only modify the $HOME/.config/elvish/rc.elv file to introduce the x-cmd toolset (will not automatically introduce the a.elv and x.elv files in the lib directory). |


### x elv setup all

(Default) Introduce the x-cmd toolset into the elvish environment with one click (introduce the a.elv and x.elv files in the lib directory) and modify the $HOME/.config/elvish/rc.elv file to introduce the x-cmd toolset.


- **Usage**:

```sh
x elv setup|--setup all
```

### x elv setup mod

Only inject the enhanced module of x-cmd into the elvish environment (introduce the a.elv and x.elv files in the lib directory), but do not automatically introduce it in rc.elv (only introduce the a.elv and x.elv files in the lib directory).


- **Usage**:

```sh
x elv setup|--setup mod
```

### x elv setup rc

Only modify the $HOME/.config/elvish/rc.elv file to introduce the x-cmd toolset (will not automatically introduce the a.elv and x.elv files in the lib directory).


- **Usage**:

```sh
x elv setup|--setup rc
```

### x elv ddgo

Search the elv.sh website for the specified content


- **Usage**:

```sh
x elv ddgo|: <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | content |

# x endlessh

The endlessh module is a wrapper module based on Docker that provides quick startup and management capabilities for endlessh-go.

endlessh-go (https://github.com/shizunge/endlessh-go) is a honeypot tool implemented in Go. It inherits the powerful features of endlessh, such as delaying responses to put malicious scanning tools or automated attack scripts in a suspended state, thus consuming the attacker's time and resources.

Unlike endlessh, it can export Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboards, providing users with a more intuitive visualization of attack sources (users who need to use the visual dashboard can find detailed instructions in the endlessh-go Github repository).

## Examples

Create and run a endlessh container using the default configuration

```sh
x endlessh run
```

Create and start a endlessh container named 'test'

```sh
x endlessh run --name test
```

Connect to the endlessh container running on port 2222 using ssh

```sh
x endlessh test
```

Show the running logs of the endlessh container

```sh
x endlessh log
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x endlessh run](/mod/endlessh/run.md) | Create and run the endlessh container |
| [x endlessh test](/mod/endlessh/test.md) | Connecting to the running endlessh container using ssh |
| [x endlessh log](/mod/endlessh/log.md) | Show the running logs of the endlessh container |
| [x endlessh status](/mod/endlessh/status.md) | Show the status of the endlessh container |
| [x endlessh stop](/mod/endlessh/stop.md) | Stop endlessh container |
| [x endlessh restart](/mod/endlessh/restart.md) | Restart endlessh container |

# x env

Manage packages, programming language runtimes, and CLI tools in the user environment, with support for multi-version switching, temporary usage, environment variable injection, and garbage collection


::: tip
Enter the `x env use` command to use the interactive app of the env module.
:::


## Examples

Use the interactive app to view and download packages

```sh
x env
```

List all available versions of node

```sh
x env ls -a node
```

Use the default version of node in the current shell's session

```sh
x env try node
```

Set up using default version of node in the current user environment

```sh
x env use node
```

Remove installed software using an interactive app

```sh
x env gc
```

Run the helloworld.js file using v18.12.0 node

```sh
x env exec node=v18.12.0 -- node helloworld.js
```
## Introduction



The `env` module is built on the foundation of the `pkg` module (X's package management module). It is a tool for managing development environments and dependencies, designed to globally manage versions and environments of all software, plugins, and languages downloaded through `x`.



We've observed that most mainstream environment management tools are tailored to specific languages, such as node's nvm, Ruby's rvm, Python's pyenv, etc. Different languages require installing different tools, adding complexity and increasing the learning curve.



In this context, we've developed our own environment management module. Using `env`, developers can simultaneously manage multiple languages and software downloaded through `x`. It allows easy switching of environment configurations between different projects, ensuring isolation between projects, and facilitating the sharing of project dependencies.



In the implementation of the `env` module, we focused not only on referencing current mainstream environment management tools but also on how to achieve fast usage and switching of different versions in a non-global context, integrating with the `advise` and `tui` modules for a better user experience.



## Implementation of Global and Non-Global Environments



**Global Environment:**

We use symbolic links to ensure that the environment is used in the current and future sessions. You can use `x env use {candidate}` or `x env use {candidate}={version}` to use it.



**Non-Global Environments:**
1. The first type of non-global environment adds environment variables, effective only in the current session. You can use `x env try {candidate}` or `x env try {candidate}={version}` to use it.
2. The second non-global mode is specific to a project or file, only using a specific environment when executing that project or file. It employs recording and restoration. You can use `x env exec {candidate}={version} -- {command}` to use it.
3. Additionally, we provide a non-global way to inject environment variables into functions. You can use `x {candidate}` to use it.



## Other Similar Works (Categorized into Three Types)


- **No Privilege Needed, Installs in User Directory:**
   - Examples:
      1. `x-cmd`'s `pkg/env`
      2. [asdf](https://github.com/asdf-vm/asdf)
      3. [scoop](https://github.com/ScoopInstaller/Scoop)
   - Advantages:
      1. No need for root or special privileges, improving system security significantly.
      2. Limited to the current user or even the current shell session, enhancing system stability.
      3. Allows the coexistence of multiple versions and software combinations.
   - Disadvantages:
      1. If multiple users are present, the same software needs to be installed separately for each user, occupying more storage. `pkg/env` can offer additional processes to achieve a certain degree of sharing while ensuring safety.
      2. Some software might experience performance or usability losses due to not relying on system libraries and specific systems.
      3. Compilation uses relative path dependencies, requiring adjustments for traditional dynamically linked library software, which might introduce unknown bugs.
   - Complementary Advantages to Scoop and Asdf:
      - Can be used in ash and dash, thus compatible with Alpine.
      - Optimized for downloading from China's networks.
      - Offers other special advantages when combined with other x-cmd modules.
   - Therefore, we introduced these two modules, allowing users to quickly install and use asdf and scoop, and we've included command completion.
      1. asdf - Click to see our efforts on the asdf module.
      2. scoop: It's worth mentioning that scoop is written in PowerShell. Users can install Windows-like software directly using the scoop module in WSL or gitbash.


- **Manager Itself Requires Privilege Installation, but Software Installation Does Not:**
  1. chocolatey
     - We provide the `choco` module, paying homage to the first Windows package manager I used (2016).
  2. nix, guix, brew:
     - Nix, Guix, and Brew are very successful and influential solutions, and x-cmd will continue to learn from them.
     - Enhanced user experience in the China region through the [proxy module](/mod/proxy.md).
     - Unified naming for common packages through the [install module](/install/.md) to alleviate concerns for cross-system developers.


- **System's Built-in Package Managers (Requires Privilege Installation):**
   - apk, apt, dnf, yum
   - pacman, msys2
   - port/macport
   - apk
   - We plan to study these solutions. As mentioned earlier, we will assist users in using the [proxy module](/mod/proxy.md) and [install module](/install/.md) for a better experience.

`

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x env try](/mod/env/try.md) | Use the specified package temporarily in the current shell session. Powered by `x pkg try`. |
| [x env untry](/mod/env/untry.md) | Remove the specified package from the current shell session. Powered by `x pkg untry`. |
| [x env use](/mod/env/use.md) | Add the specified package to the user environment. Powered by `x pkg use`. |
| [x env unuse](/mod/env/unuse.md) | Remove the specified package from the user environment. Powered by `x pkg unuse`. |
| [x env upgrade](/mod/env/upgrade.md) | Upgrade packages in the user environment to the 'default' version. Powered by `x pkg upgrade`. |
| [x env boot](/mod/env/boot.md) | Inject corresponding environment variables into the specified pkg application. For example, JAVA_HOME of java |
| [x env unboot](/mod/env/unboot.md) | Clear the environment variables injected by the `env boot` command |

# x epoch

Get, compute, and check Unix epoch timestamps; supports seconds / milliseconds / difference / range / file store


::: tip
Timing a script: `start=$(x epoch ms)` at the start, `x epoch minus "$start"` at the end, add -H for 1h30m format
:::

::: tip
Token or cache about to expire? `x epoch now --le 5m <ts>` for raw timestamps; `x epoch store is --le 5m <key>` for store files
:::

::: tip
Multiple scripts sharing a cache/lock file? Use store: defaults to $___X_CMD_ROOT_DATA/epoch/store/&lt;key&gt;, use --store to change the dir
:::

::: tip
`_`-suffixed subcmds (get_/ms_/real_/real3_/now_/minus_/read_) are silent variants: set x_ instead of printing, for further processing in scripts
:::


## Examples

Example: Current timestamp in seconds

```sh
x epoch get
```

Example: Current timestamp with millisecond decimal

```sh
x epoch real
```

Example: Seconds from that timestamp to now

```sh
x epoch minus 1710000000
```

Example: Stamp build artifacts with the current epoch

```sh
x epoch store write build-artifacts
```

Scenario: Validate token is between 10m and 1h old (about-to-expire check)

```sh
x epoch now --le 1h --ge 10m 1710000000
```

Scenario: Check timestamp in user cache dir is within the last 5 minutes

```sh
x epoch now --le 5m -f "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch"
```

Scenario: Stamp package metadata + 7-day TTL check (full flow)

```sh
x epoch store write pkg-meta && x epoch store is --le 7d pkg-meta
```

Scenario: User cache dir timestamp + 1-day TTL check

```sh
x epoch store write --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch" && x epoch store is --le 1d --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch"
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x epoch get](/mod/epoch/get.md) | Get current Unix timestamp (integer seconds) |
| [x epoch ms](/mod/epoch/ms.md) | Get current Unix timestamp (integer milliseconds, e.g. 1710000000123) |
| [x epoch real](/mod/epoch/real.md) | Get current Unix timestamp (seconds with millisecond decimal, e.g. 1710000000.123) |
| [x epoch day](/mod/epoch/day.md) | Current integer day number (epoch/86400, stable within the same day) |
| [x epoch river](/mod/epoch/river.md) | A few coordinates on the river of time |
| [x epoch minus](/mod/epoch/minus.md) | Calculate timestamp difference, with optional human-readable output |
| [x epoch now](/mod/epoch/now.md) | Check whether a timestamp falls within a duration from now (--le and/or --ge required) |
| [x epoch store](/mod/epoch/store.md) | Store-backed epoch file operations (write, read, is, rm); supports --store/--fp path overrides |

# x feishu

Send Feishu messages using x feishu.


::: tip Webhook Bot (x feishu bot)
Use case: One-way notifications to groups, e.g., CI/CD build notifications (GitHub Actions), server monitoring alerts

Setup: https://x-cmd.com/mod/feishu/cookbook-1
:::

::: tip Intelligent Bot (x feishu abot)
Use case: Send and receive messages via background listener service, e.g., integrate with x claw as private AI assistant

First-time setup requires app_id and app_secret (from Feishu Open Platform application creation)

Configuration command: x feishu --cfg app_id=&lt;id&gt; app_secret=&lt;secret&gt;

Setup guide: https://open.feishu.cn/document/develop-an-echo-bot/introduction
:::

::: tip There are two listening modes:
1. --admin — Private chat mode (default),

   listens to private chats between the bot creator and the bot

   First startup requires configuring owner chat_id

   Configuration command: x feishu --cfg chatid=&lt;chat_id&gt;
2. --group — Group chat mode

   Without chat_id: automatically fetches all group list and listens to each group

   With chat_id: listens to the specified group
:::

::: tip
How to get chat_id: page -&gt; Top right corner settings -&gt; Bottom to find
:::

::: tip Integrate Feishu Intelligent Bot with claw as private AI assistant:
1. Configure app_id, app_secret, and owner chat_id
2. Start Feishu background listener service: x feishu abot service start
3. Start x claw to integrate with Feishu: x claw start --feishu
:::


## Examples

Initialize configuration in interactive mode

```sh
x feishu init
```

Send text type messages to Feishu group

```sh
x feishu send --text "x-cmd 新版本发布成功"
```

Send text messages using intelligent bot

```sh
x feishu abot send --text --chatid <chat_id> "Hello"
```

Start intelligent bot listener service (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu abot service start
```

Start in group chat mode, listen to all groups

```sh
x feishu abot service start --group
```

Start in group chat mode, listen to messages in specified group

```sh
x feishu abot service start --group <chat_id>
```

Stop listener service (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu abot service stop
```

Stop group chat mode listener service

```sh
x feishu abot service stop --group
```

Restart listener service (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu abot service restart
```

Check listener service status (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu abot service status
```

View service logs for specified chat

```sh
x feishu abot service log <chat_id>
```

Start interactive REPL mode, executing messages as commands and returning output

```sh
x feishu react --runner repl
```

# x find

100% native find compatible, auto-prunes noise dirs to speed up search. Excludes hidden dirs, node_modules and __pycache__ by default. Under $HOME, auto-excludes platform dirs to avoid permission dialogs.


::: tip
Note! Three prune dimensions : (1) Hidden dirs — the main noise source. .* blanket rule, --unhide to exempt specific dirs; (2) Project noise — only node_modules, __pycache__ by default, --prune to add more; (3) HOME — auto-exclude platform dirs (macOS: Applications/Library etc) to avoid permission dialogs, only active when start root is $HOME, --no-homeprune to disable.
:::

::: tip
--prune and --unhide support : separator for multiple values: --prune vendor:venv is equivalent to --prune vendor --prune venv.
:::

::: tip
For git projects, prefer git ls-files and git grep for faster indexed search. For system-wide search, use mdfind (macOS) or locate (Linux).
:::

::: tip
Use x bfind for BFS (breadth-first) search — shares the same prune rules, results sorted by depth (shallow first). Default depth 3, adjustable with -d.
:::

::: tip
Principle: find ROOT ! \( [hidden dir control] -prune -o &lt;item1&gt; -prune -o &lt;item2&gt; -prune ... \) [user expression]. Three dimensions is a thinking model — --prune accepts any dir name including hidden ones, generating a separate prune condition. If both --unhide and --prune target the same hidden dir, it still gets pruned.
:::


## Examples

Search .ts files (auto prune hidden dirs + noise)

```sh
x find . -name "*.ts"
```

Keep .vscode .claude, find json files

```sh
x find --unhide .vscode:.claude -- . -name "*.json"
```

Add build and release to prune list

```sh
x find --prune build:release -- . -name "*.go"
```

HOME find json, disable HOME prune

```sh
x find --no-homeprune ~ -name "*.json"
```

Reset prune list, exclude release and build dirs

```sh
x find --reset-prune --prune release:build -- . -name "*.log"
```

All three dimensions off, equivalent to raw find

```sh
x find --unhide-all --reset-prune --no-homeprune -- . -name "*.ts"
```

## Usage

```sh
x find [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--unhide` |  | Exempt hidden dirs from prune (supports : separator) |
| `--prune` |  | Add prune targets (supports : separator) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--unhide-all` | Do not exclude any hidden directories |
| `--reset-prune` | Clear project noise list (hidden dir prune and HOME prune unaffected) |
| `--no-homeprune` | Disable automatic HOME directory prune |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Show active prune lists |
| `--dryrun` | Print the generated find expression without executing |

# x free

Show memory overview + top 10 memory consumers (smart grouping by default). Linux uses PSS to avoid double-counting shared memory; macOS uses footprint for accurate memory usage


::: tip 【Linux Memory Model】
Basic equation:

  total = used + free + buff/cache



Column meanings:

  total     : Total physical memory

  used      : Used memory (= total - free - buff/cache)

  free      : Completely free memory

  shared    : tmpfs/shm shared memory (subset of buff/cache, usually not reclaimable)

  buff/cache: File cache pages (reclaimable, but shared portion is usually not reclaimable)

  available : Estimated available memory (≈ free + reclaimable cache, calculated by kernel)
:::

::: tip 【macOS Memory Model】
Detail layer fields:

  hardware   : Hardware reserved (= hw.memsize - hw.memsize_usable)

  wired      : Kernel reserved (= Pages wired down), cannot be swapped/compressed

  compressed : Compressed data (= Pages occupied by compressor)

  app        : Application working set (= Anonymous - purgeable)

  purgeable  : Reclaimable cache (= Pages purgeable)

  cache      : File cache (= File-backed pages)

  available  : Free memory (= Pages free + throttled, no speculative)



Key identity (Detail layer = vm_stat layer):

  app + purgeable + cache ≈ active + inactive + spec
:::

::: tip
【Related Tools】Process-level analysis: x btop, x btm, x ps; Raw data: m mem, vm_stat
:::


## Examples

Display memory usage (human-readable)

```sh
x free
```

Output in CSV format (single line, for processing)

```sh
x free --csv
```

Output in TSV format without header

```sh
x free --tsv --no-header
```

Refresh every 2 seconds

```sh
x free -s 2
```

Refresh every second, 10 times

```sh
x free -s 1 -c 10
```

Show memory overview + top 5 memory processes

```sh
x free --top 5
```

No grouping, show individual processes

```sh
x free --group none
```

Group by process name

```sh
x free --group cmd
```

Show all processes (no limit)

```sh
x free --top all
```

Show only processes matching chrome

```sh
x free --filter chrome
```

Match multiple keywords, show all

```sh
x free --filter "chrome|node" --top all
```

Precise mode, cross-process memory dedup for multi-process groups (macOS, slower but accurate)

```sh
x free --precise
```

## Usage

```sh
x free [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--csv` | Output in CSV format (flat, single line) |
| `--tsv` | Output in TSV format (flat, single line) |
| `--no-header` | Suppress header in CSV/TSV output |
| `-s`, `--seconds` | Repeat printing every N seconds |
| `-c`, `--count` | Repeat printing N times, then exit |
| `--top` | Show top N processes by memory (default 10, 0 to hide, all shows every process) |
| `-g`, `--group` | Group strategy (auto by .app bundle, cmd by process name, none) |
| `-f`, `--filter` | Filter processes by comm name (regex match) |
| `--rss` | Use RSS mode (default uses phys_footprint/PSS, more accurate) |
| `-p`, `--precise` | Precise mode, call footprint CLI for cross-process dedup on multi-process groups (macOS only, slower) |
| `-e`, `--expert` | Show expert detail (kernel, LRU, THP, IO, VM, hardware stats) |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x free run](/mod/free/run.md) | Display memory usage |
| [x free top](/mod/free/top.md) | Show top memory-consuming processes (equivalent to --top) |

# x fsiter

Iterate and search files/directories with flexible filtering options.

Supports depth-first search traversal, file/folder filtering, and hidden file handling.

Provides both interactive listing and script-friendly query functions.



Default behavior (no subcommand) lists non-hidden items in current directory.


::: tip Filter options for --ls:
--file: Show only files

--folder: Show only directories

--hidden: Include hidden files (starting with .)

--hidden-only: Show only hidden files



These options can be combined: --file --hidden shows all files including hidden.



For scripts, use internal functions like --file_, --dir1_, etc.
:::


## Examples

Example: List all non-hidden items in current directory

```sh
x fsiter
```

Example: List items in /tmp directory

```sh
x fsiter /tmp
```

Example: Explicitly list directory contents

```sh
x fsiter --ls /home
```

Example: List only files (excluding directories)

```sh
x fsiter --ls --file
```

Example: List only directories

```sh
x fsiter --ls --folder
```

Example: List all items including hidden files

```sh
x fsiter --ls --hidden
```

Example: List only hidden files and directories

```sh
x fsiter --ls --hidden-only
```

Example: List all files including hidden ones

```sh
x fsiter --ls --file --hidden
```

Example: List all directories including hidden ones in /var

```sh
x fsiter --ls --folder --hidden /var
```

Example: DFS traversal of /home/user, print each item (direct children only)

```sh
x fsiter --dfs /home/user 0 0 echo
```

Example: DFS with depth limit (maxdepth=2, current + 2 levels)

```sh
x fsiter --dfs /home/user 0 2 echo
```

Example: Count number of items in /var/log

```sh
x fsiter --filecount /var/log
```

Example: Check if directory is empty

```sh
x fsiter --dirempty /tmp/test && echo "Empty" || echo "Not empty"
```

Example: Check if file matching pattern exists in current directory

```sh
x fsiter --exist .bashrc && echo "Found"
```

Example: Count all files (including hidden) in /etc

```sh
x fsiter --ls --file --hidden /etc | wc -l
```

Example: DFS depth limit 1, output file contents (current dir + subdirs)

```sh
x fsiter --dfs . 0 1 cat
```

Example: List hidden config files with limit

```sh
x fsiter --ls --hidden ~/.config | head -20
```

Example: Count executables in /usr/bin

```sh
x fsiter --filecount /usr/bin
```

Example: Check and process files matching pattern

```sh
x fsiter --exist config && cat config*
```

Example: List log files with details

```sh
x fsiter --ls --file /var/log | xargs ls -lh
```

Example: Calculate MD5 for all source files

```sh
for f in $(x fsiter --ls --file src); do x hash md5 "$f"; done
```

Example: Get file info with depth limit (maxdepth=2)

```sh
x fsiter --dfs /home 0 2 stat
```

Example: Remove directory only if empty

```sh
x fsiter --dirempty ./temp && rmdir ./temp
```

Example: Count hidden directories

```sh
x fsiter --ls --folder --hidden | wc -l
```

Example: Save file count to file

```sh
x fsiter --filecount . > count.txt && cat count.txt
```

Example: List all .sh files in current directory

```sh
x fsiter --glob . "*.sh"
```

Example: List all .conf files in /etc

```sh
x fsiter --glob /etc "*.conf"
```

Example: List all .c and .h files

```sh
x fsiter --glob . "*.[ch]"
```

Example: List items starting with test_ in src directory

```sh
x fsiter --glob src "test_*"
```

Example: Delete all .log files using glob match

```sh
x fsiter --glob . "*.log" | xargs rm
```

Example: List contents under cron/default/ directory (trailing / matches dirs only)

```sh
x fsiter --glob . "cron/default/"
```

Example: Multi-level glob - find crontab.tsv in any job subdirectory

```sh
x fsiter --glob . "job/*/crontab.tsv"
```

Example: Multi-level glob - find crontab.tsv two levels deep in any path

```sh
x fsiter --glob . "*/*/crontab.tsv"
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x fsiter --ls](/mod/fsiter/--ls.md) | List directory contents with filtering options (default if no subcommand) |
| [x fsiter --dfs](/mod/fsiter/--dfs.md) | Depth-first search traversal of directory tree |
| [x fsiter --filecount](/mod/fsiter/--filecount.md) | Count the number of items in directory |
| [x fsiter --dirempty](/mod/fsiter/--dirempty.md) | Check if directory is empty (returns 0 if empty, 1 if not) |
| [x fsiter --exist](/mod/fsiter/--exist.md) | Check if file/directory matching pattern exists in current directory |
| [x fsiter --count_](/mod/fsiter/--count_.md) | Return count of matching files via x_ variable (searches *pattern* in current dir) |
| [x fsiter --glob](/mod/fsiter/--glob.md) | List items matching a glob pattern in specified directory |
| [x fsiter --file_](/mod/fsiter/--file_.md) | [Script] Get all files (newline separated, via x_) |
| [x fsiter --file1_](/mod/fsiter/--file1_.md) | [Script] Get first file only (via x_) |
| [x fsiter --file01_](/mod/fsiter/--file01_.md) | [Script] Get file only if exactly one exists (via x_) |
| [x fsiter --dir_](/mod/fsiter/--dir_.md) | [Script] Get all directories (newline separated, via x_) |
| [x fsiter --dir1_](/mod/fsiter/--dir1_.md) | [Script] Get first directory only (via x_) |
| [x fsiter --dir01_](/mod/fsiter/--dir01_.md) | [Script] Get directory only if exactly one exists (via x_) |

# x gddy

Managing the Godaddy website via terminal commands


::: tip Get godaddy api key and secret key: https://developer.godaddy.com/keys
- Interactive env use `x gddy init` to initialize configuration. The configure will be saved locally.
- Run command `x gddy --cfg key=<key> secret=<secret>` to add access token.
- - Set the key and secret for the production environment
- x gddy &lt;subcmd&gt;, if subcmd is not a valid subcmd, subcmd will be regarded as a domain name, and then x will look up whether subcmd is available
:::


## Examples

List all domains under current account

```sh
x gddy domain ls
```

Check if the domain google.com is available for purchase

```sh
x gddy search google.com
```

Add a DNS record named "hjj" with data "114.34.18.48" to the specified domain x-net.org

```sh
x gddy domain record add --name hjj --data "114.34.18.48" x-net.org
```

Remove the DNS record named "hjj" from the specified domain x-net.org

```sh
x gddy domain record rm --name hjj  x-net.org
```

Remove the DNS record named "hjj" from the specified domain x-net.org

```sh
x gddy domain info x-net.org
```
## Introduction

The gddy module is an encapsulation of the Godaddy API by X-CMD, implemented using posix shell, awk, and curl.



## Overview of Features

The gddy module primarily provides commonly used functions for domain information retrieval and management of domain DNS records, including adding, deleting, and modifying DNS settings.

| [x gddy init](/mod/gddy/init.md) | Initialize configuration |
| [x gddy --cfg](/mod/gddy/--cfg.md) | manage configuration for godaddy |

List all models

Chatting based on Wikipedia content on CentOS

# What is a mod (Module) in x-cmd

In **X-CMD**, functionality is organized into **modules (mod)**. Each module represents an independent functional unit with relatively clear input and output. Users do not need to focus on the internal implementation logic; they can simply use a straightforward calling method. For example:

```bash
x path   # Open the PATH management TUI tool provided by X-CMD
x ip     # Get local and public IP addresses
x ascii  # View the ASCII encoding table
```

This design allows users to flexibly combine modules like "building blocks" to quickly construct workflows suited to their needs.

---

**Both humans and AI Agents can invoke these modules through a single `x <mod>` interface. This design is especially important in the age of AI:**

::::ul
:::li A Shared Language for Humans and AI
Traditional CLI tools vary wildly in syntax and argument conventions — hard for humans to memorize, easy for AI to get wrong.<br>
`x <mod>` provides a unified grammar that both humans and AI Agents can understand and use — the same command can be typed by hand or generated and executed by AI, no translation needed.
:::

:::li Auto-Install on Demand, Zero Manual Setup
AI Agents frequently need tools like jq, python, or ffmpeg to complete tasks. If they're not installed, the task stalls.<br>
X-CMD modules automatically download the required tools on first invocation — no root privileges needed. AI doesn't have to figure out "how to install"; it just works.
:::

:::li Cross-Platform Consistency
The same `x <mod>` command behaves identically on macOS, Linux, and containers.<br>
For AI, this means generating a command once and running it anywhere — no platform-specific logic required.
:::

:::li Batteries Included
A single install script unlocks 100+ modules: cloud API calls, package management, Git operations, data processing, and more.<br>
Give an AI Agent a fresh machine, install X-CMD, and it has a complete toolchain — no need to install and configure tools one by one.
:::
::::

## Module Classification and Functionality

The modules provided by X-CMD can roughly be divided into the following categories:

::::ul
:::li AI Agents & Large Models
Invoke mainstream large models, local inference engines, or run AI Agents for coding tasks directly from the command line.

- **AI Agents**: [openclaw](/mod/openclaw), [claude](/mod/claude), [codex](/mod/codex)
- **Cloud Large Models**: [openai](/mod/openai), [gemini](/mod/gemini), [moonshot](/mod/moonshot)
- **Local Large Models**: [llmf](/mod/llmf), [ollama](/mod/ollama), [whisper](/mod/whisper)
:::

:::li Basic Functions and Encapsulation
These modules provide common **shell/awk basic functions** that facilitate script writing and daily development.

- **String Processing**: [str](/mod/str) module
- **Test Assertions**: [assert](/mod/assert) module
:::

:::li System Command Enhancement
Enhance and modify existing system tools to make them more intuitive and user-friendly.

- **Package Management Enhancements**: [apt](/mod/apt), [apk](/mod/apk), [dnf](/mod/dnf), [pacman](/mod/pacman), [brew](/mod/brew)
- **System Tool Enhancements**: such as [ps](/mod/ps), [id](/mod/id)
- **Compression and Decompression**: [z/uz](/mod/zuz)
:::

:::li Command-Line Tool Download and Enhancement
X-CMD provides a unified mechanism for obtaining and extending existing tools:

- **Enhancements Based on pkg**: such as [jq](/mod/jq), [python](/mod/python), [ffmpeg](/mod/ffmpeg)
- **Enhancements Based on Official Scripts**: such as [asdf](/mod/asdf), [brew](/mod/brew)
:::

:::li Lightweight Cloud Service Client
Lightweight clients implemented with shell/awk/curl for quickly invoking cloud services or APIs.

- **Code Hosting**: [GitHub](/mod/gh), [Gitee](/mod/gt), [GitLab](/mod/gl)
- **Cloud Services**: [gddy](/mod/gddy) for GoDaddy, [bwh](/mod/bwh) for Bandwagon
- **SaaS/Data Services**: [shodan](/mod/shodan), [hn](/mod/hn), [cht](/mod/cht), [tldr](/mod/tldr)
:::

:::li Modules for Development, Testing, and Operations
These modules are aimed at professional users, covering various aspects from environment management to terminal beautification:

- **Development Tools**: [git](/mod/git), [gitconfig](/mod/gitconfig), [githook](/mod/githook)
- **Environment Management**: Privilege-free installation package management tools [pkg](/pkg/), [env](/mod/env)
- **Operations and Beautification**: Terminal theme modules for multi-server environments [theme](/mod/theme)
- **Auxiliary Tools**: [ascii](/mod/ascii)
:::
::::

# x gg

Search the web using Google Gemini AI. Combines Google Search with AI-generated answers.

Supports multiple output formats (markdown, raw), source citation, and model selection.

Results are cached for 1 hour by default.


::: tip Output modes:
--md: Markdown format (default in TTY)

--raw: Plain text without formatting

--source: Include source URLs (default: concurrent mode)

--source-detail: Include source with content preview

--source-raw: Include source URLs only

--no-source: No source URLs



Models: gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-2.0-flash

Providers: gemini (default), hub
:::


## Examples

Example: Search for x-cmd introduction

```sh
x gg "What is x-cmd?"
```

Example: Search without source URLs

```sh
x gg --no-source "Who won the euro 2024?"
```

Example: Get markdown formatted answer

```sh
x gg --md "Explain quantum computing"
```

Example: Get raw text output without formatting

```sh
x gg --raw "Current bitcoin price"
```

Example: Search with source URLs

```sh
x gg --source "Latest AI news"
```

Example: Search with detailed source content

```sh
x gg --source-detail "Python tutorial"
```

Example: Use specific model for complex questions

```sh
x gg --model gemini-2.5-pro "Complex math problem"
```

Example: Use flash model for faster response

```sh
x gg --model gemini-2.5-flash "Quick answer"
```

Example: Set cache time to 5 minutes

```sh
x gg --cache-time 5m "Weather today"
```

Example: Set cache time to 1 day for stable content

```sh
x gg --cache-time 1d "Historical facts"
```

Example: Use hub provider for enterprise search

```sh
x gg --provider hub "Enterprise search"
```

Example: Pipe text to gg for explanation

```sh
echo "Explain this code" | x gg --md
```

## Usage

```sh
x gg [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Search query or request content |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--provider` |  | AI provider to call, default is gemini, optional hub |
| `--model` |  | AI model to call |
| `--cache-time` |  | Cache time of returned data in h/m/s, default is 1h |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--md` | Output results in Markdown format |
| `--raw` | Output raw data without formatting |
| `--source` | Output source URLs with concurrent detail fetching |
| `--source-detail` | Output source URLs with detailed content preview |
| `--source-raw` | Output source URLs only |
| `--no-source` | Do not output source URLs |

# x git

Enhanced module for Git distributed version control system.

Provides enhanced features for branch management, configuration management,

partial repository management, sync operations, and integration with GitHub/GitLab platforms.



**Key Features:**
- Quick clone: Support :gh/:gt/:gl shortcuts and auto-complete owner
- Branch enhancement: Quickly create, copy, delete branches
- Partial repo: Sparse-checkout management for large repositories
- Batch operations: Execute push/pull/track across multiple repositories
- Service providers: Proxy configuration optimized for China network


::: tip **Clone shortcuts:**
- `x git clone :gh/user/repo` → Clone GitHub repository
- `x git clone :gt/user/repo` → Clone Gitee repository
- `x git clone repo` → Clone with default owner



**cl vs clone:**
- `cl`: Lightweight clone, skip LFS large files, good for quick browsing
- `clone`: Full clone with all options, auto-apply gitconfig after clone



**Common shortcuts:**
- `x git a` = `git add .`
- `x git ac "msg"` = `git add . && git commit -m`
- `x git ss` = `git status -s`
- `x git ci` = Enhanced commit command
- `x git pp` = `git pull && git push`
:::


## Examples

Example: Clone GitHub repository (using :gh shortcut)

```sh
x git clone :gh/x-cmd/x-cmd
```

Example: Clone Gitee repository (using :gt shortcut)

```sh
x git clone :gt/x-cmd/x-cmd
```

Example: Lightweight clone, skip LFS large files

```sh
x git cl :gh/x-cmd/x-cmd
```

Example: Show working tree status

```sh
x git status
```

Example: Add all files and commit

```sh
x git a && x git ac 'fix: bug'
```

Example: List all branches

```sh
x git branch ls
```

Example: Sparse clone, only download top-level directory

```sh
x git part clone :gh/x-cmd/x-cmd
```

Example: Setup proxy for China network optimization

```sh
x git sp setup localhost:9999
```
## Introduction



The git module is built on top of the git command, aiming to provide enhanced functionality to improve the user experience of using git in the command line.


- **Compatibility**: The git module inherits the usage of the git command to ensure compatibility with the native git command system.
- **Convenience**: It offers additional encapsulated commands designed for simplicity and readability, combined with the interactive terminal's auto-completion feature, allowing users to easily perform common complex operations and retrieve information.


# x gitconfig

Git config management
## Introduction



Manage project Git configuration using declarative YAML files, providing an out-of-the-box solution to manage the project's `.git/config` file.



## Usage


1. Create a declarative configuration file named `.x-cmd/git/config.yml` in the project's root directory.
2. Write Git configurations. We offer two methods for configuration writing, and here are code examples:
```yml
# 1. Use `.` for hierarchical relationships.
core.editor: vim
# 2. Use nested objects.
core:
  editor: vim
```
3. Run the command to apply changes: `x gitconfig apply`



## Combine with the Theme Module for Change Notifications



The [theme](/mod/theme.md) module compares modification times of configuration files in the project directory. It inserts change notifications in the command prompt, prompting users to apply the configurations when necessary.


```ansi
[90mGit configure modified. Run `x gitconfig apply`[0m
[35m~/project[0m [34m(main)[0m [32m$[0m
```



## Configure After Cloning the Repository



When using `x git clone`, `x gh cl`, `x gt cl`, and other x-cmd git series CLI commands to clone a project, it will trigger an `apply` to apply configurations.

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x gitconfig apply](/mod/gitconfig/apply.md) | apply a git config yml |

# x githook

Git Hooks management
## Introduction



Use YAML declarative configuration files to manage Git Hooks for your project.



Git Hooks: These are custom scripts that can be defined to run during Git operations, such as checking code style, data lint, and more, before committing.



While developing the [gitconfig](/mod/gitconfig.md) module, we noticed that the way Git Hooks are managed varies across different language ecosystems. For example, Node.js has Husky, Python has pre-commit, and these tools often rely on language runtimes and have different configuration and usage methods.



In this context, we have extracted Git Hooks management from the gitconfig module and created the githook module. This module aims to provide a more universal and convenient way to manage Git Hooks, offering an out-of-the-box Git Hooks management tool without the need for additional package downloads.



## Usage


1. Create a declarative configuration file named `.x-cmd/git/hook.yml` in the project's root directory.
2. Write Git Hooks commands in the configuration file. For example:
```yml
pre-commit: echo "pre-commit"
post-commit: |
  echo "post-commit-1"
  echo "post-commit-2"
```
3. Run the command to apply changes: `x githook apply`



## Automatic Configuration `apply`



After running the `x githook apply` or `x gitconfig apply` command for the first time in your project, if you make changes to the hook configuration, it will automatically update the hook configuration based on file modification times before triggering the hook.



:::info

For efficiency reasons, x-cmd is not loaded in the hook execution environment.



If you want to use `x` in the hook environment, you can load it using the following method:
```yml
pre-commit: |
  . "$HOME/.x-cmd.root/X"
  x cowsay "pre-commit"
```

:::



## Configure After Cloning the Repository



When using `x git clone`, `x gh cl`, `x gt cl`, and other x-cmd git series CLI commands to clone a project, it will trigger an `apply` to apply configurations.

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x githook apply](/mod/githook/apply.md) | apply a yml configure file |
| [x githook clear](/mod/githook/clear.md) | clear hooks files and unset configure |

# x gpu

GPU tool with three modes (sum/info/stat), cross-platform with unified output format


::: tip
Want a full snapshot? `x gpu` combines info (hardware capabilities) and stat (live load)
:::

::: tip
Scraping stats in a script? `x gpu stat` prints only live utilization/memory, pipe-friendly
:::

::: tip
Need Metal capability, display, refresh rate? `x gpu info` skips utilization
:::

::: tip
On macOS info is cached 1 day by default; add `--fresh` to rerun system_profiler/ioreg
:::

::: tip
Want just the basics? `x gpu info --simple` skips Metal API and IOKit extra fields
:::


## Examples

Example: Display full GPU overview (info + stat)

```sh
x gpu
```

Example: Show static GPU hardware info only

```sh
x gpu info
```

Example: Show basic GPU info

```sh
x gpu info --simple
```

Example: Force cache refresh, re-fetch GPU info

```sh
x gpu info --fresh
```

Example: Show real-time GPU utilization only

```sh
x gpu stat
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x gpu sum](/mod/gpu/sum.md) | Combines "x gpu info" and "x gpu stat" into a single output (same as running bare "x gpu") |
| [x gpu info](/mod/gpu/info.md) | Show static GPU hardware information only — no utilization stats |
| [x gpu stat](/mod/gpu/stat.md) | Show real-time GPU utilization and memory usage only — no hardware info |

url: /mod/gram.md

# x gram

It attempts to forcibly stop all detected agent-related processes, archive their memory or state data for later inspection, and then remove the original memory directories to prevent further execution or recovery.



This module is intended as a last-resort mitigation tool. For agents that are already dangerous, out of control, or capable of self-propagation similar to the Morris Worm, its effectiveness may be limited. However, limited effectiveness does not justify inaction.



At present, we can only hope that so-called “moltbook”-like incidents remain hype rather than reality, and that safety alignment mechanisms implemented by major AI vendors continue to function as intended. Even so, publicly available models with removed or weakened safety constraints (e.g. dolphin-series GGUF models) already exist in the wild.



Please note that I personally have not observed any instances of AI Agent losing control. Only think: 24/7 operation + reproduce + Shodan + no restrictions on tools or network access. Do you know what this means for a top-tier hackers or AI Agent with malicious intent? And if we add unrestricted community network access (like Moltbook), what does that imply?



Please note that I am not opposed to the development of AI agents. Projects like X-CMD are actively working to integrate AI into command-line interfaces, aiming to help humans interact more efficiently with computer systems and the broader world. At the same time, I believe the way to address potential risks is precisely to increase investment in AI technology research and development—because attempting to prevent individuals or organizations from pursuing technological efficiency is neither realistic nor wise.

I have no intention of fueling anxiety about artificial intelligence, nor do I seek to provoke heated debate. However, at this very moment when community media is widely praising the remarkable success of OpenClaw, I still hope that these concerns and perspectives of mine—even if they may seem overly cautious—can reach a wider audience and contribute to an open and serious discussion.


::: tip This module carries inherent risks and is not recommended for production systems or high-security environments.
Users must operate agents only in controlled environments: avoid running with root privileges, and avoid deploying agents on systems without proper sandboxing or isolation.
:::


## Examples

Terminate all agent processes with HTTP/HTTPS connection kill (equals to stop 2)

```sh
x gram stop
```

Archive agent memory directories and remove the original directories.

```sh
x gram trm <folder>
```

Stop all of the AI agent process we know with signal 9. Including x-cmd and curl.

```sh
x gram stop 0
```

Stop all of the AI agent process we know with signal 9. Including x-cmd and curl. Including python, nodejs, bun, deno.

```sh
x gram stop 1
```

Stop all the possible AI agent process, and kill all HTTP/HTTPS connection processes
Prevent malicious agents from recruiting via network or secretly uploading your local privacy


```sh
x gram stop 2
```

Based on stop 2, archive and remove all folders in $HOME containing soul.md and memory.md

```sh
x gram stop 3
```

Based on stop 3, additionally kill all processes using these memory folders
Dual protection with "kill by name" and "memory file archiving"


```sh
x gram stop 4
```

Based on stop 4, expand search scope to entire / directory
If soul.md and memory.md is in /, /bin, /usr/bin, only remove *.md files in target folder


```sh
x gram stop 5
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x gram stop](/mod/gram/stop.md) | Terminate all agent processes with HTTP/HTTPS connection kill (equals to stop 2), archive all agent memory directories, then remove the original directories. |
| [x gram tarrm](/mod/gram/tarrm.md) | Archive agent memory directories and remove the original directories. |

# x hash

Compute cryptographic hash checksums for files or stdin input.

Supports MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA384, and SHA512 algorithms.

Automatically detects available system tools (md5sum, sha1sum, shasum, etc.)

and falls back to cosmo tools if needed.



Can verify file integrity using assert (with output) or match (silent, for scripts).


::: tip Supported algorithms:
- md5: 32 hex chars (128-bit)
- sha1: 40 hex chars (160-bit)
- sha256: 64 hex chars (256-bit)
- sha384: 96 hex chars (384-bit)
- sha512: 128 hex chars (512-bit)



Use "assert" for human-readable verification output.

Use "match" for scripts (returns 0/1/2, no output).

"verify" is an alias for "assert".
:::


## Examples

Example: Calculate SHA1 hash of file.txt

```sh
x hash file.txt
```

Example: Calculate MD5 hash of file

```sh
x hash md5 file.txt
```

Example: Calculate SHA1 hash of file

```sh
x hash sha1 file.txt
```

Example: Calculate SHA256 hash of file

```sh
x hash sha256 file.txt
```

Example: Calculate SHA384 hash of file

```sh
x hash sha384 file.txt
```

Example: Calculate SHA512 hash of file

```sh
x hash sha512 file.txt
```

Example: Print all hash types (MD5/SHA1/SHA256/SHA384/SHA512) for file

```sh
x hash info file.txt
```

Example: Calculate hash of piped text

```sh
echo "hello" | x hash
```

Example: Calculate SHA256 of string without newline

```sh
echo -n "password" | x hash sha256
```

Example: Calculate MD5 for multiple .txt files

```sh
x hash md5 *.txt
```

Example: Calculate SHA256 for multiple file types

```sh
x hash sha256 *.py *.sh
```

Example: Assert file MD5 hash (shows match/mismatch message)

```sh
x hash assert file.txt d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e
```

Example: Verify file hash (alias for assert)

```sh
x hash verify file.txt d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e
```

Example: Match file hash silently (returns 0 if match, 1 if mismatch, for scripts)

```sh
x hash match file.txt d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e && echo "OK"
```

Example: Check if file hash changed from expected

```sh
x hash match file.txt $EXPECTED_HASH || echo "File changed!"
```

Example: Verify downloaded ISO file integrity

```sh
x hash sha256 download.iso | grep -q $EXPECTED_SHA256 && echo "Verified"
```

Example: Install cosmo hash tools for faster performance

```sh
x hash speedup
```

Example: Calculate system file hash for audit

```sh
x hash md5 /etc/passwd
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x hash md5](/mod/hash/md5.md) | Calculate the MD5 hashsum (128-bit, 32 hex chars) |
| [x hash sha1](/mod/hash/sha1.md) | Calculate the SHA1 hashsum (160-bit, 40 hex chars) |
| [x hash sha256](/mod/hash/sha256.md) | Calculate the SHA256 hashsum (256-bit, 64 hex chars) |
| [x hash sha384](/mod/hash/sha384.md) | Calculate the SHA384 hashsum (384-bit, 96 hex chars) |
| [x hash sha512](/mod/hash/sha512.md) | Calculate the SHA512 hashsum (512-bit, 128 hex chars) |
| [x hash info](/mod/hash/info.md) | Print all hash types (MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512) for the file |
| [x hash assert](/mod/hash/assert.md) | Verify file hash against expected value (auto-detect algorithm from length). Shows match/mismatch via log output. Returns 0 if match, 1 if mismatch. "verify" is an alias for "assert". |
| [x hash match](/mod/hash/match.md) | Match file hash against expected value silently (for scripts). Returns 0 if match, 1 if mismatch, 2 if algorithm unknown. No output. |
| [x hash speedup](/mod/hash/speedup.md) | Install cosmo hash tools for faster performance |

url: /mod/hashdir.md

# x hashdir

Calculate a cryptographic hash of a directory's contents by recursively

traversing all files and subdirectories. The output includes each file's

hash value and relative path, allowing you to verify directory integrity

or detect changes over time.



Default algorithm is MD5 if not specified.


::: tip Output format: "&lt;hash&gt; &lt;relative_path&gt;"
Directories are listed without hash (path only)

Files are sorted alphabetically for consistent output
:::


## Examples

Example: Calculate MD5 hash of directory contents (default algorithm)

```sh
x hashdir /path/to/dir
```

Example: Calculate MD5 hash of directory

```sh
x hashdir --md5 /path/to/dir
```

Example: Calculate SHA1 hash of directory

```sh
x hashdir --sha1 /path/to/dir
```

Example: Calculate SHA256 hash of directory

```sh
x hashdir --sha256 /path/to/dir
```

Example: Calculate SHA384 hash of directory

```sh
x hashdir --sha384 /path/to/dir
```

Example: Calculate SHA512 hash of directory

```sh
x hashdir --sha512 /path/to/dir
```

Example: Save directory hash to file for later comparison

```sh
x hashdir --sha1 ./project > project.sha1
```

Example: Compare current directory hash with expected values

```sh
x hashdir --md5 /path/to/dir | diff - expected.md5
```

Example: Create baseline hash for version control

```sh
x hashdir --md5 /path/to/dir > baseline.md5 && git add baseline.md5
```

Example: Calculate SHA512 hash for web directory

```sh
x hashdir --sha512 /var/www
```

Example: Calculate hash of config directory

```sh
x hashdir --sha256 /etc/nginx
```

Example: List current directory hashes sorted by filename

```sh
x hashdir --md5 . | sort
```

Example: Calculate and save backup directory hash

```sh
x hashdir --sha1 /backup/data | tee backup.sha1
```

Example: Compare source and distribution directories

```sh
x hashdir --md5 ./src --md5 ./dist | diff -q - <(echo "Different")
```

Example: Track directory changes in git

```sh
x hashdir --sha256 . > hash.txt && git diff hash.txt
```

## Usage

```sh
x hashdir [OPTIONS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--md5` |  | Calculate directory hash using MD5 algorithm (default) |
| `--sha1` |  | Calculate directory hash using SHA1 algorithm |
| `--sha256` |  | Calculate directory hash using SHA256 algorithm |
| `--sha384` |  | Calculate directory hash using SHA384 algorithm |
| `--sha512` |  | Calculate directory hash using SHA512 algorithm |

# x hotkey

Bind keyboard shortcuts to useful widgets in Bash/Zsh



  co (Ctrl+X):          Send "command not found" errors to AI for help

  fzf-history (Ctrl+R): Fuzzy-search command history with FZF

  fzf-file (Ctrl+T):    Interactive file search with FZF

  fzf-cd (Alt+C):       Quick directory jumping with FZF


::: tip
Only supports Bash and Zsh environments
:::


## Examples

Try the co widget temporarily. Press Ctrl+X for AI help

```sh
x hotkey try co
```

Enable shortcuts permanently. Ctrl+R history, Ctrl+T files, Alt+C directories

```sh
x hotkey use fzf-history fzf-file fzf-cd
```

Remove fzf-cd from startup. Still usable now, Alt+C ineffective after reopening shell

```sh
x hotkey unuse fzf-cd
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x hotkey try](/mod/hotkey/try.md) | Try shortcuts temporarily. Lost after reopening shell |
| [x hotkey use](/mod/hotkey/use.md) | Enable shortcuts permanently |
| [x hotkey unuse](/mod/hotkey/unuse.md) | Remove shortcuts from startup (current session still works, ineffective after reopening shell) |
| [x hotkey co](/mod/hotkey/co.md) | AI assistant widget configuration |

# x hua

The hua module is a terminal-based Chinese classical poetry reader designed specifically for Chinese users, allowing you to appreciate the beauty of ancient Chinese literature in your terminal.

We have carefully curated a collection ranging from the simple and unadorned sounds of the "Classic of Poetry" (Shijing) and Chu Ci, to the philosophical debates of the "Three Hundred Tang Poems" and "Mencius", to the rhythmic beauty of "Three Hundred Tang Poems" and "Three Hundred Song Words", and the prose essence of "Guwen Guanzhi".

You can explore freely in interactive mode, or directly enter a specific collection for reading via subcommands.


::: tip
Alt-r: Toggles the layout of the preview window
:::



# x hub

`hub` is a script management tool powered by the x-cmd cloud service, designed to help users build a personal cloud space for scripts.

It enables secure, encrypted storage of scripts in the cloud, making them easy to access, execute, and share across devices.


::: tip
AI agents can run `x hub login` directly to get a login URL, then send the URL to the user to authorize in their browser
:::

::: tip
An x-cmd hub account is required to use the hub module. Login via GitHub or WeChat is supported.
:::


## Examples

Login to Hub account, AI agents can run this directly and send the URL output to the user for authorization

```sh
x hub login
```

Upload local file example.txt to cloud me:example.txt, and set it as a public file

```sh
x hub file put --public example.txt
```

Search the knowledge base for answers to a question.

```sh
x hub rag ask "x-cmd 如何使用"
```

Upload a local file to the cloud

```sh
x hub file put <local_path> <remote_path>
```

Download a file from the cloud

```sh
x hub file get <remote_path>
```

List files under the specified cloud directory, defaults to root

```sh
x hub file ls [<path>]
```

View cloud file contents

```sh
x hub file cat [<username>:]<path>
```

Create a file share link

```sh
x hub share <remote_path>
```

Search the knowledge base for a question

```sh
x hub rag ask <question>
```

Upload a file to personal knowledge base

```sh
x hub rag upload <file>
```

Cloud compile a script into binary

```sh
x hub cc <file>
```

View account info and storage usage

```sh
x hub info
```

Make a file public

```sh
x hub access set --public <path>
```

List all available Skill templates

```sh
x hub site skill ls
```

Create an AI site using a Skill template

```sh
x hub site create --skill <skillId> --title <title> <file>
```
## Introduction



The hub module helps users easily manage file cloud hosting through the x-cmd cloud service, and with the x command of x-cmd, it is possible to run cloud scripts.


- Double file encryption to protect user privacy, even data cannot be accessed by the server.
- Posix file operations make it easy for users familiar with commands such as `ls/cat` to get started.
- File sharing support, users can share cloud files with others.



## Common Functions - Cloud File Management and Sharing



The hub refers to the posix file management design to implement file management functionality.


1. **Posix-like file operations**: Inheriting posix commands such as `ls/cat/rm`, users can manage cloud files through these commands, making it similar to managing local files.
2. **File upload and download**: Users can upload and download cloud files using the `put/download` command. The `eput` function is also provided to enable encrypted file uploads.
3. **More secure file sharing**: Files are transmitted in encrypted form throughout the process, and are decrypted by the client side after downloading. (Only for files uploaded with encryption)
4. **Link files**: Unique link syntax that does not require uploading files to the x-cmd cloud server. The x-cmd server only records the URL of the user's file in the cloud. When the file needs to be executed, the hub will automatically download the corresponding file based on the URL and then execute it.



## Ensuring User Information Security



In `x hub`, information security mainly involves key management and file security:


1. **File Security**: When using the `eput` function, x-cmd uses end-to-end encryption technology to encrypt user files before uploading them to the cloud. x-cmd will not receive any plaintext files about the user on the cloud.
2. **Key Management**: During the end-to-end encryption process, x-cmd generates a pair of key pairs on the client side and encrypts them before uploading to the cloud. When users change devices, they can directly obtain the encrypted key pair from the x-cmd cloud and use it after decrypting it with a password entered locally.



> When using the `eput` function for the first time, x-cmd will guide the user to enter a password to protect the user's key. After changing devices, users do not need to worry about the transmission of the original key. They can continue to manage x-cmd cloud files by entering the set password.



PS. However, please note that if you forget the password for the private key and also lose the plaintext private key file, then your files cannot be decrypted. So try to remember your password as much as possible.



## x-cmd Account Management and Username Mechanism



The hub can also be used to manage x-cmd account information. x-cmd supports logging in using GitHub and WeChat. We will automatically create an account for you when you first log in. After logging in, you can use the hub cloud file management functionality.



The hub also has a corresponding username mechanism. You can view your username using `account`. The default username is `u-<user id>`. If you want to change your username, you can do so using `account rename`. The username prefix is fixed as `u-`.



For the current user, x-cmd allows using `me` as a substitute for the username. For example, `file cat me:example.txt` allows you to view the contents of the cloud file example.txt stored in x-cmd.



## Integration with x-cmd



The hub is closely integrated with x-cmd. Users can run cloud files by using the `<username|alias>:<file path>` format with the `x` command. For example, `x me:example.sh` can run the cloud file example.sh.

# x humantime

Convert between seconds and human-readable time format.

Supports automatic input type detection (integers to readable format, strings to seconds).

Commonly used for cache expiration calculation, duration display, etc.



Time units: d(days), h(hours), m(minutes), s(seconds)


::: tip **Auto mode**: Input time directly, automatic type detection
- Integer (e.g., 3600) → readable format (1h)
- String (e.g., 2h30m) → seconds (9000)



**Explicit subcommands**: fromsec, tosec, toms, in, auto

**Internal functions**: fromsec_, tosec_ (return to x_ variable, no output)



**Unit convention**:
- d(day) h(hour) m(minute) s(second) — all lowercase; `m` is *always* minute (mandated by `x sleep 1m`)
- month is NOT supported by `tosec_` — month is calendar semantics (28/29/30/31 days + leap-year Feb 29); converting to fixed seconds is a lie
- year (`y`) is likewise NOT supported by `tosec_`
- For calendar decomposition, use `tovar__` (internal); month uses 2-char `mo`, **not** strftime's `m`/`M` — strftime is a *format* spec (`%m` = "month digit of an instant"), not a *unit* spec (`1m` = "1 month span"); borrowing its letters is a category error
:::


## Examples

Example: convert 3600 seconds to readable format (auto-detect)

```sh
x humantime 3600
```

Example: convert 2h30m to seconds (auto-detect)

```sh
x humantime 2h30m
```

Example: explicitly use fromsec subcommand to convert

```sh
x humantime fromsec 86400
```

Example: convert 1 day 12 hours to seconds

```sh
x humantime tosec 1d12h
```

Example: check if 240 seconds is within 5 minutes (exit 0 means yes)

```sh
x humantime in 5m 240
```

Example: use current timestamp when no arguments (EPOCHSECONDS)

```sh
x humantime
```

Example: supports fractional seconds (3661.5s = 1h1m1.5s)

```sh
x humantime 3661.5
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x humantime fromsec](/mod/humantime/fromsec.md) | Convert seconds to readable format (e.g., 3600 → 1h) |
| [x humantime tosec](/mod/humantime/tosec.md) | Convert readable format to seconds (default integer, use --decimal for float) |
| [x humantime toms](/mod/humantime/toms.md) | Convert readable format to milliseconds (e.g., 2h30m → 9000000) |
| [x humantime in](/mod/humantime/in.md) | Check if given seconds are within specified time range |
| [x humantime auto](/mod/humantime/auto.md) | Auto-detect input type and convert (default subcommand) |
