# x skill

Manage Agent Skills to enhance LLM task execution.



Skills are reusable capabilities that extend LLM abilities for specific tasks.

This module allows you to browse, add, remove, and manage skills for various AI agents.


::: tip Quick start:
1. Run 'x skill lr' to see all available skills
2. Run 'x skill ls' to see activated skills in current project
3. Run 'x skill suggest' to get AI-recommended skills for your project
:::

::: tip Skill source prefixes:
- clawhub/*        — Clawhub platform
- x-mod/*          — x-cmd built-in module
- &lt;author&gt;/&lt;name&gt;  — awesome list, auto-cached (e.g. anthropics/pptx)
- GitHub URL       — install directly from repo
:::

::: tip x-mod/* represents an x-cmd built-in module.
Use 'x &lt;mod&gt; --help' for documentation.

To keep across sessions, note it in AGENTS.md.
:::

::: tip Agent skill directories (when --agent is specified):
claude → .claude/skills/    gemini → .gemini/skills/

codex  → .codex/skills/     others → .agents/skills/

Without --agent, installs to both .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/.

Global scope: ~/.&lt;agent&gt;/skills/

Override with --skill-dir.
:::


## Examples

Example: list all available skills

```sh
x skill lr
```

Example: list activated skills in current project

```sh
x skill ls
```

Example: auto-apply AI-recommended skills

```sh
x skill suggest --auto
```

Example: add pptx skill

```sh
x skill add anthropics/pptx
```

Example: add pptx skill for claude-code agent only

```sh
x skill add anthropics/pptx --agent claude
```

Example: add multiple skills from GitHub repo

```sh
x skill add https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-skills --skill gemini-api-dev --skill gemini-interactions-api
```

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x skill0</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span>

Skill0 is a special class of skill, designed as the zero-skill. It aggregates meta-knowledge across domains, including best practices + data/behavioral conventions (e.g., rule, score). We reduce information density and urge the LLM to use tools to fetch in real time from first-party docs, the network, and the skill community based on the current environment (e.g., x rfc, x cve, x wkp, agent-browser), execute based on understanding, and form the most suitable personalized skill set + memory.


::: tip
General skills provide latest operational guides, data, knowledge, and methodology (rich content, but may not be continuously updated). Skill0 aggregates meta-knowledge across domains (best practices + data/behavioral conventions, e.g., rule, score), carries less (by design), and urges the LLM to use the right tools (x wkp / x rfc / x cve, browsers, search engines, etc.) to fetch the latest knowledge and the practices most suited to the current environment.
:::

::: tip The LLM continuously updates its training data, methodology, and chain-of-thought, but data hallucinations have no solution — you can't expect it to be lossless compression. Community and personal skills may be outdated or have security issues.
The idea: leverage the LLM's continuously-updating ability to read external skills; once understood, verify via first-party data + formal logic given the current environment, and form a personalized skill set + memory.
:::


## Examples

List all sub-skills.

```sh
x skill0 ls
```

TSV output for downstream processing.

```sh
x skill0 ls --tsv
```

Resolve ccal to its SKILL.md path.

```sh
x skill0 which ccal
```

By bucket/slug form.

```sh
x skill0 which data/ccal
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x skill0 ls](/mod/skill0/ls.md) | List skill0 catalog. Table on TTY, TSV on pipe. |
| [x skill0 which](/mod/skill0/which.md) | Resolve a sub-skill name to its absolute path. |

# x sleep

Pause execution for a specified time, or schedule periodic tasks.

Supports human-readable time formats like 1s, 1m, 1h, 1d.

Also provides beacon for periodic timestamp output and schd for scheduled command execution.


::: tip Time formats: s (seconds), m (minutes), h (hours), d (days)
Examples: 30s, 5m, 2h, 1d
:::


## Examples

Example: Pause for 5 seconds

```sh
x sleep 5s
```

Example: Pause for 30 seconds

```sh
x sleep 30s
```

Example: Pause for 1 minute

```sh
x sleep 1m
```

Example: Pause 1 minute then execute command

```sh
x sleep 1m echo "Hello"
```

Example: Pause for 5 minutes

```sh
x sleep 5m
```

Example: Pause for 1 hour

```sh
x sleep 1h
```

Example: Pause for 2 hours

```sh
x sleep 2h
```

Example: Pause for 1 day

```sh
x sleep 1d
```

Example: Pause for compound time (1 hour 30 minutes)

```sh
x sleep 1h 30m
```

Example: Output timestamp every 5 seconds (infinite loop)

```sh
x sleep beacon
```

Example: Output timestamp every second

```sh
x sleep beacon 1s
```

Example: Output timestamp every 10 seconds

```sh
x sleep beacon 10s
```

Example: Output timestamp every minute

```sh
x sleep beacon 1m
```

Example: Execute command every 5 seconds (infinite)

```sh
x sleep schd -i 5s echo "tick"
```

Example: Execute command every 5 seconds for 10 times

```sh
x sleep schd -i 5s -n 10 echo "tick"
```

Example: Run ls every minute (infinite)

```sh
x sleep schd -i 1m -- ls -la
```

Example: Run tests every 10 seconds for 5 times

```sh
x sleep schd -i 10s -n 5 -- make test
```

Example: Run backup script every hour

```sh
x sleep schd -i 1h -- backup.sh
```

Example: Sleep then chain with another command

```sh
x sleep 5s && echo "Done"
```

Example: Use in loop with counter

```sh
for i in 1 2 3; do x sleep 1s; echo $i; done
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x sleep beacon](/mod/sleep/beacon.md) | Output timestamp periodically (infinite loop, use Ctrl-C to stop) |
| [x sleep schd](/mod/sleep/schd.md) | Schedule command execution with specified interval |

# x smart

smartctl is a tool for control and monitor disks, used to check disk health, including SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Technology) data.

This module aims to help users quickly use the smartctl tool without installation and provides an interactive way to list local disk devices, making it easy for users to choose the disk they want to check.


::: tip The smartctl command needs to be run with root privileges to allow access to the disk's SMART data.
If you are a Linux user, the sudo module will be automatically invoked to run the command, without the need to add the sudo prefix
:::


## Examples


```sh

```


Open an interactive Gemini session to discuss the SMART information of the disk

```sh
x smart -a /dev/disk0 | @gemini
```

Search the smartmontools.com website for content related to "disk health" and display the search results in an interactive table format.

# x starship

Starship is a minimal, blazing-fast, and infinitely customizable prompt for any shell!

For a detailed guide on getting started, have a look at the docs at https://starship.rs



The starship module is an enhanced module designed for Starship, allowing users to easily switch themes with a single command.

This module also includes a theme preview feature that lets users preview different themes directly in the command line, streamlining the process of selecting and changing themes.


::: tip
This module's try/untry feature is currently only compatible with bash and zsh environments.
:::

::: tip
Using the starship module's theme will override the current environment's STARSHIP_CONFIG variable
:::


## Examples

```sh
x starship
```


```sh

```

Cancel the theme that is currently used globally

```sh
x starship unuse
```

Try to use the 'pastel-powerline' theme in this current Shell

```sh
x starship try pastel-powerline
```

View the currently used theme settings

```sh
x starship current
```

# x str

High-performance string manipulation module providing rich string operations.

Supports case conversion, trim, split, replace, encoding/decoding, hash calculation, etc.

Low-level module, subcommand-level help not supported.


::: tip This is a low-level high-performance module, all TLDR examples are at root level.
Supports both pipe input and argument input.
:::


## Examples

Example: convert string to uppercase

```sh
x str upper hello
```

Example: convert string to lowercase via pipe

```sh
echo "Hello World" | x str lower
```

Example: trim whitespace from both ends

```sh
x str trim "  hello  "
```

Example: trim leading whitespace

```sh
x str triml "  hello"
```

Example: trim trailing whitespace

```sh
x str trimr "hello  "
```

Example: slice index 1 to 3 (result: bc)

```sh
x str slice abcdef 1:3
```

Example: slice excluding last char (result: abcde)

```sh
x str slice abcdef 0:-1
```

Example: slice excluding last 2 chars (result: abcd)

```sh
x str slice abcdef 0:-2
```

Example: slice from index 2 to end (result: cdef)

```sh
x str slice abcdef 2:
```

Example: slice from start to index 3 (result: abc)

```sh
x str slice abcdef :3
```

Example: slice last 3 chars (result: def)

```sh
x str slice abcdef -3:
```

Example: slice from -5 to -2 (result: bcd)

```sh
x str slice abcdef -5:-2
```

Example: extract 3 chars from index 2, C-style (result: cde)

```sh
x str substr abcdef 2 3
```

Example: split string by comma

```sh
x str split "," a,b,c
```

Example: split string via pipe

```sh
echo "a,b,c" | x str split ","
```

Example: replace first occurrence

```sh
x str replace "hello world" world bash
```

Example: replace all occurrences

```sh
x str replace_all "a,b,a" a x
```

Example: join strings with comma

```sh
x str join "," a b c
```

Example: calculate string length

```sh
x str len hello
```

Example: check if string starts with 'he'

```sh
x str startswith "hello" "he"
```

Example: check if string ends with 'lo'

```sh
x str endswith "hello" "lo"
```

Example: Base64 encode

```sh
x str base64 hello
```

Example: Base64 decode

```sh
x str unbase64 aGVsbG8=
```

Example: calculate MD5 hash

```sh
x str md5 hello
```

Example: calculate SHA256 hash

```sh
x str sha256 hello
```

Example: convert DOS to Unix line endings

```sh
x str dos2unix file.txt
```

Example: convert Unix to DOS line endings

```sh
x str unix2dos file.txt
```

Example: repeat character 10 times

```sh
x str repeat "*" 10
```

Example: find substring index

```sh
x str indexof "hello world" world
```

# x sudo

Wraps sudo/doas/su to run commands with elevated privileges while preserving

the user's PATH and environment variables in the privileged process.


::: tip Fallback order: prefers sudo, then doas, then su.
If sudo auth fails, prompts whether to retry with su.
:::

::: tip su vs sudo: su runs via `su <user> -s /bin/sh <script>`, requires the
root password (not your user password), defaults to root.

Use --suuser to specify a user; defaults to root if unset.
:::

::: tip Why x sudo over bare sudo: e.g. you installed jq via `x env use jq` under HOME,
`sudo jq` fails with "command not found" because sudo resets PATH.

`x sudo jq` works because PATH is preserved. Same for any software

installed under HOME (node, python, etc.).
:::


## Examples

Edit system hosts file with root privileges

```sh
x sudo vim /etc/hosts
```

Update package index (auto-selects sudo/doas/su)

```sh
x sudo apt update
```

Run as specific user using su

```sh
x sudo --suuser admin whoami
```

Execute x-cmd command with sudo (preserves PATH)

```sh
x sudo hostname set myhost
```

## Usage

```sh
x sudo [OPTIONS] <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | Command and arguments to run with elevated privileges |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--suuser` |  | Specify the username for the su command |

# x tailer

Message queue framework for Agents.



Supports multi-writer single-reader mode for A2A (Agent to Agent) messaging.


::: tip Use run to start listener, use send to send messages.
Set ___X_CMD_TAILER_HANDLE env var to customize message handler.
:::


## Examples

Example: Start message queue listener

```sh
x tailer run /tmp/mq
```

Example: Send message to queue

```sh
x tailer send /tmp/mq "hello world"
```

Example: Set GC threshold to 20000 messages

```sh
x tailer run --gc 20000 /tmp/mq
```

Example: Query pending message count

```sh
x tailer pending /tmp/mq
```

Example: Subscribe mymq queue to subscription directory

```sh
x tailer sub /tmp/subscriptions mymq /tmp/mq
```

Example: One-time subscription, auto-unsubscribe after publish

```sh
x tailer sub --once /tmp/subscriptions mymq /tmp/mq
```

Example: Unsubscribe mymq

```sh
x tailer unsub /tmp/subscriptions mymq
```

Example: Publish message to all subscribers

```sh
x tailer pub /tmp/subscriptions
```

Example: Publish to one-time subscribers

```sh
x tailer pub --once /tmp/subscriptions
```

Example: Test throughput and latency with 10000 messages

```sh
x tailer test --count 10000
```

Example: Run sender in Docker container for testing

```sh
x tailer test --docker 10000
```

Example: Test with bash:3 image and sh shell

```sh
x tailer test --docker --docker-image bash:3 --docker-shell sh 20000
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x tailer run](/mod/tailer/run.md) | Start message queue listener, continuously read and process messages |
| [x tailer send](/mod/tailer/send.md) | Send message to the queue |
| [x tailer pending](/mod/tailer/pending.md) | Query the number of pending messages in the queue |
| [x tailer stop](/mod/tailer/stop.md) | Stop a running message queue listener |
| [x tailer sub](/mod/tailer/sub.md) | Subscribe a message queue |
| [x tailer unsub](/mod/tailer/unsub.md) | Unsubscribe a message queue |
| [x tailer pub](/mod/tailer/pub.md) | Publish message to all subscribers |
| [x tailer test](/mod/tailer/test.md) | Test tailer throughput and latency performance |
| [x tailer sublist](/mod/tailer/sublist.md) | List all subscribers |
| [x tailer service](/mod/tailer/service.md) | Manage Gateway Service |

# x tee

Execute command and write its output to both stdout and file.

Unlike traditional pipe tee, this preserves the command's exit code

and environment variable changes by using named pipe technique.

## Examples

Example: Build and log (preserves exit code for CI checks)

```sh
x tee output.txt -- make build
```

Example: Deploy with logging (exit code available on failure)

```sh
x tee deploy.log -- ./deploy.sh
```

Example: Run tests and save results (keeps failure status)

```sh
x tee results.txt -- pytest tests/
```

Example: Multiple commands (use eval to wrap shell operators)

```sh
x tee -a build.log -- eval 'make clean && make'
```

Example: Capture both stdout and stderr to file

```sh
x tee /tmp/build.log -- make 2>&1
```

## Usage

```sh
x tee
```

# x telegram

Use x telegram send messages to your Telegram group or channel. The first use requires configuring bot token.


::: tip Group Bot (x telegram bot)
Use case: One-way notifications to groups/channels, e.g., CI/CD build notifications, server monitoring alerts

First-time setup requires bot token

Configuration command: x telegram --cfg token=&lt;token&gt;

Setup guide: https://core.telegram.org/bots#how-do-i-create-a-bot
:::

::: tip Integrate with x claw as private AI assistant:
1. Configure bot token
2. Start Telegram gateway service: x telegram bot service start
3. Start x claw with Telegram: x claw start --telegram
:::


## Examples

Initialize configuration in interactive mode

```sh
x telegram init
```

Set the group bot's token

```sh
x telegram --cfg token=<token>
```

Send text type messages to Telegram group

```sh
x telegram send --text "x-cmd v1.0 released successfully"
```

Send text type messages to Telegram channel

```sh
x telegram send --text --chatid "@channelusername" "x-cmd v1.0 released successfully"
```

Send a.png images to Telegram group

```sh
x telegram send --image --chatid "-967810017" --file_path ./a.png
```

Start Telegram gateway service

```sh
x telegram bot service start
```

Show gateway service status

```sh
x telegram bot service status
```

Show gateway service log

```sh
x telegram bot service log
```

Stop gateway service

```sh
x telegram bot service stop
```

## Usage

```sh
x telegram [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Options

| `--cfg` |  | manage configuration for telegram |

| `--cur` | current session default value management |

# x termux

Comprehensive Termux utility for Android. Features include:
- Package management (pkg wrapper)
- System property viewer (getprop wrapper)
- Termux:API integration (sms, battery, volume, etc.)
- PRoot distro management (run Linux distros without root)



Note: Termux:API features require installing Termux:API app and termux-api package.


::: tip Shortcuts:
- m = x termux (default alias)
- x termux alp = Alpine Linux
- x termux deb = Debian
- x termux ubu = Ubuntu
:::


## Examples



```sh

```

Read and list SMS content


sending a text message

```sh

```

Speak the entered text

```sh

```

Vibrates the device for a specified duration in milliseconds (default 200ms).

```sh
x termux vibrate <number>
```

# x theme

Use command line prompt theme, Globally manage the display style of all x related interactive compoments.

If you want to view more themes online, please visit https://x-cmd.com/theme/


::: tip
The variable `___X_CMD_THEME_RELOAD_DISABLE` controls whether the theme is loaded
:::


## Examples

Open theme preview client to choose theme

```sh
x theme
```

View the currently used theme settings.

```sh
x theme current
```

Use and set 'robby' theme as prompt theme

```sh
x theme use robby
```

Try to use festival emoji in the current theme

```sh
x theme feature try emoji -t festival
```

Set the global theme feature to enable transient features by default

```sh
x theme feature use transient_enable always
```

Set the global theme feature to disable transient features by default

```sh
x theme feature use transient_enable never
```
## Introduction



The `theme` module is used to globally manage the display style of all `x` related widgets. Similar to the compatibility of x-cmd, `theme` can be used for ash, dash, bash, and zsh. 



The themes set in `theme` not only affect the display of the command prompt, but also affect the color scheme of the interactive widgets provided by x-cmd, such as the color scheme of the commonly used table widget in x-cmd, which will be adjusted as the `theme` theme color changes.



There are already many good solutions for enhancing command line display, such as oh-my-zsh, oh-my-bash, and zinit. 



In the process of implementing the `theme` module, in addition to trying our best to catch up with the above-mentioned predecessors in terms of functionality, we are most concerned about how the `theme` module can perceive the environment in order to achieve adjustments and provide the best user experience.



In terms of performance, we have already discovered the efficiency issues when using **MSYS** on Windows (such as git-for-windows), and have made adjustments and adaptations.



## Attempts in Environment Perception and Adaptation


1. Automatic line wrapping in long path environment - When the current path to be displayed is very long, the Prompt will automatically break into multiple lines to ensure the visibility and comfort of inputting commands.
2. Perceive whether it is vscode, gnome (the system terminal with the default deep red background in Ubuntu), or apple terminal, and change the theme of the command line accordingly.
3. Use htag (host tag) to mark whether the local server is in the production environment or the development environment. For more details, please refer to htag `x htag --help`, and provide reminders for important production environments.
4. Perceive whether the terminal supports 8 colors, 256 colors, or true colors, and automatically adjust the colors.
5. Show or hide information based on the type of project folder (git? node? python?).



## Themes and `l`



The above-mentioned environment perception features are not provided by all current theme schemes. The most complete default theme scheme that currently provides these features is `l`.



Regarding the design of the official `l` series themes, the design priorities are:
1. Command interaction experience (assisting in quickly inputting correct commands, clearly obtaining command results and completion status).
2. Survivability in various default terminals (designed with the system's 8 colors to simplify the effects and reduce the impact on system performance).
3. Comfort for long-term use takes priority over visual effects.



## Custom Themes



We have considered configurability, but since we are still observing and adjusting, we recommend users to use the provided themes first. We provide three design options for users who want to customize their themes:
1. Customize the color scheme based on a theme using environment variables.
2. Customize the widget display by re-implementing certain functions based on a theme.
3. Redefine theme functions and create a new theme, but the official theme widget functions can be reused.

## Usage

```sh
x theme [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--app` | Open theme preview client to choose theme |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x theme ls](/mod/theme/ls.md) | List all theme |
| [x theme use](/mod/theme/use.md) | Using the command line prompt theme globally |
| [x theme unuse](/mod/theme/unuse.md) | Unset theme |
| [x theme try](/mod/theme/try.md) | Try theme in the current session |
| [x theme untry](/mod/theme/untry.md) | Cancel setting theme in 'try' command |
| [x theme update](/mod/theme/update.md) | Update theme resource pack |
| [x theme font](/mod/theme/font.md) | Using font module to download fonts |
| [x theme current](/mod/theme/current.md) | Display the currently used prompt theme |
| [x theme feature](/mod/theme/feature.md) | Manage features of the current theme |
| [x theme statusline](/mod/theme/statusline.md) | Manage the status line component for Claude Code |

# x timeout

A portable wrapper around the `timeout` command with automatic busybox/cosmo fallback.

Supports signal selection, kill-after timeout, verbose mode, foreground, and preserve-status.


::: tip
To timeout a shell function instead of an external command, use the `tmo` module
:::

::: tip
Duration format: 1s, 1m, 1h, 1d (seconds, minutes, hours, days)
:::

::: tip
If the command finishes before timeout, it exits with the command's own status
:::


## Examples

Example: Run command with 10-second timeout

```sh
x timeout 10s command arg1 arg2
```

Example: Run script with 30s timeout, send TERM signal

```sh
x timeout -s TERM 30s ./script.sh
```

Example: Run script with 30s timeout, force kill after 5s

```sh
x timeout -k 5s 30s ./script.sh
```

Example: Run command with timeout, show verbose output

```sh
x timeout --verbose 10s ping example.com
```

Example: Run command with timeout, preserve exit status

```sh
x timeout --preserve-status 60s some_command
```

## Usage

```sh
x timeout [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-s`, `--signal` |  | Specify the signal to send on timeout |
| `-k`, `--kill-after` |  | Wait for a duration after timeout before force killing |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--verbose`, `-v` | Show verbose output |
| `--preserve-status` | Preserve command exit status even on timeout |

# x tmp

Cross-platform temporary file and directory management tool.

Supports getting temp paths, creating temp files/directories, setting temp root.

Automatically recognizes system temp directory ($TMPDIR).


::: tip Uses system $TMPDIR environment variable as default temp directory.
Use `x tmp root set <path>` to set custom temp root.

Use `x tmp root` or `x tmp root get` to view current setting.



**For Developers**: Subcommands with `_` suffix (path_, mkdir_, mkfile_, root_) are internal 

high-performance versions that store results in `x_` variable instead of stdout,

suitable for reuse in scripts. No help or completion support to minimize overhead.
:::


## Examples

Example: get system temp directory path

```sh
x tmp path
```

Example: get full temp path for subpath

```sh
x tmp path myapp/logs
```

Example: view current temp root (default get)

```sh
x tmp root
```

Example: get current temp root directory

```sh
x tmp root get
```

Example: set custom temp root directory

```sh
x tmp root set /var/tmp
```

Example: create subdirectory in temp directory

```sh
x tmp mkdir mydir
```

Example: create temp directory with random suffix

```sh
x tmp mkdir --prefix myapp
```

Example: create empty file in temp directory

```sh
x tmp mkfile myfile.txt
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x tmp path](/mod/tmp/path.md) | Get temp directory path, optionally with subpath |
| [x tmp mkfile](/mod/tmp/mkfile.md) | Create empty file in temp directory |
| [x tmp mkdir](/mod/tmp/mkdir.md) | Create temp subdirectory, use --prefix for random suffix |
| [x tmp root](/mod/tmp/root.md) | Temp root directory management (default: get) |

# x tping

This module leverages the TCP protocol and utilizes curl to establish a straightforward, plain-text TCP connection from your local machine to the target host and port.


::: tip To address the issue where versions of curl prior to v8.4 and curl.exe on Windows require manual disconnection of the TCP connectionwhen retrieving data from the target host,
use 'x cosmo curl' to invoke cosmo's curl binary.

For information about cosmo, use 'x cosmo -h'
:::


## Examples

Output the results of ping using the default mode (verbose mode, port 80)

```sh
x tping bing.com
```

Show the ping results as a heatmap

```sh
x tping --heatmap bing.com
```

Show the ping results as a bar graph

```sh
x tping --bar bing.com:80
```

Ping 10 times then stop (limit number of pings)

```sh
x tping -n 10 bing.com
```

## Usage

```sh
x tping [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-n` |  | Limit number of pings (e.g., -n 10 stops after 10 pings) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--verbose` | Output in verbose mode (default mode) |
| `--heatmap`, `-m` | Output in heatmap mode |
| `--bar`, `-b` | Output in bar chart mode |
| `--raw`, `-r` | Output in raw data |
| `--csv` | Output in CSV format |
| `--tsv` | Output in TSV format |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x tping run](/mod/tping/run.md) | Send a TCP connection |

# x uptime

Enhanced `uptime` command with structured YAML output.

Displays system uptime, logged-in users, and load averages (1/5/15 min).

Supports native uptime, busybox, and cosmo (for Windows) backends.



Load averages indicate how busy the system is - the number of processes

waiting for CPU or I/O. Three values show short-term (1m), medium-term (5m),

and long-term (15m) trends.


::: tip Windows doesn't have native uptime. x uptime automatically uses cosmo binary.
Use `x cosmo -h` for more info about cosmo.
:::


## Examples

Display uptime and load in YAML format (default)

```sh
x uptime
```

Show raw uptime command output

```sh
x uptime --raw
```

Print uptime in seconds

```sh
x uptime get
```

Print cumulative idle seconds since boot (total across all cores)

```sh
x uptime idle
```

Show uptime, core count, and idle percentage

```sh
x uptime summary
```

## Usage

```sh
x uptime [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--yml`, `-y` | YAML format output (default) |
| `--raw` | Raw command output, supports additional arguments |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x uptime get](/mod/uptime/get.md) | Print system uptime in seconds |
| [x uptime get_](/mod/uptime/get_.md) | Internal interface, returns uptime seconds via variable x_ |
| [x uptime idle](/mod/uptime/idle.md) | Print cumulative idle seconds since boot (total across all cores) |
| [x uptime idle_](/mod/uptime/idle_.md) | Internal interface, returns idle seconds via variable x_ |
| [x uptime summary](/mod/uptime/summary.md) | Show system uptime, CPU core count, and idle percentage |

# x usb

USB tool with three modes:
- "x usb" (default = sum): detailed device info + compact device table
- "x usb info": detailed USB device info in key:value format

  (name, vendor, serial, speed, product ID, vendor ID, device version, location)
- "x usb ls": compact device table (DEVICE, VENDOR, SPEED, SERIAL)

Cross-platform (macOS/Linux) with TTY color support.

Speed shows human-readable labels: 12M (USB 1.1), 480M (USB 2.0),

5G (USB 3.0), 10G (USB 3.1/3.2).

## Examples

Example: Display full USB overview (info + ls table)

```sh
x usb
```

Example: Show USB device details only

```sh
x usb info
```

Example: List USB devices in compact table

```sh
x usb ls
```

| [x usb info](/mod/usb/info.md) | Show detailed USB device info in key:value format. |
| [x usb ls](/mod/usb/ls.md) | Show compact USB device table. |

# x uuid

Generate UUIDs (Universally Unique Identifiers), including UUIDv4 and UUIDv7 formats. UUIDv7 is time-ordered (RFC 9562, 2024), offering natural sortability and better database index locality than UUIDv4.


::: tip
This module was extracted from `x rand uuid` (since v0.8.13); `x rand uuid` now redirects to `x uuid`
:::

::: tip
Use v4 (`x uuid get`) for stronger randomness and timestamp concealment; use v7 for ordered scenarios like logging and sorting
:::


## Examples

Example: Generate a UUID

```sh
x uuid
```

Example: Generate a UUID (uses system command first, falls back to pv4)

```sh
x uuid get
```

Example: Generate a UUIDv7 (uses system UUID randomness with current v7 timestamp)

```sh
x uuid v7
```

Example: Generate a UUIDv4 (system command first, falls back to urandom)

```sh
x uuid v4
```

Example: Extract millisecond timestamp from a UUIDv7

```sh
x uuid parsev7 "019dd021-c7c0-7xxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x uuid get](/mod/uuid/get.md) | Generate UUID (uses system uuid/uuidgen command first, falls back to pv4) |
| [x uuid v4](/mod/uuid/v4.md) | Generate UUIDv4 (uses system command first, falls back to pure urandom generation) |
| [x uuid pv4](/mod/uuid/pv4.md) | Pure UUIDv4 generation (uses /dev/urandom, no dependency on system uuid/uuidgen) |
| [x uuid v7](/mod/uuid/v7.md) | Generate UUIDv7 (RFC 9562 time-ordered format).

Prefers system UUID randomness (/proc/sys/kernel/random/uuid or uuid/uuidgen) with a current v7 timestamp;

falls back to pure UUIDv7 (pv7) if no system UUID source is available. |
| [x uuid pv7](/mod/uuid/pv7.md) | Pure UUIDv7 generation (uses /dev/urandom, no dependency on system uuid/uuidgen) |
| [x uuid parsev7](/mod/uuid/parsev7.md) | Extract the encoded millisecond Unix timestamp from a UUIDv7 string |

# x webtop

The webtop module is a wrapper built on Docker commands that provides advanced management features for the linuxserver/webtop image. It aims to simplify how users interact with and manage the linuxserver/webtop image.

linuxserver/webtop is a series of Linux-based Docker images built and maintained by the linuxserver.io community, enabling users to seamlessly access the container's desktop environment through a browser.


::: tip
- The interactive environment has a default alias set as `alias xwt='x webtop'`.
- The administrator username inside the webtop container is "abc," and by default, using sudo privileges does not require a password.
- By default, the container only allows access from users on localhost, and other hosts cannot directly access it via `http://<IP>:<PORT>`.
- linuxServer.io/webtop documentation: https://docs.linuxserver.io/images/docker-webtop/
:::


## Examples

Create an ubuntu-kde desktop system container from a webtop image

```sh
x webtop run ubuntu-kde
```

Create an arch-xfce desktop system container from a webtop image

```sh
x webtop run arch-xfce
```

List all the webtop containers

```sh
x webtop ps
```

Open the desktop environment of the webtop container in your browser

```sh
x webtop open
```

Log into the x-webtop-40000 container and open a bash session

```sh
x webtop bash x-webtop-40000
```

Stop the x-webtop-40000 container

```sh
x webtop stop x-webtop-40000
```

Delete the HOME directory mapping of the x-webtop-40000 container

```sh
x webtop home rm x-webtop-40000
```

Forcefully remove all webtop containers

```sh
x webtop container rmfa
```

Initialize the webtop module configuration.

```sh
x webtop init
```
# Webtop Module Introduction



The Webtop module simplifies the deployment and use of Webtop by integrating the open-source remote Linux desktop solution, Kasm, with the `linuxserver/webtop` container image provided by LinuxServer.



This module is specifically optimized for Chinese/Korean/Japanese users and offers enhanced features for a better user experience.



## Designed Use Cases


- Easily experience various Linux distributions and desktop environments locally.
- Utilize a browser as the primary work tool within a containerized desktop environment.



## Limits



Due to recent criticism, I want to set some realistic expectations to avoid any misunderstandings.


- This is a desktop system installed within a container, so it will naturally differ from a Linux desktop distribution installed on a virtual machine or physical machine.
- Because of the container's security restrictions on the host system, snap, flatpak, and AppImage are unusable. However, you can still install desktop software through the system package manager.  The webtop community is also exploring proot-app as a solution, which I'll touch on later.
- Installed software won't offer the same polished experience as native applications on the host.  However, by increasing the stream quality to lossless and with kasm's interactive improvements, it comes remarkably close.



Given these limitations, webtop's value is somewhat limited for my current command-line-centric workflow, even though each container only uses 750MB-1GB of RAM and has virtually zero CPU/power impact when idle.



However, webtop images offer several benefits:


- It provides a non-command-line alternative for users using containers as development environments, even with tools like VS Code's container workspaces.
- It is useful for users who need to keep web pages open.
- It allow users to encapsulate a specific workflow involving web pages and local applications within a container desktop, easily paused when not in use.
- Developers can debug applications directly in the container desktop's browser using localhost.



If you discover any other interesting uses, please share them with us on GitHub Discussions, Bilibili, or YouTube.





## Key Features


- **Simplified Operation:**  Interactive TUI and command completion are provided through the x-cmd script library, enhancing user experience.
- **Locale perception** Automatic language configuration is performed at container startup, utilizing the values defined in the environment variables.
- **Multiple Distributions and Desktop Environments:**  Easily explore different Linux distributions and desktop environments.
- **Browser-First Approach:** Optimized for usage scenarios where the browser serves as the primary tool within the containerized desktop.
- **Image Fine-tuning**: This feature provides scripts that allow for the modification of the base image, consequently reducing the startup time for each subsequent launch.



## Security



By default, the Webtop module only permits access from localhost. This means other hosts cannot directly access the container desktop via `http://<IP>:<PORT>`.  Therefore, for ease of use, setting a container password is not mandatory by default.



**If you need to restrict access for other users, please use the `--password {password}` option to set a password.**



## Installing Additional Desktop Software within the Container



To protect the host system's security, the Webtop container operates with restricted permissions.  Application managers like Flathub, Snap, and AppImage do not function correctly.



Software can be installed through the following methods:


- **System Package Manager:** Use the system's built-in package manager, for example, `apt install flameshot`.
- **proot-apps (Experimental):** The [proot-apps](https://github.com/linuxserver/proot-apps) tool provided by LinuxServer allows for the installation of more applications. However, this method consumes significant storage space. Improvements and more comprehensive support are planned for the future.





## Important KASM Usage Tips



The above content has corresponding demonstration images, please refer to the images/video demonstrations at the beginning of this article.



### Enhancing Image Quality



The default `stream quality` is set to `medium`. However, since webtop runs directly on the local host, bandwidth considerations are less critical.  It's recommended to increase the quality to `extreme` or even `lossless`.



### Enabling Audio


- KASM supports high-quality audio synchronization.
- Click on the KASM settings sidebar on the left.
- Three icons will appear in the center of the screen at the top. The middle icon enables sound, and the third icon enables the microphone.



### (For Chinese, Japanese, and Korean Users) Input Method


- The best input method configuration is often the host environment's input method.
- Open the KASM settings sidebar on the left.
- Find "IME input mode," click to enable it. Now you can directly use your host environment's input method within the remote desktop.



### Using Chrome Browser's PWA


- KASM supports PWA (Progressive Web App) functionality. Using this feature provides a user experience close to native desktop applications.
- When you open the webpage, an icon will appear on the right side of the URL bar. Hovering over it will display a tooltip like "Install `40000-ubuntu-kde`".
- Click to install the PWA application. Afterwards, this application can directly open the container's applications.
- On macOS, the current `x webtop open` command will attempt to open the PWA first. If it fails, it will fall back to opening in a browser. We plan to gradually extend this behavior to Linux and Windows.



### Beyond Stop: Using Pause


- When some containers are not in use, you can choose to `stop` them to reduce CPU and memory usage. Note that after stopping, any open web pages or applications within the desktop will be closed.
- Alternatively, you can use `pause`. The next time you `unpause`, your open web pages and applications will be preserved.
- Pausing will free up CPU usage, but it may not release the container's memory usage. However, modern Linux memory management is increasingly efficient, and inactive memory can be swapped or compressed.  So, users can choose between stopping and pausing based on their specific scenario and hardware resources.



Personally, due to frequent switching between development tasks, I've left three webtop containers running in the background for two weeks without realizing it.  I haven't noticed any significant impact on CPU, memory, battery life, or heat generation during this time – though it's possible I'm just not very sensitive to these things.



## For Advanced Users: Managing the Container's HOME Directory



**TLDR**:



Assuming you start the container named `40000-ubuntu-kde`:


- using `x webtop rm x-webtop-40000` or `docker rm x-webtop-40000` will only remove the container itself.  It will not remove the container's home directory (`/config`). This is because the webtop module creates a directory on your host machine and maps it to `/config` inside the container when it starts.
- To access this directory, you can use the interactive `x webtop home cd` option available within `x webtop ps`.
- Alternatively, you can learn more about managing the home directory with `x webtop home -h`.  We plan to add features like backup and cloning in the future.  Until then, you can manage this directory like any other folder on your system – back it up, customize it, or clone it as needed.



For backing up or cloning the container's home directory now, you'll need to understand how we map ports, container names, and the home directory data.  More details on this follow below.



Understanding our port, container name, and HOME directory mapping design is necessary for backing up or cloning the container environment's HOME directory.



### Port and Container Naming Conventions



The Webtop module introduces a convention where each system-desktop combination has a fixed port prefix:



For example:


- `400xx` — ubuntu-kde
- `401xx` — ubuntu-mate
- `410xx` — debian-kde
- `411xx` — debian-mate



Assuming a user launches a maximum of 10 local container desktops simultaneously:


- The first ubuntu-kde container export kasm port as `40000`, the second uses `40010`, and so on.
- The first debian-mate instance export kasm port as `41100`, the second uses `41110`, and so on.



We've reserved nine ports for mapping to each container.



**Containers are named `x-webtop-<PORT>`**, while the default name for web tab or PWA will be `<PORT>-<OS>-<DESKTOP>`.



For example, a container named `x-webtop-40000` would have a corresponding tab named `40000-ubuntu-kde`.



Since users typically stick with one OS-DESKTOP combination, they'll quickly memorize the pattern after a couple of uses.  While this approach sacrifices some flexibility, it eliminates the hassle of naming things every time.  We're considering ways to incorporate custom labels down the line.





### HOME Directory Persistence Design


- **Default Mapping:** The container's HOME directory (`$HOME`) is automatically mapped to `/config` on the host file system.
- **Consistent UID and GID:** The container user's UID and GID are kept consistent with the host, ensuring proper file permissions.



**No HOME Directory Data Loss on Restart**



Unless the host's HOME data is explicitly deleted, each time the container restarts, as long as the container name remains the same, the previous HOME data is automatically mapped to the new container. This preserves settings such as:


- Desktop configurations (like wallpaper and themes)
- Installed x-cmd and proot-apps software



### Preventing Conflicts and Confusion



The same series of system/desktop combinations use the same series of ports and container names, ensuring that configuration data for different systems/desktops are not mixed within a single HOME directory.



### proot-apps Software



proot-apps is a containerized desktop software manager provided by LinuxServer.



Similar to x-cmd, software is installed within the user space, eliminating the need for privileges and modifications to global dependencies.  The software persists upon subsequent loading of the same HOME directory. The primary drawback is the substantial size of the software due to the underlying proot technology.



We are actively exploring and improving related technologies and plan to provide more comprehensive support in the future.



## Other Issues



### Key User Experience Concerns with Remote Desktops



For a containerized desktop solution to be effective, it must address two key challenges, which kasm handles exceptionally well:


1. Chinese Input Method Support – Utilizing the local input method is crucial.
2. Video Playback
3. Audio Playback



Issue 1:  I discovered the need to activate this in the settings during the October 1st holiday.



Issue 3: I haven't found a solution within the kasm version, while enabling audio is straightforward in the webtop image.





### Reasons for Not Using the kasm Image:


- The development strategy prioritized the kasm module, with webtop development following later.
- The kasm image assumes a remote server environment, thus requiring certificate configuration, HTTPS, and password setup by default.  x-cmd, however, is geared towards local execution for testing, sandboxing, and development.
- The webtop image aligns better with this local usage model.  Furthermore, the webtop author is addressing desktop software installation challenges (present in both projects) using proot-apps.
- The kasm module is not currently included in the public x-cmd release.  Future development and release plans for kasm will have a different focus.



## Future Plans


- Automatic installation of the local x-cmd version upon container startup.
- Addition of `clone` and `backup` subcommands.
- Secure local desktop sharing functionality.
- More customization options.
- Optimization of proot-apps storage usage.
- Support for generating Docker Compose files.
- Potential implementation of a Webtop server solution.



This version provides a clearer explanation of the Webtop module's features, security policies, software installation methods, and future plans, along with practical, user-experience-oriented advice.

# x whisper

Local AI speech recognition. For more information about whisper.cpp, please visit https://github.com/ggerganov/whisper.cpp


::: tip
- First-time users will automatically download whisper.cpp.
:::


## Examples

Interactively select the model and recognize the audio file as text

```sh
x whisper <audio file>
```

Use the medium model for audio recognition

```sh
x whisper -m medium -f <audio file>
```

Save the results to a test.srt subtitle file

```sh
x whisper dictate --srt -o test <audio file>
```

Merge srt subtitles into your video

```sh
x whisper merge <srt file> <video file>
```

Start WhisperLiveKit server (default base model)

```sh
x whisper livekit
```

Auto-pull medium model with speaker diarization and Chinese

```sh
x whisper livekit run --model medium --diarization --language zh
```

Transcribe an audio file (no server needed)

```sh
x whisper livekit transcribe meeting.wav
```

## Usage

```sh
x whisper [OPTIONS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-f`, `--file` &lt;file dir&gt; |  | The file path of the audio file to be recognized |
| `-m`, `--model` &lt;name&gt; |  | Explicitly specify the model for recognition |

| Name | Description |

# x wifi

WiFi tool with multiple modes:
- "x wifi" (default = sum): interface hardware info + all available networks table
- "x wifi info": WiFi adapter hardware info (card type, MAC, firmware, PHY modes)
- "x wifi stat": compact table of all available networks (current + scanned),

  current network marked with *, like "x disk stat"
- "x wifi scan": scan nearby networks with SAVED column showing known networks
- "x wifi connect": connect to a WiFi network
- "x wifi enable/disable": turn WiFi on/off
- "x wifi prefer": manage saved/preferred networks

Cross-platform (macOS/Linux/Windows) with TTY color support.

## Examples

Example: Display full WiFi overview (info + networks table)

```sh
x wifi
```

Example: Force cache refresh, re-fetch WiFi info

```sh
x wifi info --fresh
```

Example: Show all available networks table

```sh
x wifi stat
```

Example: Scan nearby WiFi networks

```sh
x wifi scan
```

Example: Connect to a secured network

```sh
x wifi connect MyNetwork mypassword
```

Example: List saved networks

```sh
x wifi prefer ls
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x wifi sum](/mod/wifi/sum.md) | Display full WiFi overview (same as running bare "x wifi"). |
| [x wifi info](/mod/wifi/info.md) | WiFi adapter hardware info. Use --simple for interface/card/MAC/status only. |
| [x wifi stat](/mod/wifi/stat.md) | Compact table of all available networks. Signal colored: green/cyan/yellow/red. |
| [x wifi scan](/mod/wifi/scan.md) | Scan nearby networks. Shows SSID, PHY, channel, security, SAVED (*=known), signal. |
| [x wifi connect](/mod/wifi/connect.md) | Connect to WiFi by SSID. Provide password for secured networks. |
| [x wifi enable](/mod/wifi/enable.md) | Turn WiFi on. |
| [x wifi disable](/mod/wifi/disable.md) | Turn WiFi off. |

# x worker

Background worker process manager with start, stop, query, alive check, and list.

Isolates workers by namespace and name, uses process fingerprint for alive verification.


::: tip Three-way comparison: worker = persistent background process (e.g. daemon); bgjob = one-shot background task; cron = recurring scheduled task.
See x bgjob --help for full comparison.
:::


## Examples

Example: Start a background worker named mytask

```sh
x worker run --name mytask -- my_command arg1
```

Example: Stop the background worker named mytask

```sh
x worker stop --name mytask
```

Example: Check if worker is alive

```sh
x worker isalive --name mytask
```

Example: Show worker info (PID, start time, status)

```sh
x worker info --name mytask
```

Example: List all workers

```sh
x worker ls
```

Example: Start worker in custom namespace

```sh
x worker run --ns myapp --name worker1 -- my_script.sh
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x worker run](/mod/worker/run.md) | Start a background worker process |
| [x worker stop](/mod/worker/stop.md) | Stop the specified worker process and remove its state file |
| [x worker isalive](/mod/worker/isalive.md) | Check if the specified worker process is still running |
| [x worker info](/mod/worker/info.md) | Show worker details |
| [x worker ls](/mod/worker/ls.md) | List all workers |

# x wttr

wttr is a weather forecast module that retrieves real-time weather information and 3-day forecasts for any location via wttr.in. It supports cities, airports (IATA codes), GPS coordinates, and area codes. You can also view moon phases and customize temperature/wind speed units.

## Examples

Example: Show weather for current location

```sh
x wttr
```

```sh
x wttr zhongshan
```

```sh
x wttr Beijing
```

Example: View current moon phase

```sh

```

Example: View moon phase for specific date

```sh
x wttr moon@2024-01-01
```

Example: View weather in interactive app

```sh
x wttr --app
```

Example: Show today's weather (concise format)

```sh
x wttr --api "?1n"
```

```sh
x wttr --unit m
```

Example: Show weather in US units

```sh

```

# x yq

yq (YAML Query) is a lightweight processor for YAML, JSON, and XML, primarily used for querying and extracting YAML data.

`x yq` is an enhancement module based on the yq command, designed to improve the yq user experience. The specific enhancements are as follows:
1. Simplified yq command installation: If yq is not found in the current environment, `x yq` will download and install yq through the x-cmd pkg system in a way that does not affect the user's environment.
2. Provides the `repl` command: This offers an interactive way to read and explore YAML data using fzf.

## Examples

Enable interactive mode to process the results of the `x ascii --yml` command.

```sh
x ascii --yml | x yq r
```

Enable interactive mode to process test.yml

```sh
x yq r test.yml
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x yq repl](/mod/yq/repl.md) | Read and explore YAML data using an interactive YAML viewer |
| [x yq --cmd](/mod/yq/--cmd.md) | Run the yq command directly |

# x zig

zig command enhancements


::: tip
Run `x zig help` to get help for zig native commands
:::


## Examples

Initialize C compilation

```sh
x zig initcc
```

List available zig packages

```sh
x zig pm la
```

Output the build.zig.zon file in YAML format

```sh
< build.zig.zon  x zig zon toyml
```

Reformat Zig code into canonical form

```sh
x zig fmt path/to/file.zig
```

Compile the project in the current directory

```sh
x zig build
```
## Targeting v0.12



This module is designed with v0.12 in mind and will cease support for previous versions. The decision is driven by several factors:


- In our practical usage (primarily for compiling and installing third-party libraries with Lua and LuaRocks), version v0.12 will address some of the compilation failures on macOS that were present in v0.11.
- It's worth noting that there are interface differences in subcommands between zig v0.11 and v0.12. Considering zig is still undergoing rapid iteration, and current zig users are likely to swiftly migrate to v0.12, we decisively chose v0.12 as the design target.
- We've observed that many zig projects directly adopt the zig master version rather than stable releases.
- Zig 0.12 itself introduces numerous new features, details of which can be found [zig pkg](/pkg/zig.md).



It's worth noting that while the module is designed with v0.12 in mind, the x-cmd/pkg still offers downloads and installations for v0.11, ensuring users can continue to use it seamlessly:


```sh
x env use zig=v0.11.0
zig run hi.zig          # Usage remains normal
```



## Goals and Current Status



This module is still in the early stages of development and currently employs the x-cmd library to enhance zig in the following three aspects:


- Zig code can be rapidly deployed and executed:
  - Users simply need to run `x hi.zig` to execute Zig files.
  - For users of the hub, Zig files stored on the hub can be executed directly using `x {username}:hi.zig`. For more about the hub, please refer to [hub](https://hub.x-cmd.com).
- Simulating a C compiler environment with Zig: `x zig initcc`.
- Enhanced visualization of Zig commands:
  - `x zig zen`.
  - `x zig target`.



As our understanding of Zig deepens, we'll continue to enhance Zig's functionality, providing a better development experience for Zig developers.

# x zuz

This module supports multiple decompression formats such as tar, gz, xz, 7z, zst, zip, bz, Z, and rar(Decompression only). It prioritizes using system software, but if unavailable, it will automatically download the necessary software (7zip, zstd, etc.).


::: tip Since compression and decompression are commonly used, x-cmd also provides two aliases:
- `x zuz z`  -&gt; `x z`
- `x zuz uz` -&gt; `x uz`
:::


## Examples

Compress the specified file or folder into a specified format archive.

```sh
x z <file name>.<Compression format> <file or folder>
```

Extract the specified archive to the specified directory, defaulting to the current directory.

```sh
x uz <Compressed file name> <Target directory>
```

Extract the specified file and delete the source file after extraction.

```sh
x uzr <Compressed file name>
```

Lists the files contained inside the test.tar.gz file

```sh
x zuz ls <Compressed file name>
```
![zuz meme image](https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/tar.png)

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x zuz z](/mod/zuz/z.md) | Compress file |
| [x zuz uz](/mod/zuz/uz.md) | Decompress file |
| [x zuz uzr](/mod/zuz/uzr.md) | Decompress file then remove the original file |
| [x zuz ls](/mod/zuz/ls.md) | List compress inside file |
| [x zuz show](/mod/zuz/show.md) | View the file formats supported by zuz |

# AI/LLM Work

x-cmd is committed to introducing AI/LLM capabilities in the simplest way to enhance user work efficiency.


## Local Models and Cloud Models Complement Each Other, Each Showing Their Strengths

1. We have encapsulated various LLM service CLIs in a consistent way. Users can seamlessly use `@gpt`, `@gpt4`, `@gpt`, `@gemini`, `@o` (ollama), combined with current shell environment (variables, files), to dialogue with LLM.
2. We believe that local LLM can protect privacy and complement cloud LLM; our solution is built with seamless interaction between local LLM and cloud LLM, each showing their strengths.
3. On local model services, we focus on supporting [ollama](https://ollama.ai); based on actual usage experience, we have enhanced `ls` (view downloaded models locally), `la` (view available model list), `run`, `pull`; additionally based on ollama api, we have also implemented interfaces consistent with openai, gemini, mistral, moonshot modules as encapsulation.


Here are demonstrations of interacting with gemini, ollama, and gpt-4o to complete tasks.

## AI Application Modules

We focus on improving LLM experience in command line usage, assisting users to complete tasks more efficiently with LLM加持 (jiāchí - empowerment):

1. [co module -- copilot](https://x-cmd.com/mod/co): x-cmd will enhance all traditional commands that can be LLM-enhanced. We will add prompts to reduce LLM hallucinations, with the ultimate goal of enabling models like llama 3 8B to correctly generate commands based on user natural language in most scenarios.
2. All command line results can be piped to LLM CLIs implementing the chat interface -- @o ([ollama](/mod/ollama.md)), @gpt ([openai](/mod/openai.md), gpt3.5), @gpt4 ([openai](/mod/openai.md) gpt4), @gemini ([gemini](/mod/gemini.md)) -- either generating text based on user prompts or starting chat to discuss results.
3. x-cmd will fully leverage LLM capabilities to provide LLM application modules such as translation (tran), writing ([writer](/mod/writer.md)), local image-to-text (llava), and local audio-to-text ([whisper](/mod/whisper.md)).

Under development, stay tuned:

1. Each domain can be tailored. Thanks to x-cmd's shell being easy to粘合 (niánhé) and extend, we will use x-cmd module mechanism and LLM Agent technology to extend traditional command functions.
2. x-cmd will leverage its 500+ open-source pkgs to inject more行动力 (xíngdònglì) into LLM.


Here are attempts with co and tran.


## Related [AI/LLM Modules](/mod/llmf.md)

- API Client:
  - [openai](/mod/openai.md): OpenAI Webservice Client
  - [gemini](/mod/gemini.md): Gemini Webservice Client

  - llava
  - [whisper](/mod/whisper.md): Local AI Speech Recognition

- Applications:
  - tran: Translation module suitable for multiple formats and batch processing environments (TODO)
  - txt: Text content management via command line
  - md: More elegantly preview Markdown documents through syntax highlighting. (TODO)
  - chat: Chatgpt command line tool
  - coco: coco provides code-related operations; our language modules provide `,` and `,,` support
  - co: abbreviation for copilot, generates shell commands executable locally, preferably one-liners

# Air-Gap Installation

To install x-cmd without internet access, you have two options:

- **Option 1**: SSH one-click deployment (x-cmd installed on external machine)
- **Option 2**: Manual installation package (x-cmd not installed on external machine)

## Option 1: SSH One-Click Deployment

If you're already using x-cmd, this is the quickest method.

::::ol
:::li Run the deployment command
Push from external machine to internal target:

```bash
x ssh setup user@hostname
```

This automatically: packages x-cmd code → uploads via SSH/SCP → runs install → configures startup.
:::

:::li Verify installation
SSH into target machine and check:

```bash
ssh user@hostname
x version
```
:::
::::

:::tip Prerequisites
- External machine has x-cmd installed
- Can SSH into target machine
- Only code is transferred, **not** custom configurations
:::

## Option 2: Manual Installation Package

If you don't have x-cmd yet, or can't SSH into internal machines, use the installation package.

::::ol
:::li Download, transfer and install
Download on external machine, transfer to internal and install:

```bash
# 1. Download on external machine
curl --fail -L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/x-cmd/release/main/dist/latest.tgz > latest.tgz

# 2. Copy latest.tgz to internal machine, then extract and install
mkdir -p ./tmp/latest
tar -zxf latest.tgz -C ./tmp/latest/
./tmp/latest/mod/boot/lib/setup-x-cmd.sh
```
:::

:::li Verify installation
Reload shell config:

```bash
source ~/.bashrc
x version
```
:::
::::

## Comparison

| Aspect | Option 1: SSH Deployment | Option 2: Manual Package |
|--------|-------------------------|--------------------------|
| Prerequisite | External machine **has** x-cmd | External machine **does not need** x-cmd |
| Network | Requires SSH | Completely offline |
| Steps | One command | Download → Transfer → Extract → Install |
| Use case | Internal machines accessible via SSH | Fully air-gapped environments |

## Available Features After Installation

The following features work fully offline:

::::ul
:::li Shell Experience
[theme](/mod/theme.md) customization, smart Tab completion, syntax highlighting, enhanced history, quick directory jump
:::

:::li File & System Tools
Enhanced file listing ([ls](/mod/ls.md)), path operations ([path](/mod/path.md)), process viewing ([ps](/mod/ps.md)), disk usage ([df](/mod/df.md))
:::

:::li Development Tools
Git enhancement ([git](/mod/git.md)), Git config ([gitconfig](/mod/gitconfig.md)), Git hooks ([githook](/mod/githook.md)), Docker shortcuts ([docker](/mod/docker.md))
:::

:::li AI & Local LLM
Local LLM framework support ([llmf](/mod/llmf.md)) — call locally deployed open-source models
:::
::::

:::warning Limited Features
These require internet access:
- Package installation ([env](/mod/env.md), [install](/mod/install.md))
:::

## Further Reading

- [Module Get Started](/mod/get-started.md) — Learn about x-cmd modules
- [Theme Module](/mod/theme.md) — Configure terminal appearance
- [LLMF Module](/mod/llmf.md) — Local LLM framework support

# Alacritty - A Fast, Cross-Platform OpenGL Terminal Emulator

**Alacritty** is a terminal emulator built for performance, widely popular among developers for its **minimalist design, exceptional speed**, and **cross-platform compatibility**. Developed in Rust and using OpenGL for GPU-accelerated rendering, it maintains smooth scrolling and responsiveness even in text-intensive scenarios.

Unlike many terminals that integrate complex features like tabs, remote connections, and multi-pane layouts, Alacritty focuses on **doing one thing and doing it well**: providing a **fast, stable, and aesthetically pleasing terminal experience**. If you are a command-line enthusiast, system administrator, or programmer looking for a clean and highly efficient terminal tool, Alacritty is an ideal choice.

![alacritty.bat](/image/start/alacritty.bat.webp)

## Installation

Alacritty supports mainstream platforms. Users can choose from official prebuilt packages or build from source as needed.

::::ul
:::li Windows
Two installation methods are available:

- **[Installer (.msi)](https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty/releases)**: [Alacritty-v0.15.1-installer.msi](https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty/releases/download/v0.15.1/Alacritty-v0.15.1-installer.msi) — Click to install automatically and create a Start Menu shortcut
- **[Portable (.exe)](https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty/releases)**: [Alacritty-v0.15.1-portable.exe](https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty/releases/download/v0.15.1/Alacritty-v0.15.1-portable.exe) — Suitable for running from a USB drive or in environments without installation
:::

:::li Linux
Alacritty does not provide prebuilt packages for all distributions, but it can be easily built from source:

1. Install dependencies (using Ubuntu as an example):
   ```bash
   sudo apt install cmake pkg-config libfreetype6-dev libfontconfig1-dev libxcb-xfixes0-dev python3
   ```

2. Install Rust toolchain:
   ```bash
   curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
   rustup override set stable
   rustup update stable
   ```

3. Clone source and compile:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty.git
   cd alacritty
   cargo build --release
   ```

The compiled binary is located at `target/release/alacritty`.

👉 View complete installation instructions: [Linux Install Guide](https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty/blob/master/INSTALL.md)
:::

:::li macOS
Official `.dmg` package available: [Alacritty-v0.15.1.dmg](https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty/releases/download/v0.15.1/Alacritty-v0.15.1.dmg)

After downloading, double-click to open and drag **Alacritty** to the Applications folder to complete installation.

Or install via Homebrew:
```bash
brew install --cask alacritty
```
:::
::::

## Configuration

Alacritty uses TOML format for configuration files, which are clear, readable, and easy to modify. Users can freely adjust font styles, color schemes, key bindings, cursor styles, window behavior, and other details through the configuration file.

::::ul
:::li Configuration File Location
- Linux/macOS: `~/.config/alacritty/alacritty.toml`
- Windows: `%APPDATA%\alacritty\alacritty.toml`

If no configuration file is detected on first launch, Alacritty uses built-in defaults.
:::

:::li Font Configuration Example
Configure Alacritty to use `FiraCode Nerd Font` at size 14:

```toml
[font]
normal.family = "FiraCode Nerd Font"
size = 14.0
```

For more comprehensive configuration documentation, see: [Official Config Manual](https://alacritty.org/config-alacritty.html)
:::

:::li Using with X-CMD
After configuring the font, use the `x-cmd` `theme` module to switch theme styles with one command:

```bash
x theme --app
```

![alacritty.theme.1](/image/start/alacritty.theme.1.webp)

You can also use third-party beautification tools integrated with `x-cmd`, such as [Oh My Posh](/mod/ohmyposh.md) and [Starship](/mod/starship.md):

![alacritty.theme.2](/image/start/alacritty.theme.2.webp)
:::
::::

## Project Resources

- GitHub Repository: [github.com/alacritty/alacritty](https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty)
- Color Scheme Repository: [alacritty/alacritty-theme](https://github.com/alacritty/alacritty-theme)

# BSD

🎯 This document describes how to install `x-cmd` on `BSD` systems such as `FreeBSD`, `OpenBSD`, and `NetBSD`.

:::warning
`x-cmd` support for `BSD` systems is still under development
:::

## FreeBSD

```sh
eval "$(fetch -o - https://get.x-cmd.com)"
```

Status: Installation succeeds, but some modules do not function properly.

## OpenBSD

```sh
eval "$(ftp -o - https://get.x-cmd.com)"
```

Status:
- Tar command decompression issues need to be addressed
- OpenBSD uses ksh; library-level support is not currently provided. It will automatically download portable bash as the runtime

## NetBSD

Status: Development environment needs to be prepared.

## FAQ

:::details SSH Remote Deployment Installation {open}
If you connect to the target host via ssh, you can use the ssh remote installation method.

The basic principle is to deploy the x-cmd all-in-one installation package to the remote server's user directory via scp, and trigger extraction and automatic configuration.
:::

    alt="GitCode:x-cmd/x-cmd"
    class="inline-block mr-2" />
</a>

To ensure domestic user experience, extensive work has been done:

::::ul
:::li Chinese-English Bilingual Support
In addition to logs, all help documents and demonstrations provide Chinese and English bilingual versions for easy understanding and use. Default language automatically switches based on environment language.

To facilitate troubleshooting, logs are uniformly recorded in English. Since solutions may involve multiple languages, using English logs ensures users can get more comprehensive search results when searching for problem solutions, regardless of which language they use, by pasting English logs, avoiding missing potential solutions.
:::

:::li China Mirror Acceleration
All released index metadata files are simultaneously published in China, ensuring faster download speeds for required resources.
:::

:::li Dual Platform Binary Package Release
Binary packages are published to GitHub internationally while also being published domestically to codeberg.org or NPM, ensuring Chinese users can also enjoy high-speed download experiences.
:::

:::li Resource Packaging and Hosting
For repackaged external resources, such as [tldr](/mod/tldr.md), China region mirrors are provided to further improve download speeds.
:::

:::li Convenient Mirror Source and Proxy Configuration Tools
Modules like [apt](/mod/apt.md), [apk](/mod/apk.md), [brew](/mod/brew.md) provide mirror subcommands for configuring domestic mirror sources (such as Tsinghua source), without manually modifying configuration files, simplifying the operation process. Additionally, proxy subcommands within modules can easily set application-specific proxies.
:::
::::

## How to Check if Experience Optimization is Enabled?

Generally, <u>experience optimization is automatically enabled during X-CMD installation by sensing network and current environment configurations</u>. If not enabled, it can be checked through the following methods.

::::ul
:::li Language Settings
**Help documents, data information, and completion items prioritize Chinese**: Driven by `lang` module

```sh
# View current preferred language
x lang get
# Set preferred language to Chinese
x lang use zh
```
:::

:::li Download Source Settings
**X-CMD binary packages, external information, and index source files enable domestic download mirrors**: Driven by `websrc` module

```sh
# View current download source
x websrc
# Set download source to domestic mirror
x websrc use cn
```
:::
::::

## We Are Still Working

Some software internal code pointing to download sources (such as Terraform plugin downloads) may have access issues. Although these can be solved by modifying source code and recompiling or making system-level certificate modifications and redirections, these methods are too invasive and therefore not currently adopted.

For example, [asdf](/mod/asdf.md) depends on github. In addition to setting the current shell environment proxy via `http_proxy`, users can also use the `x asdf proxy set` command to set asdf's proxy. In the future, when users use `x asdf`, x-cmd will automatically read the proxy configuration file and use asdf through the proxy.

# About x-cmd

`x-cmd` (pronounced "x command") is a **command-line toolset and library** written in `POSIX shell`, designed to help users accomplish tasks more efficiently and comfortably in the command line.

`x-cmd` organizes code internally as [mod (modules)](/mod/.md), and externally invokes different functional modules through `x <mod>` commands, such as [`x ip`](/mod/ip.md) to call IP information-related functionality.

## Main Modules

::::ul
:::li Optimizing Traditional Command Tools
Wrapping traditional command tools to make them more usable and provide more readable output, such as [`x ping`](/mod/ping.md), [`x cd`](/mod/cd.md), [`x apt`](/mod/apt.md), [`x git`](/mod/git.md)
:::

:::li Package Manager
A [package manager](/pkg/get-started.md) that works without `root` privileges, implemented in `POSIX shell` and `awk`, obtaining and using third-party open source software tools (such as [`node`](/pkg/node.md), [`fzf`](/pkg/fzf.md), [`nvim`](/pkg/nvim.md)) in a lightweight and secure way
:::

:::li Lightweight Script CLI
Integrating common command-line functions, provided in a more lightweight and efficient way, such as [`x theme`](/mod/theme.md), [`x tldr`](/mod/tldr.md), [`x ws`](/mod/ws.md), [`x openai`](/mod/openai.md)
:::
::::

## As a Command-Line Toolset

In command-line interactive scenarios, `x-cmd` is the "Infinity Gauntlet" of the "command-line universe," with modules like individual "Infinity Stones":

::::ul
:::li x theme
Beautify the command line, providing 130+ command-line prompt themes, `symbol` features, `emoji` features, and `transient` functionality

![x theme](/image/start/other-theme.webp)
:::

:::li x advise
Complete partial commands, use `Tab` key to get command completion items and corresponding suggestions

![x advise](/image/start/other-advise.en.webp)
:::

:::li x install / x pkg
Download and install third-party software tools, providing installation methods for 1000 software tools

![x install](/image/start/other-install.en.webp)
:::

:::li AI Modules
`x openai` and other modules have access capabilities to `openai` and other `LLMs`, such as using `ChatGPT` services in the command line

![@gpt](/image/start/other-gpt.en.webp)
:::
::::

## As a Shell Tool Library

`x-cmd` can be used as a `POSIX shell` tool library, providing important but lacking functionality for modern scripting:

- Use `x jq` and `x yq` modules to automatically download `jq`, `yq`, processing json/yml data obtained from Web APIs with minimal environmental impact
- Use interactive Terminal UI components provided by `x ui` module to enhance script interaction experience with minimal dependencies

::: warning Not Recommended as Library Before v1
- **Current development focus is on application modules**. Planning to rapidly accumulate application module practical experience, clarify requirements and design element balance, continuously polish `x-cmd`'s interface and design as a library
- **No forward compatibility guaranteed before v1**. Although we try to maintain forward compatibility for modules already documented as public, ultimately for v1 simplicity and user experience, library interfaces will be continuously streamlined and adjusted
- Still exploring the best library function calling methods on various `POSIX shell`, making balanced adjustments based on performance, current mainstream hardware performance, usage scenarios, and other factors
:::

## x-cmd and Native Commands

For traditional command tools and native commands (such as `ping`), `x-cmd`'s corresponding modules are not replacements but **enhancements**, like Iron Man and Tony:

- `x-cmd` modules focus on improving the user experience of native commands' commonly used features (about 20%), without (and without needing to) encapsulate all native command functionality
- System-installed native commands usually prioritize **stability**; `x-cmd` modules focus more on providing convenient **interaction and user experience**
- For features that native commands aren't convenient to integrate, `x-cmd` can leverage `shell` script advantages to download third-party software tools on demand and extend their functionality

Taking `x docker` module as an example:
- `x docker` command can execute all `docker` subcommands; module enhancements mainly focus on images, containers, networks, and logs and other common functions
- `x docker` provides richer visualization enhancements, such as `x docker ps` viewing and managing `docker` containers through interactive APP in the command line
- Common commands have shorter aliases; for example, `x docker` can be abbreviated as `xd`, `x docker image` can be abbreviated as `xd img`

## Security and Privacy

::::ul
:::li Code Transparency
Implemented in `shell` and `awk`, every line of code can be reviewed and verified
:::

:::li Reliable Package Sources
Packages in the pkg system are confirmed by the `x-cmd` team from official sources, and repackaged to minimize potential security issues
:::

:::li Container Sandbox Priority
Prioritize isolating applications and services in sandbox environments to reduce risk and enhance security
:::

:::li Secure Permission Control
Prioritize technologies with built-in permission control mechanisms like `Deno`, `WASM` to ensure execution environment security
:::

:::li Minimized Data Sharing
Designed services only use and share absolutely necessary information when collecting, transmitting, and processing data. For example, when using MAC address query services, only the first ten digits of the device MAC address are uploaded
:::
::::

## Finally

The `x-cmd` team, guided by `Unix` philosophy, aims to make `x-cmd` a secure, transparent, powerful, and interesting tool collection.

`x-cmd` started with `bash`, took shape with `shawk`, and blends with modern scripting ecosystems, open source binary tools, cloud services, AI/LLM. Based on `Unix/POSIX` environments, `x-cmd` will eventually become the Infinity Gauntlet for open source free developers, gathering collective wisdom in the palm, clearing obstacles for imagination and creativity, and opening up infinite possibilities.

- Quick install: `eval "$(curl https://get.x-cmd.com)"`
- More detailed installation guide: [start/install](/start/.md)
- Looking forward to starring on `Github` or recommending `x-cmd` to friends
