# x abox cmd

Execute command in container (non-interactive)


::: tip Executes command in specified container without allocating TTY.
If no command is specified, defaults to bash.

If no container name is specified, uses container named "abox-0" by default.
:::


## Examples

Execute ls -la in mybox container

```sh
x abox cmd -n mybox ls -la
```

Execute apt update as root in default container

```sh
x abox cmd -r apt update
```

## Usage

```sh
x abox cmd [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Command to execute |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-n`, `--name` |  | Container name |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `-r`, `--root` | Execute command as root user |

## Examples

Start container with SSH public key and port mapping

```sh
x abox start --key <ssh-pubkey-file> --port 2222
```

Remove default container

```sh
x abox rm
```

Start default container (no SSH)

```sh
x abox start
```

Start container with random password and connect via SSH (see startup output for password)

```sh
x abox start --pass - --port 2222 && ssh -p 2222 ai@localhost
```

Start container named mybox with SSH public key and connect using the corresponding private key

```sh
x abox start --key ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub --port 2223 -n mybox && ssh -p 2223 -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa ai@localhost
```

Start container sharing host Docker (docker commands work directly inside the container)

```sh
x abox start --dind
```

## Usage

```sh
x abox start [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--key` |  | SSH public key file path (requires --port) |
| `--pass` |  | SSH password (requires --port, use "-" to auto-generate random password) |
| `--port`, `-p` |  | SSH port mapping (host port) |
| `--name`, `-n` |  | Container name |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--dind` | Mount the host Docker socket so the host Docker is usable inside the container (same as x docker run --dind) |

# x advise autoload

Manage the auto-load mode for x-cmd command completions


::: tip auto: Automatic loading (default). Before loading 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion', it checks if 'bash/zsh-completion' and 'carapace' are already loaded to avoid overwriting by 'x-cmd' completions.
all: Loads all completions, including 'x-cmd' commands, as well as 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion'.

x: Only loads 'x-cmd' command completions without loading 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion'.

never: Disables all 'x-cmd' command completion functionalities.
:::


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x advise autoload get](#x-advise-autoload-get) | Get the current auto-load mode (default is auto) |
| [x advise autoload set](#x-advise-autoload-set) | Set the current auto-load mode |


### x advise autoload get

Get the current auto-load mode (default is auto)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x advise autoload get
```

### x advise autoload set

Set the current auto-load mode


- **Sub Commands**:


| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x advise autoload set auto](#x-advise-autoload-set-auto) | Automatic loading (default). Before loading 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion', it checks if 'bash/zsh-completion' and 'carapace' are already loaded to avoid overwriting by 'x-cmd' completions |
| [x advise autoload set all](#x-advise-autoload-set-all) | Loads all completions, including 'x-cmd' commands, as well as 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion' |
| [x advise autoload set x](#x-advise-autoload-set-x) | Only loads 'x-cmd' command completions without loading 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion' |
| [x advise autoload set never](#x-advise-autoload-set-never) | Disables all 'x-cmd' command completion functionalities |


### x advise autoload set auto

Automatic loading (default). Before loading 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion', it checks if 'bash/zsh-completion' and 'carapace' are already loaded to avoid overwriting by 'x-cmd' completions


- **Usage**:

```sh

```

### x advise autoload set all

Loads all completions, including 'x-cmd' commands, as well as 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion'


- **Usage**:

```sh

```

### x advise autoload set x

Only loads 'x-cmd' command completions without loading 'x-cmd/advise' and 'bash/zsh-completion'

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x agent</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> chat

Launch interactive AI chat with session reuse and workspace binding


::: tip chat is an interactive conversation mode that launches the native AI tool interface
Ideal for multi-turn communication, clarification, and real-time exploration

--reference-workspace references external workspace as read-only context

| `--no-thinking` | Skip AI thinking process, output result directly (save tokens) |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x agent</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> init

Initialize agent config, interactively select and set default AI tool


::: tip What does `x agent init` do?
It picks and configures your default AI tool (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, Kimi CLI).

You usually run it once; use `x agent --cfg` to view or change the default later.

Note: init is not setup.
- init: choose your default AI tool and verify login / API key.
- setup: install x-cmd prompts and skills into the AI tool directories.

Recommended: run `x agent init` first, then `x agent setup`.

Want to temporarily switch tools without changing defaults? Use `x agent --cur set zero_harness=<tool-name>`.
:::

::: tip Supported AI tools:
- claude / claude-* — Claude Code and provider variants
- codex — OpenAI Codex
- cursor — Cursor Agent
- gemini-cli — Google Gemini
- opencode — Open-source multi-model tool
- kimi-cli — Kimi CLI
:::


## Examples

Example: Initialize config, interactively select default AI tool (minimal mode)

```sh
x agent init
```

Example: Full configuration mode, show all supported AI tools

```sh
x agent init --full
```

## Usage

```sh
x agent init
```

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x agent</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> job

Manage long-term iterative tasks (create, execute, monitor, stop)


::: tip Job workflow explained:
1. run creates task, AI auto-generates execution plan and iterates
2. Each iteration AI executes one subtask, updates progress
3. Stops when all subtasks complete or max-iterations reached, generates DONE.md
4. Use status anytime to check progress, stop to force terminate



init, iter, and exec are internal implementations. Users create tasks through run.
:::

::: tip Job-id usage tips:
- Custom ID: `x agent run --job-id fix-bug-123 "Fix login"`
- Cross-command tracking: `run --job-id mytask` → `status --job-id mytask` → `stop --job-id mytask`
- Default ID: timestamp format, e.g. 260527_193035
:::

::: tip Output format choices:
- Default (tty): Interactive table with selectable actions
- --tsv: Tab-separated, good for CLI filtering `x agent job ls --active | grep error`
- --yml: YAML structured, good for AI parsing and scripting
- --csv: Comma-separated, compatible with Excel
:::


## Examples

Example: Create and run task, auto-iterate until completion

```sh
x agent run "Refactor authentication module"
```

Example: Specified job-id + iteration limit, easy to track

```sh
x agent run --job-id auth-fix --max-iterations 50 "Fix OAuth"
```

Example: YAML list of active tasks (AI-parseable)

```sh
x agent job ls --yml --active
```

Example: View complete task status (YAML with file list and running state)

```sh
x agent job status --job-id auth-fix --yml
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x agent job ls](#x-agent-job-ls) | List all tasks with multiple formats and filters |
| [x agent job status](#x-agent-job-status) | View detailed status of a single task (progress, iterations, files, running state).

Colored highlight in tty, pure structured data with --yml. |
| [x agent job run](#x-agent-job-run) | Run task using predefined agent config, auto-build prompt and execute. |
| [x agent job stop](#x-agent-job-stop) | Stop background process of specified task (task state is preserved) |
| [x agent job retry](#x-agent-job-retry) | Re-run an existing job, preserve description/config, clear old execution state |
| [x agent job rm](#x-agent-job-rm) | Remove the specified job directory (running jobs must be stopped first) |


### x agent job ls

List all tasks with multiple formats and filters


- **Examples**:

Example: Interactive select in terminal, TSV otherwise

```sh
x agent job ls
```

Example: YAML list of active tasks (AI-readable)

```sh
x agent job ls --active --yml
```

Example: CSV export of completed tasks

```sh
x agent job ls --completed --csv > done.csv
```

Example: YAML list of failed tasks

```sh
x agent job ls --failed --yml
```

Example: View tasks in custom directory

```sh
x agent job ls --job-dir ~/custom-jobs
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x agent job ls [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--job-dir` |  | Specify parent directory for jobs (default ~/.x-cmd/data/agent/job/) |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--active` | Show only active tasks (has PLAN.md but no DONE.md) |
| `--completed` | Show only completed tasks (has DONE.md) |
| `--failed` | Show only failed tasks (ERROR.md exists or non-zero exit code) |
| `--csv` | CSV format (suitable for Excel import) |
| `--tsv` | TSV format (default for non-tty, good for piping) |
| `--yml` | YAML format (structured, good for AI parsing and scripting) |
| `--app` | Interactive app mode (tty default, clickable view/delete) |


### x agent job status

View detailed status of a single task (progress, iterations, files, running state).

Colored highlight in tty, pure structured data with --yml.



::: tip Status output fields:
- job/jobdir: Task ID and full directory path
- status: Task state (active/completed/failed/interrupted/unknown)
- running: Whether background process is alive (via worker isalive)
- progress: Completion percentage and TODO progress
- iteration: Current / maximum iterations
- ai: AI status, work type, exit signal, recommendation
- stats: Files modified, test status, response count
- time: Creation and update timestamps
- core_files: Core file list (AGENTS.md, PLAN.md, DONE.md, SUMMARY.md, ERROR.md, etc.)
- response_files: Historical iteration response files

--yml stable fields: job_id, job_dir, status, exit_code, done, error_type, error_summary, summary_file, done_file, error_file, iter, max_iterations, progress, started_at, updated_at, completed_at, description status values: COMPLETE &#124; FAILED &#124; RUNNING &#124; INTERRUPTED &#124; PENDING
:::


- **Examples**:

Example: View most recent task status (colored)

```sh
x agent job status
```

Example: Specified job-id, YAML output (AI-parseable)

```sh
x agent job status --job-id mytask --yml
```

Example: View by directory path

```sh
x agent job status --job-dir ~/.x-cmd/data/agent/job/260527_193035
```

Example: Get status and summarize via AI

```sh
x agent job status --yml | x agent request --pipe "Summarize this task"
```

Example: LLM-optimized format with reading guide and DONE.md content

```sh
x agent job status --llms
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x agent job status [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Task directory path (positional, alternative to --job-dir) |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--job-dir` |  | Specify task directory path |
| `--job-id` |  | Specify job ID (most convenient, no need for full path) |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--yml` | Force pure YAML output (no colors, structured, AI-friendly) |
| `--llms` | LLM-optimized output (reading guide + YAML data + auto-embedded DONE.md) |


### x agent job run

Run task using predefined agent config, auto-build prompt and execute.



::: tip Shortcut alias: `x agent run` is equivalent to `x agent job run`
See `x agent run --help` for full parameters and examples
:::


- **Usage**:

```sh
x agent job run
```

### x agent job stop

- **Examples**:

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x agent</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> request

Single-shot AI invocation — send prompt, get response, exit immediately (non-interactive)


::: tip request vs job:
- request: One-off Q&A, e.g. "explain code", "generate regex"
- job: Complex long-term tasks with auto-iteration, e.g. "refactor entire module"
:::

::: tip
--file can be used multiple times to attach files (content injected into prompt)

--output saves response to file, use with --overwrite to force replace

--json requests structured JSON output for script parsing
:::

::: tip
--workspace enables state memory; AI can create/read state files in working directory

--reference-workspace references external workspace as read-only context
:::


## Examples

Example: One-off Q&A — explain code

```sh
x agent request "Explain this code"
```

Example: Specific AI tool + attach code file for review

```sh
x agent request --harness claude --file main.py "Review and suggest improvements"
```

Example: Attach multiple files to generate API docs

```sh
x agent request -f api.ts -f types.ts "Generate API documentation"
```

Example: Generate content and save to file (force overwrite)

```sh
x agent request --output result.md --overwrite "Write a README"
```

Example: Request JSON output for script parsing

```sh
x agent request --json "List all exported functions in this module"
```

Example: Bind working directory, AI can read/write project files

```sh
x agent request --workspace ./myproject "Analyze codebase structure"
```

Example: Simple conversion, skip thinking to save tokens

```sh
x agent request --no-thinking "Convert 2024-01-15 to Unix timestamp"
```

Example: Pipe input + AI analysis

```sh
echo "Error log content" | x agent request --pipe "Analyze this error"
```

## Usage

```sh
x agent request [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | Prompt content, supports natural language task description |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--harness` |  | Specify AI tool (override default config) |
| `-f`, `--file` |  | Attach file to prompt (can be used multiple times) |
| `-o`, `--output` |  | Save AI response to specified file |
| `--stdout-file` |  | Capture AI execution stdout to file |
| `--stderr-file` |  | Capture AI execution stderr to file |
| `--timeout` |  | Request timeout in seconds, 0 means no timeout |
| `--workspace` |  | Bind working directory, enable file memory and state persistence |
| `--session-desc` |  | Custom description for the current session |
| `--reference-workspace` |  | Reference external workspace as read-only context |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--overwrite` | Force overwrite existing output file (use with --output) |
| `--debug` | Output raw JSON and event logs for troubleshooting |
| `--json` | Request JSON formatted output from AI |
| `--pipe` | Read content from stdin/pipe to append to prompt |
| `--new-workspace-session` | Bind workspace but create a new session per request |
| `--no-thinking` | Skip AI thinking process, output result directly (save tokens) |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x agent</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> run

[Shortcut alias] Equivalent to `x agent job run`, run task with predefined agent config


::: tip
Shortcut alias: `x agent run` is a shortcut for `x agent job run`, fully equivalent
:::

::: tip run vs exec:
- run: Requires agent.md config, good for standardized reusable workflows
- exec: Direct description, good for one-off exploratory tasks

run supports all exec parameters (--harness, --max-iterations, etc.)
:::

::: tip Example agent.md format:
```
# Role
You are a senior frontend developer.

# Rules
- Use TypeScript
- Follow React best practices
```

Supported files: GOAL.md, AGENTS.md, AGENT.md, agent.md, SKILL.md, skill.md, CLAUDE.md, CODEX.md, GEMINI.md
:::

::: tip Common parameter combinations:
--yolo: Auto-confirm dangerous operations (e.g. file deletion)

--skill: Load extra skills, e.g. `x agent run --skill python --skill docker ./agent.md "deploy"`

--goal: Override task goal from config file

--prompt: Append system prompt
:::


## Examples

Example: Execute standardized task with agent.md config

```sh
x agent run ./agent.md "Implement OAuth2 login"
```

Example: Yolo mode auto-deploy (skip dangerous op confirmations)

```sh
x agent run --yolo ./deployment-agent/ "Deploy to production"
```

Example: Specified job-id + skills, easy to track status later

```sh
x agent run --job-id auth-refactor --skill python ./backend-agent/ "Refactor auth"
```

Example: Limit iterations + debug mode, quickly locate issues

```sh
x agent run --max-iterations 10 --debug ./test-agent/ "Fix failing tests"
```

Example: Specific harness + continuous session for long tasks

```sh
x agent run --harness claude --continuous ./chat-agent/ "Implement chat feature"
```

## Usage

```sh
x agent run [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1> <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Agent config file or directory path |
| `#n` | Additional arguments/description text |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--skill` |  | Load additional skills (can be used multiple times) |
| `--job-dir` |  | Parent directory for job records |
| `--job-id` |  | Job ID (auto-generated as timestamp, e.g. 260527_193035) |
| `--goal` |  | Override task goal description |
| `--prompt` |  | Append system prompt |
| `--exp` |  | Inject historical experience and lessons (influences AI decisions) |
| `--harness` |  | Specify AI tool interface |
| `--max-iterations` |  | Maximum iterations (prevents infinite loops, default 100) |
| `--inrow` |  | Consecutive no-progress threshold to stop (default 2) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--continuous` | Continuous session mode (all iterations share one session, preserving full context) |
| `--debug` | Output debug logs, view internal requests for each iteration |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x agent</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> stat

[Experimental] Extract per-turn cost & efficiency statistics from AI agent session logs


::: tip ⚠️ Experimental feature
Command name, subcommand structure, and output field formats may change in future releases — do not use in production scripts.

Feedback welcome at https://github.com/x-cmd/x-cmd
:::

::: tip stat extracts per-turn structured statistics from AI agent session logs for cost accounting and efficiency review.
A turn = from the user sending a message to the AI completing its full response (including tool-call loops).

Each turn yields 12 fields: input/output/thinking/cache token counts, API call count, human wait duration, human_ratio, human_message (human prompt text, a semantic anchor for grouping by task type), etc.
:::

::: tip Pick output format by audience:
text   human-readable: summary + model usage + referenced turns + anomalies + highlights (default)

  brief  human, compact: one-screen summary + labelled anomalies + trends, for terminal/chat windows

  tsv    for AI agents: header + tab-separated, full per-turn fields, for awk/Excel

  json   for AI agents: JSON array, full per-turn fields, for jq/scripts
:::

::: tip Two ways to locate a session (mutually exclusive):
&lt;file&gt;          pass the JSONL file path directly

  --session-id    pass a session UUID, auto-resolved under ~/.claude/projects/

                  searches the cwd-derived project first, then all projects
:::

::: tip
Cost estimates are in CNY. Built-in pricing covers Claude / DeepSeek / GLM / MiniMax mainstream models.
:::

::: tip The cross subcommand provides cross-session statistics — parses multiple session JSONLs at once, emitting per-turn data.
Adds a session_id column (for traceability) beyond parse's columns; only supports tsv / json (no text / brief).

AI Agents consume the tsv output, classify by task via human_message, then aggregate with awk.

Session selection: --session-id id1,id2,... (specific sessions) or --all (all sessions, with optional --since / --until / --project filters).
:::

::: tip
The pricing subcommand outputs the built-in model pricing table (CNY/million tokens). AI Agents call pricing to get unit prices, then multiply by cross token data to estimate costs.
:::


## Examples

Example: Parse a Claude Code session by UUID (human-readable report)

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id 16dee4f1-08ba-4964-a7b0-7c0073acc1ef
```

Example: Parse a JSONL file by path

```sh
x agent stat parse claude ~/.claude/projects/-Users-me-proj/session.jsonl
```

Example: Compact summary for feeding as AI agent context

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid> --format brief
```

Example: Export TSV for Excel/awk processing

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid> --format tsv > stats.tsv
```

Example: Show all turns (default shows only those referenced)

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid> --all
```

Example: Cross-session stats — get all turns from last 30 days as TSV; AI Agent groups by human_message for task-level aggregation

```sh
x agent stat cross claude --all --since $(date -v-30d +%s) --format tsv
```

Example: Cross-session stats — specify multiple session UUIDs, JSON output

```sh
x agent stat cross claude --session-id <uuid1>,<uuid2> --format json
```

Example: Cross-session stats — filter by project, awk aggregate by model

```sh
x agent stat cross claude --all --project='-Users-me-myproj' --format tsv | tail -n +2 | awk -F'\t' '{input[$2]+=$3; output[$2]+=$4} END{for(m in input) printf "%s\t%d\t%d\n",m,input[m],output[m]}'
```

Example: Output built-in model pricing table (CNY/million tokens) for AI Agent cost calculation

```sh
x agent stat pricing --format tsv
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x agent stat parse](#x-agent-stat-parse) | Parse AI agent session log, extract per-turn statistics |
| [x agent stat cross](#x-agent-stat-cross) | Cross-session statistics — parse multiple Claude Code sessions into a single per-turn data stream with a session_id column, for AI Agent task-level aggregation by human_message |
| [x agent stat pricing](#x-agent-stat-pricing) | Output built-in model pricing table (CNY/million tokens) for AI Agent cross-session cost calculation |


### x agent stat parse

Parse AI agent session log, extract per-turn statistics


- **Sub Commands**:


| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x agent stat parse claude](#x-agent-stat-parse-claude) | Parse Claude Code session JSONL file |


### x agent stat parse claude

Parse Claude Code session JSONL file


- **Examples**:

Example: Parse by UUID (most common, auto-locates file)

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id 16dee4f1-08ba-4964-a7b0-7c0073acc1ef
```

Example: Parse by file path

```sh
x agent stat parse claude ./session.jsonl
```

Example: Compact summary for AI consumption

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid> --format brief
```

Example: JSON output + jq to extract per-turn models

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid> --format json | jq '.[].model'
```

Example: Incremental parse (skip first 1MB)

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid> --offset 1048576
```

Example: Show all turns (incl. housekeeping)

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid> --all
```

Example: Hide human prompts (code, secrets, etc.) when sharing/exporting output

```sh
x agent stat parse claude --session-id <uuid> --format tsv --no-human-message
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x agent stat parse claude [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Claude Code session JSONL file path (alternative to --session-id) |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--session-id` |  | Claude Code session UUID, auto-resolved under ~/.claude/projects/ (alternative to &lt;file&gt;) |
| `--offset` |  | Byte offset for incremental parsing (skip already-processed bytes) |
| `--format` |  | Output format |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--all` | Show all turns in the detail table (default shows only those referenced by anomalies/highlights) |
| `--no-human-message` | Suppress the human_message field (tsv empty cell, json null; column/field structure unchanged). Use when sharing/exporting output — human prompts may contain code, secrets, or business text. |

| [x agent stat cross claude](#x-agent-stat-cross-claude) | Parse multiple Claude Code session JSONL files, output per-turn statistics with session_id. Only tsv / json formats (no human-readable report); designed for AI Agent consumption. |

# x apk - Alpine Linux Package Manager Enhancement

Alpine Linux is favored for its lightweight and secure design, and `apk` as its official package manager is equally concise and efficient. But sometimes, we want a more user-friendly interaction, easier mirror switching, and more proactive security protection. `x apk` is designed for this purpose, bringing you a brand new experience on top of the native `apk`.

<Terminal demo="/cookbook/mod/apk.1.cn.json" size="large" />

## Interactive Exploration: Browse Packages Like an App Store

Forget the days of memorizing exact package names! Just run `x apk`, and you'll enter an interactive package exploration interface (using the powerful `fzf` tool by default). Here, you can:

*   **Fuzzy Search:** Type keywords in real-time to dynamically filter the package list.
*   **Live Preview:** Select a package, and detailed information appears instantly in the right panel.
*   **Convenient Actions:** After choosing a package, you can directly select to install or view more detailed information.

> If you don't have `fzf` installed, `x-cmd` will automatically download and launch `fzf` when you execute `x apk`, no manual pre-installation needed.

```sh
x apk
```

![x apk](/image/mod/apk.1_1.webp)

This interactive approach greatly lowers the barrier to finding and installing packages, especially useful when you're not sure of the exact package name.

## One-Click Mirror Switch: Say Goodbye to Slow Downloads

In domestic network environments, connecting directly to Alpine official sources can sometimes be slow. `x apk` thoughtfully integrates mirror management, allowing you to easily switch to faster domestic mirrors.

Want to see what mirror sources are recommended?

```sh
x apk mirror ls
```

After executing this command, you'll see a list similar to below, containing official sources and commonly used domestic mirrors like Alibaba Cloud, Huawei Cloud, Tsinghua University, etc.

```
Code          Url                                  Name
official      dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org               Official
ali           mirrors.aliyun.com                   Alibaba Cloud
huawei        mirrors.huaweicloud.com              Huawei Cloud
tuna          mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn         Tsinghua University
ustc          mirrors.ustc.edu.cn                  USTC
sjtu          mirrors.sjtug.sjtu.edu.cn            SJTU
```

Once you find your preferred mirror (e.g., Tsinghua's `tuna`), a single command completes the switch:

```sh
x apk mirror set tuna
```

`x apk` automatically backs up your original configuration, modifies the `/etc/apk/repositories` file, and runs `apk update` to refresh the index. From now on, enjoy blazing-fast download speeds! To restore the official source, use `x apk mirror unset`.

## Security Scanning: Proactive Defense, Preventing Issues Before They Happen

Software supply chain security is increasingly important. Are there known vulnerabilities in the packages installed on your system? `x apk` integrates `osv-scanner`, allowing you to conveniently scan installed packages and their dependencies for security flaws.

```sh
x apk osv
```

This command analyzes the `/lib/apk/db/installed` file and submits the list of installed packages to OSV-Scanner for detection. After scanning, it reports any potential vulnerabilities found, helping you assess risks and take appropriate actions (such as upgrading packages) in a timely manner. This is crucial for maintaining system security.

::: tip
`x apk` greatly enhances the native `apk` experience through its interactive interface, convenient mirror management, and integrated security scanning. Whether you're new to Alpine or a long-time user, `x apk` helps you manage your packages more efficiently and securely. Give it a try!
:::

# x apt - Smarter Debian/Ubuntu Package Management

For those who frequently work on Debian, Ubuntu, or their derivatives (like Kali, Raspberry Pi OS), the `apt` command is certainly familiar. But have you ever felt that native `apt` is somewhat inconvenient when searching for packages, switching to domestic mirrors, or checking for security vulnerabilities? `x apt` was born to solve these pain points! It includes all the functionality of `apt` while providing numerous enhancements to make your package management workflow more efficient and pleasant.

<Terminal demo="/cookbook/mod/apt.1.cn.json" size="large" />

## Feature Highlights

::::ul
:::li Interactive Exploration
Say goodbye to the flood of information from `apt search`. Use the `fzf` or `pick` powered interface to easily find, preview, and select packages.
:::

:::li One-Click Mirror Switch
Built-in support for domestic mirrors (Alibaba, Tsinghua, USTC, etc.). `x apt mirror` lets you switch effortlessly without manually editing `sources.list`.
:::

:::li Security Scanning
Integrated `osv-scanner`. `x apt osv` helps you scan installed packages for known vulnerabilities with one command, protecting your system security.
:::

:::li Smart Proxy
`x apt proxy` makes it easier to configure and manage network proxies for `apt` operations.
:::

:::li Seamless sudo
For operations requiring root privileges (installation, updates, mirror switching), `x apt` intelligently uses `sudo`, no need to manually add it.
:::
::::

## Interactive Exploration: Browse Software Like an App Store

Tired of scrolling through `apt search` results? Just run `x apt` (or `x apt fz`) and try it out!

```sh
x apt
```

This launches an interactive interface based on `fzf` (if your environment supports it). You can:

1.  **Real-time Search:** Type keywords to dynamically filter packages.
2.  **Detailed Preview:** Select a package, and the right panel shows `apt show` information including description, version, dependencies, with syntax highlighting for comfortable reading.
3.  **Quick Actions:** After selecting a package, a menu pops up for you to choose the next step: install, reinstall, view details, or even browse the package's official repository page!

![x apt](/image/mod/apt.1_1.webp)

This interactive approach greatly improves the efficiency of finding and deciding which software to install.

## Say Goodbye to Manual Mirror Switching: Easy Domestic Mirror Switching

In domestic network environments, official `apt` sources may not be ideal. `x apt mirror` makes switching mirror sources easier than ever.

First, see which mirrors are currently supported:

```sh
x apt mirror ls
```

You'll see a list similar to this, containing commonly used domestic mirror sites and their aliases:

```
Code          Url                                  Name
ali           mirrors.aliyun.com                   Alibaba Cloud
tuna          mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn         Tsinghua University
bfsu          mirrors.bfsu.edu.cn                  BFSU
ustc          mirrors.ustc.edu.cn                  USTC
tencent       mirrors.tencent.com                  Tencent Cloud
```

Want to switch to Tsinghua's mirror? Just execute:

```sh
x apt mirror set tuna
```

`x apt` automatically backs up your current source configuration, then intelligently modifies `/etc/apt/sources.list` or related files based on your system (Ubuntu/Debian/Kali/Raspberry Pi) and architecture, replacing official sources with Tsinghua (security update sources typically remain official or use specific mirrors). Finally, it automatically runs `apt update` to refresh the package list. The entire process requires no manual file editing, done in one step! To restore your previous configuration, use `x apt mirror unset`.

## System Security Scanning: Prevent Issues Before They Happen

Are there known vulnerabilities in packages installed on your system? `x apt osv` can help you check.

```sh
x apt osv
```

This command invokes the powerful `osv-scanner` tool to scan all packages installed via `dpkg` (i.e., packages managed by `apt`) and compares them against the OSV (Open Source Vulnerability) database, listing any security vulnerabilities found. This is crucial for maintaining the security of servers or development environments.

::: tip
`x apt` greatly enhances the native `apt` experience through these carefully designed features. It preserves all of `apt`'s capabilities (you can still use `x apt update`, `x apt upgrade`, `x apt remove <package>`, etc.), while making you more proficient in Debian/Ubuntu package management through its interactive interface, convenient mirror and proxy management, and security scanning features.
:::

Try `x apt` now and experience smarter, more efficient command-line package management!

# x arp - View ARP Cache Table Information

The `x arp` module displays local system ARP cache table information. It supports multiple output formats, including interactive TUI applications, CSV, and TSV formats, allowing users to view and analyze ARP table data in different ways.

## Quick Start

The simplest way to use it is to run the `x arp` command directly:

```bash
x arp
```

::: tip
This command is equivalent to `x arp --auto`. The system automatically selects the output mode based on whether stdout is connected to a terminal (tty): if connected, it launches the interactive TUI application (`--app`); otherwise, it outputs in TSV format (`--tsv`).
:::

## Output Format Options

`x arp` provides various output format options to meet different needs:

:::: ul
::: li **`--app` (interactive TUI)**
Shows the ARP table in a TUI when stdout is a terminal—default in that case.
:::
::: li **`--tsv` / `-t`**
Emits TSV for spreadsheets or scripts. Headers: `ip, mac, if, suspicious, scope, type, vendor`.
:::
::: li **`--csv` / `-c`**
Same as TSV but comma-separated.
:::
::: li **`--raw` / `-r`**
Prints the raw ARP feed.
:::
::::

## Advanced Options

In addition to basic output format options, `x arp` provides some advanced options:

:::: ul
::: li **`--all` / `-a`**
Lists every entry, including `incomplete` MAC rows (defaults may hide some).
:::
::: li **`--no-vendor` / `-n`**
Skips vendor resolution for quieter, faster output.
:::
::::

## Examples

Here are some examples of `x arp` commands:

:::: ul
::: li **View ARP table in interactive TUI mode**

```bash
x arp --app
```
:::
::: li **Output ARP table in TSV format**

```bash
x arp --tsv
```
:::
::: li **Output ARP table in CSV format with all entries**

```bash
x arp --csv --all
```
:::
::: li **Output ARP table in raw format without vendor information**

```bash
x arp --raw --no-vendor
```
:::
::::

## More Information

Visit [https://x-cmd.com/mod/arp](https://x-cmd.com/mod/arp) for more information.

---

# x arp ls

Retrieving the ARP table

## Usage

```sh
x arp ls [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--all`, `-a` | Display all ARP cache tables, including entries in an incomplete state |
| `--no-vendor`, `-n` | Do not display the manufacturer or organization information associated with the MAC address |
| `--auto` | If the standard output is connected to a terminal (tty), it starts in interactive mode (`--app`); otherwise, it outputs in TSV format (`--tsv`). This is the default behavior for `x arp` |
| `--app` | Check ARP cache table with the tui app |
| `--tsv`, `-t` | Output in TSV format |
| `--csv`, `-c` | Output in CSV format |
| `--raw`, `-r` | Output in the raw data format |

# x ascii - ASCII Art and Tools

The `x ascii` module provides a series of commands for ASCII-related tasks, including querying ASCII tables, generating ASCII art text, converting images to ASCII art, drawing ASCII line charts, rendering Mermaid diagrams, and simulating ASCII art fireworks.

## Query ASCII Table

Use the `table` subcommand to query the ASCII table. This command supports multiple output formats and can filter specific character ranges as needed.

::::ul
::: li Output ASCII table as CSV

```bash
# Output ASCII table in CSV format
x ascii table --csv
```

:::
::: li List lowercase letter codes

```bash
# List ASCII codes for all lowercase letters
x ascii table lower
```

:::
::: li Look up Ctrl-A

```bash
# Return ASCII code for Ctrl-A
x ascii table ^A
```

:::
::: li Look up `0x11`

```bash
# Return ASCII code for 0x11
x ascii table 0x11
```

:::
::::

## Generate ASCII Art Text

The `cfonts` (or `cfont`) subcommand converts text into ASCII art. You can customize fonts, colors, background colors, and text alignment.

::::ul
::: li Render `x-cmd` as ASCII art

```bash
# Convert "x-cmd" string to ASCII art
x ascii cfont x-cmd
```

:::
::: li Gradient `red,blue`

```bash
# Convert "x-cmd" to ASCII art with red and blue gradient
x ascii cfont x-cmd -g red,blue
```

:::
::: li Red background, centered

```bash
# Convert "x-cmd" to ASCII art with red background and center alignment
x ascii cfont x-cmd -a center -b red
```

:::
::::

## Image to ASCII Art

The `imagec` subcommand uses `ascii-image-converter` to convert images to ASCII art. You need to provide the image file path as an argument.

::::ul
::: li Image to ASCII art

```bash
# Convert image to ASCII art (replace <image_path> with your path)
x ascii imagec <image_path>
```

:::
::::

::: tip
Please replace `<image_path>` with your actual image file path. Common formats like PNG, JPG, GIF are supported.
:::

## Draw ASCII Line Charts

The `graph` subcommand draws ASCII line charts based on input data. Input data is typically a column of values, such as generated by the `seq` command.

::::ul
::: li Simple ASCII line chart

```bash
# Draw a simple ASCII line chart
seq 1 10 | x ascii graph
```

:::
::::

## Render Mermaid Diagrams

The `mermaid` subcommand allows rendering Mermaid diagrams in the terminal. You need to provide Mermaid code as input.

::: tip
Mermaid code is typically piped to the command, for example:
```bash
echo 'graph TD; A-->B;' | x ascii mermaid
```
:::

## Simulate ASCII Art Fireworks

The `firework` subcommand downloads and runs `firework-rs` to simulate ASCII art fireworks. You can choose different demo effects.

::::ul
::: li Fireworks demo 1

```bash
# Display ASCII art fireworks using demo 1
x ascii firework -d 1
```

:::
::::

::: warning
Press `esc` to exit the fireworks program
:::

## Summary

The `x ascii` module provides a rich set of tools to help you easily create and process various ASCII art works. From simple ASCII code queries to complex image conversion and fireworks simulation, this module provides convenient command-line interfaces.

Visit [https://x-cmd.com/mod/ascii](https://x-cmd.com/mod/ascii) for more information.

# x asdf - Master Multi-Version Environments with Ease

As a CLI enthusiast, have you ever struggled with managing different development language and tool versions across projects? Ruby, Node.js, Python, Java... Each project may have its own specific version requirements. Manual switching and configuration is not only tedious but also error-prone. Now, with `x asdf`, all of this becomes simple!

`asdf` itself is a powerful extensible version manager, and x-cmd's `asdf` module builds upon it with careful refinement and enhancement, aiming to provide you with a smoother, more intuitive command-line experience. Say goodbye to lengthy commands and complex configuration. Let `x asdf` become your capable assistant for managing development environments!

<Terminal demo="/mod/asdf.cn.json" size="large" />

## Interactive Exploration: Your Personal Software Manager

When you first run `x asdf`, it acts like an intelligent software manager. If `asdf` isn't installed on your system yet, `x-cmd` will thoughtfully ask and automatically download and install it for you.

```sh
x asdf
```

::: tip
If you just want to explore `x asdf` features, simply run `x asdf` to launch the interactive interface
:::

Once ready, `x asdf` presents you with a clean interactive interface. Here, you can easily browse all software supported by `asdf`, use fuzzy search to quickly locate the tools you need. Whether you want to install the latest Node.js or a specific Python version, just select with up/down arrows and press Enter. `x asdf` handles the subsequent installation and configuration for you.

![x asdf](/image/mod/asdf.1_1.webp)

This interactive interface frees you from memorizing tedious plugin names and version numbers. Manage your development tools as easily as browsing an app store.

## One-Click Ready: Easy Installation and Switching

Tired of the step-by-step operations of `plugin add`, `install`, `global`? The `use` command in `x asdf` combines all these steps into one! Want to install and globally use the latest version of `nodejs` on your system? Just one line:

```sh
x asdf use nodejs
```

`x asdf` automatically helps you:

1.  Add the `nodejs` plugin for `asdf`.
2.  Install the latest stable version of `nodejs`.
3.  Set the newly installed version as the global default.

::: tip
You can also specify a version number, like `x asdf use nodejs 18.17.0`
:::

The entire process flows smoothly, letting you focus on the code itself rather than environment configuration details.

## Clean Up: Uninstalling is Just as Simple

When a tool or version is no longer needed, cleanup can be just as simple. `x asdf` provides the `unuse` command, allowing you to uninstall specified software and its `asdf` plugin with one click. For example, to uninstall `nodejs` you installed earlier:

```sh
x asdf unuse nodejs
```

`x asdf` cleanly removes all installed versions of `nodejs` and deletes the related `asdf` plugin information. Keeping your development environment clean and organized has never been easier.

## Precise Control: Activate and Deactivate

`asdf` manages different versions of executables through the `shims` directory and environment variables. `x asdf` automatically activates `asdf` for you upon first use, meaning versions installed by `asdf` will be prioritized by the system.

But sometimes, you may want to temporarily disable `asdf` management and use system-default or otherwise installed tool versions. The `--deactivate` parameter comes in handy:

```sh
x asdf --deactivate
```

After executing this command, `asdf`'s `shims` path is removed from your `PATH` environment variable. Software installed by `asdf` will no longer be directly available in the current terminal session (unless you specify the full path). This provides more flexible environment control. When you need to re-enable `asdf`, simply run `x asdf --activate`.

---

`x asdf` is more than just a simple wrapper for `asdf`. Through its intelligent interactive interface and convenient `use` / `unuse` commands, it greatly simplifies the complexity of multi-version environment management. Whether you're an experienced developer or new to the command line, `x asdf` helps you manage your development tools more efficiently and elegantly. Open your terminal, type `x asdf`, and start your efficient development journey now!

# x aur - Your AUR Assistant for Arch Linux

Arch Linux is known for its "rolling release" and "user-contributed" design philosophy, and AUR (Arch User Repository) is the heart of this philosophy. AUR hosts a vast collection of community-contributed packages, allowing users to easily access applications not found in the official repositories. However, searching and browsing AUR packages in the terminal typically requires manual queries and copy-pasting package names—a cumbersome process.

`x aur` is designed to solve this pain point. It provides Arch Linux users with a smooth interactive interface, combined with `fzf` for intuitive package filtering and selection. It also offers features like viewing popular package rankings, helping you quickly discover high-quality and popular applications.

## Quick Start: Interactive AUR Package Search

The most common and intuitive way to use `x aur` is to run the command directly, which launches an interactive interface for fuzzy searching packages.

```sh
# Launch interactive search interface
x aur
```

<!-- ![aur_app](/image/mod/aur.1.webp) -->

This command starts the fzf interactive interface, showing the package list on the left and preview information on the right. You can fuzzy search by typing keywords, use up/down arrows to select packages, and press Enter to confirm your selection.

## View Package Details

If you already know the package name, use the `info` subcommand to view its detailed information:

```sh
# View details for x-cmd
x aur info x-cmd
```

<!-- ![aur_info](/image/mod/aur.2.webp) -->

This command displays the complete package information, including package name, version, description, maintainer, vote count, popularity score, last update date, and other key data. This information helps you decide whether a package is worth installing.

## Browse Package Lists

The `ls` subcommand lists packages in AUR, convenient for batch viewing or data processing:

```sh
# Export in TSV format for easy script processing
x aur ls --tsv
```

<!-- ![aur_ls](/image/mod/aur.3.webp) -->

TSV format output is especially suitable for data analysis or integration with other tools—you can easily import results into spreadsheet software or further process them.

## Discover Popular Packages

Want to find the most popular applications in AUR? Use the `top` subcommand to view popular package rankings:

```sh
# View the top 1000 most popular packages (default)
x aur top

# View top 200
x aur top 200
```

<!-- ![aur_top](/image/mod/aur.4.webp) -->

This feature is especially useful for discovering high-quality applications—you can quickly find community-approved premium packages based on vote counts and popularity.

## Update Local AUR Database

To ensure search results reflect the latest AUR state, you can manually update the local database:

```sh
# Update AUR package list
x aur update
```

When first using `x aur` search functionality, the system automatically updates the database. Subsequent uses rely on the local cache. Run this command to manually refresh if you want the latest package information.

## More Information

Visit our homepage for more information: https://x-cmd.com/mod/aur

# x brew (1) - Interactive UI and Mirror Management

## Interactive Software Search

Running the `x brew` command, **x-cmd** provides an `fzf` interactive APP where users can search for various software tools and installation information.

```sh
x brew
```

![x brew](/image/mod/brew.1_1.webp)

In the interactive APP, the left column shows package names of software tools, and the right panel displays installation information such as version and dependencies.

## Change Homebrew Mirror Source

`x brew` uses the `$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/etc/homebrew/brew.env` file to configure `Homebrew` download sources.

Use the following command to set `Homebrew` download source to Tsinghua University mirror:

```sh
x brew mirror set tuna
```

Additionally, `x brew` supports setting mirrors from Alibaba Cloud, USTC, and others. You can run `x brew mirror ls` to view them.

## Common Commands

::::ul
:::li Install Package
```sh
x brew install node
```
:::

:::li Search Package
```sh
x brew search python
```
:::

:::li List Installed
```sh
x brew list
```
:::

:::li Upgrade All
```sh
x brew upgrade all
```
:::
::::

::: tip
Experiencing slow downloads with Homebrew on macOS? Try `x brew mirror set tuna` to switch to Tsinghua mirror!
:::

[More] To learn more about the brew module, please visit x-cmd official website - x-cmd.com/mod/brew

# x brew (2) - Homebrew Download Statistics and Privacy Settings

## Obtaining Homebrew's Official Software Download Statistics

`x brew` supports viewing download and installation data for core Homebrew packages and cask software.

```sh
x brew analytics data
```

![x brew analytics data](/image/mod/brew.2_1.webp)

Additionally, it supports specifying the output format and the number of days to query. For example, to output the top 10 Homebrew cask software packages downloaded in the last 30 days in CSV format:

```sh
x brew analytics data cask --csv --30 | head -n 10
```

## Disabling Homebrew's Analytics Tracking

Homebrew defaults to collecting usage data, such as software installation, uninstallation, and update actions, to optimize the software installation and user experience.

If you have concerns about this, you can run the following command to disable it:

```sh
x brew analytics off
```

# x btop - Real-Time System Resource Monitoring

## Introduction

The `x btop` module provides a convenient way to monitor your system resources, including CPU, memory, disk, network, and processes. It prioritizes using the locally installed `btop` command. If `btop` is not installed on your system, `x btop` automatically downloads and runs it via `pixi` (Linux/macOS) or `scoop` (Windows), requiring no manual installation and without affecting your system environment.


## Quick Start

Simply run the following command to start `btop`:

::::ul
::: li Start `x btop`

```bash
x btop
```
:::

::::

This launches `btop` and displays real-time system resource usage. You can interact with `btop` via mouse or keyboard to view more detailed information.


### Run btop Commands Directly

You can pass arguments directly to `btop` using the `--` parameter:

::::ul
::: li Pass flags to `btop` with `--`

```bash
x btop -- -h  # Equivalent to running btop -h, view help information
```
:::

::::

This allows you to use all features and options of `btop`.


### Future Enhancements

We plan to add more features in the future, such as:

::::ul
:::li **Custom Configuration:** Allow users to customize `btop` display and parameters.
:::li **Data Export:** Export `btop` monitoring data to files.
::::



## Integration with Other Tools

`x btop` seamlessly integrates with other `x-cmd` modules. For example, you can combine `x btop` output with other tools to create more powerful monitoring and analysis tools.


## Summary

`x btop` provides a simple yet powerful way to monitor your system resources. Whether or not `btop` is installed on your system, you can easily use it to get real-time system information. We encourage you to try `x btop` and explore its features.

# Control Browser with Natural Language

`x buse` is an enhanced module for the [browser-use](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use) project. Combining AI and command line, it lets you **drive the browser to complete tasks with just one natural language command**, such as opening web pages, searching content, taking screenshots, filling forms, and even navigating and clicking buttons.

::: tip
For first-time use, it's recommended to run `x buse --init` to configure default model and options
:::

## Prerequisites

Before using `x buse`, ensure these basic requirements are met:

::::ul
:::li Install `browser-use` and its dependencies
Including Python, playwright Chrome browser, etc. If `browser-use` is not locally available, `x buse` will automatically install it for you.
:::

:::li Have an AI model API Key
At least one available AI model API Key (such as OpenAI, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek).
:::
::::

## Basic Usage

### Launch Interactive Console

```bash
x buse
```

Enter an interactive TUI interface and input natural language commands to control the browser directly, such as "Open OpenAI's official website and take a screenshot". The command will be parsed by the AI model, and Chrome will be driven via CDP to perform clicks, screenshots, and other actions.

### Initialize Configuration with `--init`

For first-time use, it's recommended to execute:

```bash
x buse --init
```

This command guides you to configure the default model, whether to use headless mode, and whether to enable MCP mode. After configuration, it saves to x-cmd's configuration system for subsequent use.

### Run Tasks with Specified AI Model

```bash
x buse --model gpt-4o
```

If no model is explicitly specified, the system reads the model configuration from settings, or defaults to `gemini-2.0-flash`.

You can also pass other model names via `--model` (provided you have configured the corresponding API key):

::::ul
:::li `gpt-4o`
OpenAI model
:::

:::li `gemini-pro` / `gemini-2.0-flash`
Google model
:::

:::li `deepseek-coder`
DeepSeek model
:::
::::

## Run Single Tasks Directly (Prompt Mode)

You can skip the interactive interface and write task commands directly in the command line:

```bash
x buse -p "Search for 'Python decorator usage' and screenshot the first page of results"
```

This will automatically:

::::ol
:::li Launch browser
:::

:::li Perform search
:::

:::li Find and screenshot search results
:::

:::li Save file to local directory
:::
::::

## Advanced Features

### Run Browser in Headless Mode

Use browser headless mode:

```bash
x buse --headless
```

::: tip
Headless mode is suitable for automation tasks, CI environments, or server script execution
:::

### Use MCP Mode for System Integration

MCP (Machine Command Protocol) mode exposes a JSON-RPC interface through standard input/output (stdin/stdout).

This allows `x buse` to be embedded into larger systems, such as:

::::ul
:::li Integration with backend services
:::

:::li Access to web control panels
:::

:::li Embedding into VS Code plugins or GUI frontends
:::
::::

Launch MCP mode:

```bash
x buse --mcp
```

You can send standard JSON-RPC requests from stdin, such as:

```json
{
  "method": "run",
  "params": {
    "prompt": "Open GitHub and take a screenshot"
  }
}
```

### Custom Browser Parameters

You can customize browser window size, user profile directory, and other options:

```bash
x buse --window-width 1280 --window-height 720
x buse --user-data-dir ~/.config/buse/chrome --profile-directory Default
```

Or connect to your existing Chrome instance (debug port needs to be enabled):

```bash
x buse --cdp-url http://localhost:9222
```

## Combine with Shell Scripts for Automation

Through the `x buse -p` format, you can easily embed it into bash scripts:

```bash
#!/bin/bash

keyword="$1"

x buse -p "Search for $keyword and screenshot the first result"
```

After saving as `screenshot.sh`, run:

```bash
chmod +x screenshot.sh
./screenshot.sh "linux command cheat sheet"
```

## Configuration Management and Model API Keys

You can set API keys for each model separately:

```bash
x openai --cur set apikey=sk-xxx
x gemini --cur set apikey=xxx
x grok --cur set apikey=xxx
x deepseek --cur set apikey=xxx
```

View current settings:

```bash
x buse --cur
```

Modify default model:

```bash
x buse --cfg set model=gpt-4o
```

## FAQ and Troubleshooting

::::ul
:::li Missing API Key prompt?
Confirm whether you've set `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable, or configured the key via `x xxx --cfg set apikey`.
:::

:::li Cannot screenshot or click?
It may be due to incomplete page loading or CDP call failure. Try running in non-headless mode to observe:

```bash
x buse --headless
```
:::
::::

# x bwh --cfg

Manage the configuration file.


::: warning
After using the x bwh --cfg load command to load the relevant file contents, you cannot use the x bwh --cfg cat command to view the file contents in the current terminal environment.
:::


## Examples

Set the value of the configuration item veid in the configuration file to 1234567, and the value of apikey to private_XXXXXXXX

```sh
x bwh --cfg set veid=1234567 apikey=private_XXXXXXXX
```

Get the value of veid in the profile file named X, and then output it to stdout

```sh
x bwh --cfg get --profile X veid
```

Get the value of the corresponding field in the config yml file, then assign it to the corresponding variable and output it to stdout

```sh
x bwh --cfg var veid=veid && echo $veid
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x bwh --cfg init](#x-bwh-cfg-init) | Set the values of VEID and API KEY again |
| [x bwh --cfg load](#x-bwh-cfg-load) | Loads variables that specify the config yml file to generate corresponding prefixes, and uses the default config when empty |
| [x bwh --cfg unload](#x-bwh-cfg-unload) | Unloads variables that specify the corresponding prefix generated by the config yml file |
| [x bwh --cfg reload](#x-bwh-cfg-reload) | Reloads variables that specify the corresponding prefix generated by the config yml file, using the default config when empty |
| [x bwh --cfg isloaded](#x-bwh-cfg-isloaded) | Determines whether the variable with the specified variable prefix has been loaded |
| [x bwh --cfg current](#x-bwh-cfg-current) | View current profile information |
| [x bwh --cfg rm](#x-bwh-cfg-rm) | Remove configuration file |
| [x bwh --cfg cat](#x-bwh-cfg-cat) | Read and display configuration files |
| [x bwh --cfg set](#x-bwh-cfg-set) | Set the values corresponding to the VID and apikey of the configuration items in the configuration file |
| [x bwh --cfg get](#x-bwh-cfg-get) | Gets the configuration information for the configuration file |
| [x bwh --cfg var](#x-bwh-cfg-var) | Set variables for configuration files |


### x bwh --cfg init

Set the values of VEID and API KEY again


- **Examples**:

Set the values of VEID and API KEY again

```sh
x bwh --cfg init <VEID> <API KEY>
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh --cfg init <#1> <#2>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | veid |
| `#2` | apikey |


### x bwh --cfg load

Loads variables that specify the config yml file to generate corresponding prefixes, and uses the default config when empty


- **Examples**:

Loads the specified config yml file

```sh
x bwh --cfg load <config yml file>
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh --cfg load
```

### x bwh --cfg unload

Unloads variables that specify the corresponding prefix generated by the config yml file


- **Examples**:

Unloads the specified config yml file


# x bwh current

View or modify the current VPS configuration.

## Examples

Sets the VEID for the current environment.  This changes which VPS the subsequent commands will affect.

```sh
x bwh current set veid=<new_veid>
```

Prints the current VPS configuration (config path, profile name, VEID, API key, and proxy settings) to the console.

```sh
x bwh current print
```

Gets the path to the current VPS configuration file and assigns it to the variable `x_`.

```sh
`x bwh current get_ config` or `x bwh current config_`
echo "$x_"

```

Gets the VEID of the currently selected VPS.

```sh
x bwh current getor veid
```

Sets the API key for the current VPS.

```sh
x bwh current import apikey:=<API KEY>
```

Clears the current VPS configuration variables.

```sh
x bwh current clear
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x bwh current set](#x-bwh-current-set) | Set the value of the current VPS field, store it in the current environment with variables, and set multiple fields at once. |
| [x bwh current ls](#x-bwh-current-ls) | Lists the values for all fields of the current VPS |
| [x bwh current lsi](#x-bwh-current-lsi) | Lists all the fields of the current VPS and the corresponding environment variables |
| [x bwh current get](#x-bwh-current-get) | Obtain the value of the corresponding field of the current VPS and output it to stdout |
| [x bwh current get_](#x-bwh-current-get) | Gets the value of the profile field corresponding to the current VPS and assigns the value to the specified variable 'x_'. |
| [x bwh current getor](#x-bwh-current-getor) | Get the value of the field corresponding to the current VPS, take the default value if not, and output it to stdout |
| [x bwh current print](#x-bwh-current-print) | Displays the specified parameter information of the current VPS. |
| [x bwh current import](#x-bwh-current-import) | Obtain the value of the field corresponding to the current VPS, and then assign the value to the corresponding variable, you can assign multiple variables at once |
| [x bwh current clear](#x-bwh-current-clear) | clear the specified config yml file, empty use default config |
| [x bwh current let](#x-bwh-current-let) | TODO |


### x bwh current set

Set the value of the current VPS field, store it in the current environment with variables, and set multiple fields at once.


- **Usage**:


### x bwh current ls

- **Usage**:


- **Usage**:

# x bwh info

View detailed information about your VPS.

## Examples

Get VPS information and print to terminal

```sh
x bwh info get
```

View running VPS information

```sh
x bwh info live
```

Get VPS system information currently in use and optionally installed

```sh
x bwh info availableos
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x bwh info get](#x-bwh-info-get) | Get VPS information |
| [x bwh info live](#x-bwh-info-live) | View running VPS information |
| [x bwh info availableos](#x-bwh-info-availableos) | Get information about installed and available VPS systems |
| [x bwh info auditlog](#x-bwh-info-auditlog) | Returns an array with the detailed audit log shown under Audit Log in KiwiVM. |
| [x bwh info ratelimit](#x-bwh-info-ratelimit) | When you perform too many API calls in a short amount of time, KiwiVM API may start dropping your requests for a few minutes. This call allows monitoring this matter. |
| [x bwh info rawusagestats](#x-bwh-info-rawusagestats) | Returns a two-dimensional array with the detailed usage statistics shown under Detailed Statistics in KiwiVM. |
| [x bwh info suspensiondetails](#x-bwh-info-suspensiondetails) | Retrieve information related to service suspensions. |
| [x bwh info brief](#x-bwh-info-brief) | brief report of data usage and next reset time |


### x bwh info get

Get VPS information


- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh info get
```

### x bwh info live

View running VPS information


- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh info live
```

### x bwh info availableos

Get information about installed and available VPS systems


- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh info availableos
```

### x bwh info auditlog

Returns an array with the detailed audit log shown under Audit Log in KiwiVM.


- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh info auditlog
```

### x bwh info ratelimit

When you perform too many API calls in a short amount of time, KiwiVM API may start dropping your requests for a few minutes. This call allows monitoring this matter.


- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh info ratelimit
```

### x bwh info rawusagestats

Returns a two-dimensional array with the detailed usage statistics shown under Detailed Statistics in KiwiVM.


- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh info rawusagestats
```

### x bwh info suspensiondetails

Retrieve information related to service suspensions.


- **Usage**:

```sh

```

### x bwh info brief

brief report of data usage and next reset time


- **Usage**:

```sh
x bwh info brief
```

# x bwh sh

Execute shell commands or scripts on your VPS.

## Examples

Executes the `pwd` command on the VPS and displays the current working directory.

```sh
x bwh sh --exec 'pwd'
```

## Usage

```sh
x bwh sh [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--cd` | Change current directory to new directory |
| `--exec` | Execute a shell command on the VPS (synchronously). |

| [x bwh snapshot export](#x-bwh-snapshot-export) | Generates a token with which the snapshot can be transferred to another instance. |
| [x bwh snapshot import](#x-bwh-snapshot-import) | Imports a snapshot from another instance identified by VEID and Token. |


- **Usage**:

# x cb cl

shortcut for `x cb repo clone`

## Usage

```sh
x cb cl [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | &lt;ownerPath&gt;/&lt;RepoPath&gt; (default ownerPath: current user) |
| `#2` | directory |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-o`, `--origin` &lt;name&gt; |  | use &lt;name&gt; instead of 'origin' to track upstream |
| `-b`, `--branch` &lt;branch&gt; |  | checkout &lt;branch&gt; instead of the remote's HEAD |
| `-u`, `--upload-pack` &lt;path&gt; |  | path to git-upload-pack on the remote |
| `-j`, `--jobs` &lt;n&gt; |  | number of submodules cloned in parallel |
| `--separate-git-dir` &lt;gitdir&gt; |  | separate git dir from working tree |
| `--depth` &lt;depth&gt; |  | create a shallow clone of that depth |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--recursive` | initialize all contained submodules |
| `--shallow-submodules` | any cloned submodules will be shallow |

# x cb codeurl

Get Codeberg source url

## Examples

Get the raw file URL of the README.md for the default branch of the x-cmd/x-cmd repository

```sh
x cb codeurl https://codeberg.org/x-cmd/x-cmd
```

Get the raw file URL of LICENSE/LICENSE.txt on branch X of the x-cmd/x-cmd repository

```sh
x cb codeurl https://codeberg.org/x-cmd/x-cmd/src/branch/X/LICENSE/LICENSE.txt
```

## Usage

```sh
x cb codeurl <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | The resource address starting with https://codeberg.org |

# Codeberg Introduction

## About Codeberg

Introduce the history of Codeberg

In China, Codeberg is accessible


## Some Issues with Codeberg

::::ul
:::li Occasionally inaccessible
:::li Lack of Discussion
::::

::: tip
Codeberg's Action is not enabled by default, but users may request to enable it.
:::


## Codeberg CLI

::::ul
:::li Codeberg is an operation site based on the forgejo structure. x-cmd already provides CLI for forgejo and gitea.
:::li Therefore, we wrapped a module oriented to Codeberg on top of the fjo module -- [cb module](/mod/cb.md)
:::li On the one hand, it maintains some similarity with GitHub in concept design, so x-cmd's cb module and gh module also maintain a certain similarity, allowing users to migrate easily.
::::

# x cb issue

repo issue management

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x cb issue ls](#x-cb-issue-ls) | List repo issue |
| [x cb issue create](#x-cb-issue-create) | Create issue |
| [x cb issue edit](#x-cb-issue-edit) | Edit issue |
| [x cb issue close](#x-cb-issue-close) | Close issue |
| [x cb issue reopen](#x-cb-issue-reopen) | Reopen issue |


### x cb issue ls

List repo issue


- **Examples**:

View closed issues with the label "bug" in the x-cmd/x-cmd repository

```sh
x cb issue ls --labels bug --state closed -r x-cmd/x-cmd
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x cb issue ls [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--state` &lt;state&gt; |  | Indicates the state of the issues to return |
| `--type` &lt;type&gt; |  | filter by type (issues / pulls) if set. |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--repo`, `-r` &lt;owner/repo&gt; | &lt;owner_path&gt;/&lt;repo_path&gt; |
| `--q` &lt;string&gt; | search query |
| `--labels` &lt;labels(separated ,)&gt; | Labels to associate with this issue |
| `--since` &lt;timestamp&gt; | Only show items updated after the given time |
| `--before` &lt;timestamp&gt; | Only show items updated before the given time |
| `--created_by` &lt;assignees&gt; | Only show items which were created by the the given user |
| `--assigned_by` &lt;creator&gt; | Only show items for which the given user is assigned |
| `--milestones` &lt;assignees&gt; | comma separated list of milestone names or ids |
| `--mentioned_by` &lt;user_path&gt; | Only show items in which the given user was mentioned |
| `--page` &lt;num&gt; | target page |
| `--limit` &lt;num&gt; | per page data number |
| `--json`, `-j` | output raw JSON data |
| `--csv` | output csv data |
| `--yml` | output yml data |


### x cb issue create

Create issue


- **Examples**:

Created an issue in the ollama/ollama repository with the title "A new bug", the content "it is a new bug"

```sh
x cb issue create -r ollama/ollama --title "A new bug" --body "it is a new bug"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x cb issue create [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--repo`, `-r` &lt;owner/repo&gt; | &lt;owner_path&gt;/&lt;repo_path&gt; |
| `--title` &lt;string&gt; | issue title |
| `--ref` &lt;base&gt; | base branch name or .sha=&lt;ref_SHA&gt; |
| `--body` &lt;string&gt; | The contents of the issue |
| `--labels` &lt;array&gt; | labels ID |
| `--closed` | close issue |
| `--due_date` &lt;timestamp&gt; | due date |
| `--assignees` &lt;array&gt; | User responsible for this pull request |
| `--milestone` &lt;id&gt; | milestone number |
| `--json`, `-j` | output raw JSON data |



### x cb repo create

`x cb repo create` is multi-command merge sugar to conveniently use
* `x cb user repo create`
* `x cb org repo create`

If you need more control options or using in script, Please use them


- **Examples**:

Create a public repository called x-cmd

```sh
x cb repo create --access public x-cmd
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x cb repo create [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | &lt;owner_path&gt;/&lt;repo_path&gt; |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--access` &lt;private,public&gt; | repo access |
| `--description` &lt;desc&gt; | repo description |
| `--readme` &lt;string&gt; | Readme of the repository to create |
| `--license` &lt;string&gt; | Repo License |
| `--gitignores` &lt;string&gt; | Gitignores to use |
| `--issue_labels` &lt;labels&gt; | Label-Set to use |
| `--trust_model` &lt;model&gt; | TrustModel of the repository |
| `--default_branch` &lt;branch&gt; | Default Branch of the repository |
| `--template` | Whether the repository is template |
| `--auto_init` | WWhether the repository should be auto-initialized |
| `--json`, `-j` | output raw JSON data |

# x cb team

team management

## Examples

Create a team that has access to the code

```sh
x cb team create --org <org_path> --units 'repo.code' --units_map '{"repo.code": "write"}' <team_name>

```

Lists a team's repositories

```sh
x cb team repo ls --id <team_id>
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x cb team ls](#x-cb-team-ls) | List current user or org team |
| [x cb team info](#x-cb-team-info) | Get team info by name |
| [x cb team create](#x-cb-team-create) | To create a team |
| [x cb team edit](#x-cb-team-edit) | To edit a team |
| [x cb team rm](#x-cb-team-rm) | To delete a team |
| [x cb team repo](#x-cb-team-repo) | org team repo management |
| [x cb team member](#x-cb-team-member) | team member management |


| ------- | ------- |

# x ccal - Your Terminal Lunar Calendar Assistant

For Chinese users, the lunar calendar, solar terms, traditional festivals, and almanac auspicious/inauspicious indicators are important references for daily life and festival planning. However, the standard Unix/Linux `cal` command only provides a concise Gregorian calendar view, unable to meet the needs for traditional cultural information.
`x ccal` was created for this purpose. It is a terminal calendar tool designed for Chinese users, dedicated to providing comprehensive lunar calendar and almanac information in your command line.

With `x ccal`, you can quickly view lunar dates, solar terms, traditional festivals, holiday schedules, and even almanac auspicious/inauspicious information in the terminal, without needing web pages or mobile apps. It integrates powerful interactive interfaces, fuzzy search, and multi-view switching capabilities, providing elegant and practical lunar calendar support for terminal enthusiasts.

## Quick Start: Interactive Calendar Overview

The most common and intuitive usage of `x ccal` is to run the command directly. It displays the current month's Gregorian and lunar calendar in interactive mode.

```sh
# Equivalent to x ccal fz
x ccal
```

![ccal_fz](/image/mod/ccal.1_1.webp)

When you execute `x ccal`, it enters the `fzf`-based interactive calendar interface by default (equivalent to running `x ccal fz`).
This interface clearly displays the current month's Gregorian dates, with corresponding lunar dates, weekdays, festivals, and almanac "suitable" and "avoid" items marked alongside, making lunar information clear at a glance.

::: tip Interactive Feature Overview
`x ccal` has several practical interactive features:
:::

::::ul
:::li **Page Navigation**: Use `Ctrl-p` to jump to the previous month, `Ctrl-n` to jump to the next month.
:::li **Fuzzy Search**: Input Gregorian dates (e.g., `2023-10-01`), festival names (e.g., `Mid-Autumn Festival`, `Qingming`), or even fuzzy keywords. `fzf` can quickly locate them, greatly improving search efficiency.
:::li **View Switching**: Besides the default day view, x-cmd also provides **month view** and **year view**. You can switch between different views using TAB and ENTER.
::::

### Monthly Solar Terms and Holiday Overview (Month View)

In month view, you can see at a glance the 24 solar terms, holiday dates, and adjusted workdays for each month.
Besides switching via `TAB` in day view, you can also launch the month view interactive interface directly via the `fzm` subcommand.

```sh
x ccal fzm
```

![ccal_fzm](/image/mod/ccal.1_2.webp)

### Annual Festivals and Zodiac Overview (Year View)

If you want to view traditional festival dates for a specific year, the zodiac sign for that year, and whether there is a leap month, year view is your best choice.
Similarly, besides switching via `TAB` in other views, you can also launch the year view interactive interface directly via the `fzy` subcommand.

```sh
x ccal fzy
```

![ccal_fzy](/image/mod/ccal.1_3.webp)

## Query Detailed Information for Specific Dates

The interactive interface is suitable for browsing and searching, but if you only need to quickly get detailed "almanac" information for a specific day, including lunar date, stem-branch calendar, value star, almanac auspicious/inauspicious indicators, etc., the `info` subcommand is a more direct choice.

### View Today's Details

If you want to know today's detailed information, simply run the `info` subcommand without any parameters:

```sh
x ccal info
```

![ccal_i](/image/mod/ccal.1_4.webp)

This command outputs detailed "almanac" information for the current date. You'll see the Gregorian date, lunar date, stem-branch year/month/day, the day's value star, and most importantly - the "suitable" and "avoid" items from the almanac. This information is valuable for users who follow traditional customs.

### View Specific Date

The `info` subcommand also supports querying future or past specific dates.

```sh
x ccal info 2025-6-20
```

![ccal_info](/image/mod/ccal.1_5.webp)

Just add the date you want to query after `info` (format: `YYYY`,`YYYY-MM`,`YYYY-MM-DD`), and `x ccal` will present you with detailed calendar information for that day.

## Personalization: Customize Your `x ccal`

`x ccal` provides some configuration options, allowing you to adjust the display according to personal preferences. Use the `--cfg` option to view or modify these settings.

### Change Weekday Naming (`--cfg wdtitle`)

Some people are used to calling weekdays "Monday" (zhōuyī 周一), "Tuesday" (zhōuèr 周二), while others prefer "lǐbàiyī (礼拜一)", "lǐbàièr (礼拜二)". `x ccal` allows you to easily switch via the `--cfg` option.

```sh
x ccal --cfg wdtitle=libai
```

![ccal_cfg](/image/mod/ccal.1_6.webp)

This command changes the weekday display in the calendar from the default "zhōu (周)" to "lǐbài (礼拜)". You can view all configurable options and their current values via `x ccal --cfg`.

## More Information

Please visit our homepage for more information: https://x-cmd.com/mod/ccal
