# Put Claude Code in Your WeChat — Let AI Work for You Anytime

Compared to openclaw, `x claw` has three significant advantages:

- **Lightweight & Efficient**: Built in pure bash, small footprint, no dependencies required — deploys quickly on servers and in containers
- **Safe & Secure**: No network ports exposed, no firewall configuration needed — eliminates security risks from the source
- **Official Subscription Compatible**: Safely use Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, and other official subscription plans without risking account bans

## Quick Start

### Step 1: Connect to WeChat

```bash
x weixin login
```

![weixin](/image/mod/claw.1_2.webp)

A QR code will appear — scan it with WeChat to connect.

### Step 2: Start Claw

```bash
x claw start
```

### Step 3: Start Using

Simply send a message to Claude Code on WeChat, and `x claw` will automatically receive, process, and reply.

![run](/image/mod/claw.1_3.webp)

## FAQ

### Q: What if the service is interrupted unexpectedly?

`x claw` has a built-in auto-reconnect mechanism — it will resume receiving missed messages after service recovery with no data loss.

### Q: How do I view AI work records?

`x claw` saves every conversation and work result as Markdown files in the `memory/` directory of your local workspace — browse anytime for historical records.

### Q: Will using Claude Code or other official subscriptions get my account banned?

No. `x claw` invokes locally installed Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, and other official commands to execute tasks — this constitutes normal use of these official tools and does not violate subscription agreements.

### Q: How do I configure Claude Code to use other models?

If you want Claude Code to use **DeepSeek V4** or other models, please [refer to the integration guide](/mod/claude/cookbook-5.md).

### Q: How do I switch to Codex or Kimi CLI as the Agent engine?

Run the interactive setup command:

```bash
x agent init
```

Follow the prompts to select your target engine and complete the switch.

# Server Down? x claw Analyzes Root Cause Instantly, Pushes to Feishu

For SREs, DevOps engineers, or indie developers managing server stability, nothing is worse than getting an alert at 3 AM or having a service go down with no clue where to start debugging. Traditional monitoring is either too late — users are already affected — or the alerts are too bare to give any useful context.

## AI Monitoring & Alerting System

With x claw, you can turn Feishu into a **smart monitoring hub** — letting x claw watch your systems, analyze issues.

::::ul
:::li Automatic Anomaly Detection
A background script runs on your server; x claw continuously monitors CPU, memory, disk, API response times — triggering alerts the moment something goes wrong

:::li Intelligent Log Analysis
Once an anomaly is detected, x claw grabs the relevant log slices before and after, calls in a large language model for root cause analysis — determining whether it's an OOM, traffic spike, or infinite loop

:::li Feishu Rich Card Notifications
x claw compiles the analysis into a structured card: affected service, timestamp, core error message, x claw's conclusion, and recommended action — everything at a glance

:::li Remote Control from Your Phone
When the alert fires, no need to open a laptop — just reply with an command or tap a button in Feishu group to trigger a server-side script for restart or other operations
:::
::::

## Core Config

x claw supports multiple IM platforms. Refer to [Feishu AI Agent](/mod/claw/2-cn.md) for basic setup.

## Results

**Fault Response Time: Hours → Minutes**

1. OOM occurs — x claw detects it within 30 seconds
2. x claw captures relevant logs and analyzes: high concurrency caused memory overflow
3. Feishu group receives a rich alert card with full context and action plan
4. SRE handles it from phone with one-tap restart; service recovers in 2 minutes

**Human-in-the-Loop Safety**

- x claw provides analysis, humans make final decisions — avoiding the data corruption risk of blind automated restarts
- All remote operations are logged in the group — traceable and auditable

# Connect AI Agent to Feishu

When integrating AI with Feishu, many developers face a common problem: existing solutions (like openclaw) often require binding to their built-in Agent engine to process messages. But if your workflow heavily depends on local engines like Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex, this forced binding becomes a limitation.

The `x claw` + `x feishu` toolchain provided by **`x-cmd`** solves this problem: you decide how to receive Feishu messages and which AI engine (Claude / Codex / Kimi / Gemini) processes them — **you have full control**.

## Connect to Feishu Private Chat

The following steps integrate the AI Agent with Feishu private chat, turning the Agent into your personal AI assistant — chat with it directly in Feishu, and have it help you anytime.

### Step 1: Login to Feishu and Configure Bot

Run the following command and scan the QR code to login to Feishu:

```bash
x feishu login
```

<img src="/image/mod/claw.2_1.webp" alt="feishu login" style="max-width: 400px; width: 100%;" />

After scanning the QR code with the Feishu App, you'll be prompted to choose:

- **Select Existing Bot**: If you've created a Feishu bot before, you can select it directly
- **Create New Bot**: Choose this for first-time use, and the system will automatically create a Feishu bot

After successful login, the bot credentials (app_id and app_secret) are automatically saved, and the bot sends you a message to get the private chat id (required to start the private chat monitoring service).

### Step 2: Configure AI Agent

Run the interactive configuration command and select the Agent tool you want to use:

```bash
x agent init
```

- **Existing Configuration**: If you've previously configured Claude Code or Codex, you can select it directly from the list
- **First-time Configuration**: For first-time use, taking "Claude Code + Minimax" as an example, simply select `claude-minimax` in the TUI interface launched by x-cmd, enter your API Key, and press Enter to complete the configuration quickly

### Step 3: Connect to Feishu

After completing the above configuration, start the `claw` service with the following command to bridge Feishu messages with your selected AI Agent:

```bash
x claw start --feishu
```

After a successful connection, you can chat with it directly in your Feishu private chat window, making it your personal assistant for daily tasks.

## FAQ

### Q: Why is the AI sometimes slow to reply?

This is because x feishu uses an **Adaptive Polling** mechanism. To avoid hitting Feishu API rate limits and optimize resource usage, x feishu dynamically adjusts the message polling interval based on each group's recent activity:

| Group Activity | Time Since Last Message | Polling Interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active | Within 1 minute | 2 seconds |
| Normal | Within 5 minutes | 10 seconds |
| Inactive | Over 5 minutes | 30 seconds |

url: /mod/claw/cookbook-3.md

# Connect to Feishu Group Chats

This guide helps you quickly configure and start Feishu group chat monitoring. Follow the steps below to connect the bot to a Feishu group, and choose between **private chat commands** or **terminal commands** to control monitoring based on your preference.

## Prerequisites

Before starting group chat monitoring, make sure the following requirements are met:

- **Bot is added to the group chat**: First, add the bot to the Feishu group you want to monitor
- **App has the "Receive all messages in group" permission**: Apply for the `im:message.group_msg` app permission in the [Feishu Developer Console](https://open.feishu.cn/app)

![feishu scope](/image/mod/claw.2_2.webp)

Once the prerequisites are in place, you can choose one of the two methods below:

## Activate Group Chat Monitoring via Private Chat

> 💡 **Prerequisite for this method**: x claw must be running in the background with at least one IM platform connected — the private chat channel isn't limited to Feishu. You can send the command in **WeChat / Feishu / Telegram / WeChat Work** private chat to activate Feishu group monitoring. Setup guides: [WeChat](/mod/claw/cookbook-1.md) · [Feishu](/mod/claw/cookbook-2.md) · [WeChat Work](/mod/claw/cookbook-4.md) · [Telegram](/mod/claw/cookbook-5.md).

Just send it a command in private chat and it will open the channel in the background:

- **Enable monitoring for a specific group**: Tell it `"Help me enable monitoring for [Dev Tech Group]"`
- **Enable monitoring for all groups**: Tell it `"Enable monitoring for all my Feishu groups"`

## Manage Group Chat Connections via Terminal

If you prefer precise control from the local or server terminal, follow these steps:

### Step 1: Connect Group Chats

Based on your needs, choose the corresponding command:

- **Connect a specific group chat**:

```bash
# 1. Get the group ID (starts with oc_)
x feishu group ls
# 2. Replace the ID below with the one you just found, then run
x claw connect feishu:oc_xxx
```

- **Connect all group chats**:

```bash
x claw connect feishu:groups

```

### Step 2: Start or Check the Service

- **If `x claw` is not yet running**, run: `x claw start`
- **If `x claw` is already running**: No need to restart — go straight to the Feishu group and test the bot's response.

## FAQ

### Q: Why is the AI sometimes slow to reply?

This is because x feishu uses an **Adaptive Polling** mechanism. To avoid hitting Feishu API rate limits and optimize resource usage, x feishu dynamically adjusts the message polling interval based on each group's recent activity:

| Group Activity | Time Since Last Message | Polling Interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active | Within 1 minute | 2 seconds |
| Normal | Within 5 minutes | 10 seconds |
| Inactive | Over 5 minutes | 30 seconds |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> cron

Scheduled task management (wraps x cron)


::: tip 'x claw cron' wraps 'x cron'.
All subcommands except 'add' are passed through directly.

'add' performs basic validation: warns if command does not start with 'x claw agentrequest'.

The namespace is managed internally; do NOT attempt to override it.
:::

::: tip
Before adding your first task, confirm the user's timezone and use the tz subcommand if needed.
:::


## Examples

Example: Send morning report via WeChat daily at 9 AM (message includes Goal/Tools/Steps/Output/Delivery)

```sh
x claw cron add --name "morning-report" --desc "Morning Report" "0 9 * * *" "x claw agentrequest weixin clawbot '
  Complete the following task:
    Goal: Fetch HN top stories for morning report.
    Tools: x hn top.
    Steps:
      1) Get top 5 posts
      2) Extract title, URL, and score
      3) Format into a numbered list.
    Output: Numbered list.
    Delivery: x claw weixin send --chatid "<CHATID>" --text <result>
'

```



```sh
x claw cron tz CST-8
```

Example: Run an agent-generated backup script daily at 2 AM

```sh
x claw cron add --name "backup-daily" "0 2 * * *" "bash /path/to/agent-generated-backup.sh"
```

Example: Push Guangzhou Baiyun weather forecast daily at 8 AM

```sh
x claw cron add --name "weather-guangzhou" --desc "Baiyun Weather Forecast" "0 8 * * *" "x claw agentrequest weixin clawbot '
  Complete the following task:
    Goal: Get weather for Baiyun, Guangzhou and push to user.
    Tools: x wttr Baiyun,Guangzhou.
    Steps:
      1) Query weather for Baiyun, Guangzhou
      2) Summarize temperature, condition, and clothing advice
      3) Format into readable text.
    Output: Plain text weather broadcast.
    Delivery: x claw weixin send --chatid "<CHATID>" --text <result>
'

```

Example: Remove the morning-report task

```sh
x claw cron rm --name "morning-report"
```

Example: List all scheduled tasks

```sh
x claw cron ls
```

Example: Test if the expression matches current time

```sh
x claw cron match "0 9 * * *"
```

Example: Execute the morning-report task immediately

```sh
x claw cron exec --name "morning-report"
```

Example: Set timezone to Asia/Shanghai

```sh
x claw cron tz Asia/Shanghai
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x claw cron add](#x-claw-cron-add) | Add a scheduled task. The 2nd argument MUST be an executable command string. |
| [x claw cron rm](#x-claw-cron-rm) | Remove a scheduled task |
| [x claw cron ls](#x-claw-cron-ls) | List all tasks |
| [x claw cron match](#x-claw-cron-match) | Test if a given time matches a cron expression |
| [x claw cron run](#x-claw-cron-run) | Run the cron daemon in foreground |
| [x claw cron exec](#x-claw-cron-exec) | Execute a task's command directly (ignore schedule, for testing) |
| [x claw cron tz](#x-claw-cron-tz) | Set or view the timezone |
| [x claw cron history](#x-claw-cron-history) | View task execution details (omitting timestamp shows the most recent run) |


### x claw cron add

Add a scheduled task. The 2nd argument MUST be an executable command string.



::: tip The 2nd argument (command) MUST be an executable string, not an interactive TTY command.
To notify the user or spawn an AI Agent: use 'x claw agentrequest &lt;im&gt; &lt;chatid&gt; '&lt;msg&gt;''.

&lt;msg&gt; goes to a NEW agent with ZERO memory, so it MUST include: Goal, Tools, Steps, Output, and Delivery.

For standalone tasks (no Agent/message): use any executable command, e.g. 'bash /path/to/agent-generated-backup.sh'.
:::

::: tip
Before adding your first task, confirm the user's timezone and use the tz subcommand if needed.
:::


- **Examples**:

Example: Send morning report via WeChat daily at 9 AM (message includes Goal/Tools/Steps/Output/Delivery)

```sh
x claw cron add --name "morning-report" --desc "Morning Report" "0 9 * * *" "x claw agentrequest weixin clawbot '
  Complete the following task:
    Goal: Fetch HN top stories for morning report.
    Tools: x hn top.
    Steps:
      1) Get top 5 posts
      2) Extract title, URL, and score
      3) Format into a numbered list.
    Output: Numbered list.
    Delivery: x claw weixin send --chatid "<CHATID>" --text <result>
'

```

Example: Run an agent-generated backup script daily at 2 AM

```sh
x claw cron add --name "backup-daily" "0 2 * * *" "bash /path/to/agent-generated-backup.sh"
```

Example: Push Guangzhou Baiyun weather forecast daily at 8 AM

```sh
x claw cron add --name "weather-guangzhou" --desc "Baiyun Weather Forecast" "0 8 * * *" "x claw agentrequest weixin clawbot '
  Complete the following task:
    Goal: Get weather for Baiyun, Guangzhou and push to user.
    Tools: x wttr Baiyun,Guangzhou.
    Steps:
      1) Query weather for Baiyun, Guangzhou
      2) Summarize temperature, condition, and clothing advice
      3) Format into readable text.
    Output: Plain text weather broadcast.
    Delivery: x claw weixin send --chatid "<CHATID>" --text <result>
'

```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw cron add [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Cron expression (e.g. '0 9 * * *') |
| `#2` | Command to execute. Usually 'x claw agentrequest &lt;im&gt; &lt;chatid&gt; "&lt;msg&gt;"'
to spawn an AI Agent and notify the user. If no Agent/message needed, must still be an executable command (not interactive).
 |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--name` | Task name (must be unique) |
| `--desc` | Task description |
| `--once` | Run once and auto-delete after execution |


### x claw cron rm

Remove a scheduled task


- **Examples**:

Example: Remove the morning-report task

```sh
x claw cron rm --name "morning-report"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw cron rm [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--name` | Task name |


### x claw cron ls

List all tasks


- **Examples**:

Example: List all scheduled tasks

```sh
x claw cron ls
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw cron ls
```

### x claw cron match

Test if a given time matches a cron expression


- **Examples**:

Example: Test if the expression matches current time

```sh
x claw cron match "0 9 * * *"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw cron match
```

### x claw cron run

Run the cron daemon in foreground


- **Examples**:

Example: Start cron daemon in foreground

```sh
x claw cron run
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw cron run
```

### x claw cron exec

Execute a task's command directly (ignore schedule, for testing)


- **Examples**:

Example: Execute the morning-report task immediately

```sh
x claw cron exec --name "morning-report"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw cron exec [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--name` | Task name |


### x claw cron tz

Set or view the timezone


- **Examples**:

Example: Set timezone to Asia/Shanghai

```sh
x claw cron tz Asia/Shanghai
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw cron tz
```

### x claw cron history

View task execution details (omitting timestamp shows the most recent run)


- **Examples**:

Example: View the most recent execution details of the morning-report task

```sh
x claw cron history morning-report
```

Example: View execution details of morning-report at the specified timestamp

```sh
x claw cron history morning-report 1752300000
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw cron history <#1> <#2>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Task name |
| `#2` | Execution timestamp (unix epoch), omit to show the most recent run |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> disconnect

Disconnect from IM platform(s) and stop the message listener. Supports multiple platforms at once.

## Examples

Scenario: Temporarily disconnect WeChat, Telegram, and Feishu groups while keeping the service running

```sh
x claw disconnect weixin telegram feishu:groups
```

Scenario: Disconnect only a specific Feishu group without affecting others

```sh
x claw disconnect feishu:oc_xxx
```

Scenario: Disconnect all WeChat connections entirely

```sh
x claw disconnect weixin
```

## Usage

```sh
x claw disconnect <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | IM platform identifier, multiple allowed. Same format as connect: `im` or `im:chatid`.
Omitting chatid disconnects all connections for that platform.
<br>`weixin` &#124; `telegram` &#124; `qywx` &#124; `feishu` &#124; `feishu:groups` |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> feishu

Feishu message query tools

## Examples

Scenario: Send a text message to the Feishu chat with chatid mychatid

```sh
x claw feishu send --chatid mychatid --text 'hello'
```

Scenario: Batch review messages line 100-200 for chatid mychatid

```sh
x claw feishu get-msg mychatid 100:200
```

Scenario: After processing 100 messages, update read offset for this chatid

```sh
x claw feishu update-offset mychatid 100
```

Scenario: Get unread count for chatid to decide whether to spawn an Agent

```sh
x claw feishu unread-count mychatid
```

Scenario: Conditional read — fetch messages only when unread detected (has-unread uses exit code 0/1)

```sh
if x claw feishu has-unread mychatid; then
    x claw feishu recent-msg mychatid
fi

```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x claw feishu get-msg](#x-claw-feishu-get-msg) | Get messages by line range |
| [x claw feishu unread-count](#x-claw-feishu-unread-count) | Show unread message count (outputs number to stdout) |
| [x claw feishu recent-msg](#x-claw-feishu-recent-msg) | Show all recent unread messages |
| [x claw feishu has-unread](#x-claw-feishu-has-unread) | Check if there are unread messages. Exit code 0 means yes, 1 means no. No stdout output; consume the exit code with if or &&/&#124;&#124; in scripts. |
| [x claw feishu send](#x-claw-feishu-send) | Send text/image/file messages |
| [x claw feishu update-offset](#x-claw-feishu-update-offset) | Update the read offset to the specified line number, marking messages up to that line as read |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> init

Initialize the AI Agent configuration required by claw (runs x agent init internally)


::: tip Initialize the agent configuration before first use.
You can also run `x agent init` directly for the same result.

In non-interactive environments, claw will try to invoke this automatically if the agent is not ready.
:::


## Examples

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> log

Show gateway service log (sorted by timeline)


::: tip Logs include message processing and heartbeat records for all IM platforms.
Shows the last 50 log entries by default, then follows live output.

Supports multi-line entries (e.g. Agent output).

`D|claw:` debug logs are hidden by default; use --debug to show them.

Heartbeat logs are prefixed with [HB] for easy identification.
:::


## Examples

Scenario: View the last 50 log entries in real time to troubleshoot recent message handling or heartbeat issues

```sh
x claw log
```

Scenario: View logs from the last 30 minutes

```sh
x claw log --since 30m
```

Scenario: View the last 100 log entries

```sh
x claw log --last 100
```

Scenario: View full historical logs

```sh
x claw log --all
```

Scenario: View full logs including claw debug information

```sh
x claw log --debug
```

## Usage

```sh
x claw log [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--since` |  | Show logs since the given time |
| `--last` |  | Show only the last N top-level log entries |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--all` | Output full history (default shows last 50 entries) |
| `--debug` | Show claw module debug logs (hidden by default) |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> manager

Default subcommand of x claw. Talk to the core administrator to manage IM platforms, chat history, and scheduled tasks.


::: tip Type x claw to enter this mode.
In interactive mode, describe complex needs directly, e.g. "track x-cmd GitHub issues and notify me of updates".

Single-shot mode gets it done in one sentence, e.g. x claw 'what are the important messages in the Feishu group today'.
:::


## Examples

First-time setup — one sentence and AI connects your IM platforms

```sh
x claw
> "我刚装好，帮我连上微信和飞书群"

```

Let AI monitor news daily and push relevant content to you

```sh
x claw
> "每天早上 8 点帮我扫一遍 Hacker News 和 GitHub Trending，有 AI 相关的推给我"

```

Vibe coding: hand off dev tasks to AI and get notified when done

```sh
x claw
> "帮我重构这个模块，不用等我，搞完通知我"
> "issue #123 那个功能，帮我实现一下，后台跑，搞完通知我"

```

Cross-platform: summarize from one group and push to others

```sh
x claw
> "把飞书群今天的重要讨论整理成公告，发到企业微信和 Telegram"

```

Quick task: summarize discussions and extract action items in one sentence

```sh
x claw '总结一下飞书群今天的讨论，把待办事项列出来'
```

## Usage

```sh
x claw manager
```

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> qywx

Qywx message query tools

## Examples

Scenario: Send a text message to the Qywx chat with chatid mychatid

```sh
x claw qywx send --chatid mychatid --text 'hello'
```

Scenario: Batch review messages line 100-200 for chatid mychatid

```sh
x claw qywx get-msg mychatid 100:200
```

Scenario: After processing 100 messages, update read offset for this chatid

```sh
x claw qywx update-offset mychatid 100
```

Scenario: Get unread count for chatid to decide whether to spawn an Agent

```sh
x claw qywx unread-count mychatid
```

Scenario: Conditional read — fetch messages only when unread detected (has-unread uses exit code 0/1)

```sh
if x claw qywx has-unread mychatid; then
    x claw qywx recent-msg mychatid
fi

```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x claw qywx get-msg](#x-claw-qywx-get-msg) | Get messages by line range |
| [x claw qywx unread-count](#x-claw-qywx-unread-count) | Show unread message count (outputs number to stdout) |
| [x claw qywx recent-msg](#x-claw-qywx-recent-msg) | Show all recent unread messages |
| [x claw qywx has-unread](#x-claw-qywx-has-unread) | Check if there are unread messages. Exit code 0 means yes, 1 means no. No stdout output; consume the exit code with if or &&/&#124;&#124; in scripts. |
| [x claw qywx send](#x-claw-qywx-send) | Send text/image/file messages |
| [x claw qywx update-offset](#x-claw-qywx-update-offset) | Update the read offset to the specified line number, marking messages up to that line as read |


### x claw qywx get-msg

Get messages by line range


- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw qywx get-msg <#1> <#2> <#3>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Qywx chatid |
| `#2` | Line range (e.g. 100:200) or start line |
| `#3` | End line number (optional, used with start line) |


### x claw qywx unread-count

Show unread message count (outputs number to stdout)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw qywx unread-count <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Qywx chatid |


### x claw qywx recent-msg

Show all recent unread messages


- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw qywx recent-msg <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Qywx chatid |


### x claw qywx has-unread

Check if there are unread messages. Exit code 0 means yes, 1 means no. No stdout output; consume the exit code with if or &&/&#124;&#124; in scripts.


- **Examples**:

Scenario: Poll and read only when unread exists, avoiding empty runs

```sh
if x claw qywx has-unread mychatid; then
    x claw qywx recent-msg mychatid
fi

```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw qywx has-unread <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Qywx chatid |

Send a file to the specified chat

| Name | Description |

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> restart

Restart the x claw background service and reconnect IM platforms


::: tip Restart the x-claw-service daemon and restore all active IM connections.
If no IM chat is active, no platform will be connected automatically.

Use `x claw connect <im>` / `x claw disconnect <im>` to manage connections.
:::


## Examples

Scenario: Restart service and restore active IM connections

```sh
x claw restart
```

Scenario: Restart the gateway after configuration changes

```sh
x claw restart
```

## Usage

```sh
x claw restart
```

# <span class="flex items-center justify-between gap-1"><span>x claw</span> <span class="text-x-brand">🔥</span></span> service

Manage the x claw background service


::: tip Service operations can also be invoked directly via x claw start/stop/restart/status/log.
Use install/uninstall to register or remove startup service entries.
:::


## Examples

Example: Start the claw background service

```sh
x claw service start
```

Example: Register claw as a startup service

```sh
x claw service install
```

Example: Remove claw from startup services

```sh
x claw service uninstall
```

Example: Check claw service status

```sh
x claw service status
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x claw service start](#x-claw-service-start) | Start the x claw background service |
| [x claw service stop](#x-claw-service-stop) | Stop the x claw background service |
| [x claw service restart](#x-claw-service-restart) | Restart the x claw background service |
| [x claw service status](#x-claw-service-status) | Show x claw service status |
| [x claw service log](#x-claw-service-log) | Show x claw service logs |
| [x claw service install](#x-claw-service-install) | Register x claw as a startup service |
| [x claw service uninstall](#x-claw-service-uninstall) | Remove x claw from startup services |


### x claw service start

Start the x claw background service



::: tip Start only the x-claw-service daemon; no IM platform is connected automatically.
After startup, connect a platform with `x claw connect <im>`, e.g.:

  x claw connect weixin

  x claw connect telegram

  x claw connect qywx

  x claw connect feishu:groups

  x claw connect feishu:oc_xxx

If active IM chats exist, the service heartbeat will keep them alive.

Otherwise, a recommended ready platform will be logged.
:::


- **Examples**:

Scenario: Start the claw background service

```sh
x claw start
```

Scenario: Manually connect WeChat after starting the service

```sh
x claw connect weixin
```

Scenario: Manually connect all Feishu groups after starting the service

```sh
x claw connect feishu:groups
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw service start
```

### x claw service stop

Stop the x claw background service



::: tip
Stop the X-Claw background service and heartbeat worker. To disconnect IM platforms, use `x claw disconnect`.
:::


- **Examples**:

Scenario: Fully stop the claw background service and heartbeat worker

```sh
x claw stop
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw service stop
```

### x claw service restart

Restart the x claw background service



::: tip Restart the x-claw-service daemon and restore all active IM connections.
If no IM chat is active, no platform will be connected automatically.

Use `x claw connect <im>` / `x claw disconnect <im>` to manage connections.
:::


- **Examples**:

Scenario: Restart service and restore active IM connections

```sh
x claw restart
```

Scenario: Restart the gateway after configuration changes

```sh
x claw restart
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw service restart
```

### x claw service status

Show x claw service status



::: tip Defaults to a human-friendly block format with Overview / Heartbeat / IM Connections / Cron Jobs.
Use `x claw status --yaml` for machine-readable output.
:::


- **Examples**:

Scenario: Quickly check if the gateway is running and review IM connections and Agent status

```sh
x claw status
```

Scenario: Output YAML for script parsing

```sh
x claw status --yaml
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw service status [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--yaml` | Output machine-readable YAML (same as the legacy x claw status behavior) |


### x claw service log

Show x claw service logs



::: tip Logs include message processing and heartbeat records for all IM platforms.
Shows the last 50 log entries by default, then follows live output.

Supports multi-line entries (e.g. Agent output).

`D|claw:` debug logs are hidden by default; use --debug to show them.

Heartbeat logs are prefixed with [HB] for easy identification.
:::


- **Examples**:

Scenario: View the last 50 log entries in real time to troubleshoot recent message handling or heartbeat issues

```sh
x claw log
```

Scenario: View logs from the last 30 minutes

```sh
x claw log --since 30m
```

Scenario: View the last 100 log entries

```sh
x claw log --last 100
```

Scenario: View full historical logs

```sh
x claw log --all
```

Scenario: View full logs including claw debug information

```sh
x claw log --debug
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw service log [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--since` |  | Show logs since the given time |
| `--last` |  | Show only the last N top-level log entries |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--all` | Output full history (default shows last 50 entries) |
| `--debug` | Show claw module debug logs (hidden by default) |


### x claw service install

Register x claw as a startup service



::: tip If the service is not running, it will be started before registration.
After registration, claw will auto-start on system boot.
:::


- **Examples**:

Example: Register claw as a startup service

```sh
x claw service install
```

Example: Enable auto-start after deployment

```sh
x claw service install
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw service install
```

### x claw service uninstall

Remove x claw from startup services



::: tip
The service will no longer auto-start on boot, but a currently running service is not stopped.
:::


- **Examples**:

Example: Remove claw from startup services

```sh
x claw service uninstall
```

Example: Clean up startup entries before uninstalling

```sh
x claw service uninstall
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x claw service uninstall
```

Scenario: Batch review messages line 100-200 for chatid mychatid

```sh
x claw weixin get-msg mychatid 100:200
```

Scenario: After processing 100 messages, update read offset for this chatid

```sh
x claw weixin update-offset mychatid 100
```

Scenario: Get unread count for chatid to decide whether to spawn an Agent

```sh
x claw weixin unread-count mychatid
```

Scenario: Conditional read — fetch messages only when unread detected (has-unread uses exit code 0/1)

```sh
if x claw weixin has-unread mychatid; then
    x claw weixin recent-msg mychatid
fi

```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x claw weixin send](#x-claw-weixin-send) | Send text/image/file/video messages. Note: the underlying `x weixin bot send` does not yet support `--chatid`, so all messages are still sent by a single WeChat account; `--chatid` is only used by claw to isolate sent records per chat. |
| [x claw weixin get-sent](#x-claw-weixin-get-sent) | Get sent message history for the specified chatid |
| [x claw weixin get-msg](#x-claw-weixin-get-msg) | Get messages by line range |
| [x claw weixin unread-count](#x-claw-weixin-unread-count) | Show unread message count (outputs number to stdout) |
| [x claw weixin recent-msg](#x-claw-weixin-recent-msg) | Show all recent unread messages |
| [x claw weixin has-unread](#x-claw-weixin-has-unread) | Check if there are unread messages. Exit code 0 means yes, 1 means no. No stdout output; consume the exit code with if or &&/&#124;&#124; in scripts. |
| [x claw weixin update-offset](#x-claw-weixin-update-offset) | Update the read offset to the specified line number, marking messages up to that line as read |

# `x codex` - Zero Barrier to Use Codex, One Command to Connect DeepSeek/Kimi/Zhipu, Turn Your Terminal into an Intelligent Programming Assistant!

This guide will help you understand x codex's common features in minutes and quickly get started with OpenAI Codex, experiencing the powerful capabilities of an intelligent AI programming agent.

## 1. Zero Barrier! Auto-Install and Launch OpenAI Codex

::: tip
You don't need to manually install Codex
:::

**You don't need to manually install Codex**. When you run the x codex command, x-cmd automatically detects whether Codex is installed in the current environment.
If not yet installed, x-cmd will automatically download, install, and configure it for you, with no manual operation required throughout the process. No need to manually deploy Node.js or handle dependency installation.

## 2. Model Freedom! Connect ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Kimi, Zhipu, and More AI Models

### Connect ChatGPT Models

Codex uses ChatGPT series models (such as gpt-5-codex, gpt-5, etc.) by default. To use these models, you need to log in with a ChatGPT account or configure an API Key.

Login method: When you first run x codex, the system will automatically prompt you to log in. You can choose either of the following methods:

::::ul
:::li ChatGPT Account Login
Suitable for ChatGPT Plus or Team subscription users. Simply log in with your ChatGPT account, no additional configuration needed
:::

:::li API Key Connection
Suitable for developers and enterprise users. Billed by actual usage, can provide higher concurrency and call quotas
:::
::::

![1](/image/mod/codex.1_1.webp)

After login is complete, your credentials will be automatically encrypted and saved locally. No need to repeat login for subsequent use, the system will automatically read the saved credential information.

### Connect DeepSeek/Kimi and Other Models

::: warning Important Notice
Starting from Codex v0.80.0+, Codex uses the Responses API as the sole inference interface and no longer supports the chat/completions API. If your target model does not support the Responses API (such as DeepSeek), please use one of the following solutions:

1. **Downgrade Version**: Use `x env use codex=v0.80.0` to downgrade to an older version
2. **Alternative**: Use Claude Code with your target model

Related Discussions:
- [x-cmd/issues/363](https://github.com/x-cmd/x-cmd/issues/363)
- [openai/codex/discussions/7782](https://github.com/openai/codex/discussions/7782)
:::

Besides ChatGPT series models, x codex also supports connecting other AI models as the backend driver for Codex.

For example, you can easily switch Codex to use the DeepSeek model:
```bash
x deepseek init
x codex ds
```

![2](/image/mod/codex.1_2.webp)

After executing the above commands, Codex will automatically use the DeepSeek model for dialogue and programming assistance. Similarly, you can also connect Kimi, Zhipu, and other models as needed.

::: info
For more detailed model connection methods, please refer to the corresponding documentation
:::

For more detailed model connection methods, please refer to the corresponding documentation:
- [Connect DeepSeek Model](/mod/codex/cookbook-2.md)

## 3. Extend AI Skills! Manage Codex Agent Skills with x-cmd

Codex officially supports the Agent Skills mechanism, allowing your Codex to better handle specific complex tasks through extended Skills, such as writing technical documents following brand guidelines, performing advanced data analysis, or reviewing code according to best practices. You can manage these Skills through the `skill` command of the `x codex` module. Here are common usage examples:

1. Query available professional skills (Skills): You can use the `x codex skill ll` command to query the list of Agent Skills shared by the **x-cmd platform and community**.
2. Add professional skills for Claude Code: After determining the needed skills, use the `x codex skill use` command to quickly install from remote repositories or local paths.

For more content about `x codex skill`, please refer to the following article:
- [x codex skill - AI Agent Professional Skill Management](/mod/codex.md)

# `x codex ds` - No need for a ChatGPT account! Zero threshold for connecting Codex to the DeepSeek AI model

The DeepSeek V4 series now supports the OpenAI Responses API, so Codex can use DeepSeek directly as its backend model. If you experience access, latency, or cost issues with the OpenAI model, switching to DeepSeek offers a more stable and lower-cost option.

## Get a DeepSeek API Key

::::ol
:::li Register and sign in to the DeepSeek platform
Visit the [DeepSeek platform](https://platform.deepseek.com/api_keys) to create an account.
:::

:::li Create an API key
Generate a new key on the "API Keys" page. It is recommended to create separate keys for different projects to make management and usage tracking easier.
:::
::::

## Launch Codex with DeepSeek

Once the key is configured, start Codex with the x-cmd shortcut.

::::ol
:::li Configure DeepSeek in x-cmd
```bash
x deepseek init
# Or set manually: x deepseek --cfg apikey="<your_api_key>"
```
:::

:::li Launch Codex
```bash
x codex ds
```
:::
::::

You can also start it directly via an environment variable:

```bash
export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY="<your_deepseek_api_key>"
x codex ds
```

`x codex ds` uses the `deepseek-v4-flash` model by default and connects to the DeepSeek Responses API endpoint at `https://api.deepseek.com`. The agent workflow and CLI interaction are almost identical to the native ChatGPT model.

## How is this different from the official DeepSeek setup script?

The official DeepSeek setup guide usually asks you to edit `~/.codex/config.toml` and `models.json` directly, writing the DeepSeek model and provider entries into the global configuration. This works, but has some downsides:

- **It modifies your existing configuration**: if `~/.codex/config.toml` already contains custom `model`, `provider`, approval policies, MCP, hooks, and so on, editing it directly can break those settings.
- **Switching models is cumbersome**: to go back to OpenAI, you need to edit the configuration again.

`x codex ds` takes a different approach by using Codex's `--config` argument to pass DeepSeek settings as **overrides for the current launch only**:

- **No global config changes**: only the current Codex process is affected; your original `config.toml` and `models.json` remain untouched.
- **OpenAI and DeepSeek can coexist**: running `x codex` normally still uses your OpenAI configuration, while `x codex ds` temporarily switches to DeepSeek.

# `x codex zhipu` - Say Goodbye to ChatGPT Limitations, Enable Codex to Seamlessly Access the Zhipu GLM Model

::: warning Important Notice
Starting from Codex v0.80.0+, Codex uses the Responses API as the sole inference interface and no longer supports the chat/completions API. If your target model does not support the Responses API, please use one of the following solutions:

1. **Downgrade Version**: Use `x env use codex=v0.80.0` to downgrade to an older version
2. **Alternative**: Use Claude Code with your target model

Related Discussions:
- [x-cmd/issues/363](https://github.com/x-cmd/x-cmd/issues/363)
- [openai/codex/discussions/7782](https://github.com/openai/codex/discussions/7782)
:::

By default, Codex uses the ChatGPT series of models (such as GPT-4, GPT-3.5). However, for domestic users, accessing ChatGPT may face network or account restrictions. At this point, you can choose to access the GLM series models provided by Zhipu AI.

Zhipu AI is one of the leading large model providers in the country, with its GLM models (such as GLM-4.5, GLM-4.5-Air, GLM-4.5-Flash, etc.) demonstrating outstanding performance in tasks like general understanding, code generation, and knowledge Q&A. By using the `x codex zhipu` command, you can switch Codex to the Zhipu models, allowing you to enjoy faster responses and lower network barriers in domestic environments (no need for VPNs or overseas accounts)!

## Get Zhipu API Key

1. Visit the [Zhipu AI Open Platform](https://bigmodel.cn/usercenter/proj-mgmt/apikeys) to register.

2. After registering your account, create a new key on the “API Keys” page. It is advisable to create different API Keys for different projects to facilitate management and usage tracking.

## Start Codex and Access Zhipu AI Model

Once you have obtained your key, you can import it into x-cmd's configuration or enable it via environment variables.

* Sample configuration and startup:

```bash
# Configure Zhipu API key
x zhipu init
# You can also configure the API Key for Zhipu via x-cmd -> x zhipu --cfg apikey="<your_api>"

# Start Codex and access Zhipu AI model
x codex zhipu
```

* Alternatively, use the environment variable approach:

```bash
export CODEX_API_KEY="<your_zhipu_api_key>"
x codex zhipu
```

Once configured, Codex will use the Zhipu model to handle your programming requests. The functionality remains almost identical to that of the native ChatGPT models, and the entire proxy process and command line interaction logic remains the same, so there’s no need to learn a new way to interact.

# `x codex skill` - Aggregating community wisdom, enabling your AI assistant to instantly master parsing and automation capabilities.

**Skill** is an extension of the capabilities of an AI assistant. If we consider the large model as the "brain," then Skill is its "toolbox." Through the x codex skill command, you can quickly obtain ready-made skills (such as document parsing, code analysis, API calls, etc.) from the x-cmd community and seamlessly integrate them into your workflow.

## Discover Skills: Explore Community Wisdom

Before you begin, you can browse the pre-set skill library in the x-cmd community. These skills have been deeply optimized for various productivity scenarios.

```bash
# Query the list of community-shared Agent Skills
x codex skill ll
```

![1](/image/mod/codex.4_1.webp)

- Identify Identifiers: The list will display identifiers such as anthropics/docx (Word parsing) or anthropics/frontend-design (frontend design), etc.

- View Details: You can quickly locate a suitable Skill for your current task through this command.

## Install Skills: Plug and Play

When you find a skill that meets your project needs, use the add command to achieve "one-click enhancement."

```bash
# Add the docx deep parsing skill to the current project
x codex skill add anthropics/docx
```

- Automated Operation: This command will automatically create a `.codex/skills` directory and download the related files for the anthropics/docx skill into it.
- Zero Configuration Loading: There is no need to modify any global configuration. When you run x codex, the AI will automatically scan this directory and "awaken" the relevant capabilities.

## Manage Skills: Keep Your Project Lightweight

As your project evolves, you may need to clean up or update your toolbox.

### View Installed Skills

Confirm what "superpowers" the AI has in the current project environment:

```bash
x codex skill ls
```

### Remove Unnecessary Skills

Keep your project tidy and avoid interference by having too many skills when the AI processes simple tasks:

```bash
x codex skill rm anthropics/docx
```

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

### Q: Can I customize skills?

Of course! You just need to create a folder under `.codex/skills` and write an execution script and SKILL.md.

### Q: Can I add skills directly from a GitHub URL?

The `x codex skill add` command is constantly evolving and will support adding skills directly through a GitHub URL or private Git repository address in the future.

# x codex deepseek

Launch codex and connect to the DeepSeek model.


::: tip
By default, it uses the `x deepseek` module to configure the model and API key. You can run `x deepseek init` to switch models or reconfigure your API key.
:::

::: tip
Codex will deprecate chat/completions API from v0.80.0+, only responses API is supported. To continue using models that don't support responses API, run `x env use codex=v0.80.0` to downgrade.
:::


## Examples

The API key for deepseek is configured interactively. This particular configuration will be utilized by the codex module and will concurrently be applied to various Large Language Model (LLM) application modules, including deepseek, and claude.

```sh
x deepseek init
```

With a single command, DeepSeek's API key can be directly configured. This specific configuration will then be employed by the codex module and will furthermore be extended to various other LLM application modules, including deepseek, and claude.

```sh
x deepseek --cfg apikey="<your api key>"
```

Launch codex and connect to the DeepSeek model.

```sh
x codex ds
```

## Usage

```sh
x codex deepseek|ds
```

# x coin - CoinCap Platform Information Viewer

The `x coin` module is a powerful command-line tool for conveniently accessing and viewing cryptocurrency information from the CoinCap platform. Without tedious web operations, you can get the data you need with simple commands.

::: tip
Due to the unavailability of the dependent Public API, the coin module is currently unavailable. We are looking for alternative solutions, please stay tuned
:::

## Quick Start

After installing `x-cmd`, you can directly use the `x coin` command. This module provides multiple ways to view CoinCap platform information: interactive application, CSV format, and JSON format.

### Interactive Application (`--app`)

Want to view data more intuitively? Use the `--app` parameter to launch the interactive application:

```bash
x coin --app
```

This application provides a friendly interface for you to easily browse real-time information of various cryptocurrencies.


### CSV Format (`--csv`)

If you need to import data into spreadsheets or other data analysis tools, you can use the `--csv` parameter to export data in CSV format:

```bash
x coin --csv > coin_data.csv
```

This saves CoinCap platform cryptocurrency information to the `coin_data.csv` file.


### JSON Format (`--json`)

If you prefer JSON format data, you can use the `--json` parameter:

```bash
x coin --json
```

This outputs CoinCap platform cryptocurrency information in JSON format, convenient for programmatic processing.


## Advanced Usage (May Be Supported in Future)

Future versions may add more advanced features, such as:

:::: ul
::: li **Filtering and sorting**
Narrow or order rows by metrics such as market cap or price.
:::
::: li **Custom fields**
Choose which columns to print so the table stays compact.
:::
::: li **Refresh cadence**
Let heavy users tune how often quotes refresh.
:::
::::

## Error Handling and Prompts

The `x coin` module strives to handle various error situations and provides friendly prompt messages. For example, network connection failures or API request errors will have corresponding prompts.


## More Information

Please visit our homepage for more information: [https://x-cmd.com](https://x-cmd.com)


Hope this brief introduction helps you quickly get started with the `x coin` module. If you have any questions or suggestions, please feel free to contact us.

# x colr: Your Terminal Color Assistant

`x colr` is a powerful command-line tool for easily finding and using colors in the terminal. It supports multiple color systems including 8-color, 256-color, and RGB, and provides various features to help you find the right colors and display them in different ways.

## Quick Start

Using `x colr` is very simple. The most basic usage is to run `x colr` directly, which lists all colors in the 256-color palette with their codes and approximate colors.

```bash
x colr
```

Want to view the 8-color palette? Just run:

```bash
x colr 8
```

## Find Similar Colors

The power of `x colr` lies in its ability to find similar colors based on color names or codes you provide. For example, to find colors similar to green:

```bash
x colr ls green
```

You can also use RGB color codes:

```bash
x colr rgb(0, 128, 0)  # Or use hex #008000
```

Or, directly input hex color codes:

```bash
x colr #008000
```


## Advanced Usage: Rainbow Effects and Custom Ranges

`x colr` also supports generating rainbow-colored output and allows you to customize color ranges and steps:

```bash
x colr rainbow --min 100 --max 200 --step 50
```

This generates a rainbow output with minimum RGB value 100, maximum RGB value 200, and step size 50. You can adjust the `--min`, `--max`, and `--step` parameters as needed. The `--color` parameter can specify using true color or 256-color. The `--norand` parameter can disable random color generation.


## Preset Color Schemes

`x colr` provides some preset color schemes, such as:

::::ul
::: li **`--blue`**: Display approximate colors for blue, cyan, and turquoise
:::
::: li **`--pink`**: Display approximate colors for purple, pink, and magenta
:::
::: li **`--purple`**: Display approximate colors for blue, purple, and magenta
:::
::: li **`--red`**: Display approximate colors for red, maroon, and pink
:::
::: li **`--yellow`**: Display approximate colors for yellow and orange
:::
::: li **`--green`**: Display approximate colors for green, teal, olive, and lime
:::
::: li **`--gray`**: Display approximate colors for gray
:::
::: li **`--black`**: Display approximate colors for gray and black
:::
::: li **`--white`**: Display approximate colors for gray and white
:::
::::


For example, to view approximate colors for red:

```bash
x colr --red
```


## Summary

`x colr` is a powerful color tool that helps you easily handle colors in the terminal. Whether finding similar colors, generating rainbow effects, or using preset color schemes, `x colr` meets your needs and makes your terminal more colorful. Try it out, you'll find it very useful in shell scripts and terminal applications.

# C Language "Compile Once, Run Anywhere"? A Must-See Ultimate Solution for C Developers | Cosmopolitan

In modern software development, **cross-platform building and distribution** has always been a difficult problem to completely solve. While many languages and frameworks provide cross-platform capabilities, most require sacrificing performance or relying on large runtime environments. C/C++, as high-performance system languages, although irreplaceable in low-level control and execution efficiency, require tedious multi-platform compilation and packaging processes when building and distributing cross-platform.

**Cosmopolitan C Library** (abbreviated as Cosmopolitan or Cosmo) was born in this context. Developed by Justine Tunney, its goal is to compile C programs into a special binary format - APE (Actually Portable Executable). Files in this format can run natively on **Windows, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, and even BIOS**, truly achieving "compile once, run anywhere".

## Core Value of Cosmopolitan

Cosmopolitan mainly solves the following problems:

::::ul
:::li **Unified Distribution**: Developers only need to build one binary file that can run directly on multiple operating systems, reducing the cost of maintaining multi-platform build systems.
:::li **Zero Dependencies**: No virtual machine or interpreter needed, generating native binary files that are lighter and more efficient.
:::li **Performance Guarantee**: Compared to other libc implementations, Cosmopolitan adopts vectorized optimization in basic libraries such as string processing, and common CLI tools can even achieve higher performance.
::::

## Running Cosmopolitan Applications

To lower the barrier to using Cosmopolitan, **x-cmd** provides the `x cosmo` module, which offers unified running, installation, and management capabilities for Cosmopolitan-compiled applications. Compared to manually downloading and calling APE files directly, `x cosmo` is closer to daily usage habits, allowing users to quickly experience and manage Cosmo applications.

### 1. Basic Execution

The simplest usage of `x cosmo` is to directly run a Cosmopolitan-compiled application. For example, running Lua:

```bash
x cosmo lua [args]
```

At this point, if it's the first execution, the tool will automatically download the APE loader and cache it locally, then run directly. Users don't need to worry about underlying binary formats or compatibility issues.

You can also select the program to run in interactive mode:

```bash
x cosmo
```

After entering the TUI interface, you can select the Cosmo application to run via keyboard.


### 2. Installation and Deployment

Unlike simply running, `x cosmo` also supports installing programs to specified directories or PATH for long-term use.

::::ul
:::li Install Lua to specified directory:

```bash
x cosmo -i lua ~/tools
```

This allows users to find the Lua executable under `~/tools`.

:::li Select installation directory in PATH and place `make`:

```bash
x cosmo -i make
```

The tool interactively lists all directories in PATH. After users select a directory, the program automatically installs `make`, ready to use immediately.
::::

This approach is particularly suitable for team environments, where developers can quickly deploy a batch of common tools on their development machines or container environments.


### 3. Global Environment Management

`x cosmo` provides package manager-like functionality, allowing applications to be added to or removed from the global environment.

::::ul
:::li Add tool to global environment:

```bash
x cosmo --use lua
```

:::li Remove from global environment:

```bash
x cosmo --unuse lua
```
::::

This way, users can conveniently enable or disable an application system-wide without manually modifying PATH.


### 4. Program Location and Information Query

::::ul
:::li Query installation path of an application:

```bash
x cosmo --which lua
```

:::li View all available applications interactively:

```bash
x cosmo --ls
```

:::li List all supported Cosmo applications:

```bash
x cosmo --ll
```

:::li View Cosmopolitan author information:

```bash
x cosmo --author
```
::::

These features make `x cosmo` serve as both a tool runner and a "Cosmo application indexer", helping users quickly locate and understand applications.


### 5. Usage Scenario Examples

::::ul
:::li **Quickly Experience Cross-Platform Applications**: New users can simply `x cosmo <bin>` to experience a zero-dependency cross-platform program.
:::li **Team Development Environment**: Teams can use `x cosmo -i` to batch install tools (such as `make`, `vim`, `lua`), avoiding environment inconsistencies due to operating system differences.
:::li **Temporary Tool Usage**: For occasionally needed programs, you can `x cosmo --use` to enable globally, then `x cosmo --unuse` to disable, avoiding environment pollution.
:::li **Container and CI/CD Environments**: When building container images or CI/CD pipelines, directly install binaries via `x cosmo`, reducing dependency layers and improving image lightness.
::::


## Typical Application Scenarios

1. **Cross-Platform Distribution**
   Cosmo applications compiled by developers can be delivered directly to users. Combined with `x cosmo` management, no need to distinguish operating systems, greatly reducing release and maintenance costs.

2. **Research and Education**
   Teachers can quickly distribute experimental tools via `x cosmo`, ensuring students get consistent execution results across different systems.

3. **Operations and Emergency Response**
   Operations personnel can quickly install necessary tools (such as `curl`, `vim`) on different platforms via `x cosmo`, without dealing with complex dependency issues, suitable for emergency scenarios.

# x cowsay - Make Your Terminal Speak

Still using monotonous text output? Want to add some fun and personality to your command line interface? The `x cowsay` command is your secret weapon! It's a fun ASCII art module that lets a cute ASCII cow (or Tux the penguin we'll see later!) speak your message in a speech bubble in your terminal. Whether surprising colleagues or adding humor to script output, `x cowsay` handles it easily.

## Classic Cow, Speak Up!

The most basic and classic usage is to have an ASCII cow say what you specify. For example, want it to say "Hello world!"? Very simple:

```sh
x cowsay 'Hello world!'
```

After execution, you'll see this in your terminal:

![cowsay.1_1](/image/mod/cowsay.1_1.webp)

::: tip
When running in color-supported terminals, x-cmd thoughtfully adds rainbow colors to the cow
:::

Isn't it fun? The cow's expression combined with the speech bubble makes simple text messages instantly vivid. And if you run it directly in a color-supported terminal, `x-cmd` will thoughtfully add rainbow colors to the cow, making it even more eye-catching!

## Not Just Cows, Tux Penguin Arrives!

If you find cows a bit monotonous, or if you're a loyal Linux fan, `x cowsay` also prepares the cute Tux penguin for you! Just add the `tux` parameter before the message:

```sh
x cowsay tux 'Hello world!'
```

Now, Tux penguin will appear in your terminal with your "Hello world!" message:

![cowsay.1_2](/image/mod/cowsay.1_2.webp)

::: tip
Similarly, Tux will also be dressed in rainbow colors in color-supported terminals
:::

Instantly, your terminal is filled with geek style!

## Summary

`x cowsay` is a simple yet fun command. It not only adds color to your daily command-line work but also provides a unique way to prompt users when writing scripts. Go try it and make your terminal "speak" too!

# No more digging through sysctl for CPU info

Scripts sometimes need CPU info for branching logic: how many cores, what architecture, P-core vs E-core counts. `sysctl -a | grep cpu` floods the terminal — the useful fields are buried in there, and you have to pick them out yourself.

`x cpu` lays out the key fields directly, and also shows real-time load down to per-core utilization.

## Quick Start

```bash
x cpu              # hardware info + real-time load
```

![x cpu](/image/mod/cpu.1_1.webp)

`x cpu` subcommands are organized by purpose:

- **`x cpu`**: hardware info + real-time load in one view, the most commonly used mode
- **`x cpu info`**: hardware info only — architecture, core counts, P/E cores, frequency and other static fields
- **`x cpu stat`**: real-time load only, down to per-core utilization
- **`x cpu endianness`**: detect byte order, handy for cross-compilation

## FAQ

### Q: stat shows an error or no data?

On macOS, `x cpu stat` requires python3 to call system APIs (`host_statistics64` for overall load, `host_processor_info` for per-core utilization). On Linux, it reads `/proc/stat` directly with no extra dependencies.

### Q: How do I use P-cores and E-cores in scripts?

P-cores are performance cores (high frequency, large cache), E-cores are efficiency cores (low power). For specific usage in scripts, see the "Compile tuning" section above. A few practical tips:

- **Compile tuning**: P-core count determines the optimal parallelism for `make -j`, typically set to P-cores + 1
- **Background task scheduling**: Limit low-priority tasks (like log rotation, backup sync) to within the E-core count to avoid competing for P-core resources
- **Performance monitoring**: In `x cpu stat`'s per-core utilization, the first N cores are typically P-cores — watch whether their loads are balanced

### Q: info shows too many fields — what should I focus on?

For a quick overview of CPU specs, `x cpu info --simple` is enough. The full output is useful for script integration or deep debugging, with fields like cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3), flags, ARM feature flags, and other low-level details.

# x cron add

Add a cron job


::: tip
Not sure if your cron expression is correct? Test it with x cron match first
:::


## Usage

```sh
x cron add [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Cron time expression (min hour day month dow) |
| `#2` | Command to execute |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--ns` |  | Specify the namespace (default DEFAULT) |
| `--name` |  | Specify the job name (must be unique) |
| `--desc` |  | Job description |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--once` | Run only once, auto-delete after execution |

# x cve data

Manage the local CVE cache; query its location, status, and base URL

## Examples

Show cache location, mirror, and per-year file age

```sh
x cve data status
```

Refresh the manifest and every year file in parallel

```sh
x cve data update
```

Print the cache root directory

```sh
x cve data root
```

Print the upstream base URL the fetcher talks to

```sh
x cve data base
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x cve data status](#x-cve-data-status) | Show cache directory, mirror, and per-year file age (default subcommand) |
| [x cve data update](#x-cve-data-update) | Refresh the manifest + every year file (HTTP/2 parallel) |
| [x cve data root](#x-cve-data-root) | Print the on-disk cache root path |
| [x cve data index](#x-cve-data-index) | Print the on-disk path of index.tsv |
| [x cve data year](#x-cve-data-year) | Print the on-disk path of cve-YYYY.tsv for the given year |
| [x cve data base](#x-cve-data-base) | Print the upstream base URL (depends on --tag / --ghproxy) |
| [x cve data ensure-index](#x-cve-data-ensure-index) | Download index.tsv if missing or stale (1-day TTL) |
| [x cve data ensure-year](#x-cve-data-ensure-year) | Download cve-YYYY.tsv if missing or stale (1 day for current year, 30 days for older years) |
| [x cve data ensure-years](#x-cve-data-ensure-years) | Batch-download several years in one curl invocation (HTTP/2 multiplexing) |
| [x cve data fetch](#x-cve-data-fetch) | Fetch a single URL to a file (escape hatch) |
| [x cve data fetch-parallel](#x-cve-data-fetch-parallel) | Fetch multiple URLs in parallel (escape hatch) |


### x cve data status

Show cache directory, mirror, and per-year file age (default subcommand)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data status
```

### x cve data update

Refresh the manifest + every year file (HTTP/2 parallel)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data update|refresh
```

### x cve data root

Print the on-disk cache root path


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data root
```

### x cve data index

Print the on-disk path of index.tsv


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data index
```

### x cve data year

Print the on-disk path of cve-YYYY.tsv for the given year


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data year <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | 4-digit year, e.g. 2024 |


### x cve data base

Print the upstream base URL (depends on --tag / --ghproxy)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data base
```

### x cve data ensure-index

Download index.tsv if missing or stale (1-day TTL)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data ensure-index
```

### x cve data ensure-year

Download cve-YYYY.tsv if missing or stale (1 day for current year, 30 days for older years)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data ensure-year
```

### x cve data ensure-years

Batch-download several years in one curl invocation (HTTP/2 multiplexing)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data ensure-years
```

### x cve data fetch

Fetch a single URL to a file (escape hatch)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data fetch
```

### x cve data fetch-parallel

Fetch multiple URLs in parallel (escape hatch)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cve data fetch-parallel
```

# x cve detail

Fetch the FULL upstream record from CVEProject/cvelistV5 (affected products, CWE, references, metrics, timeline, ADP)

## Examples

Fetch the full upstream record — yml block: metadata, descriptions, affected, CWE, CVSS, references, timeline, ADP

```sh
x cve detail --yml CVE-2024-0001
```

Stream the raw upstream JSON

```sh
x cve detail --json CVE-2024-0001
```

One TSV row per affected product/version pair (id / state / vendor / product / version / cwe / score / vector / desc)

```sh
x cve detail --tsv CVE-2024-0001
```

Fetch multiple records in one call

```sh
x cve detail CVE-2024-0001 CVE-2026-9999
```

## Usage

```sh
x cve detail [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--yml` | Render as rich yml blocks (default mode) |
| `--tsv` | Compact TSV: one row per affected product/version pair |
| `--json` | Pass-through raw upstream JSON |
| `--ghproxy` | Fetch through the gh-proxy.com mirror |

# x cve info

Look up one or more CVE records by id (slim per-year cache; quick fields only)

## Examples

Look up a single CVE

```sh
x cve info --yml CVE-2024-0001
```

Look up several CVEs at once; year files are downloaded in parallel

```sh
x cve info --yml CVE-2024-0001 CVE-2023-0567 CVE-2026-15895
```

Output as raw TSV (good for piping)

```sh
x cve info --tsv CVE-2024-0001
```

## Usage

```sh
x cve info [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--yml`, `--yaml` | Render the result as YAML (default) |
| `--tsv` | Render the result as TSV (the raw row) |
| `--csv` | Render the result as CSV |
| `--json` | Render the result as JSON |
| `--raw` | Print only the CVE id (one per line, no other fields) |
| `--ghproxy` | Fetch through the gh-proxy.com mirror (helps when GitHub raw is slow/blocked) |
| `--tag` | Use a non-default cache tag (e.g. a local mirror URL) |
| `--offline` | Do not touch the network; fail if the year file is not already cached |

# x cve ls

Stream every cached CVE row. TTY → fzf picker; pipe → TSV. Auto-refreshes this year + last year if stale (&gt;1h).

## Examples

Auto: fzf picker if stdout is a TTY, raw TSV if piped; auto-refreshes this year + last year if older than 1h

```sh
x cve ls
```

Force raw TSV (good for piping to awk/grep/fzf --filter)

```sh
x cve ls --tsv
```

Stream every row as human-readable blocks

```sh
x cve ls --yml
```

Stream every row as JSON (one record per line)

```sh
x cve ls --json
```

Stream every row as CSV

```sh
x cve ls --csv
```

Pretty fixed-width table (header + aligned columns)

```sh
x cve ls --table
```

Force interactive fzf picker (with --yml preview pane)

```sh
x cve ls fz
```

## Usage

```sh
x cve ls [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--all`, `-a` | `x cve ls` 默认就是 --all；显式提供以便脚本使用 |
| `--no-refresh` | Skip the automatic 1-hour freshness check on this year + last year |
| `--yml` | Render each row as a human-readable block |
| `--tsv` | Emit raw TSV (default for pipes) |
| `--csv` | Emit raw CSV |
| `--json` | Emit raw JSON (one record per line) |
| `--table` | Pretty fixed-width table with header |
| `--ghproxy` | Fetch through the gh-proxy.com mirror |
| `--tag` | Use a non-default cache tag |

# x cve year

Browse CVEs published in a given year

## Examples

Stream every CVE published in 2024 (raw TSV)

```sh
x cve year --tsv 2024
```

Only CVEs with CVSS score ≥ 9

```sh
x cve year --tsv 2024 --score 9
```

Filter rows whose cve / ghsa / desc contains 'chromium' (case-insensitive)

```sh
x cve year --tsv 2024 --grep chromium
```

Stream three years at once

```sh
x cve year --tsv 2023 2024 2025
```

## Usage

```sh
x cve year [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--score` | Minimum CVSS base score (float); rows without a score are excluded |
| `--grep` | Case-insensitive substring match against cve / ghsa / desc |
| `--yml` | Pretty-print as human-readable text (one block per CVE) |
| `--tsv` | Emit raw TSV (default for piping) |
| `--csv` | Emit raw CSV |
| `--json` | Emit raw JSON |
| `--ghproxy` | Fetch through the gh-proxy.com mirror |
| `--tag` | Use a non-default cache tag |
| `--offline` | Use only the local cache; do not fetch missing year files |

# x cwe data

Manage the local CWE cache; query its location, status, and base URL

## Examples

Show cache location, mirror, and catalog age

```sh
x cwe data status
```

Re-download the catalog from MITRE

```sh
x cwe data update
```

Print the cache root directory

```sh
x cwe data root
```

Print the upstream base URL the fetcher talks to

```sh
x cwe data base
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x cwe data status](#x-cwe-data-status) | Show cache directory, mirror, and catalog age (default subcommand) |
| [x cwe data update](#x-cwe-data-update) | Refresh the catalog from MITRE (forces re-download) |
| [x cwe data root](#x-cwe-data-root) | Print the on-disk cache root path |
| [x cwe data csv](#x-cwe-data-csv) | Print the on-disk path of the cached 2000.csv |
| [x cwe data zip](#x-cwe-data-zip) | Print the on-disk path of the cached 2000.csv.zip |
| [x cwe data base](#x-cwe-data-base) | Print the upstream base URL (depends on --tag) |
| [x cwe data ensure](#x-cwe-data-ensure) | Download the catalog if missing or stale (30-day TTL) |
| [x cwe data fetch](#x-cwe-data-fetch) | Fetch a single URL to a file (escape hatch) |


### x cwe data status

Show cache directory, mirror, and catalog age (default subcommand)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cwe data status
```

### x cwe data update

Refresh the catalog from MITRE (forces re-download)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cwe data update|refresh
```

### x cwe data root

Print the on-disk cache root path


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cwe data root
```

### x cwe data csv

Print the on-disk path of the cached 2000.csv


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cwe data csv
```

### x cwe data zip

Print the on-disk path of the cached 2000.csv.zip


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cwe data zip
```

### x cwe data base

Print the upstream base URL (depends on --tag)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cwe data base
```

### x cwe data ensure

Download the catalog if missing or stale (30-day TTL)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cwe data ensure
```

### x cwe data fetch

Fetch a single URL to a file (escape hatch)


- **Usage**:

```sh
x cwe data fetch
```

# x cwe info

Look up one or more CWE records by id (full description, related weaknesses, mitigations, consequences, etc.)

## Examples

Print the full record for CWE-79 (XSS) as a YAML block

```sh
x cwe info CWE-79
```

Bare-id form (the `CWE-` prefix is optional)

```sh
x cwe info 79
```

Look up several CWE ids in one call

```sh
x cwe info CWE-79 CWE-89 CWE-1004
```

Emit one JSON line per id

```sh
x cwe info CWE-79 --json
```

Emit just the canonical id (good for pipelines)

```sh
x cwe info CWE-79 --raw
```

## Usage

```sh
x cwe info [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--yml`, `--yaml` | Render the record as a human-readable YAML block (default) |
| `--json` | Emit the record as a single JSON line |
| `--raw` | Emit only the canonical CWE id |
| `--no-refresh` | Skip the automatic 30-day freshness check on the catalog |
| `--offline` | Use only the local cache; do not attempt to refresh |
| `--tag` | Use a non-default cache tag |

# x date dump

Format the current time or a timestamp; defaults to ISO when --&lt;fmt&gt; is omitted

## Examples

Example: Output current time in ISO (dump default)

```sh
x date dump
```

Example: Explicitly request ISO format for current time

```sh
x date dump --iso
```

Example: UTC zero-timezone ISO format

```sh
x date dump --iso0
```

Example: String format suitable for filenames

```sh
x date dump --str
```

Example: Varname format

```sh
x date dump --varname
```

Example: UTC varname format (no timezone offset)

```sh
x date dump --varname0
```

Example: UTC short ID

```sh
x date dump --vlid
```

Example: Output in RFC 3339 format

```sh
x date dump --rfc
```

Example: Email header format (RFC 2822 / RFC 5322)

```sh
x date dump --email
```

Example: Custom strftime-style format output

```sh
x date dump --fmt '%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S'
```

Example: Go-style time format output

```sh
x date dump --go '2006-01-02 15:04:05 Z07:00'
```

Example: Convert timestamp to ISO (supports s/ms/decimal)

```sh
x date dump --iso 1743038674
```

Example: Convert timestamp to string format

```sh
x date dump --str 1743038674
```

Example: Convert timestamp to varname format

```sh
x date dump --varname 1743038674
```

Example: Convert timestamp to UTC short ID

```sh
x date dump --vlid 1743038674
```

Example: Specify timezone offset for output

```sh
x date dump --offset '+0000' --iso
```

Example: Add 1 day to now then format

```sh
x date dump -v 1d --iso
```

Example: Reverse: output raw epoch seconds

```sh
x date dump --second 1743038674
```

## Usage

```sh
x date dump [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Optional timestamp (seconds/milliseconds/decimal); uses current time when omitted |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--iso` | ISO format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss+tz |
| `--str` | String format YYYY-MM-DD_hh:mm:ss+tz (suitable for filenames) |
| `--varname` | Varname format YYYY_MM_DD_hh_mm_ss_tz |
| `--vlid` | UTC short ID YYMMDD_hhmmss (variable length ID) |
| `--rfc` | RFC 3339 format YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss+tz (ISO 8601 compatible, space-separated) |
| `--email` | Email header format (RFC 2822 / RFC 5322): 'Fri, 27 Mar 2026 09:24:34 +0800' |
| `--fmt` | Custom strftime format string; supports %Y %y %m %d %H %M %S %z %:z %_z %a %A %b %B %N %[1-9]N %% |
| `--go` | Go-style time format (reference 2006-01-02 15:04:05 MST); auto-translated to --fmt |
| `--offset` | Explicit timezone offset (e.g. +0800 / -0500 / +0000); defaults to system TZ when omitted |
| `--second` | Reverse: output raw epoch seconds (other --&lt;fmt&gt; flags produce date strings) |
| `-v` | Apply time delta (humantime units: 1d/2h/30m/1y1mo or bare seconds), then format |

# x dbnomics align

Fetch multiple series aligned to a unified time axis


::: tip
Without a format flag, interactive terminals open csv app; pipe or redirect outputs TSV.
:::

::: tip
Internally uses JSON API (align_periods=1) for true alignment, missing values filled with null.
:::

::: tip
Align series from the same provider with the same frequency to avoid excessive nulls.
:::

::: tip
See x dbnomics --help for alias and full ID lookup methods
:::


## Examples

Compare US/Germany/Japan CPI; interactive terminal opens csv app, pipe outputs TSV

```sh
x dbnomics align imf.us.cpi imf.de.cpi imf.jp.cpi
```

CSV format: Compare US/China GDP, suitable for database import, spreadsheets, or scripting

```sh
x dbnomics align --csv imf.us.gdp imf.cn.gdp
```

TSV format: Compare US Treasury yield curve, suitable for piping with awk/grep

```sh
x dbnomics align --tsv fed.10y fed.2y fed.3m
```

JSON format: Compare US/China/Germany CPI, full API response for programmatic use

```sh
x dbnomics align --json imf.us.cpi imf.cn.cpi imf.de.cpi
```

Compare US CPI vs PPI (BLS monthly)

```sh
x dbnomics align bls.cpi bls.ppi
```

Compare China/Germany/Japan GDP growth (IMF annual)

```sh
x dbnomics align imf.cn.gdp.growth imf.de.gdp.growth imf.jp.gdp.growth
```

Compare China/India/Vietnam GDP growth (emerging Asia)

```sh

```

Compare US government revenue vs expenditure (% GDP)

```sh

```

Compare US/Japan/Germany government debt (% GDP)

Compare US/China/India PPP GDP

Compare US/Singapore/Korea GDP per capita PPP


Compare US/Germany/France unemployment rate

## Usage

```sh
x dbnomics align [FLAGS] <#1> <#2> <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | First series ID or alias |
| `#2` | Second series ID or alias |
| `#n` | Additional series IDs or aliases (same provider and frequency recommended) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--csv` | Output in CSV format (default) |
| `--tsv` | Output in TSV format |
| `--json` | Output in JSON format |
| `--raw` | Raw API JSON response |
| `--limit` | Number of observations to return |
| `--offset` | Number of observations to skip |
