# x eget cache

Unified management of eget caches (raw archives + extracted snap binaries)


::: tip eget keeps two caches:
- `cache/<owner>--<repo>/<version>/<asset>` — raw downloaded archive, SHA-256 verified.
  - `snap/<owner>--<repo>/<version>/bin/<binary>` — extracted ready-to-run binary.

`snap` / `use` / `upgrade` all share the snap cache; `download` defaults to the archive cache.
:::

::: tip `clear` uses different policies: archive keeps N versions per repo (default 5); snap keeps only `.default-version` (the active binary).
The snap default version is protected by `clear` — to wipe it, use `rm <owner/repo>` or `purge`.
:::


## Examples

List all cache entries (with KIND / REPO / VERSION / BYTES columns)

```sh
x eget cache ls
```

Show path and size of the three caches (archive / snap / use list)

```sh
x eget cache info
```

Clear: archive keeps 5 versions per repo; snap keeps .default-version only

```sh
x eget cache clear 5
```

Remove a repo's archive + snap cache

```sh
x eget cache rm jqlang/jq
```

Remove by URL (equivalent to owner/repo)

```sh
x eget cache rm https://github.com/jqlang/jq
```

Purge everything (irreversible)

```sh
x eget cache purge
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x eget cache ls](#x-eget-cache-ls) | List archive + snap cache entries (TSV: KIND / REPO / VERSION / BYTES / PATH) |
| [x eget cache info](#x-eget-cache-info) | Show path and size of the three caches |
| [x eget cache clear](#x-eget-cache-clear) | Prune old versions (archive keeps N per repo, default 5; snap keeps .default-version) |
| [x eget cache purge](#x-eget-cache-purge) | Wipe both caches (irreversible) |
| [x eget cache rm](#x-eget-cache-rm) | Remove a single repo from both caches |


### x eget cache ls

List archive + snap cache entries (TSV: KIND / REPO / VERSION / BYTES / PATH)


- **Examples**:

List all cache entries

```sh
x eget cache ls
```

Show first few entries

```sh
x eget cache ls | head
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x eget cache ls
```

### x eget cache info

Show path and size of the three caches


- **Examples**:

Show path and size of archive / snap / use list

```sh
x eget cache info
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x eget cache info
```

### x eget cache clear

Prune old versions (archive keeps N per repo, default 5; snap keeps .default-version)


- **Examples**:

Clear: archive keeps 5 versions per repo; snap keeps .default-version only

```sh
x eget cache clear 5
```

Remove all archives, snap keeps .default-version only

```sh
x eget cache clear 0
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x eget cache clear
```

### x eget cache purge

Wipe both caches (irreversible)


- **Examples**:

Purge everything (irreversible; next use/snap re-downloads)

```sh
x eget cache purge
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x eget cache purge
```

### x eget cache rm

Remove a single repo from both caches


- **Examples**:

Remove by owner/repo

```sh
x eget cache rm jqlang/jq
```

Remove by URL (equivalent to owner/repo)

```sh
x eget cache rm https://github.com/jqlang/jq
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x eget cache rm
```

# The Must-Have Open Source AI Tools of 2026 — All Installed with x eget

It's 2026, and AI coding tools are everywhere. Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode — they've become daily drivers for a lot of developers. The tools themselves are great, but after using them for a while, a few pain points start to surface: tokens burning too fast, juggling multiple agents at once, and never quite knowing what each agent is up to. Below, let's look at the tools that tackle these specific pain points:

```bash
eval "$(curl https://get.x-cmd.com)"
x eget use rtk
x eget use abtop
x eget use ogulcancelik/herdr
```

## rtk: Every AI-Powered Developer Should Install This

[rtk-ai/rtk](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk), 68k stars.

```bash
x eget use rtk
```

Put simply, it's a CLI proxy — it sits between your AI agent and the shell, compressing command output before passing it to the model.

Picture this: you ask Claude Code to help debug something. It runs `ls`, `cat`, `grep`, `git diff`, `cargo test`, one after another. Every command's output gets stuffed into the context window, and most of it is noise the model doesn't need. rtk intelligently filters and compresses those outputs. The official number is 60–90% token savings.

From my own experience, **the token savings are nice, but the real win is faster responses**. When the context window isn't crammed full, the agent replies noticeably quicker and is less likely to "forget" earlier context mid-conversation. This is especially noticeable with Rust projects — `cargo test` error logs can run hundreds of lines, and rtk strips it down to what actually matters.

It's a single Rust binary with sub-10ms overhead, supporting filtering rules for over 100 commands. That covers pretty much every CLI tool you'd reach for in day-to-day development.

## abtop: See What Your Agents Are Doing at a Glance

[graykode/abtop](https://github.com/graykode/abtop), 3,200+ stars.

```bash
x eget use abtop
```

If you've used btop or htop, abtop's interface will feel right at home — same TUI style, except it's monitoring your AI agent sessions instead of system processes.

It automatically discovers running Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenCode sessions on your machine, then displays each agent's token usage, context window remaining ratio, rate limit status, child processes, and occupied ports — all in real time.

I first installed it because I had three Claude Code windows going at once — one refactoring the backend, one building the frontend, and one fixing CI config. Switching between them, I'd quickly lose track of which one was waiting for input, which was rate-limited, and which had already finished. abtop consolidates all of that into one screen. Agent status is immediately clear: working, waiting for input, rate-limited, complete.

## herdr: tmux for AI Agents

[ogulcancelik/herdr](https://github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr), 10k+ stars.

```bash
x eget use ogulcancelik/herdr
```

If abtop helps you _see_ all your agents, herdr helps you _manage_ them. It's a terminal-based agent multiplexer — think of it as tmux, but for agents.

Each agent runs in its own real terminal panel (not an emulated pseudo-terminal, so even full-screen TUIs render correctly), with a sidebar that marks each agent's status: 🔴 blocked / 🟡 working / 🔵 complete / 🟢 idle. You can split panes, use tabs and workspaces, and drag with the mouse — just like tmux.

What sold me on herdr is **session persistence**. Close your terminal, shut your laptop — the agents don't die. A background server keeps running, and you can reconnect from another terminal (or even over SSH from your phone) and pick up right where you left off, with all agent state intact. For long-running tasks like large-scale refactors, you don't have to live in fear of your terminal connection dropping.

Unlike a lot of agent management tools, herdr isn't a GUI app. It's a single Rust binary (around 10MB), no Electron shell, no OS restrictions, no account registration, no telemetry. It runs in your terminal and feels as natural as using tmux.

## x eget: Installing Open Source AI Tools

You probably noticed something: all three tools share the exact same install command pattern — `x eget use` followed by a repo name.

[x eget](https://x-cmd.com) does something simple: it grabs the author's pre-compiled binary from the official GitHub / GitLab / Codeberg Release page, extracts it, and drops it into `~/.local/bin`. It solves a real problem: **a lot of fast-rising new tools haven't made it into Homebrew or apt yet, and waiting for package manager inclusion can take weeks or even months**. x eget pulls straight from the official release, so you're running the latest version the day an AI tool ships.

Another thing I value: GitHub downloads are often painfully slow from certain network environments. When a download stalls, `x eget` automatically falls back to x-cmd's accelerated hosting — no need to configure proxies or mirrors yourself.

Day-to-day usage comes down to two commands:

- `x eget use <repo>` — installs to `~/.local/bin`
- `x eget upgrade --all` — upgrades every tool installed via x eget to the latest version with a single command

Best of all, x eget is a submodule within the x-cmd toolset, implemented in pure shell — no sudo, zero dependencies. It works whether you're on your local machine, a server, in a container, or in a CI pipeline.

## Wrapping Up

These four tools are my current setup: rtk for token savings, abtop for monitoring, herdr for agent management, and x eget to handle the installations. If you haven't tried them yet, give them a spin.

```bash
eval "$(curl https://get.x-cmd.com)"
x eget use rtk
x eget use abtop
x eget use ogulcancelik/herdr
```

# x eget download

Download and install binary — the default behavior; the subcmd can be omitted (`x eget <repo>`)

## Examples

Download the default binary to the current directory

```sh
x eget BurntSushi/ripgrep
```

Download to a specific directory

```sh
x eget --to ~/.local/bin BurntSushi/ripgrep
```

Download a specific version

```sh
x eget --tag v2.42.1 cli/cli
```

Cross-platform download

```sh
x eget --system linux/amd64 cli/cli
```

Download only, skip extraction

```sh
x eget --download-only cli/cli
```

## Usage

```sh
x eget download [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--to` |  | Install directory (default: current directory) |
| `-t`, `--tag` |  | Specify version tag |
| `-s`, `--system` |  | Specify target platform (e.g., linux/amd64, darwin/arm64) |
| `--speed-limit` |  | Stall threshold (bytes/sec); below this for N seconds, abort and retry via mirror (default 50000) |
| `--speed-time` |  | Seconds of sustained slow speed before aborting to mirror (default 5) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--download-only` | Download the archive to tmp only, no extraction |
| `--source` | Download source tarball instead of pre-built binary |
| `--pre-release` | Allow pre-release versions |
| `--forge` | Specify forge (github / gitlab / codeberg) |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | Quiet mode |
| `--no-verify` | Skip SHA-256 verification |
| `--no-mirror` | Disable eget hosting; download directly throughout |

# x eget html

Scrape the GitHub releases page HTML for release info (fallback when the API is rate-limited)


::: tip When api.github.com is rate-limited (60 req/hr unauthenticated quota exhausted), the download / use / snap paths automatically fall back to this HTML scraping path.
`x eget html <repo>` invokes the scraper directly without going through the API — handy for diagnosing what eget actually sees when rate-limited.

Mirrors the community's `curl .../releases/expanded_assets/<tag> | grep <repo> | grep download`, but anchors owner/repo into the pattern to avoid wrong matches on multi-repo pages.

Output is a JSON object in the same `{tag_name, assets[]}` shape as the API path; digest is empty and size is 0 (the HTML page doesn't expose them).
:::


## Examples

Scrape the latest release (no API)

```sh
x eget html ljh-sh/zhhz
```

Scrape a specific tag

```sh
x eget html --tag v0.7.7 ljh-sh/zhhz
```

## Usage

```sh
x eget html [OPTIONS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-t`, `--tag` |  | Specify release version tag |

# x eget ls

Without args, list all eget-installable packages from the x install database; with a repo, list its releases or a specific release's artifacts


::: tip Calling `x eget ls` with no args filters the x install TSV for rows whose rule column contains `/eget`, emitting a 3-column TSV: NAME / REPO / DESCRIPTION.
The list is large (~800 entries) and pipe-friendly: `x eget ls | grep ripgrep`, `x eget ls | head`, `x eget ls | fzf`.
:::


## Examples

List all eget-installable packages (from x install)

```sh
x eget ls
```

Filter by keyword

```sh
x eget ls | grep ripgrep
```

List all releases of a repo

```sh
x eget ls BurntSushi/ripgrep
```

List artifacts in a specific release

```sh
x eget ls BurntSushi/ripgrep 14.1.0
```

List GitLab releases

```sh
x eget ls gl:owner/repo
```

## Usage

```sh
x eget ls [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Repository (user/repo or gh:/gl:/cb: short name) |
| `#2` | Release tag (omit to list all releases) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--forge` | Specify forge |
| `--limit` | Max releases to list (default 20) |
| `--no-ccmd` | Skip cache, force fresh API request |

# x eget snap

Download and run instantly without PATH install; like npx


::: tip
First run downloads and caches locally; subsequent runs have zero network overhead.
:::

::: tip
--auto-check-update 1d: auto-check GitHub Release for new versions after 1 day. Minimum interval 5m; on failure, same 5m cooldown before retry.
:::


## Examples

Run ripgrep directly

```sh
x eget snap BurntSushi/ripgrep --version
```

Search files by extension

```sh
x eget snap sharkdp/fd -e py -e js .
```

Run fzf inside tmux

```sh
x eget snap junegunn/fzf --tmux
```

Auto-check for updates daily

```sh
x eget snap --auto-check-update 1d BurntSushi/ripgrep --version
```

Run a specific version

```sh
x eget snap --tag 14.1.0 BurntSushi/ripgrep -- -V
```

Force check for updates

```sh
x eget snap --update BurntSushi/ripgrep --version
```

## Usage

```sh
x eget snap [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--auto-check-update` |  | Periodically check GitHub Release for new versions (e.g. 1d, 1h, 5m, minimum 5m) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--update` | Force check for updates, ignore cache |
| `-t`, `--tag` | Specify version tag |
| `-s`, `--system` | Specify target platform (e.g. linux/amd64) |
| `-q`, `--quiet` | Quiet mode |

# x eget upgrade

Refresh use-installed binaries to their latest release (snap cache means repeated 'use' won't auto-upgrade)


::: tip `x eget use <name>` does NOT auto-check for upgrades — after the first install, repeated calls always hit the snap cache with zero network.
To get the latest release you must explicitly run `x eget upgrade`.

Bare `x eget upgrade` (no args, no --all) errors out to avoid footguns — pass either a name or --all.

`update` is an alias for `upgrade` (eget has no package index, so the two are synonymous).
:::


## Examples

Preview all upgradable binaries (no filesystem changes)

```sh
x eget upgrade --dry-run --all
```

Upgrade every use-tracked binary

```sh
x eget upgrade --all
```

Upgrade only entries matching by binname or owner/repo

```sh
x eget upgrade fzf
```

## Usage

```sh
x eget upgrade [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Name or owner/repo (exact match on binname, otherwise substring match on owner/repo) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--all` | Upgrade every use-tracked binary |
| `--dry-run` | Print current→latest comparison only; do not download or replace files |

# x emoji - Your Command-Line Emoji Assistant

Still troubled by inputting or finding specific emoji in the command line? Or want to know which category an emoji belongs to? The `x emoji` command is your powerful partner! It not only lets you easily browse and search massive amounts of emoji but also conveniently use them in scripts or documents, and even keep your local emoji library synchronized with Unicode standards.

Let's quickly get started with the core functions of `x emoji` through a few simple and practical examples!

::: tip Tip
`x emoji` is a powerful command-line tool supporting interactive browsing, precise filtering, data export, and automatic updates.
:::

## Interactive Exploration: Your Portable Emoji Encyclopedia

Sometimes, you may just want to browse what interesting emoji are available, or find one based on a general impression. In this case, the simplest and most direct way is to start `x emoji`'s interactive application.

Just enter in the terminal:

::::ul
::: li Run `x emoji`

```sh
x emoji
```

:::
::::

![emoji.1_1](/image/mod/emoji.1_1.webp)

:::: ul
::: li **Arrow navigation**
Move through the list with ↑/↓.
:::
::: li **Details pane**
Inspect the glyph, description, group, and related metadata.
:::
::: li **Search**
Most pickers bind `/` to search so you can jump quickly.
:::
::::

This is like having a constantly updated, readily available emoji dictionary—very intuitive and convenient.

## Precise Finding: Filter by Category and Subcategory

If you have a more specific target for the emoji you want, such as knowing it belongs to the "smileys" category under the "face-smiling" subcategory, the `x emoji ls` command can help you precisely locate it.

Suppose you want to find all emoji under the "smileys" (Smileys & Emotion) category, "face-smiling" (Smiling Faces) subcategory, you can operate like this:

::::ul
::: li List by category and subcategory

```sh
x emoji ls smileys face-smiling
```

:::
::::

![emoji.1_2](/image/mod/emoji.1_2.webp)

After execution, the terminal will list all emoji meeting these two conditions. This is very useful for quickly finding a series of related emoji, for example, when you want to use a set of specific theme emoji in an article or script comments.

::: tip Tip
You can view all available category and subcategory options through `x emoji ls --help`.
:::

## Data Export: CSV Format for Further Processing

`x emoji` not only lets you view emoji but also export results in different formats for subsequent processing. CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is a common tabular data format, easily parsed by various spreadsheet software or scripting languages.

If we want to export the results of the previous command (finding `smileys` category `face-smiling` subcategory emoji) in CSV format, just add the `--csv` parameter:

::::ul
::: li Export as CSV

```sh
x emoji ls smileys face-smiling --csv
```

:::
::::

![emoji.1_3](/image/mod/emoji.1_3.webp)

Each row represents an emoji, containing description, emoji character itself, subgroup, main group, Unicode code point, status, and Unicode version information. You can easily import this data into spreadsheets or analyze and use it with scripts.

## Stay Fresh: Update Your Emoji Library

The world of emoji is also constantly evolving. Unicode standards regularly release new emoji. To ensure your `x emoji` command uses the latest emoji list, you need to regularly update the local emoji resource package.

The update operation is very simple:

::::ul
::: li Update local emoji data

```sh
x emoji update
```

:::
::::

After executing this command, `x emoji` will download the latest emoji data file from official or mirror sources (such as `unicode.org` or its mirrors). It is recommended to run this command regularly to ensure you can access all the latest, coolest emoji!

::: warning Note
Regularly updating the emoji library ensures you use the latest emoji, but the first download may take some time depending on network speed.
:::

---

Through these `tldr` examples, we have mastered the core usage of the `x emoji` command. Whether quickly browsing, precise finding, data export, or staying updated, `x emoji` provides CLI users with a powerful and convenient emoji solution. Now, go try these commands in your terminal and add more fun and color to your command-line experience!

# x env (1) - Interactive Search and Install Software Tools

## Interactive Search and Install Software Tools

The `x env` module is a development environment and dependency management tool built on the `x-cmd pkg` system, capable of installing and managing `500+` software tools without requiring `root` permissions.

Execute the following command to open the interactive APP and easily search for and install required tools and dependencies.

```sh
x env
```

<!-- [image] Show x env interactive APP -->
![x env --app 1](/image/mod/env.1_1.webp)
<!-- [image] Show x env next step quick action menu -->
![x env --app 2](/image/mod/env.1_2.webp)

- In the interactive APP:
    - **Left column**: Displays software tool categories and package names, such as `lang/python`, `lang-js-ts/node`, `data-line/fzf`, etc.
    - **Middle column**: Shows available versions of the selected software tool, helping users choose the appropriate version for installation.
    - **Right column**: Provides relevant information about the software, including brief introduction, official website link, open source license, etc., to help users quickly understand software details.
    - After selecting software and pressing Enter, a next-step quick action menu will be provided, such as install and use the software.


## Install and Use Specified Software Tools

Use the `x env use` command to install software to the global environment. Whether restarting the terminal or opening a new session, the software will remain activated for easy access anytime.

If you need to use a specific version of software, you can specify the version number in the command. Taking installing and using `python` as an example:

```sh
x env use python
x env use python=v3.11.0+23.11.0-1
```

<!-- [image] Show x env use python installation process -->
![x env use](/image/mod/env.1_3.webp)

## Remove Specified Software Tools from Global Environment

If you want to cancel the use of a certain software from the global environment, you can use the `x env unuse` command. For example, to remove `python` from the global environment:

```sh
x env unuse python
```

<!-- [image] Show x env unuse python command output -->
![x env unuse](/image/mod/env.1_4.webp)

## Install and Use Specified Software Tools Only in Current Environment

Sometimes you may want to try new software or new versions without affecting the global environment configuration.

For example, trying out `fzf` and version `v23.9.0` of `node`:

```sh
x env try fzf node=v23.9.0
```

<!-- [image] Show x env try command installation and usage process -->
![x env try](/image/mod/env.1_5.webp)

Software or versions installed through the above method will only be effective in the current session. After closing the terminal or exiting the current session, they will be automatically cleared—very suitable for development testing or temporary tasks.

---
[More] If you want to learn more about the env module, please visit x-cmd official website - x-cmd.com/mod/env

url: /mod/env/cookbook-2.md

# x env (2) - Managing and Upgrading Software Tools

## Upgrading Installed Software

`x env` simplifies software management. If you need to upgrade installed software tools to access new features or fix known issues, use the `x env upgrade` command.

For example, to upgrade `deno`:

```sh
x env upgrade deno
x env upgrade deno=v2.2.2
```

<!-- [image] x env upgrade output -->
![x env upgrade](/image/mod/env.2_1.webp)

## Viewing Globally Enabled Software Tools

For easy viewing of software tools installed using `x env use`, `x env ls` provides an interactive app by default in interactive environments.

```sh
x env ls
```

<!-- [image] Showing x env ls interactive app -->
![x env ls 1](/image/mod/env.2_2.webp)
<!-- [image] Showing x env ls next step shortcut menu -->
![x env ls 2](/image/mod/env.2_3.webp)

- Within the interactive app:
    - **Real-time Search:** Type keywords in the input box to quickly search for specific software tools.
    - **Shortcut Menu:** After selecting a software tool, press Enter to display a series of options, such as upgrading or deleting the software.

If you prefer a simple list view, use the following:

```sh
x env ls | cat
```

<!-- [image] Showing x env ls list view -->
![x env ls 3](/image/mod/env.2_4.webp)

This will output a line-by-line list, helping you quickly understand the software tools enabled in the global environment.

## Listing All Installed Software Tools

To view all installed software tools, regardless of whether they are enabled globally, use the `-i` option:

```sh
x env ls -i
```

# x env gc

Uninstalls the specified package (if any) without affecting active packages or dependencies, then removes orphaned packages to free disk space.

## Examples

Interactive selection of specified pkg package for garbage collection

```sh
x env gc
```

Remove yq, jq and delete other recyclable packages. q

```sh
x env gc yq jq
```

## Usage

```sh
x env gc|cleanup [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | package name |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--force` | Force execution of the recycling mechanism |

# x env upgrade

Upgrade packages in the user environment to the 'default' version. Powered by `x pkg upgrade`.

## Examples

Upgrade all packages used in the user environment to the default version

```sh
x env upgrade --all
```

Upgrade the jq, yq, and fzf packages used in the user environment to the default version

```sh
x env upgrade jq yq fzf
```

## Usage

```sh
x env upgrade [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND] <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | Package and its version, format: &lt;package_name&gt;[=&lt;version_to_upgrade&gt;] |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--sphere` |  | sphere name |
| `--sphereroot` |  | sphere root path |
| `--osarch` |  | The system and CPU architecture that the package matches, in the format &lt;os&gt;/&lt;arch&gt;, such as linux/x64. If not specified, the system and CPU architecture of the current environment will be used. |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--default` | Upgrade to the default version (the latest stable version, relatively) |
| `--latest` | Upgrade to the latest version (which may be less stable and not recommended for use) |
| `--force` | After upgrading, enforce the recycling mechanism for the old version |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x env upgrade --all](#x-env-upgrade-all) | Upgrade the versions of all packages used in the global environment |


### x env upgrade --all

Upgrade the versions of all packages used in the global environment


- **Usage**:

```sh
x env upgrade --all
```


Upgrade all packages used in the user environment to the default version

```sh
x env use --upgrade --all
```

Upgrade the jq, yq, and fzf packages used in the user environment to the default version

# x epoch minus

Calculate timestamp difference, with optional human-readable output


::: tip
How long did my task run? `start=$(x epoch ms)` at the start, `x epoch minus "$start"` at the end; add -H for 1h30m format
:::

::: tip
Compare two timestamps? `x epoch minus 1710000000 1700000000` gives the difference directly
:::


## Examples

Example: Seconds from that timestamp to now

```sh
x epoch minus 1710000000
```

Example: Difference between two timestamps (10,000 seconds)

```sh
x epoch minus 1710000000 1700000000
```

Example: Output time difference in 1h30m format

```sh
x epoch minus -H 1710000000
```

## Usage

```sh
x epoch minus
```

# x epoch now

Check whether a timestamp falls within a duration from now (--le and/or --ge required)


::: tip
Cron job running too often? In your script, `x epoch now --le 1m $(cat ts.txt)` exits 1 if not within 1 minute
:::

::: tip
Integer epoch uses second precision; fractional epoch (e.g. 1710000000.123) auto-uses millisecond precision, is detects this too
:::


## Examples

Example: Check whether the timestamp is within the last 5 minutes (typical token expiration check)

```sh
x epoch now --le 5m 1710000000
```

Example: Check whether the timestamp is between 10 minutes and 1 hour old

```sh
x epoch now --le 1h --ge 10m 1710000000
```

Example: Check 30-day TTL on user cache dir timestamp

```sh
x epoch now --le 30d -f "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch"
```

## Usage

```sh
x epoch now
```

# x epoch store

Store-backed epoch file operations (write, read, is, rm); supports --store/--fp path overrides


::: info
Path resolution: --fp &lt;path&gt; overrides everything; otherwise &lt;--store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; with default --store=$___X_CMD_ROOT_DATA/epoch/store
:::

::: tip
Quick freshness check on a store file? Just `x epoch store --le 5m <key>` — omitting the subcmd defaults to is
:::

::: tip
Wrote metadata lines (e.g. key=v version=2)? `read` only takes line 1 (the epoch); use `cat` / `tail -n +2` / `awk` for the rest
:::

::: tip
Need millisecond precision? Add --real to write; the file becomes 1710000000.123; is detects the decimal and auto-uses millisecond precision
:::


## Examples

Example: Stamp build artifacts with the current epoch

```sh
x epoch store write build-artifacts
```

Example: Build artifacts are fresh if stamped within the last hour

```sh
x epoch store is --le 1h build-artifacts
```

Example: Read the build timestamp (comparable in scripts)

```sh
x epoch store read build-artifacts
```

Example: Clean up the build stamp (no error if missing)

```sh
x epoch store rm build-artifacts
```

Scenario: Package metadata + 7-day TTL check (full flow)

```sh
x epoch store write pkg-meta && x epoch store is --le 7d pkg-meta
```

Scenario: Inspect the full file (including metadata lines) after writing

```sh
x epoch store write pkg-meta && cat "$(x epoch store which pkg-meta)"
```

Scenario: User cache dir timestamp + 1-day TTL check

```sh
x epoch store write --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch" && x epoch store is --le 1d --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch"
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x epoch store write](#x-epoch-store-write) | Write the current epoch to &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; (line 1 = epoch, following lines = metadata) |
| [x epoch store read](#x-epoch-store-read) | Read and print &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; (only line 1, the epoch) |
| [x epoch store is](#x-epoch-store-is) | Check whether &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; is within a duration from now (--le and/or --ge required) |
| [x epoch store exist](#x-epoch-store-exist) | Check whether &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; exists (via store resolve; exit 0/1, no output) |
| [x epoch store rm](#x-epoch-store-rm) | Remove &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; (no error if the file is missing) |
| [x epoch store which](#x-epoch-store-which) | Print the resolved path of &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; (no file I/O, just path resolution) |


### x epoch store write

Write the current epoch to &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; (line 1 = epoch, following lines = metadata)


- **Examples**:

Example: Stamp build artifacts with the current epoch

```sh
x epoch store write build-artifacts
```

Example: Write in real format (is auto-detects millisecond precision)

```sh
x epoch store write --real build-artifacts
```

Example: Write epoch then append metadata lines; use --fp for user cache dir

```sh
x epoch store write --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch" k=v ver=2
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x epoch store write [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--real` | Write fractional seconds (e.g. 1710000000.123); is auto-uses millisecond precision |
| `--store` &lt;dir&gt; | Override the store dir (default $___X_CMD_ROOT_DATA/epoch/store) |
| `--fp` &lt;path&gt; | Use an explicit full file path (overrides --store + &lt;key&gt;) |


### x epoch store read

Read and print &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; (only line 1, the epoch)


- **Examples**:

Example: Read the build artifacts timestamp

```sh
x epoch store read build-artifacts
```

Example: Use --fp for an explicit path in user cache dir

```sh
x epoch store read --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x epoch store read [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--store` &lt;dir&gt; | Override the store dir |
| `--fp` &lt;path&gt; | Use an explicit full file path |


### x epoch store is

Check whether &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; is within a duration from now (--le and/or --ge required)


- **Examples**:

Example: Build artifacts are fresh if stamped within the last hour

```sh
x epoch store is --le 1h build-artifacts
```

Example: Package metadata is between 1 and 5 minutes old

```sh
x epoch store is --le 5m --ge 1m pkg-meta
```

Example: Use --fp to check 1-day TTL on user cache dir

```sh
x epoch store is --le 1d --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch"
```

Example: Cache exists but is over 1 hour old — needs regeneration

```sh
x epoch store is --ge 1h build-artifacts
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x epoch store is [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--le`, `--in` &lt;duration&gt; | Upper bound: must be within this duration from now (required unless --ge given); --in is a synonym |
| `--ge` &lt;duration&gt; | Lower bound: must be at least this duration old (e.g. 1h = at least 1 hour ago) |
| `--store` &lt;dir&gt; | Override the store dir |
| `--fp` &lt;path&gt; | Use an explicit full file path (overrides --store + &lt;key&gt;) |


### x epoch store exist

Check whether &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; exists (via store resolve; exit 0/1, no output)


- **Examples**:

Example: Continue only if the cache file exists

```sh
x epoch store exist build-artifacts
```

Example: Cache exists and is over 1 hour old — needs regeneration

```sh
x epoch store exist build-artifacts && x epoch store is --ge 1h build-artifacts
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x epoch store exist [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--store` &lt;dir&gt; | Override the store dir |
| `--fp` &lt;path&gt; | Use an explicit full file path |


### x epoch store rm

Remove &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; (no error if the file is missing)


- **Examples**:

Example: Clean up the build stamp (no error if missing)

```sh
x epoch store rm build-artifacts
```

Example: Use --fp to remove an explicit path in user cache dir

```sh
x epoch store rm --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x epoch store rm [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--store` &lt;dir&gt; | Override the store dir |
| `--fp` &lt;path&gt; | Use an explicit full file path |


### x epoch store which

Print the resolved path of &lt;store&gt;/&lt;key&gt; (no file I/O, just path resolution)


- **Examples**:

Example: Print the full path of &lt;store&gt;/build-artifacts

```sh
x epoch store which build-artifacts
```

Example: Use --store to see the resolved path under a custom dir

```sh
x epoch store which --store /tmp/alt build-artifacts
```

Example: --fp just prints the explicit path in user cache dir

```sh
x epoch store which --fp "$HOME/.local/cache/myapp.start.epoch"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x epoch store which [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--store` &lt;dir&gt; | Override the store dir |
| `--fp` &lt;path&gt; | Use an explicit full file path |

# x feishu abot

Send messages and manage listener service using Feishu intelligent bot

## Examples

Send text messages using intelligent bot

```sh
x feishu abot send --text --chatid <chat_id> "Hello"
```

Reply to a specified message using intelligent bot

```sh
x feishu abot reply --msgid <message_id> "Hello"
```

Add an emoji reaction to a specified message

```sh
x feishu abot reaction add --msgid <message_id> THUMBSUP
```

Remove an emoji reaction from a specified message

```sh
x feishu abot reaction rm --msgid <message_id> <reaction_id>
```

Start the intelligent bot listener service

```sh
x feishu abot service start
```

Show data file path for specified chat

```sh
x feishu abot data which <chat_id>
```

Get basic information of the current app

```sh
x feishu abot info
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x feishu abot info](#x-feishu-abot-info) | Get basic information of the Feishu app |
| [x feishu abot send](#x-feishu-abot-send) | Send messages using Feishu intelligent bot |
| [x feishu abot reply](#x-feishu-abot-reply) | Reply to a specified message using Feishu intelligent bot |
| [x feishu abot reaction](#x-feishu-abot-reaction) | Manage emoji reactions on messages |
| [x feishu abot service](#x-feishu-abot-service) | Manage intelligent bot listener service |
| [x feishu abot data](#x-feishu-abot-data) | Manage intelligent bot data files |


### x feishu abot info

Get basic information of the Feishu app



::: tip app_id is the unique identifier of a Feishu app (format: cli_xxxxx), obtained when creating the app on the Feishu Open Platform
Omit --appid to use me, equivalent to querying the currently configured app

Querying other apps requires the "Get app info" scope (admin:app.info:readonly)
:::

::: tip open_id (default) — identifies a user within the current app; same user has different open_ids across apps
--id_type specifies the ID type for user fields in the response (e.g. creator_id, owner_id)


union_id — identifies a user within the app vendor's apps, useful for correlating the same user across apps from the same vendor

user_id — identifies a user within a tenant; shared across all apps in the tenant (requires the contact:user.employee_id:readonly scope)

Keep the default open_id in most cases; only switch when you need to correlate users across apps or tenants
:::


- **Examples**:

Get current app info (equivalent to --appid me)

```sh
x feishu abot info
```

Get info of a specific app

```sh
x feishu abot info --appid <app_id>
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x feishu abot info [OPTIONS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--appid` &lt;app_id&gt; |  | App ID (defaults to me, the current app) |
| `--lang` &lt;lang&gt; |  | Language (zh_cn / en_us / ja_jp, default zh_cn) |
| `--id_type` &lt;id_type&gt; |  | User ID type (open_id / union_id / user_id, default open_id) |

| [x feishu abot send --file](#x-feishu-abot-send-file) | Send files to specified chat |
| [x feishu abot send --card](#x-feishu-abot-send-card) | Send a Markdown card message (Feishu Schema 2.0 interactive card, supports full Markdown including code blocks and tables) |


### x feishu abot send --text

Send text messages to specified chat


- **Examples**:

Send text message to specified chat

```sh
x feishu abot send --text --chatid <chat_id> "Hello"
```

With --messageid, reply to that message instead of sending

```sh
x feishu abot send --text --messageid <message_id> "Hello"
```

Send text message and save it to the data file

```sh
x feishu abot send --text --chatid <chat_id> --fp "Hello"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x feishu abot send --text [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--chatid` &lt;chat_id&gt; |  | Chat ID |
| `--messageid` &lt;message_id&gt; |  | Target message ID; when set, delivers as a reply to that message (uses the reply API; --chatid can be omitted) |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--fp` | Record sent message content to the data file |

| `--messageid` &lt;message_id&gt; |  | Target message ID; when set, delivers as a reply to that message (uses the reply API; --chatid can be omitted) |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--fp` | Save a local copy of the image, and record its path to the data file |

### x feishu abot send --card

Send a Markdown card message (Feishu Schema 2.0 interactive card, supports full Markdown including code blocks and tables)


- **Examples**:

Send a Markdown file as a card (most common)

```sh
x feishu abot send --card --chatid <chat_id> -f ./README.md
```

Send a single-line Markdown string (bold, links, emoji supported)

```sh
x feishu abot send --card --chatid <chat_id> '**任务完成** ✅ 详见 [构建报告](https://github.com/x-cmd/x-cmd)'
```

Pipe command output from stdin as the card body

```sh
git log --oneline -10 | x feishu abot send --card --chatid <chat_id> -
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x feishu abot send --card [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--chatid` &lt;chat_id&gt; |  | Chat ID |
| `--messageid` &lt;message_id&gt; |  | Target message ID; when set, delivers as a reply to that message (uses the reply API; --chatid can be omitted) |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `-f`, `--file` &lt;path&gt; | Read Markdown content from a file |
| `--fp` | Record sent card content to the data file |
| `-j`, `--json` | Output raw JSON response from Feishu API |

### x feishu abot reaction

Manage emoji reactions on messages



::: tip For available emoji_type values, see the Feishu emoji reference:
https://open.feishu.cn/document/uAjLw4CM/ukTMukTMukTM/reference/im-v1/message-reaction/emojis-introduce

Common values: SMILE, THUMBSUP, DONE, OK, HEART, etc.

add returns a reaction_id needed by rm; you can only remove reactions you added yourself
:::


- **Examples**:

Add a THUMBSUP reaction to the specified message

```sh
x feishu abot reaction add --msgid <message_id> THUMBSUP
```

Remove the specified emoji reaction from the message

```sh
x feishu abot reaction rm --msgid <message_id> <reaction_id>
```

### x feishu abot service

Manage intelligent bot listener service



::: tip There are two listening modes:
1. --admin — Private chat mode (default), listens to private chats between the bot creator and the bot

   First startup requires configuring owner chat_id, service name: x-feishu-admin-listener

   Configuration command: x feishu --cfg chatid=&lt;chat_id&gt;
2. --group — Group chat mode

   Without chat_id: automatically fetches all group list and listens to each group, service name: x-feishu-group-listener

   With chat_id: listens to the specified group, service name: x-feishu-group-&lt;chat_id&gt;-listener
:::

::: tip
How to get chat_id: page -&gt; Top right corner settings -&gt; Bottom to find
:::


- **Examples**:

Start listener service (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu abot service start
```

Start in private chat mode

```sh
x feishu abot service start --admin
```

Start in group chat mode, listen to all groups

```sh
x feishu abot service start --group
```

Start in group chat mode, listen to messages in specified group

```sh
x feishu abot service start --group <chat_id>
```

Stop listener service (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu abot service stop
```

Stop group chat mode listener service

```sh
x feishu abot service stop --group
```

Check listener service status (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu abot service status
```

Check group chat mode service status

```sh
x feishu abot service status --group
```

Restart listener service (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu abot service restart
```

View service logs for specified chat

```sh
x feishu abot service log <chat_id>
```

- **Sub Commands**:


| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x feishu abot service start](#x-feishu-abot-service-start) | Start intelligent bot listener service |
| [x feishu abot service stop](#x-feishu-abot-service-stop) | Stop intelligent bot listener service |
| [x feishu abot service restart](#x-feishu-abot-service-restart) | Restart intelligent bot listener service |
| [x feishu abot service status](#x-feishu-abot-service-status) | Show intelligent bot listener service status |
| [x feishu abot service log](#x-feishu-abot-service-log) | Show intelligent bot listener service logs |

# x feishu bot

Send messages using Feishu group bot (webhook)

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x feishu bot send](#x-feishu-bot-send) | Send messages using Feishu group bot (webhook) |


### x feishu bot send

Send messages using Feishu group bot (webhook)


- **Examples**:

Send text messages to Feishu via Webhook

```sh
x feishu bot send --text "x-cmd 新版本发布成功"
```

A message with the title "Demo of Feishu" will be sent, linking to "https://x-cmd.com/mod/feishu"

```sh
x feishu bot send --richtext   \
  --title "Demo of Feishu" \
  --text "Welcome to x-cmd's website for details:" \
  --url "website" "https://x-cmd.com/mod/feishu"

```

- **Sub Commands**:


| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x feishu bot send --raw](#x-feishu-bot-send-raw) | send raw json |
| [x feishu bot send --text](#x-feishu-bot-send-text) | Send text type messages |
| [x feishu bot send --richtext](#x-feishu-bot-send-richtext) | Send a rich text message composed of text, images, and hyperlinks |
| [x feishu bot send --image](#x-feishu-bot-send-image) | Send image type messages |
| [x feishu bot send --share_chat](#x-feishu-bot-send-share-chat) | Share group business cards |


### x feishu bot send --raw

send raw json


- **Examples**:

Send text type messages to Feishu group

```sh
x feishu send --raw - <<A
  {
      "msgtype": "text",
      "text": {
          "content": "<content>"
      }
  }
  A
```

Reading JSON data from a file and sending a message

```sh
cat markdown.json | x feishu send --raw -
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x feishu bot send --raw [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | The original JSON message content that was sent. You can read JSON data from standard input using "-" |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--json`, `-j` | Output in Json format |
| `--webhook` | The webhook used by the specified group of bots to send messages |


### x feishu bot send --text

Send text type messages


- **Examples**:

Send text type messages to Feishu group

```sh

```

- **Arguments**:

| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | The content of the message |

# x feishu - Send Messages via Feishu Group Bot

## Initialize Configuration, Set Webhook URL

To start sending messages via Feishu group bot, you first need to get the Webhook URL. Please follow these steps:

::::ol
:::li Add Bot
In your Feishu group, click the "..." button in the upper right corner
:::

:::li Select Add Bot
Select "Add Bot"
:::

:::li Select Custom Bot
Select "Custom Bot"
:::

:::li Create and Get URL
After successful creation, you can find the webhook URL on the bot details page (note: select `v3` version bot)
:::
::::

After obtaining the Webhook URL, you can use the `init` command to paste the webhook URL into the designated position to quickly complete the initialization configuration.

```sh
x feishu init
```

**image demo**

Additionally, you can add the Webhook URL by running the following command:

```sh
x feishu --cfg webhook=<webhook_URL>
```

## Send Simple Text Messages

After completing the initialization configuration, you can easily send messages to the group chat by specifying the message type and content.

```sh
x feishu send --text "x-cmd new version released successfully"
```

**image demo**

## Send Rich Text Messages

Feishu bots support sending rich text messages containing text, images, links, etc.

```sh
x feishu send --richtext \
   --title "Demo of feishu"  \
   --text "Welcome to x-cmd's website for details." \
   --url "website" "https://x-cmd.com/mod/feishu"
```

**image demo**

## Send Image Messages

You can send image messages via `image_key`. The `image_key` needs to be obtained through Feishu's image upload interface.

```sh
x feishu send --image --image_key <image_key>
```

**image demo**

## Send Share Group Card Messages

You can share group cards to Feishu groups.

```sh
x feishu send --share_chat --chat_id <chat_id>
```

**image demo**

## Send Messages Using Different Group Bots

`x feishu` can choose different group bots to send messages as needed.

### Use `--webhook` Parameter

If you want to temporarily use another group bot's Webhook URL, you can use the `--webhook` parameter.

```sh
x feishu send --text --webhook <webhook> "A test"
```

**image demo**

### Use Configuration File Profile

Additionally, you can manage different group bots through configuration files.
First, create a Profile named `xbot` and save the specified `<webhook>` to this Profile:

```sh
x feishu --cfg set --profile xbot webhook=<webhook>
```

Then, you can send messages using the Webhook URL configured in the `xbot` Profile:

```sh
# `:` prefix is used to specify the Profile to use
x feishu :xbot send --text "A test"
```

**image demo**

Through this method, you can quickly switch to other bots without modifying the global configuration.

::: warning
Please remember to replace all `/image/mod/feishu.*.webp` with actual image paths and filenames.
:::

# x feishu listen

Long-polling listener for Feishu messages


::: tip There are two listening modes:
1. --admin — Private chat mode (default), listens to private chats between the bot creator and the bot
2. --group — Group chat mode, automatically fetches all group list and listens to each group if chat_id not provided
:::

::: tip There are two output modes:
1. --fp — Save received messages to data file (default path ~/.x-cmd-feishu/data_&lt;chat_id&gt;.tsv)
2. --json — Output messages in JSON format to stdout
:::


## Examples

Start long-polling listener for Feishu messages (private chat mode)

```sh
x feishu listen
```

Listen in private chat mode

```sh
x feishu listen --admin
```

Listen in group chat mode for all group messages

```sh
x feishu listen --group
```

Listen in group chat mode for messages in specified group

```sh
x feishu listen --group <chat_id>
```

Start listener and save messages to data file

```sh
x feishu listen --fp
```

Output messages in JSON format

```sh
x feishu listen --json
```

## Usage

```sh
x feishu listen [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--group` |  | Listen in group chat mode, automatically fetches all group list if chat_id not provided |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--admin` | Listen in private chat mode |
| `--fp` | Save received messages to data file |
| `--json` | Output messages in JSON format |

# x feishu login

Login to create a Feishu bot via QR code scan


::: tip Feishu Bot Login (x feishu login)
Use case: Create a Feishu intelligent bot by scanning a QR code with the Feishu App

This command retrieves app_id and app_secret and automatically saves them to the config

After successful login, you can directly use the intelligent bot features



Auto-detect runtime environment:

  Interactive terminal - Blocking mode, waits for QR scan and saves config

  Non-terminal (Agent/piped) - Non-blocking mode, returns QR code and session immediately



Agent workflow:
  1. x feishu login          - Get QR code
  2. x feishu login --check   - Check status, saves config on successful scan
:::


## Examples

Scan QR code to login and create Feishu bot

```sh
x feishu login
```

Check login status (agent mode)

```sh
x feishu login --check
```

## Usage

```sh
x feishu login
```

# x feishu parse

Parse Feishu messages, automatically download media files

## Examples

Parse message records from line 1 to 10 for chat oc_xxxxx

```sh
x feishu bot parse oc_xxxxx 1:10
```

Parse message records starting from line 5 for chat oc_xxxxx

```sh
x feishu bot parse oc_xxxxx 5
```

## Usage

```sh
x feishu parse <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Feishu chat ID or conversation ID |
| `#2` | Message line range, format as start:end or start |

# x feishu react

Listen for Feishu messages and reply automatically based on the specified mode

## Examples

Start in default mode (echo), returning the original message

```sh
x feishu react
```

Start interactive REPL mode, executing messages as commands and returning output

```sh
x feishu react --runner repl
```

Start a simple echo service to test if communication is working

```sh
x feishu react --runner echo
```

## Usage

```sh
x feishu react [OPTIONS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--timeout` &lt;ms&gt; |  | Timeout for the message reactor |
| `--runner` &lt;name&gt; |  | The execution mode of the reactor |

# x feishu send

Send messages using Feishu group bot (webhook) (equivalent to `x feishu bot send`)

## Examples

Send text type messages to Feishu group

```sh
x feishu send --text "x-cmd 新版本发布成功"
```

A message with the title "Demo of Feishu" will be sent, linking to "https://x-cmd.com/mod/feishu"

```sh
x feishu send --richtext   \
  --title "Demo of Feishu" \
  --text "Welcome to x-cmd's website for details:" \
  --url "website" "https://x-cmd.com/mod/feishu"

```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x feishu send --raw](#x-feishu-send-raw) | send raw json |
| [x feishu send --text](#x-feishu-send-text) | Send text type messages |
| [x feishu send --richtext](#x-feishu-send-richtext) | Send a rich text message composed of text, images, and hyperlinks |
| [x feishu send --image](#x-feishu-send-image) | Send image type messages |
| [x feishu send --share_chat](#x-feishu-send-share-chat) | Share group business cards |


### x feishu send --raw

send raw json


- **Examples**:

Send text type messages to Feishu group

```sh
x feishu send --raw - <<A
  {
      "msgtype": "text",
      "text": {
          "content": "<content>"
      }
  }
  A
```

Reading JSON data from a file and sending a message

```sh
cat markdown.json | x feishu send --raw -
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x feishu send --raw [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | The original JSON message content that was sent. You can read JSON data from standard input using "-" |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--json`, `-j` | Output in Json format |
| `--webhook` | The webhook used by the specified group of bots to send messages |

# x fjo cl

shortcut for `x fjo repo clone`

## Usage

```sh
x fjo cl [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | &lt;ownerPath&gt;/&lt;RepoPath&gt; (default ownerPath: current user) |
| `#2` | directory |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-o`, `--origin` &lt;name&gt; |  | use &lt;name&gt; instead of 'origin' to track upstream |
| `-b`, `--branch` &lt;branch&gt; |  | checkout &lt;branch&gt; instead of the remote's HEAD |
| `-u`, `--upload-pack` &lt;path&gt; |  | path to git-upload-pack on the remote |
| `-j`, `--jobs` &lt;n&gt; |  | number of submodules cloned in parallel |
| `--separate-git-dir` &lt;gitdir&gt; |  | separate git dir from working tree |
| `--depth` &lt;depth&gt; |  | create a shallow clone of that depth |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--recursive` | initialize all contained submodules |
| `--shallow-submodules` | any cloned submodules will be shallow |

# x fjo issue

repo issue management

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x fjo issue ls](#x-fjo-issue-ls) | List repo issue |
| [x fjo issue create](#x-fjo-issue-create) | Create issue |
| [x fjo issue edit](#x-fjo-issue-edit) | Edit issue |
| [x fjo issue close](#x-fjo-issue-close) | Close issue |
| [x fjo issue reopen](#x-fjo-issue-reopen) | Reopen issue |


### x fjo issue ls

List repo issue


- **Examples**:

View closed issues with the label "bug" in the x-cmd/x-cmd repository

```sh
x fjo issue ls --labels bug --state closed -r x-cmd/x-cmd
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x fjo issue ls [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--state` &lt;state&gt; |  | Indicates the state of the issues to return |
| `--type` &lt;type&gt; |  | filter by type (issues / pulls) if set. |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--repo`, `-r` &lt;owner/repo&gt; | &lt;owner_path&gt;/&lt;repo_path&gt; |
| `--q` &lt;string&gt; | search query |
| `--labels` &lt;labels(separated ,)&gt; | Labels to associate with this issue |
| `--since` &lt;timestamp&gt; | Only show items updated after the given time |
| `--before` &lt;timestamp&gt; | Only show items updated before the given time |
| `--created_by` &lt;assignees&gt; | Only show items which were created by the the given user |
| `--assigned_by` &lt;creator&gt; | Only show items for which the given user is assigned |
| `--milestones` &lt;assignees&gt; | comma separated list of milestone names or ids |
| `--mentioned_by` &lt;user_path&gt; | Only show items in which the given user was mentioned |
| `--page` &lt;num&gt; | target page |
| `--limit` &lt;num&gt; | per page data number |
| `--json`, `-j` | output raw JSON data |
| `--csv` | output csv data |
| `--yml` | output yml data |


### x fjo issue create

Create issue


- **Examples**:

Created an issue in the ollama/ollama repository with the title "A new bug", the content "it is a new bug"

```sh
x fjo issue create -r ollama/ollama --title "A new bug" --body "it is a new bug"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x fjo issue create [FLAGS]
```

- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--repo`, `-r` &lt;owner/repo&gt; | &lt;owner_path&gt;/&lt;repo_path&gt; |
| `--title` &lt;string&gt; | issue title |
| `--ref` &lt;base&gt; | base branch name or .sha=&lt;ref_SHA&gt; |
| `--body` &lt;string&gt; | The contents of the issue |
| `--labels` &lt;array&gt; | labels ID |
| `--closed` | close issue |
| `--due_date` &lt;timestamp&gt; | due date |
| `--assignees` &lt;array&gt; | User responsible for this pull request |
| `--milestone` &lt;id&gt; | milestone number |
| `--json`, `-j` | output raw JSON data |

| Name, Shorthand | Description |

# x fjo pr

repo pull request management

## Examples

List state is open pull requests

```sh
x fjo repo pr ls --state open --repo <owner/repo>
```

Created an pull request in the x-cmd/x-cmd repository with the title "The bug is fixed"

```sh
x fjo repo pr create --repo x-cmd/x-cmd --base develop --head main --title "The bug is fixed"
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x fjo pr ls](#x-fjo-pr-ls) | List pull requests |

- **Flags**:

# `x font` -- Font Installation and Terminal Beautification

We often receive questions in the background about why the terminal displays garbled text and how to have Powerline symbols or various programming icons. If you also have this problem, then the `x font` module is built for you.

The `x font` module is designed to provide a fast and convenient way to install [Nerd Fonts](https://www.nerdfonts.com/) and [Noto Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/noto). This module mainly solves the following core problems:

::::ul
:::li Automated Installation
Help users automatically identify and use `brew`, `apt`, or direct download methods to install fonts globally based on required scenarios
:::

:::li China Region Optimization
For users in China, we have optimized installation methods and download sources to avoid potential network issues, ensuring fonts can be downloaded and installed smoothly
:::

:::li Beautify Terminal
By installing Nerd Fonts containing a large number of icon glyphs, let your terminal, TUI software (such as Neovim, tmux, lazygit, etc.), and various prompts (such as Oh My Posh, Starship) correctly display various icons and symbols, saying goodbye to "tofu blocks" and garbled text
:::
::::

## Say Goodbye to Garbled Text, Embrace a Beautiful Terminal

In modern development environments, a beautiful and powerful terminal is key to improving efficiency and mood. Many popular terminal tools, plugins, and themes (such as Oh My Posh, Starship, Neovim plugins, Powerline, etc.) rely on specific fonts to display various icons, symbols, and ligatures. If your terminal font is not configured correctly, you may see:

::::ul
:::li Garbled text or "tofu blocks"
Unable to display specific characters, showing as boxes or question marks
:::

:::li Missing icons
Pretty icons in prompts or tools cannot be displayed
:::

:::li Poor typography
Code ligatures cannot take effect, affecting code reading experience
:::
::::

`x font` was born to solve these problems.

## What is Nerd Fonts?

![nerd-fonts](/image/mod/font.1_1.webp)

[Nerd Fonts](https://www.nerdfonts.com/) is a project that merges popular programming fonts (such as Fira Code, JetBrains Mono, Hack, Cascadia Code, etc.) with a large number of icon glyphs. These icon glyphs come from multiple popular icon libraries, including:

- **Font Awesome**
- **Devicons**
- **Octicons**
- **Powerline Symbols**
- **Material Design Icons**
- ...and more!

By installing Nerd Fonts, your terminal can display these rich icons, making your command-line interface more intuitive and beautiful.

## What is Noto Fonts?

[Noto Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/noto) is a series of fonts developed by Google, aiming to support all languages in the world and eliminate "tofu blocks" (the boxes that appear when fonts don't support certain characters). Among them, **Noto Color Emoji** font is crucial for correctly displaying full-color emoji in the terminal, especially when handling text containing Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and other characters.

## `x font` Command Details

The `x font` module aims to simplify the font installation process, letting you not worry about whether the underlying method is `brew` or `apt`, and without manually downloading and extracting.

### TLDR (Quick Start)

Enable `fzf` interactive TUI to select and download fonts

```sh
x font i
```

Considering terminal usage and icons and ligatures needed for beautifying common TUI software, we recommend using **Fira Code Nerd Font**.

```sh
x font install nerd/FiraCode
# Or
x font nerd installl FiraCode
```

### Core Subcommands

::::ul
:::li Install Font (`install` / `i`)
This is the most commonly used command in `x font`, used to install specified Nerd Font.
```bash
x font install nerd/<font_name>
# Examples:
x font i nerd/FiraCode         # Install Fira Code Nerd Font (recommended)
x font i nerd/CascadiaCode     # Install CaskaydiaCove Nerd Font
x font i nerd/JetbrainsMono    # Install JetBrains Mono Nerd Font
x font i nerd/CascadiaCode     # Install Cascadia Code Nerd Font
```
`x font` will automatically detect your operating system, select download sources, install to the corresponding system directory, and use `fc-cache` to refresh the font directory cache
:::

:::li List Nerd Fonts (`nerd ls`)
If you're not sure which Nerd Fonts are available for installation, you can use this command to view the supported list.
```bash
x font nerd
## Or
x font nerd ls
```
Executing this command will list all Nerd Fonts and enable `fzf` interactive TUI to preview font information and select fonts for download
:::

:::li Get Help (`-h` / `--help`)
When you forget commands or want to view more options, you can always use the help command.
```bash
x font -h
```
:::
::::

::: warning
After installing fonts to the system, you also need to apply the font to specific terminals and editors. Different editors have different configuration methods.
:::

## Note

After installing fonts to the system, <u>you also need to apply the font to specific terminals and editors</u>. Different editors have different configuration methods. We have collected some methods, please check [next chapter](/mod/font/cookbook-2.md).

## FAQ and Troubleshooting

::::ul
:::li Garbled text or "tofu blocks"
**Cause:** The most common reason is that the terminal emulator is not configured to use Nerd Fonts, or the installed font is not a Nerd Fonts version.
**Solution:** Ensure you have installed Nerd Fonts via `x font` and correctly configured your terminal emulator according to the above steps, selecting a font name ending with "Nerd Fonts".
:::

:::li Icons not displaying
**Cause:** Same as above, the terminal is not configured to use Nerd Fonts, or the tool you are using (such as Oh My Posh) has an icon set configured that doesn't fully match your installed Nerd Fonts.
**Solution:** Confirm terminal font configuration is correct. If problems persist, check your tool configuration to ensure the icon set it uses is included in your Nerd Fonts.
:::

:::li Network issues causing download failures
**Cause:** Although `x font` has optimized for China region networks, occasional network fluctuations may still be encountered.
**Solution:** Try re-running the `x font install` command. If the problem persists, check your network connection, or try manually downloading font files from the [Nerd Fonts official website](https://www.nerdfonts.com/font-downloads) and installing them.
:::
::::

## Recommended Fonts

::::ul
:::li Fira Code Nerd Font
**Reason for recommendation:** Excellent readability, beautiful ligatures features (such as `->` displaying as an arrow), extensive community support and adoption. It is the preferred programming font for many developers.
`x font nerd install FiraCode`
:::

:::li CaskaydiaCove Nerd Font
**Reason for recommendation:** [Cascadia Code](https://github.com/microsoft/cascadia-code) is a monospaced programming font designed by Microsoft specifically for developers, also the default font for Windows Terminal, with excellent readability and aesthetics. Caskaydia Cove is a repackaging by the Nerd Fonts project, additionally adding a large number of programming symbols and icons.
`x font nerd install CascadiaCode`
:::

:::li JetBrains Mono Nerd Font
**Reason for recommendation:** Designed specifically for developers, with unique glyph shapes and excellent readability, also supports ligatures, another very popular choice.
`x font nerd install JetbrainsMono`
:::

:::li NotoSansM Nerd Font
**Reason for recommendation:** Ensure your terminal can correctly display full-color emoji, avoiding black and white or missing emoji.
`x font nerd install Noto`
:::

The `x font` module greatly simplifies the installation process of Nerd Fonts and Noto Fonts, especially solving the pain point of network downloads for users in China. With simple commands, you can inject new vitality into your terminal, say goodbye to garbled text and missing icons, and enjoy a truly beautiful and efficient development environment.

From now on, make your terminal pleasing to the eye as well!

# A Crucial Step After Font Installation: Configuring Terminal Emulators and Editors

**Important Note:** Merely installing a font onto your system (for example, using the `x font install` command) does not automatically mean your terminal emulator or code editor will use it! You must manually configure these applications to instruct them to use your newly installed font, especially for fonts like Nerd Font which include special symbols.

Below are examples of configuration methods for common terminal emulators and code editors:

## VS Code Integrated Terminal

1.  Navigate to Settings in the bottom-left corner.
2.  In the search bar, type `terminal.integrated.fontFamily`.
3.  Set its value to the name of your installed Nerd Font, for example, `"FriaCode Nerd Font"`.
4.  Next, search for `terminal.integrated.fontLigatures` and check this option to enable font ligatures (if supported by the font).

or add a JSON configuration item

```json{2}
{
  "terminal.integrated.fontFamily": "FiraCode Nerd Font"
}
```

## Windows Terminal (Windows)

1.  Open Terminal settings using the shortcut <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>,</kbd>.
2.  Select 'Defaults' --> Click to modify 'Appearance' --> Choose your desired font under the 'Font face' section --> Click 'Save'.
    ![terminal_font.win](/image/start/terminal_font.win.1.webp)
2.  Alternatively, in the left navigation bar, select the `Profile` you wish to configure (e.g., `PowerShell`, `CMD`, `WSL`).
3.  Or, access and edit the `settings.json` file via the "Open JSON File" button in the bottom-left of the `Settings` interface:
    ```json{4-6}
    {
      "profiles": {
        "defaults": {
          "font": {
              "face": "FiraCode Nerd Font Mono"
          }
        }
      }
    }
    ```

## iTerm2 (macOS)

1.  Open Terminal settings using the shortcut <kbd>⌘</kbd> + <kbd>,</kbd>.
2.  Navigate to `Profiles` -> `Text`.
3.  In the `Font` section, search for and select the font.
4.  Choose your installed Nerd Font from the list, for example, `Fira Code Nerd Font`.
5.  If the font supports ligatures (e.g., Fira Code), check `Use ligatures` to enable them.

![iTerm2-SetupFont](/image/mod/font.2_1.webp)

## Terminal.app (macOS)

1.  Open Terminal settings using the shortcut <kbd>⌘</kbd> + <kbd>,</kbd>.
2.  Select 'Profiles' --> Click 'Change...' for Font --> Choose your desired font under the 'Font face' section.
    ![Terminal.app-SetupFont](/image/start/terminal_font.darwin.1.webp)

## Warp (Cross-platform)

1. Click the avatar in the top-right corner -> Select 'Settings'.
2. Search for the 'font' setting -> Select the corresponding font.

![Warp-SetupFont](/image/mod/font.2_2.webp)

## Alacritty (Cross-platform)

1.  Edit your `alacritty.yml` configuration file (typically located at `~/.config/alacritty/alacritty.yml`).
2.  Locate the `font` section and modify the `family` for `normal`, `bold`, and `italic` to the name of your installed Nerd Font.
    ```yaml
    font:
      normal:
        family: FriaCode Nerd Font # Replace with the name of your installed font
        style: Regular
      bold:
        family: FriaCode Nerd Font
        style: Bold
      italic:
        family: FriaCode Nerd Font
        style: Italic
      size: 14.0 # Font size, adjustable as needed
    ```

## Kitty (Cross-platform)

1.  Edit your `kitty.conf` configuration file (typically located at `~/.config/kitty/kitty.conf`).
2.  Add or modify the following lines:

    ```properties
    font_family         FriaCode Nerd Font # Replace with the name of your installed font
    bold_font           auto
    italic_font         auto
    font_size           14.0 # Font size, adjustable as needed
    disable_ligatures   never # Enable ligatures
    ```

## Ghostty (Cross-platform)

Edit your `config` configuration file (typically located at `~/.config/ghostty/config`)

```properties{1}
font-family = FriaCode Nerd Font
font-style = Medium
font-size = 18
```

## GNOME Terminal (Linux)

1.  Open `GNOME Terminal` -> Right-click or select from the navigation -> `Preferences`.
2.  Select the `Profile` you wish to configure.
3.  Under the `Text` tab, check `Custom font`.
4.  Click the font selection button, then choose your installed Nerd Font.

## Konsole (Linux)

1. In the navigation bar, select 'Settings' to open the settings.
2. In `Profiles`, click 'New' or 'Edit' for the target `Profile`.
3. After entering the configuration, select 'Appearance' -> Click Font 'Choose...', then choose your installed Nerd Font.

## Termux (Android)

1. Rename the target font file and move it to `~/.termux/font.ttf`.
2. Run the `termux-reload-settings` command to apply the changes.

:::tip
After downloading font resources with the `font` module, it will detect if it's a Termux environment and enter a single-font interactive selection mode. Pressing <kbd>Enter</kbd> after selecting will automatically perform the above operations to enable the font.

```sh
x font
```
:::

## Verifying Font Activation

After configuration is complete, be sure to **restart** your terminal emulator or code editor. Then, you can try the following methods to verify if the font is displayed correctly:

*   **Display Powerline/Oh My Posh/Starship Symbols:** If you use these tools, observe whether your prompt displays the correct arrows, branches, locks, and other special symbols. This is the most direct way to verify if the Nerd Font icon character set is active.
*   **Display File Type Icons:** Use the `x yazi` or `x eza -l --icons` command. If your file manager or theme (such as `lsd` or `eza` with Nerd Font) supports it, file and folder icons will be displayed.
*   **Display Emoji:** Try typing some Emoji characters in the terminal (e.g., `😀🚀✨`) to see if they display correctly in color.
*   **Code Ligatures:** If you have installed a font that supports ligatures (such as Fira Code), type `->`, `=>`, `!=`, `===`, etc., in the terminal or VS Code to see if they merge into a more aesthetic single symbol.

If all the above verification steps are successful, congratulations! Your new font has been successfully activated in your terminal and editor!

# Fonts in System Package Managers

At times, installing x-cmd might not be convenient; however, users can still install fonts on the target host using its native package manager.

## brew -- Applicable to macOS, Linux (via Linuxbrew)

Brew font packages typically begin with `font-` and are usually located within the `homebrew/cask-fonts` Cask repository.

**Searching for Fonts**

To search for all available font packages, you can use:

```bash
brew search font-
```

Alternatively, if you know part of the font name, such as `fira-code`:

```bash
brew search font-fira-code
```

**Installing Fonts**

To install Fira Code Nerd Font:

```bash
brew install font-fira-code-nerd-font
```

To install Noto Sans CJK:

```bash
brew install font-noto-sans-cjk
```

To install Hack Nerd Font:

```bash
brew install font-hack-nerd-font
```

## apt -- Applicable to Debian, Ubuntu, Kali, and similar distributions

`apt` is the package manager for Debian and its derivative distributions (such as Ubuntu, Kali Linux, and Mint). Font packages typically begin with `fonts-`.

**Updating Package Lists**

Before searching and installing, it is recommended to update your local package list:

```bash
sudo apt update
```

**Searching for Fonts**

To search for fonts, use the `apt search` command. For example, to search for all font packages:

```bash
apt search fonts-
```

To search for specific fonts, such as `fira` or `noto`:

```bash
apt search fonts-fira
apt search fonts-noto
```

**Installing Fonts**

To install Fira Code font:

```bash
sudo apt install fonts-firacode
```

To install Noto CJK font (which includes Chinese, Japanese, and Korean characters):

```bash
sudo apt install fonts-noto-cjk
```

To install Powerline fonts (commonly used for terminal customization):

```bash
sudo apt install fonts-powerline
```

**Nerd Fonts Considerations**

The official Debian/Ubuntu repositories may not directly provide all the latest Nerd Fonts. You might need to:
1.  Install base fonts like `fonts-hack-ttf` or `fonts-fira-code`, then manually download the patched Nerd Font versions.
2.  Add a third-party PPA (Personal Package Archive), such as `ppa:rael-gc/ubuntu-fonts` (please verify its security independently).
3.  Download directly from the Nerd Fonts GitHub repository and install manually (recommended approach, offering the most flexibility).

## apk -- Applicable to Alpine Linux

`apk` is the package manager for Alpine Linux, known for its lightweight nature and security.

**Updating Package Lists**

Before searching and installing, it is recommended to update your local package list:

```bash
sudo apk update
```

**Searching for Fonts**

To search for fonts, use the `apk search` command. For example:

```bash
apk search font-
```

To search for specific fonts, such as `noto`:

```bash
apk search font-noto
```

**Installing Fonts**

To install Noto font:

```bash
sudo apk add font-noto
```

To install Fira Code font (if available):

```bash
sudo apk add font-fira-code
```

**Nerd Fonts Considerations**

Alpine Linux's official repositories offer fewer Nerd Fonts directly. Typically, you will need to:
1.  Manually download Nerd Fonts and place them in directories like `/usr/share/fonts/TTF/` or `/usr/local/share/fonts/`.
2.  Run `fc-cache -fv` to update the font cache.

## pacman -- Applicable to Arch Linux, Manjaro, EndeavourOS, and similar distributions

`pacman` is the package manager for Arch Linux and its derivative distributions (such as Manjaro).

**Updating Package Lists**

Before searching and installing, it is recommended to synchronize your local package database:

```bash
sudo pacman -Sy
```

**Searching for Fonts**

To search for fonts, use the `pacman -Ss` command. For example:

```bash
pacman -Ss font
```

To search for Nerd Fonts:

```bash
pacman -Ss nerd-font
```

**Installing Fonts**

To install Fira Code font:

```bash
sudo pacman -S ttf-fira-code
```

To install Noto CJK font:

```bash
sudo pacman -S noto-fonts-cjk
```

To install common Nerd Fonts (e.g., Hack Nerd Font):

```bash
sudo pacman -S ttf-hack-nerd
```

To install Nerd Fonts Symbols (if a separate symbols font is needed):

```bash
sudo pacman -S ttf-nerd-fonts-symbols
```

**AUR (Arch User Repository) Considerations**

Many of the latest or less common Nerd Fonts may not be found in the official repositories but can be located in the AUR (Arch User Repository). Installing AUR packages typically requires an AUR helper (such as `yay` or `paru`).

For example, to install Fira Code Nerd Font using `yay`:

```bash
yay -S ttf-fira-code-nerd
```

## scoop -- Applicable to Windows

`scoop` is a command-line installer for Windows, similar to Homebrew on macOS. It organizes software packages through "buckets."

**Installing Scoop (if not already installed)**

Run the following in PowerShell:

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser # Only needs to be run once
irm get.scoop.sh | iex
```

**Adding Font Buckets**

Scoop's fonts are typically found in buckets like `nerd-fonts` or `extras`. You must first add these buckets:

```powershell
scoop bucket add nerd-fonts
scoop bucket add extras
```

**Searching for Fonts**

To search for fonts, use the `scoop search` command. For example:

```powershell
scoop search font
```

To search for Nerd Fonts:

```powershell
scoop search nerd-font
```

**Installing Fonts**

To install Fira Code Nerd Font:

```powershell
scoop install fira-code-nerd-font
```

To install Hack Nerd Font:

```powershell
scoop install hack-nerd-font
```

To install Noto Fonts (potentially found in the `extras` bucket):

```powershell
scoop install noto-fonts
```

**Tips**

*   Fonts installed via `scoop` are typically registered automatically in the Windows font directory.
*   After installation, you may need to restart your terminal or applications for the newly installed fonts to appear.
*   `scoop` provides a very convenient way to manage fonts on Windows, especially Nerd Fonts.
