### x gt repo create

Create repo



`x gt repo create` is multi-command merge sugar to conveniently use
* `x gt user repo create`
* `x gt org repo create`
* `x gt enterprise repo create`

If you need more control options or using in script, Please use them


- **Examples**:

Create a repo named &lt;repo_name&gt; for current user

```sh
x gt repo create <repo_name>
```

Create a repo named &lt;repo_name&gt; for &lt;org_path&gt; organization

```sh
x gt repo create <org_path>/<repo_name>
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x gt repo create [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | &lt;owner_path&gt;/&lt;repo_path&gt; |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--access` &lt;private,public&gt; | repo access |
| `-p`, `--path` &lt;path&gt; | repo path |
| `--description` &lt;desc&gt; | repo description |
| `--homepage` &lt;url&gt; | repo homepage |
| `--gitignore_template` &lt;template_name&gt; | Git Ignore template |
| `--license_template` &lt;license_name&gt; | License template |
| `--no_issue` | Ban repo issue |
| `--no_wiki` | Ban repo wiki |
| `--no_comment` | Ban repo comment |
| `--auto_init` | Initialize the repository with README |


### x gt repo edit

Edit repo configure


- **Examples**:

Change the x-cmd repository to a private repository

```sh
x gt repo edit --access private user/x-cmd
```

Rename the repository "x-cmd" to "myrepo"

```sh
x gt repo edit --name myrepo user/x-cmd
```

Change the default branch of the x-cmd repository to 'main' and disable issue creation

```sh
x gt repo edit --default_branch main --no_issues user/x-cmd
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x gt repo edit|ed [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | &lt;owner_path&gt;/&lt;repo_path&gt; |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--name` &lt;rename&gt; | repo rename |
| `--access` &lt;private,public&gt; | repo access |
| `-p`, `--path` &lt;path&gt; | repo path |
| `--description` &lt;desc&gt; | repo description |
| `--homepage` &lt;url&gt; | repo homepage |
| `--default_branch` &lt;branch_name&gt; | repo default branch |
| `--default_merge_method` &lt;way&gt; | repo default merge PR way |
| `--no_issue` | Ban repo issue |
| `--no_wiki` | Ban repo wiki |
| `--no_comment` | Ban repo comment |
| `--no_security_hole` | Ban repo issue public access |
| `--no_pull_requests` | Ban repo pull request |
| `--no_online_edit` | Ban repo online edit |
| `--no_lightweight_pr` | Ban repo lightweight pr |
| `--yes`, `-y` | Ignore edit access private prompt interception |
| `--json`, `-j` | output raw JSON data |

### x gt repo cl

clone repo from Gitee


- **Usage**:

```sh
x gt repo cl|clone [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | &lt;owner_path&gt;/&lt;repo_path&gt; |
| `#2` | directory |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-o`, `--origin` &lt;name&gt; |  | use &lt;name&gt; instead of 'origin' to track upstream |
| `-b`, `--branch` &lt;branch&gt; |  | checkout &lt;branch&gt; instead of the remote's HEAD |
| `-u`, `--upload-pack` &lt;path&gt; |  | path to git-upload-pack on the remote |
| `-j`, `--jobs` &lt;n&gt; |  | number of submodules cloned in parallel |
| `--separate-git-dir` &lt;gitdir&gt; |  | separate git dir from working tree |
| `--depth` &lt;depth&gt; |  | create a shallow clone of that depth |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--recursive` | initialize all contained submodules |
| `--shallow-submodules` | any cloned submodules will be shallow |


### x gt repo fork

Fork repo from Gitee


- **Examples**:

Fork &lt;owner/repo&gt; repo to current user repositories

```sh
x gt repo fork <owner/repo>
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x gt repo fork [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Target repo &lt;ownerPath&gt;/&lt;RepoPath&gt; |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--org` &lt;org_path&gt; | Forking into an organization |
| `-p`, `--path` &lt;path&gt; | fork repo path. (default source repo path) |
| `--name` &lt;name&gt; | fork repo name. (default source repo name) |
| `--json`, `-j` | output raw JSON data |


### x gt repo apply

Manage repo by declare configure


- **Examples**:

Use repo.yml declare configure manage repo

```sh
x gt repo apply ./repo.yml
```

Use repo.yml declare configure manage repo, And alias configure's user 'bot' to 'x-cmd-bot'

```sh
x gt repo apply ./repo.yml bot=x-cmd-bot
```

Use stdin declare configure data manage repo

```sh
cat ./repo.yml | x gt repo apply -
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x gt repo apply <#1> <#n>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | declare file path(yml, json), stdin '-' |
| `#n` | alias name list |

| `--no_comment` | Ban repo comment |
| `--auto_init` | Initialize the repository with README |
| `--json`, `-j` | output raw JSON data |

# x gtb - Project Gutenberg E-book Search and Browse

The `x gtb` module provides a convenient command-line interface for searching and browsing e-books on Project Gutenberg. Project Gutenberg is a large digital library containing a vast collection of public domain books.

## Search Books

You can use the `search` or `s` command to search for books matching specific criteria.

```bash
x gtb search [keyword]
```

For example, search for books containing "Dumas":

```bash
x gtb search Dumas
```

You can use the `--csv` parameter to output results in CSV format, or use the `--app` parameter to view results in an interactive UI:

```bash
x gtb search --csv Dumas  # CSV format output
x gtb search --app Dumas  # Interactive UI view
```

## View Book Metadata

The `meta` command can view the storage location of book data and list all books:

```bash
x gtb meta
```

You can use the `which` subcommand to view the storage location of book data:

```bash
x gtb meta which
```

Similarly, the `ls` subcommand lists all books and supports `--csv` and `--app` parameters:

```bash
x gtb meta ls  # List all books
x gtb meta ls --csv # CSV format output
x gtb meta ls --app # Interactive UI view
```

## Search Using DuckDuckGo

The `x gtb : [keyword]` command uses DuckDuckGo to search for related information on the Hacker News website:

```bash
x gtb : dumas  # Search "dumas" on DuckDuckGo
```

## Get Book Text Content

The `txt` command can get the original text content of a specified book:

```bash
x gtb txt [book_id]
```

For example, get the text content of the book with ID 100:

```bash
x gtb txt 100
```

## Browse Books Interactively

The `show` command allows you to browse book content interactively:

```bash
x gtb show [book_id]
```

For example, interactively browse the book with ID 100:

```bash
x gtb show 100
```

## Open Book in Browser

The `open` command opens the book in the default browser, supporting three formats: EPUB, text, and metadata:

```bash
x gtb open [book_id] [--pub|--txt|--meta]
```

For example, open the EPUB version of the book with ID 100 in the default browser:

```bash
x gtb open 100 --pub
```

## Quick Start

Here are some commonly used `x gtb` command examples:

::::ul
:::li `x gtb`
List all books
:::

:::li `x gtb search Dumas`
Search for books containing "Dumas"
:::

:::li `x gtb : dumas`
Search for "dumas" using DuckDuckGo
:::

:::li `x gtb show 100`
Get detailed information about the book with ID 100
:::
::::

::: tip
For more command usage, please refer to the official documentation.
:::

For more information, please visit [https://x-cmd.com](https://x-cmd.com)

# x hash - Calculate File Checksums

The `x hash` command is used to calculate MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA384, and SHA512 checksums for files. It supports multiple subcommands and parameters, allowing users to flexibly calculate checksums according to their needs.

## Quick Start

The simplest usage is to directly specify the file path:

```bash
x hash <file_path>
```

This calculates and outputs the SHA1 checksum of the file. If the system supports `shasum`, it uses `shasum`; otherwise, it uses `sha1sum`.

To calculate other types of checksums, you can use the following subcommands:

::::ul
:::li `md5`
Calculate MD5 checksum
:::

:::li `sha1`
Calculate SHA1 checksum
:::

:::li `sha256`
Calculate SHA256 checksum
:::

:::li `sha384`
Calculate SHA384 checksum
:::

:::li `sha512`
Calculate SHA512 checksum
:::
::::

For example, calculate the MD5 checksum of a file:

```bash
x hash md5 <file_path>
```

## Process Multiple Files

The `x hash` command can process multiple files simultaneously. Just pass file paths as parameters in sequence:

```bash
x hash <file1> <file2> <file3>
```

Output results will display each file's SHA1 checksum in order.

## Read Data from Standard Input

If you don't need to specify a file, you can directly read data from standard input for checksum calculation:

```bash
echo "Hello, world!" | x hash
```

This calculates the SHA1 checksum of the "Hello, world!" string. Similarly, you can combine pipes with other subcommands to process standard input.

## Checksum Verification

`x hash` provides `verify` and `assert` subcommands for checksum verification:

### `verify` Command

The `verify` command compares whether a file's checksum matches a known value. It automatically infers the algorithm based on checksum length.

```bash
x hash verify <file_path> <checksum>
```

For example:

```bash
x hash verify myfile.txt a1b2c3d4e5f678901234567890abcdef
```

This command outputs verification results to the log.

### `assert` Command

The `assert` command is similar to the `verify` command but returns an exit code:

- 0: Checksum matches
- 1: Checksum does not match
- 2: Unable to determine algorithm

::: tip
The `assert` command can be conveniently used in scripts for checksum verification.
:::

```bash
x hash assert <file_path> <checksum>
```

## Information Output (`info`)

The `info` subcommand outputs the MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA384, and SHA512 checksums of a file.

```bash
x hash info <file_path>
```

## Summary

The `x hash` command is a powerful tool for conveniently calculating and verifying file checksums, suitable for various scenarios such as software package integrity checks, data consistency verification, etc. Its concise command-line interface and flexible options make it easy to use and integrate into other scripts.

# Is MD5 Secure?

In the realm of information security, the storage and protection of passwords constitute a core issue. MD5 (Message-Digest Algorithm 5), as a widely used hash function, frequently becomes the subject of discussion regarding its security: "Is MD5 secure?" This question does not have a simple "yes" or "no" answer; it depends on the specific application scenario and implementation method. This article will delve into the security of MD5 and explore the more secure practices we should adopt for modern password storage and data integrity verification.

## TLDR

1.  For information digest scenarios, it still has its uses (but be aware of collision risks; not suitable for high-security scenarios).
2.  For password storage -- insecure.
3.  For information tamper prevention -- vulnerable to Hash collisions, insecure.

## The Nature and Limitations of MD5

MD5 is a cryptographic hash function that takes an input of arbitrary length (such as a password or file) and produces a fixed-length output (128 bits, typically represented as a 32-character hexadecimal string), known as a hash value or message digest. MD5 was originally designed for data integrity verification, meaning comparing the MD5 value of a file to confirm whether it has been tampered with during transmission.

**Characteristics of MD5:**
1.  **One-way function:** Theoretically, it is impossible to derive the original input from the hash value.
2.  **Fixed output length:** Regardless of the input length, the output hash value has a fixed length.
3.  **Avalanche effect:** Even a minor change in the original input results in a drastically different hash value.
4.  **Fast computation:** MD5 is highly efficient in computation.

However, MD5's "speed" and "one-way nature" paradoxically become security vulnerabilities in password storage scenarios.

## MD5 for Password Storage: Why It's No Longer Recommended

In earlier times, MD5 was widely used for password storage due to its one-way property. Developers believed that by storing only the MD5 hash of a password, attackers could not directly obtain user passwords even if the database was leaked. However, with advancements in computing power and attack techniques, MD5 is no longer considered a secure password hashing algorithm, especially without additional protective measures.

**The primary reason lies in "Rainbow Table Attack":**

A rainbow table is a pre-computed table of hash values and their corresponding original inputs (passwords). Because MD5 computation is very fast, attackers can pre-generate a massive database containing common passwords and their MD5 hash values. Once leaked MD5 hash values are obtained, attackers can quickly find the corresponding original password by simply looking it up in the rainbow table, without needing complex computations.

For example, if your password is "password123", its MD5 hash value is `202cb962ac59075b964b07152d234b70`. An attacker only needs to look up this hash value in a rainbow table to quickly find the corresponding original password.

### "Salting": The First Step to Enhancing Password Hash Security

To counter rainbow table attacks, the concept of "Salting" was introduced.

**What is "Salt"?**
"Salt" is a randomly generated string that is combined with the user's original password (typically by concatenation) before the hashing computation. Each user's salt value is unique and is usually stored alongside the hash value in the database (the salt value is stored in plaintext because its purpose is to increase the complexity of the hash, not to be kept secret).

**How does Salting counter rainbow tables?**
By salting, even if two users set the same password, their different salt values will result in completely different final hash values. This means attackers can no longer use a single, generic rainbow table to crack all passwords. They would have to generate a separate rainbow table for every unique salt value, which significantly increases the computational cost and storage requirements for the attack, making it impractical.

**Example:**
*   User A password: "password123", salt: "abcde" -> MD5("password123abcde") -> Hash Value A
*   User B password: "password123", salt: "fghij" -> MD5("password123fghij") -> Hash Value B

Hash Value A and Hash Value B will be completely different.

### More Secure Password Hashing Algorithms: Slow Hashing Functions

Although salting effectively counters rainbow tables, MD5's inherent speed remains a weakness. Attackers can still crack salted MD5 hashes through brute-force attacks (trying passwords one by one and computing their hash values). If MD5 computation is fast, an attacker can attempt billions of password combinations per second.

To address this problem, modern password storage recommends using "Slow Hashing Functions," also known as "Adaptive Hashing Functions" or "Key Derivation Functions" (KDFs). These algorithms are designed to intentionally consume more computational resources (CPU time, memory), thereby significantly slowing down brute-force attacks.

**Common slow hashing algorithms include:**
1.  **bcrypt:** Based on the Blowfish cipher algorithm, it controls the number of computation iterations via a "work factor" or "cost factor," which can be dynamically adjusted based on hardware performance to maintain a certain computation time.
2.  **scrypt:** In addition to CPU consumption, it also increases memory consumption, making large-scale parallel attacks using specialized hardware (like GPUs) more difficult.
3.  **Argon2:** The winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition (PHC), it offers higher security and flexibility, allowing configuration of CPU time, memory, and parallelism.

These algorithms all incorporate built-in salting mechanisms and allow adjustment of their "slowness" by configuring iteration counts or memory consumption, adapting to future advancements in computing power.

### After a Database Leak, What is the Significance of Cracking Passwords?

Some might ask: "Since the database has already been compromised, and information has leaked, what's the point of cracking passwords?" This question is crucial because the harm of cracked passwords extends far beyond the initial leak:

1.  **Legitimate Website Access:** Once passwords are cracked, attackers can directly use them to log into the compromised website, obtain users' personal information, perform illicit operations, or even impersonate users.
2.  **"Credential Stuffing" Attacks:** This is one of the most common subsequent attacks. Many users habitually use the same or similar passwords across different websites. Attackers will use the usernames and passwords cracked from one website (Site A) to attempt logging into other websites (Site B, Site C, etc.). Due to the widespread phenomenon of password reuse, the success rate of such attacks is very high, potentially leading to account compromise on multiple platforms.
3.  **Identity Theft:** Combined with other leaked information (such as name, email, phone number), cracked passwords can help attackers build a more complete user profile, enabling deeper identity theft or fraud.

### Comprehensive Defense Strategies

To maximize user password security, both developers and users should adopt a multi-layered defense strategy:

**For Developers:**
1.  **Use Modern Slow Hashing Algorithms:** Abandon fast hashing algorithms like MD5 and SHA-1, and switch to bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2.
2.  **Enforce Salting:** Ensure a unique and sufficiently long random salt value is generated for each user and stored along with the hash value.
3.  **Adjust Iteration Count/Work Factor:** Regularly evaluate and adjust the iteration count or work factor of the hashing algorithm based on server performance and security requirements, ensuring computation time remains within an acceptable range (e.g., approximately 200-500 milliseconds per hash computation).
4.  **Implement Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):** Provide users with MFA options such as SMS verification codes, TOTP (e.g., Google Authenticator), or hardware keys. Even if passwords are cracked, MFA can effectively prevent unauthorized logins.
5.  **Limit Login Attempts:** Prevent brute-force and credential stuffing attacks.
6.  **Regular Security Audits:** Conduct security vulnerability scans and penetration tests on the system.

**For Users:**
1.  **Use Unique and Complex Passwords:** Set different, sufficiently long, and complex passwords containing uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols for each important online service.
2.  **Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):** Whenever a website offers MFA options, be sure to enable it. This is one of the most effective ways to prevent account theft.
3.  **Use a Password Manager:** Password managers can help users generate and store complex and unique passwords, significantly reducing the risk of password reuse.
4.  **Be Wary of Phishing Attacks:** Do not click suspicious links or enter passwords on unknown websites.

## Tamper Prevention -- Hash Collisions: Why MD5 Is No Longer Reliable?

MD5 was initially widely used for verifying data integrity. For instance, when downloading software or files, an MD5 checksum would be provided. Users could calculate the MD5 value of the downloaded file and compare it with the official checksum to confirm whether the file had been tampered with during transmission. This mechanism relies on the "collision resistance" of the hash function, meaning it is extremely difficult to find two different inputs that produce the same hash value.

However, this property of MD5 was broken in 2004 by Professor Xiaoyun Wang's team of Chinese cryptographers, followed by the emergence of more practical "chosen-prefix collision" attacks.

### MD5's Application in Everyday Tamper Prevention (and why it failed)

Let's take a common scenario as an example: you want to download an important file, such as a 1GB Linux system image (ISO file), for operating system installation.

**In the past (when MD5 was considered secure), the tamper prevention process was:**

1.  **Official Release:** The official website of the Linux distribution would release the system image file and simultaneously provide its MD5 hash value (often called an MD5 checksum or MD5sum) alongside it. This MD5 value was like a unique "digital fingerprint" for that specific file.
    *   For example, the official website might state:
        *   `Linux_Distro_v1.0.iso`
        *   `MD5: 202cb962ac59075b964b07152d234b70` (This is an example MD5 value)

2.  **User Download:** You download the 1GB Linux image file from the official website.

3.  **User Verification:** After the download is complete, you worry whether the file might have been tampered with during the download process (e.g., the website was hacked, or you downloaded it over an insecure public Wi-Fi, and the file was maliciously modified in transit). To verify, you would use a tool (such as the `certutil -hashfile` command on Windows, or the `md5sum` command on Linux/macOS) to calculate the MD5 hash value of your downloaded file.

4.  **Comparison of Results:**
    *   If the MD5 value you calculated **was exactly the same as the one provided by the official website**, you would conclude: "Great! My downloaded file is complete and hasn't been modified by anyone; I can use it with confidence."
    *   If the MD5 value you calculated **did not match the one provided by the official website**, you would know: "Oh no! The file might have been corrupted during download or maliciously tampered with. I cannot use this file and need to re-download it or find another source."

**The intention behind this process was good, relying on MD5's "avalanche effect" and "collision resistance":**
*   **Avalanche Effect:** Even if only one byte of the file content changes, the MD5 value will change drastically.
*   **Collision Resistance (ideal scenario):** Theoretically, finding two different files that produce the same MD5 value is extremely difficult, almost impossible.

### MD5's Collision Problem: Why Is It No Longer Secure?

However, MD5's "collision resistance" was broken in 2004 by Professor Xiaoyun Wang's team of Chinese cryptographers. This means that **attackers can now relatively easily construct two completely different files that produce the same MD5 hash value—a "collision."**

**What does this mean for tamper prevention?**

Imagine an attacker wants you to download a Linux image file containing a virus, but they don't want you to discover it. They can do this:

1.  **Prepare Malicious File:** The attacker first obtains the clean Linux image file released by the official source.
2.  **Create Collision:** The attacker exploits the MD5 collision vulnerability to meticulously craft a **malicious Linux image file containing a virus**. This malicious file is completely different in content from the official clean file, but miraculously, the attacker can ensure that the MD5 hash value of this malicious file **is exactly the same as the MD5 hash value of the official clean file!**
3.  **Replace File:** The attacker, through some means (e.g., by compromising the official website and replacing the file pointed to by the download link, or by performing a "man-in-the-middle attack" on your insecure network connection, secretly replacing the file during your download), replaces the official clean file with their crafted malicious file.
4.  **User Deceived:** When you download this replaced malicious file, you follow your usual habit and calculate its MD5 value. Because the attacker has meticulously designed it, the MD5 value you calculate **perfectly matches the MD5 value provided by the official website!**
5.  **Consequences:** You mistakenly believe the file is safe and untampered, then confidently install this operating system containing a virus, leading to your computer being infected, data stolen, or even becoming part of a botnet.

**Simply put, MD5's collision problem is like this:** Previously, every file had a unique fingerprint, and you could confirm if a file had been swapped by comparing fingerprints. But now, a clever forger can create two completely different files that **have identical fingerprints**. If you only check the fingerprint, you cannot distinguish between the genuine and the fake.

Therefore, MD5 is no longer suitable for high-security data integrity verification and tamper prevention scenarios. For these applications, it is strongly recommended to use more secure hash algorithms such as SHA-256, SHA-3, or BLAKE2, which are currently still considered to have sufficient collision resistance.

# x hn - Command Line Hacker News Browser

The `x hn` module provides a powerful command-line interface for browsing news and information on the Hacker News (HN) website. It allows you to view various HN posts in an interactive table format, with convenient link opening and data viewing functions.

## Quick Start

By default, `x hn` displays HN's top posts:

```bash
x hn
```

You can view other types of posts through the following commands:

::::ul
:::li New posts
`x hn new`
:::

:::li Best posts
`x hn best`
:::

:::li Ask posts
`x hn ask`
:::

:::li Show posts
`x hn show`
:::

:::li Job posts
`x hn job`
:::
::::

## View Post Details

Use the `item` subcommand to view the content of a specified post:

```bash
x hn item <item_id>
```

`<item_id>` is the post ID number. You can customize the output format through the following options:

::::ul
:::li `--browse`
Open the HN article comments page
:::

:::li `--link`
Open the HN article link page (if it exists)
:::

:::li `--reader`
Use jina reader to get information from the HN article link page
:::

:::li `--preview`
Display in preview style
:::

:::li `--csv`
Display in CSV style
:::

:::li `--json`
Display in JSON style
:::
::::

For example, view the comments page of the post with ID 12345:

```bash
x hn item 12345 --browse
```

## View User Information

Use the `user` subcommand to view HN user information:

```bash
x hn user <user_id>
```

`<user_id>` is the user ID number. Similarly, you can use `--app` (default, human-readable format), `--csv`, `--json` options to customize the output format.

## Calculate User's h-index

Use the `hi` or `hidx` subcommand to calculate a user's h-index:

```bash
x hn hi <user_id>
```

`<user_id>` is the user ID number.

## Configuration Management

`x hn` provides flexible configuration management functions:

::::ul
:::li `init`
Initialize configuration using interactive mode
:::

:::li `cfg`
Manage configuration items such as data storage time, data location, and proxy information. You can use `cfg set` to set configurations, `cfg cat` to view current configurations. `cfg clear` clears current session settings and restores defaults
:::
::::

## Search Using DuckDuckGo

`x hn` integrates DuckDuckGo search functionality, making it convenient for you to search for information on the Hacker News website:

::::ul
:::li `x hn : <keyword>`
Use DuckDuckGo to search for related information on the Hacker News website
:::

:::li `x hn :: <keyword>`
Use DuckDuckGo and AI to search for related information in Hacker News
:::
::::

## Other Features

* **Pagination:** `x hn` supports paginated display of large numbers of posts for easy browsing.
* **Translation:** Combined with other tools, such as `@zh` (Simplified Chinese translation), you can conveniently translate HN post content.
* **Data Range:** You can specify the range of posts to view, for example, `x hn top 11,20` to view the 11th to 20th top posts.

## Examples

::::ul
:::li View HN best posts and display in preview style
`x hn best --preview`
:::

:::li View HN top posts 11-20, output in JSON format
`x hn top --json 11,20`
:::

:::li Search for "nodejs" related information in Hacker News
`x hn : nodejs`
:::

:::li Search for "llama3" related information in Hacker News, using AI to assist with results
`x hn :: llama3`
:::

:::li Translate HN best posts preview style content (requires installation of corresponding translation tools)
`x hn best --preview | @zh`
:::
::::

Hope this documentation helps you use the `x hn` module better. For more information, please visit [https://x-cmd.com](https://x-cmd.com)

# x host - Local Host Table Management

The `x host` module is used to manage the mapping relationship between local hostnames and IP addresses, facilitating local domain name resolution and testing. It provides functions to view, add, modify, and delete hostname mappings.

::: warning
Note:
1. All current operations of `x host` are centered around the `/etc/hosts` file; some systems may use other files to take over hostname resolution, in which case the `x host` module may not take effect.
2. Modifying the `/etc/hosts` file affects the entire system and therefore requires sudo permissions.
:::

## View Hostname Mappings

Use the `cat` command to view all current hostname to IP address mappings:

```bash
x host cat
```

Can be abbreviated as

```bash
x host
```

## Get IP Address for Specified Hostname

Use the `get` command to get the IP address mapped to a specified hostname in the local configuration:

```bash
x host get localhost
```

This returns the IP address corresponding to `localhost`. You can replace `localhost` with any hostname you want to query. If the hostname doesn't have a mapping, no result will be returned. The command will prompt you to enter a hostname, and you can use `___x_cmd_host___advise_get_candidate` to get a list of candidate hostnames.

## Edit Hostname Mappings

Use the `ed` command to add, modify, or delete hostname mappings.

### Add or Modify Mappings

Use the `=` symbol to connect hostname and IP address, for example:

```bash
x host ed hub.x-cmd.com=192.168.3.1
```

This adds or modifies the mapping for `hub.x-cmd.com` to point to `192.168.3.1`. If `hub.x-cmd.com` already exists, its IP address will be updated; otherwise, a new mapping will be added.

### Delete Mappings

Use the `-` prefix to delete the mapping for a specified hostname:

```bash
x host ed -hub.x-cmd.com
```

This deletes the mapping for `hub.x-cmd.com`.

## Usage Examples

Here are some `x host` command examples:

::::ul
:::li View all mappings
`x host cat`
:::

:::li Get localhost IP
`x host get localhost`
:::

:::li Add mapping for hub.x-cmd.com
`x host ed hub.x-cmd.com=192.168.3.1`
:::

:::li Delete mapping for hub.x-cmd.com
`x host ed -hub.x-cmd.com`
:::
::::

Through the `x host` module, you can conveniently manage local hostname to IP address mappings, thereby simplifying the configuration of local development and testing environments.

# Can't Write Commands? Press Ctrl+X to Let AI Help

Ever find yourself in these situations when typing commands in the terminal:

- Command arguments are too complex to remember?
- Typo causing pages of errors and you don't know what's wrong?
- Spent half an hour searching Google but still unsure about the correct syntax?

**Press Ctrl+X and let AI help!** This is the terminal AI assistant feature from x-cmd. Just press a shortcut key, describe what you need, and AI gives you the correct command.

## Quick Start

```bash
# Configure AI assistant
x hotkey co init

# Bind AI assistant to Ctrl+X shortcut
x hotkey use co
```

Once enabled, **press Ctrl+X anytime you encounter a command error or don't know how to write one**.

## Use Cases

### Scenario 1: Can't Write a Command

You want to delete files modified three days ago, but can't remember the `find` command parameters. Press **Ctrl+X** to summon the AI assistant, then enter your request:

```
🤖: I want to delete files modified three days ago
```

AI immediately gives you the correct command:

```bash
find . -mtime +3 -type f -exec rm {} \;
```

### Scenario 2: Can't Understand Error Messages

You run a `docker` command and get pages of English errors, feeling overwhelmed:

```
$ docker run nginx
docker: Error response from daemon: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint web:
Error starting userland proxy: listen tcp4 0.0.0.0:80: bind: address already in use.
```

Press **Ctrl+X** to summon AI and paste the error message:

```
🤖: What does this error mean? How do I fix it?
```

AI immediately analyzes the cause and provides a solution:

```
Port 80 is occupied. Stop the process using it, or use a different port:
docker run -p 8080:80 nginx
```

**No more copying error messages to search on Google!**

### Scenario 3: Cross-Platform Commands

You use macOS at work and a Linux server at home—some command parameters differ:

```
$ tar -I pigz -cf archive.tar.gz folder/
tar: unrecognized option '-I'
```

Press **Ctrl+X** to summon AI and describe your problem:

```
🤖: Why doesn't this command work on macOS?
```

AI knows you're on macOS and provides a compatible alternative:

```
macOS doesn't have pigz. Use the built-in gzip instead:
tar -czvf archive.tar.gz folder/
```

## vs. Browser Search

| Scenario | Browser Search | Press Ctrl+X |
|----------|---------------|--------------|
| Look up command syntax | Search "linux delete files modified 3 days ago", scroll through n results, compare which is correct | Describe your need, AI gives you the answer directly |
| Fix errors | Copy error → paste to search → find blog → compare solutions | Paste error to AI → get solution instantly |
| Check parameter usage | Search "tar command parameters" → read long man pages | Ask AI → simple Chinese explanation |

**Efficiency Gains:**

- No window switching (browser ↔ terminal)
- No ads or spam to scroll through
- AI knows your system, providing more accurate answers

## FAQ

### Q: Pressing Ctrl+X does nothing?

- First run `x hotkey use co` to enable the feature
- Bash 3.x requires pressing Ctrl+X twice; Bash 4.x/Zsh only needs once
- Make sure you're using Bash or Zsh

### Q: Do I need to configure an API key?

Yes. On first use, you'll be guided to configure an AI provider (OpenAI, Claude, etc.) API key.

### Q: Which AI providers are supported?

Supports major AI services: OpenAI, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Tongyi Qianwen, and more.

# x htop - Real-time System Monitoring Tool

## Quick Install and Use htop

htop is a powerful interactive system monitoring tool that can display processes, CPU, memory, disk, and network usage in real-time. The `x htop` module simplifies the installation and usage process of htop, allowing quick startup even in environments without pre-installed htop. It uses `pixi` (a fast package manager, please visit [https://prefix.dev/](https://prefix.dev/) for details or run `x pixi --help`) to automatically complete installation in the background.

### Quick Start

```bash
x htop
```

This launches an interactive process viewing interface, distinguishing different types of processes by color, giving you a clear view of system resource usage.

This automatically installs (if needed) and starts htop, displaying real-time system resource information. You can use htop's built-in commands for navigation and operations, such as sorting processes, viewing process details, etc.

<!-- ![x htop](/image/mod/htop.1.webp) *(Screenshot should be replaced with actual image)* -->

### Directly Pass Parameters to Original Command

`x htop` supports passing parameters directly to the htop command. For example, to view htop's help information:

```bash
x htop -- -h        # This is equivalent to directly running `htop -h` command.
x htop -- -u user   # Only show processes for specified user
```

## Features

*   **Interactive Interface**: Supports mouse and keyboard operations
*   **Color Display**: Intuitively displays CPU and memory usage
*   **Process Tree**: Displays process relationships
*   **Real-time Updates**: Dynamically refreshes data

::: tip
In the htop interface:
- Press `P` to sort by CPU
- Press `M` to sort by memory
- Press `T` to sort by running time
- Press `F5` to toggle process tree view
:::

## Summary

The `x htop` module provides a simple and convenient way to use htop to monitor system resources. With pixi support, it eliminates the tedious steps of manually installing htop and allows users to directly use htop commands and their parameters. This makes `x htop` an efficient and easy-to-use system monitoring tool.

# x hua - Your Pocket Chinese Classics Library

In the digital age, how can you conveniently appreciate the treasures of Chinese classical literature? The `x hua` command opens a door to the world of ancient wisdom and poetic beauty. It is more than just a command—it is like a portable study room, allowing you to easily browse timeless classics such as the *Classic of Poetry*, *Chu Ci*, and *Three Hundred Tang Poems* right in your terminal. For those who love Chinese culture and the command line, this is undoubtedly a tool worth exploring.

::: tip
Run `x hua` directly to enter the classics selection interface
:::

## One-Click Start: Overview of Chinese Cultural Classics

When you first encounter `x hua`, the most straightforward way is to run it without any parameters:

```sh
x hua
```

![hua_1](/image/mod/hua_1.webp)

After execution, a clear text selection interface will appear, listing many well-known classic titles:

* `sj`: *Classic of Poetry* (shījīng 诗经)
* `cc`: *Chu Ci* (chǔcí 楚辞)
* `ts`: *Three Hundred Tang Poems* (tángshī sānbǎi shǒu 唐诗三百首)
* `sc`: *Three Hundred Song Words* (sòngcí sānbǎi shǒu 宋词三百首)
* `qjs`: *Poems of a Thousand Families* (qiānjiā shī 千家诗)
* `dx`: *Da Xue* (dàxué 大学)
* `zy`: *Doctrine of the Mean* (zhōngyōng 中庸)
* `ly`: *The Analects* (lúnyǔ 论语)
* `mz`: *Mencius* (mèngzǐ 孟子)
* `gwgz`: *Guwen Guanzhi* (gǔwén guānzhǐ 古文观止)
* `caocao`: *Cao Cao's Poems* (cáocāo shījí 曹操诗集)

You can use the up and down arrow keys to navigate the list, and press Enter to select and enter the corresponding classic's reading interface.

After selecting a classic of interest, such as *The Analects*, press Enter. Next, you will enter a powerful interactive selection interface. Thanks to the integration of `fzf`, you can perform fast fuzzy searches.
In this interface:

::::ul
:::li Left Side
Displays the list of chapters in the classic. You can directly type keywords (such as the author "Li Bai" or the title "Quiet Night Thoughts") to filter the list in real-time
:::

:::li Right Side
Synchronously displays a preview of the content of the chapter currently under your cursor, allowing you to quickly browse before selecting and greatly improving search efficiency
:::
::::

![hua_2](/image/mod/hua_2.webp)

Once you find the chapter you want, press Enter again to confirm.
The full text of the chapter will be output completely and clearly to your terminal interface for you to savor. From selecting the classic to reading the full text, the entire process flows smoothly and seamlessly.

![hua_3](/image/mod/hua_3.webp)

## Full of Poetry: Exploring the Three Hundred Tang Poems

If you have a special fondness for Tang poetry and want to directly access the *Three Hundred Tang Poems*, `x hua` provides a convenient path. Simply type:

```sh
x hua ts
```

![hua_4](/image/mod/hua_4.webp)

::: tip
Here `ts` is the abbreviation for `tangshi300` (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
:::

After executing the command, you will skip the main menu and directly enter the dedicated chapter selection interface for the *Three Hundred Tang Poems*.

You can directly type keywords (such as poem titles, author names, or fragments of verses) for fuzzy searching, and `fzf` will filter matching results in real-time. The right side usually has a preview window displaying the full content of the currently selected poem in real-time. After finding your desired poem, press Enter to read the full poem clearly in the terminal.

## Rhyme of Song Words: Savoring the Three Hundred Song Words

Similar to querying Tang poetry, if you want to savor the grace and boldness of Song words, use the following command:

```sh
x hua sc
```

![hua_5](/image/mod/hua_5.webp)

`sc` is the abbreviation for `songci300` (Three Hundred Song Words). Similarly, this will open an `fzf`-driven interactive interface, allowing you to efficiently browse and search through the works in the *Three Hundred Song Words*.

The interface layout and operation methods are basically the same as the query interface for the *Three Hundred Tang Poems*, including information such as tune patterns, authors, and content previews. You can quickly locate Su Shi's "The Great River Flows East" or Li Qingzhao's "Seeking, Seeking" through keywords.

## Advanced Tips: Flexibly Adjusting the Reading Experience

When using the `fzf` interactive interface (such as when reading Tang and Song poetry), `x hua` also provides a very useful tip to optimize your reading experience:

::::ul
:::li `Ctrl-r`: Toggle Preview Window Layout
This shortcut allows you to switch between different preview modes, such as moving the preview window from the right to the bottom, or temporarily hiding the preview window to focus more on the list itself. This is very useful for different terminal window sizes or personal preferences
:::
::::

![hua_6](/image/mod/hua_6.webp)

`x hua` condenses the profound Chinese classics into the small command line. Through the convenience of modern CLI tools, it makes reading and retrieving classical literature more efficient and enjoyable than ever before. Whether you want to quickly look up a verse or systematically savor a classic, `x hua` can be your capable cultural assistant. Start your command-line cultural journey now!

# x hub access

Access control — set files as public or grant access to specific users

## Examples

Make a cloud file publicly accessible

```sh
x hub access set --public <path>
```

Grant a user access to the cloud file

```sh
x hub access set --user <username> <path>
```

Grant multiple users access to the cloud file (comma-separated)

```sh
x hub access set --user <user1>,<user2>,<user3> <path>
```

Remove all non-owner access to the file

```sh
x hub access unset <path>
```

Revoke a specific user's access

```sh
x hub access unset --user <username> <path>
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x hub access set](#x-hub-access-set) | Set file access permissions (public or specific users) |
| [x hub access unset](#x-hub-access-unset) | Revoke access; without --user removes all non-owners, with --user removes specific users |


### x hub access set

- **Usage**:


- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Cloud file path |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--user` |  | Grant access to specific users (comma-separated, e.g., alice,bob) |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--public` | Make publicly accessible (anyone can access) |

### x hub account login

Login/register account, auto-register if not exists



::: tip AI Agent login flow:
1. Execute `x hub login`
2. Read the URL=xxx from the output
3. Send the URL to the user, ask them to open it in a browser and complete authorization (no need for the user to confirm, the program polls automatically)
4. Wait for STATUS=success in the output, which means login succeeded

If polling times out or is interrupted (STATUS=timeout), run

`x hub login verify` after the user completes authorization to re-check:

STATUS=success means login succeeded, STATUS=pending means the browser

authorization has not been completed yet.
:::


- **Examples**:

Login/register account, AI agents can run this directly

```sh
x hub login
```

Login with GitHub

```sh
x hub login github
```

Login with email

```sh
x hub login email <email>
```

Login with WeChat, set expiration (e.g., 1d, 7d)

```sh
x hub login --expire <duration> wechat
```

Email login with custom expiration and region

```sh
x hub login --expire <duration> --region <region> email <email>
```

Manually check if login completed (re-check after auto-poll exits)

```sh
x hub login verify
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x hub account login [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--expire` |  | Login expiration time, default 30 days (format like "n[smhdw]") |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--region` | Login region, determines account region on first login, defaults to current region |

| [x hub account login wechat](#x-hub-account-login-wechat) | WeChat login via web page |
| [x hub account login github](#x-hub-account-login-github) | GitHub login via web page |
| [x hub account login email](#x-hub-account-login-email) | Email login (requires binding email first) |
| [x hub account login verify](#x-hub-account-login-verify) | Manually check if login completed (use after auto-poll exits) |

# No USB, no Git — scripts in the cloud, x me:script.sh runs anywhere

You finished a script on one machine, and on another you just open the terminal and run `x me:dev.sh` to pick up where you left off. No USB drive, no Git, no friction — as long as the machine has x-cmd, your script is right there waiting.

That's what `x hub` delivers: scripts in the cloud, one command to run.

## Quick Start

### Step 1: Log in

```bash
x hub login
```

Supports GitHub or WeChat login. Account is created automatically on first use.

### Step 2: Upload your script

```bash
x hub file put example.sh me:example.sh
```

Uploads local `example.sh` to the cloud at path `me:example.sh` (`me:` is shorthand for your username).

### Step 3: Pull from cloud and run

```bash
x me:example.sh
```

x-cmd automatically pulls the script from the cloud and executes it locally — it feels exactly like running a local script.

## FAQ

### Q: How does the cloud file path work?

In `me:example.sh`, `me:` is shorthand for your username — equivalent to `your-username:example.sh`. When sharing with a colleague, replace `me` with your actual username (e.g. `u-123456:example.sh`).

### Q: How can a colleague run my script if they don't have x-cmd?

Ask them to install it — one command:

```bash
eval "$(curl https://get.x-cmd.com)"
```

Once installed, they can run `x u-xxx:script.sh` with your script.

### Q: What's the difference between private and public files?

By default, uploads are private (only you can see them). To share, add `--public` when uploading:

```bash
x hub file put --public example.sh me:example.sh
```

Note: even with `--public`, only you can run `x me:script.sh`. To let a colleague run your script, you need to tell them your username.

# Finished a doc? One link to share — like a blog

You finished a note or tutorial in Markdown and want to share it — before, you'd send it and they'd see unrendered raw text, which looks messy. `x hub file share` turns your doc into a beautiful web page with table of contents, code highlighting, and responsive typography — like a personal blog.

No installation needed on the viewer's end. They just open the link and read.

## Quick Start

### Step 1: Upload (as public)

```bash
x hub file put --public README.md
```

`--public` makes the doc publicly accessible. Without it, files are private — external links won't work.

### Step 2: Generate a share link

```bash
x hub file share README.md
```

Returns a publicly accessible URL.

### Step 3: Share the link

Send the link to anyone — they open it in a browser and read it like a blog post.

Uploaded docs can also be managed and viewed on the web at [hub.x-cmd.com](https://hub.x-cmd.com).

## FAQ

### Q: What formats are supported?

Markdown files (`.md`) render natively with proper headings, lists, code blocks, and tables. Code snippets get syntax highlighting.

### Q: Are share links permanent?

Links are permanent by default. To set an expiration:

```bash
x hub file share --expires 3600 README.md   # expires in 1 hour
```

### Q: What's the difference between private and public docs?

- **Private docs**: only the account owner can access — share links don't work
- **Public docs** (`--public`): anyone with the share link can view

### Q: How do I update a shared doc?

Re-upload with the same filename — the share link stays the same:

```bash
x hub file put --force --public README.md
```

`--force` overwrites the existing file.

# Self-Hosting x hub

hub is the cloud sync and sharing service of [x-cmd](https://x-cmd.com). x-cmd ships a **self-hosting package**: deploy the x-hub backend + frontend to your own Cloudflare account, with all data staying inside your own CF account (D1 / R2 / KV).

::: info Advantages of Self-Hosting
- **The free tier is enough**: the Cloudflare free plan + the R2 free quota (10 GB storage) covers everyday use for individuals and small teams
- **Your data stays in your account**: every resource is created under your own CF account, visible and manageable from the dashboard at any time
:::

## 1. Prerequisites

::::ol
:::li Have a Cloudflare account
The free plan works. If you don't have one, register a Cloudflare account at [dash.cloudflare.com](https://dash.cloudflare.com).
:::

:::li Activate R2 storage (one-time, about 1 minute)
hub stores its files on R2, so a fresh account needs to activate it once — then you never think about it again:

1. Log in to [dash.cloudflare.com](https://dash.cloudflare.com), and in the left sidebar open **Storage & Databases → R2 Object Storage**
2. Follow the prompts to activate. — **The free quota includes 10 GB storage + 1 million Class A operations per month, more than enough for personal use**
:::
::::

## 2. Quick Start

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/x-cmd-hub/x-hub/main/deploy.sh | bash
```

::: tip Want to review the script first, or have trouble downloading?
Grab the package for your platform (`vX.Y.Z_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz`) from [Releases](https://github.com/x-cmd-hub/x-hub/releases), extract it, and run `bash deploy.sh` — the rest of the flow is identical.
:::

## 3. Post-deploy Verification

```bash
# Backend health check (URL is printed when deployment finishes)
curl https://<worker-url>/ping
# should return {"ping":"pong"}

# Frontend: open the Pages URL printed at the end of deployment in a browser
```

If both checks pass, the deployment is complete — read the remaining sections as needed.

## Can't Open a Browser to Log In? (Containers / Servers)

A normal deployment opens your browser to log in to Cloudflare and authorize; containers / VMs / servers have no browser, so switch to an **API token** instead.

::::ol
:::li Open the token management page
Log in to [dash.cloudflare.com](https://dash.cloudflare.com) → left sidebar **Manage Account → Account API Tokens** → **Create Token** in the top-right corner.
:::

:::li Create a custom token
Skip the template list at the top, scroll down to **Create Custom Token → Get started**, and give the token a name (e.g. `x-hub-deploy`).
:::

:::li Set permissions
Quick way: pick **Read/Write all resources** (full read/write). The token is temporary — delete it once the deployment is done (see the note below).
:::

:::li Generate and use the token
After creating the token, copy the API token (it is shown only once). Then, in the container / VM:

```bash
export CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=<your-token>
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/x-cmd-hub/x-hub/main/deploy.sh | bash
```
:::
::::

:::details Advanced: least-privilege permissions
Prefer not to grant full access? In the Permissions section, add each row from this table (the last one is only needed with a custom domain):

| # | Scope | Resource | Action |
|---|-------|----------|--------|
| 1 | Account | Workers Scripts | Edit |
| 2 | Account | Workers KV Storage | Edit |
| 3 | Account | Workers R2 Storage | Edit |
| 4 | Account | D1 | Edit |
| 5 | Account | Pages | Edit |
| 6 (optional) | Zone | Workers Routes | Edit |

Missing any row causes a permission error at the matching step (no D1, for example, means no database).
:::

::: warning
A leaked token is equivalent to leaked account permissions. Roll or delete it from the token management page once you're done.
:::

## 4. Custom Configuration

Before deploying, edit `deploy.conf` inside the package (then re-run `bash deploy.sh` to apply):

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `WORKER_NAME` | `hub` | Backend Worker service name (lowercase letters/digits/hyphens) |
| `SHARE_DOMAIN` | empty | Root domain hosted on Cloudflare; leave empty = prompted during deployment |
| `PAGES_PROJECT` | empty | Frontend Pages project name; leave empty = prompted during deployment (default `x-hub-web`) |
| `TRAFFIC_LIMIT_BYTES` | `1073741824` | Monthly traffic limit per user (1 GB) |
| `R2_BUCKET` | `x-hub-files` | R2 bucket name (an existing bucket with the same name is reused) |
| `D1_NAME` | `x-hub-db` | D1 database name (an existing database with the same name is reused) |

### About the domain (SHARE_DOMAIN)

**Why configure a domain**: the only feature it affects is **subdomain sharing** — once configured, every user gets a personal share page at `username.your-domain` (e.g. `alice.example.com`). This requires binding a `*.domain` wildcard route to the Worker, which only works with a domain hosted on Cloudflare; `workers.dev` doesn't support it. A custom domain also gives cleaner addresses (`api.domain` / `hub.domain`) and removes the dependence on public domains like `workers.dev` / `pages.dev` (which are blocked in some networks).

**Without a domain**: everything works. The backend runs on `<worker>.workers.dev` and the frontend on `<project>.pages.dev`; sync, files, path sharing via `/s/:id`, and all other core features work fine — only subdomain sharing is unavailable. If you buy a domain later, host it on Cloudflare, set `SHARE_DOMAIN`, and re-run `bash deploy.sh` to enable it.

**With a domain**: first host the domain on Cloudflare (dashboard → Add a Site, and follow the prompts to point the registrar's nameservers to the ones CF assigns), then set `SHARE_DOMAIN` to the root domain — the deploy script configures the wildcard route and subdomain addresses automatically.

## 5. Upgrading

Download the new package from [Releases](https://github.com/x-cmd-hub/x-hub/releases), extract it, and re-run the deploy in the new directory:

```bash
tar -xzf vX.Y.Z_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz
cd vX.Y.Z_<os>_<arch>
bash deploy.sh    # when the existing Worker is detected, pick "update code" — all data is preserved
```

It's fine if the new directory has no old config: the script automatically finds the existing deployment in your account and reuses all resources.

## 6. FAQ

:::details CORS errors on the frontend {open}
Check that `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` in the deployment directory's `wrangler.toml` includes the frontend domain; add it if missing and re-run `bash deploy.sh`.
:::

:::details Email verification link returns 404 {open}
Run `grep FRONT_END_URL wrangler.toml`; the value should be `https://<pages-project>.pages.dev` (the frontend address, not the API address). Fix it if wrong and re-run `bash deploy.sh`.
:::

:::details R2 error 10042 / enable R2 {open}
R2 isn't activated on your CF account yet: dashboard → R2 Object Storage → activate it, then re-run the deploy script.
:::

## Support & Feedback

- Report issues: [Issues](https://github.com/x-cmd-hub/x-hub/issues)
- More docs in `deploy/docs/` and `docs/` inside the deployment package

# x hub file

File management — upload, download, and view cloud files

## Examples

List all files under the &lt;path&gt; folder of the current user in the cloud

```sh
x hub file ls <path>
```

View the contents of the &lt;path&gt; file of the &lt;username&gt; user in the cloud

```sh
x hub file cat [<username>:]<path>
```

Convert https://example.com/example.txt link to cloud file me:demo

```sh
x hub file link https://example.com/example.txt demo
```

Upload local file &lt;local path&gt; to cloud &lt;remote path&gt;

```sh
x hub file put <local path> <remote path>
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x hub file ls](#x-hub-file-ls) | List all files or directories under the specified folder of the current user in the cloud, the default is the root directory |
| [x hub file ll](#x-hub-file-ll) | List all files or directories under the specified folder of the current user's cloud, and display extended file metadata in table form. |
| [x hub file cat](#x-hub-file-cat) | View the contents of the cloud file |
| [x hub file put](#x-hub-file-put) | Upload file to the cloud, the default is private files |
| [x hub file get](#x-hub-file-get) | Download cloud files to local, by default download to the current directory |
| [x hub file link](#x-hub-file-link) | Convert a url link to a cloud file |
| [x hub file which](#x-hub-file-which) | Download and print the path from local, default cache 1 hour |
| [x hub file rm](#x-hub-file-rm) | Delete the cloud file |
| [x hub file update](#x-hub-file-update) | Updating local cache file. |


### x hub file ls

List all files or directories under the specified folder of the current user in the cloud, the default is the root directory


- **Examples**:

List all files or directories under the &lt;path&gt; folder of the current user in the cloud

```sh
x hub file ls <path>
```

Recursively list all files or directories under the &lt;path&gt; folder of the current user in the cloud, and display extended file metadata as a table

```sh
x hub file ls -R -l <path>
```

List all files or directories under the root directory of the current user in the cloud, and display extended file metadata as a table

```sh
x hub file ls -l
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x hub file ls [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Specify the folder path |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--recursive`, `-R` | Recursively list files in subdirectories |
| `--long`, `-l` | Display extended file metadata as a table |
| `--json` | Output in JSON format |


### x hub file ll

List all files or directories under the specified folder of the current user's cloud, and display extended file metadata in table form.


- **Usage**:

```sh
x hub file ll
```

### x hub file cat

View the contents of the cloud file


- **Usage**:

```sh
x hub file cat <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | File path |


### x hub file put

Upload file to the cloud, the default is private files



### x hub file get

```sh

```

# x hub login

Login/register account


::: tip AI Agent login flow:
1. Execute `x hub login`
2. Read the URL=xxx from the output
3. Send the URL to the user, ask them to open it in a browser and complete authorization (no need for the user to confirm, the program polls automatically)
4. Wait for STATUS=success in the output, which means login succeeded

If polling times out or is interrupted (STATUS=timeout), run

`x hub login verify` after the user completes authorization to re-check:

STATUS=success means login succeeded, STATUS=pending means the browser

authorization has not been completed yet.
:::


## Examples

Login/register account, AI agents can run this directly

```sh
x hub login
```

Login with GitHub

```sh
x hub login github
```

Login with email

```sh
x hub login email <email>
```

Login with WeChat, set expiration (e.g., 1d, 7d)

```sh
x hub login --expire <duration> wechat
```

Email login with custom expiration and region

```sh
x hub login --expire <duration> --region <region> email <email>
```

# x hub rag

RAG knowledge base — search, upload, and manage personal knowledge documents

## Examples

Search the knowledge base for answers (defaults to mod + personal knowledge).

```sh
x hub rag ask <question>
```

Search only x-cmd official module docs.

```sh

```

Upload a file and index it for AI search (charges tokens).

```sh
x hub rag upload <file>
```

List uploaded knowledge base files.

```sh
x hub rag list
```

Show this month's RAG token usage.

```sh
x hub rag quota
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x hub rag ask](#x-hub-rag-ask) | Search the knowledge base for answers. Defaults to mod and personal knowledge, scope can be specified via --scope. |
| [x hub rag upload](#x-hub-rag-upload) | Upload a file and index it for AI search. Charges tokens by file size (~1 byte = 1 token). Searchable after the next AutoRAG sync cycle (up to 1 hour). Upload is rejected entirely when token quota is insufficient. |
| [x hub rag list](#x-hub-rag-list) | List uploaded personal knowledge base files (flat listing). |
| [x hub rag delete](#x-hub-rag-delete) | Delete a file or directory from the knowledge base (directories are removed recursively). Tokens already spent on indexing are not refunded. |
| [x hub rag quota](#x-hub-rag-quota) | Show this month's RAG token usage, remaining quota, and reset time. |

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |

# x hub share

Manage share links for cloud files (default create).

When the file name ends with .zip, the backend auto-extracts it into a multi-file share; otherwise a single-file share is created.

## Examples

Create a permanent share link for cloud file me:demo/example.txt

```sh
x hub share demo/example.txt
```

Create a 1-hour share link for cloud file me:demo/example.txt

```sh
x hub share --expires 3600 demo/example.txt
```

Create a password-protected share link for cloud file me:demo/example.txt

```sh
x hub share --password <password> demo/example.txt
```

Direct-upload local file ./local.txt to create a share (does not enter the cloud file library)

```sh
x hub share --file ./local.txt
```

Direct-upload a local image with album/photo.jpg as the URL display path

```sh
x hub share --file ./photo.jpg --path album/photo.jpg
```

Create a multi-file share link for a cloud zip file (backend auto-extracts by .zip suffix)

```sh
x hub share <path/to/archive.zip>
```

Direct-upload local site.zip and auto-extract it to create a multi-file share link

```sh
x hub share --file ./site.zip
```

Direct-upload a zip, set main.html as the entry, and force-overwrite an existing folder with the same name

```sh
x hub share --file ./site.zip --entry main.html --force
```

## Usage

```sh
x hub share [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Cloud file path (reference mode) |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--expires`, `-e` |  | Set the expiration time of the share link (supports seconds or time units like 1h, 2d, 1w) |
| `--path` |  | Display path in the share URL (defaults to filename) |
| `--space` |  | Specify space name |
| `--password` |  | Set access password (single-file shares only) |
| `--entry` |  | Specify the entry file path for zip shares (default is index.html) |
| `--file` |  |  |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--require-login` | Require login to access |
| `--force` | Force overwrite when the zip share target folder already exists |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x hub share ls](#x-hub-share-ls) | List all share links |
| [x hub share rm](#x-hub-share-rm) | Delete a share link |
| [x hub share update](#x-hub-share-update) | Update share link settings |


### x hub share ls

List all share links


- **Examples**:

List all share links

```sh
x hub share ls
```

List all share links in JSON format

```sh
x hub share ls --json
```

List share links under the specified space

```sh
x hub share ls --space <name>
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x hub share ls [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--page`, `-p` |  | Page number (default 1) |
| `--limit`, `-l` |  | Items per page (default 20) |
| `--space` |  | Filter by space name |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--json`, `-j` | Output in JSON format |


### x hub share rm

Delete a share link


- **Examples**:

Delete share link &lt;fileId&gt;

```sh
x hub share rm <fileId>
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x hub share rm <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | File ID |


### x hub share update

Update share link settings


- **Examples**:


Reset share link &lt;fileId&gt; expiration to 1 hour


Set access password for share link &lt;fileId&gt;

```sh

```

Remove access password for share link &lt;fileId&gt;

```sh

```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x hub share update [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | File ID |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--expires`, `-e` |  | Reset expiration time (supports seconds or time units like 1h, 2d, 1w) |
| `--password` |  | Set or update the access password |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--require-login` | Require login to access |
| `--remove-password` | Remove the access password |

# x hub site

AI Site — query Skill templates, create and manage AI-generated web pages


::: tip Hub Site Phase 2 uses a Page→Entry (incremental append) model: template (HTML/CSS) + data (entry array) + images.
Typical AI Agent workflow:
1. Run `x hub site skill ls` to get available Skill templates
2. Run `x hub site skill info <skillId>` to get the Skill's prompt (content), entrySchema, and example HTML URL
3. Generate a single-file HTML page (or a ZIP containing index.html) based on the Skill's prompt
4. (Optional) Construct a templateSchema JSON according to pageSchema and pass it via `--data`
5. Run `x hub site create --skill <skillId> --title <title> [--data <json>] <file>` to create the Page
6. Read the Share URL from the output and present it to the user
7. Append content later with `x hub site entry add`; upload images with `x hub site media upload`; replace templates with `x hub site template update`



Notes:
- Max 5MB per template/image file; 256KB per entry JSON; 50MB per ZIP share package
- Rate limits: 10/min create page, 20/min entry/media ops, 5/min template replace
- Entry system fields (entryId/createdAt/updatedAt) are server-generated; sending them is ignored
- Template file names must be flat; `/`, `\`, `..` are forbidden
:::

::: tip ZIP file requirements: If uploading a ZIP, it must contain index.html as the entry page.
Single HTML files can be uploaded directly without zipping.
:::

::: tip The `--data` parameter in `site create` and `site template update` serves as templateSchema
(a JSON string) for page template metadata; it is optional. Entry fields are provided via

`site entry add --field key=value` and must conform to the Skill's entrySchema.
:::


## Examples

List all available Skill templates

```sh
x hub site skill ls
```

View details of Skill &lt;skillId&gt; (including prompt and schema)

```sh
x hub site skill info <skillId>
```

Create a site (Page) using a Skill template, uploading an HTML/ZIP file

```sh
x hub site create --skill <skillId> --title <title> <file>
```

List all sites

```sh
x hub site ls
```

View site details and entry count

```sh
x hub site info <siteId>
```

Append an Entry to site &lt;siteId&gt;

```sh
x hub site entry add <siteId> --field text=<hello>
```

List all entries of site &lt;siteId&gt;

```sh
x hub site entry ls <siteId>
```

Upload an image to the site, returning a relative path for use in entries

```sh
x hub site media upload <siteId> <image>
```

Replace the site template files (preserving all entry data)

```sh
x hub site template update <siteId> <file>
```

Delete site &lt;siteId&gt;

```sh
x hub site rm <siteId>
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x hub site skill](#x-hub-site-skill) | Query available Skill templates. A Skill defines the AI prompt (content), page schema (pageSchema),

and entry schema (entrySchema) for a page type. Typical Skills include diaries, resumes, portfolios, etc.

You must choose a Skill before creating a Page. |
| [x hub site create](#x-hub-site-create) | Create a Page by uploading an AI-generated HTML/ZIP template file and generating a share link.

You must first choose a Skill template via `x hub site skill ls/info`.

Returns Page ID and share URL upon success. After creation, append data with `site entry add`. |
| [x hub site ls](#x-hub-site-ls) | List all Pages of the current user, returning ID, title, Skill, share URL, and last updated time |
| [x hub site info](#x-hub-site-info) | View site details, returning:
- Basic info (ID, title, Skill, share URL)
- templateSchema: page template config (only shown if set at create time)
- entryCount: total number of entries in the Page
- createdAt / updatedAt |
| [x hub site rm](#x-hub-site-rm) | Delete a site. Soft delete, the share link will be invalidated immediately. This action cannot be undone. |
| [x hub site template](#x-hub-site-template) | Manage a Page's template files (HTML/CSS, etc.). Replacing the template does not affect existing entries. |
| [x hub site entry](#x-hub-site-entry) | Manage a Page's Entries (incremental data records). Each Entry follows the Skill's entrySchema,

with skill core fields (e.g. text, mood, images) and custom fields; system fields entryId/createdAt/updatedAt are server-generated. |
| [x hub site media](#x-hub-site-media) | Manage image assets for a Page. Uploaded images return a relative path for referencing in entry images fields or templates.

Only jpeg/png/gif/webp are allowed (SVG is blocked due to XSS risk). |

Query available Skill templates. A Skill defines the AI prompt (content), page schema (pageSchema),

- schema: includes pageSchema (page config) and entrySchema (entry field constraints with required, systemFields, properties)
- exampleHtmlUrl: Example HTML URL for style reference |

# x humantime in

Check if given seconds are within specified time range

## Examples

Example: is 240s within 5m? (yes, returns 0)

```sh
x humantime in 5m 240
```

Example: batch check multiple seconds within 1 hour

```sh
x humantime in 1h 3600 1800 900
```

## Usage

```sh
x humantime in <#1> <#n>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Time range (e.g., 5m, 1h, 1d) |
| `#n` | Seconds to check (multiple allowed, all must pass) |

# x humantime toms

Convert readable format to milliseconds (e.g., 2h30m → 9000000)

## Examples

Example: 2h30m to 9000000 milliseconds

```sh
x humantime toms 2h30m
```

Example: 1s to 1000 milliseconds

```sh
x humantime toms 1s
```

## Usage

```sh
x humantime toms <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Time string (e.g., 1d, 2h30m, 90s) |

# x humantime tosec

Convert readable format to seconds (default integer, use --decimal for float)


::: info
Does NOT accept `mo` (month) or `y` (year) — to avoid ambiguity and keep parsing unambiguous, `tosec_` only handles pure duration units.
:::


## Examples

Example: 2h30m to 9000 seconds (integer)

```sh
x humantime tosec 2h30m
```

Example: with decimal output 9000.000

```sh
x humantime tosec --decimal 2h30m
```

Example: 1 day to 86400 seconds

```sh
x humantime tosec 1d
```

## Usage

```sh
x humantime tosec <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Time string (e.g., 1d, 2h30m, 90s) |

# SSH into an unfamiliar machine, one command reveals all peripherals

SSH into an unfamiliar machine and want to know what peripherals it has — Bluetooth, camera, battery, Thunderbolt... checking them one by one is tedious. system_profiler dumps a wall of text, and the useful bits are buried in there.

`x hw` pulls everything at once: overview table plus network interfaces, so you can quickly get a read on a machine's hardware. Plugged in something new and not sure if it's recognized? Run `x hw ls` and check.

## Quick Start

```bash
x hw          # peripheral overview + network interfaces
```

![x hw](/image/mod/hw.1_1.webp)

`x hw` provides three output modes for different needs:

- **Default mode**: peripheral overview table + network interface list, for a quick scan of the machine's hardware
- **`x hw info`**: detailed peripheral info in key:value format, when you need specific parameters
- **`x hw ls`**: compact table with device names and key info, for confirming whether a device is recognized

## FAQ

### Q: Is the data real-time?

Not entirely. `system_profiler` data is cached for 1 day, while HID devices (keyboard, mouse, trackpad) are fetched in real-time via `ioreg`. If you need the latest data, use `x hw --fresh` to force a refresh.

### Q: Why do Linux and macOS show different peripherals?

The two platforms use different data sources. macOS fetches via `system_profiler` and `ioreg`, while Linux uses `/sys/class`, `bluetoothctl`, `pactl`, `ip link`, and other interfaces. The peripheral types and fields supported vary across platforms — this is determined by the underlying interfaces.

# x install --available-tool

Query available package managers in current environment

## Examples

List all supported package managers (including not-yet-installed)

```sh
x install --available-tool
```

List only installed package managers

```sh
x install --available-tool --installed
```

## Usage

```sh
x install --available-tool [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--installed` | Show only installed package managers |
| `--printname` | Print only tool names |
| `--tsv` | Output in TSV format |
| `--csv` | Output in CSV format |
| `--app` | View in interactive app mode |

# x install --best

Automatically select the best installation method based on priority

## Examples

Automatically select the best method to install bun

```sh
x install --best bun
```

Print the best install command for bun without executing

```sh
x install --best --printcmd bun
```

Install bun with brew as priority, falling back to xpkg

```sh
x install --best --priority brew,xpkg bun
```

Batch install using best method

```sh
x install --best bun vim
```

## Usage

```sh
x install --best [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Software name(s) to install |


## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-p`, `--priority` |  | Comma-separated tool priority list (e.g. brew,apt,uv) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--printcmd`, `--dry-run` | Print the best install command without executing |

# x install --withtool

Install using a specified package manager


::: tip By default, looks up recorded installation methods. Use --direct to skip and call the package manager directly:
x install --withtool brew bun — look up recorded brew method for bun

x install --withtool brew --direct bun — directly install bun via brew
:::


## Examples

Install vim and bun using brew

```sh
x install --withtool brew vim bun
```

Print brew install commands for vim and bun without executing

```sh
x install --withtool brew --printcmd vim bun
```

Directly install bun via brew (skip recorded methods)

```sh
x install --withtool brew --direct bun
```

## Usage

```sh
x install --withtool [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Package manager name (brew, apt, npm, pip, go, cargo, pixi, pkgx, etc.) |
| `#2` | Software name(s) to install |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--direct` | Skip recorded methods and directly use the package manager to install |
| `--printcmd` | Print the install command for the specified tool without executing |
