# x install - Your Cross-Platform Software Installation Swiss Army Knife

In the command-line world, installing software is a common task. But have you ever been frustrated by finding and executing the correct installation commands on different operating systems (Linux distributions, macOS, Windows/WSL)? `apt`, `yum`, `dnf`, `pacman`, `brew`, `scoop`, `winget`... Different package managers, different command formats, sometimes requiring PPAs or source configuration—all of these can interrupt your workflow.

Now, with `x install`, you can say goodbye to these troubles! Like a Swiss Army knife, it aims to be your unified software installation entry point, helping you quickly find and execute installation commands suitable for your current system.

<Terminal demo="/cookbook/mod/install.en.json" size="large" />

## Interactive Exploration: Your Personal Software Marketplace

When you only have a vague impression of the software you want to install, or want to see what treasures `x install` has in its collection, running the `x install` command directly will open a powerful interactive interface (typically based on `fzf` or similar tools).

```sh
x install
```

![x install](/image/mod/install.1_1.en.webp)

In this interface, you can:

::::ol
:::li Fuzzy Search
Type keywords, and the list will filter in real-time, quickly locating the software you need
:::

:::li Real-time Preview
Select a piece of software, and the preview window on the right will immediately display detailed information about that software, including:
- Software Name
- Official Homepage
- Description
- Primary Language
- **Key Installation Command (cmd)**: `x install` intelligently shows the most suitable installation method and its source based on your current operating system and environment
:::

:::li Select and Execute
After finding the software you want, press Enter, and `x install` will guide you to confirm and execute the selected installation command
:::
::::

This interactive experience is like having a portable, on-demand software marketplace!

## Precision Strike: Get Installation Instructions Directly

If you know exactly which software to install, such as `docker` or `dust`, you can pass the software name directly as an argument to `x install`.

```sh
x install docker
x install dust
```

`x install` will quickly look up information on `docker`, analyze your current system environment (such as whether it's Ubuntu or macOS), and then clearly list the recommended installation commands. If multiple installation methods exist (such as system package managers, official scripts, Snap, etc.), it may provide options for you to choose from. After confirmation, installation can begin.

Whether it's common development tools or niche utility programs, as long as it's in the `x install` database, you can quickly get installation instructions and execute the installation through this method.

## Stay Up-to-Date: Update Your Software Installation Database

The software world changes rapidly, with new versions and installation methods constantly emerging. To ensure the information provided by `x install` remains accurate and effective, you need to regularly update its metadata.

```sh
x install --update
```

::: tip
Running this command, x-cmd will fetch the latest software installation information database from its configured source, ensuring you can find the latest and best installation methods
:::

---

`x install` greatly simplifies the complexity of cross-platform software installation through its concise interaction and intelligent backend logic. Whether you're a command-line novice or a seasoned player, it can save you a lot of time searching for documentation and commands, allowing you to focus on what really matters. Try `x install` now and experience a smoother command-line workflow!

# x ip cidr

Displaying info related to CIDR

## Examples

Display the classful and CIDR information for the 192.168.1.0/24 network.

```sh
x ip cidr 192.168.1.0/24
```

Display the classful and CIDR information for the 192.168.1.0/24 network.

```sh
x ip 192.168.1.0/24
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x ip cidr ls](#x-ip-cidr-ls) | Illustrating the Use of Address Blocks Defined in RFC 3330 |
| [x ip cidr info](#x-ip-cidr-info) | Displaying the IP address's classification attributes, along with its subnet address and the number of IPs within that subnet. |


### x ip cidr ls

Illustrating the Use of Address Blocks Defined in RFC 3330


- **Examples**:

The address blocks defined in RFC 3330, and their purposes, were displayed in an interactive table app.

```sh
x ip cidr ls
```

Feed the address blocks and their uses, as defined in RFC 3330, into a pipe (automatically outputting in TSV format), then use awk to print columns 1 and 3.

```sh
x ip cidr ls | awk -F '\t' '{ print $1, $3 }'
```

The address blocks defined in RFC 3330, and their purposes, were displayed in CSV format.

```sh
x ip cidr ls --csv
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x ip cidr ls
```

### x ip cidr info

Displaying the IP address's classification attributes, along with its subnet address and the number of IPs within that subnet.


- **Usage**:

```sh
x ip cidr info
```

# x ip (1) - Get Local IP Address and Network Information

## Get Local Network and Public IP Addresses

Different operating systems use different commands to obtain local IP address information, and in some cases, you may even need to install additional tools using package managers.

To simplify this process, `x-cmd` provides the `x ip` command to help users get a consistent experience across all operating systems.

::::ul
::: li Run `x ip`

```sh
x ip
```

:::
::: li ![x ip](/image/mod/ip.1_1.webp)
:::
::::

After running this command, it will automatically detect and display your current local network IP address and public IP address for quick viewing and network status confirmation.

::: tip
This command automatically detects the current network environment without manual configuration or installing additional tools.
:::

## Get Geolocation of Public IP

`x ip` supports getting the geographical location of a specified IP address through the `ipinfo.io` service.

Running the following command will display the geolocation data of your machine's public IP, such as country, city, etc.

::::ul
::: li Geolocation for your public IP

```sh
x ip geolite
```

:::
::::

Additionally, you can query the location information of any other IP address to analyze the geographical distribution of network connections.

::::ul
::: li Geolocation for a specific IP

```sh
x ip geolite 8.8.8.8
x ip geolite 185.199.108.153
```

:::
::::

::: tip
Common public DNS server IPs can also be used to test the geolocation query service, such as Google's `8.8.8.8` and GitHub's `185.199.108.153`.
:::

## List Active Hosts on the Same Network

`x ip` provides a simple IP scanning function to help you quickly detect active hosts on the same local network.

For example, running the following command will scan all active hosts within the `192.168.89.0/24` subnet and display their IP addresses, suitable for device discovery and network troubleshooting within the local network.

::::ul
::: li Scan active hosts on the LAN

```sh
x ip map 192.168.89.0/24
```

:::
::: li ![x ip map](/image/mod/ip.1_2.webp)
:::
::::

::: tip
The local network scanning function is suitable for common `/24` subnets. To scan other networks, please adjust the parameters according to your actual network configuration.
:::

---
[More] To learn more about the ip module, please visit x-cmd official website - x-cmd.com/mod/ip

# x ip map

Discover ip address using ICMP ping and tcping (default for port 22, 80)

## Examples

Scan 192.168.1.0/24 for active hosts using ICMP

```sh
x ip map   192.168.1.0/24
```

Scan 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.3.11 for active hosts using ICMP

```sh
x ip map   192.168.1.0/24 192.168.3.11
```

Scan 192.168.1.1-255 for active hosts using ICMP.

```sh
x ip map   192.168.1.{1..255}
```

Scan 192.168.1-255.1 for active hosts using ICMP

```sh
x ip map   192.168.{1..255}.1
```

Scan 192.168.1.1-255 for active hosts using ICMP and TCP port 80.

```sh
x ip map -s icmp,80 192.168.1.{1..255}
```

Scan 192.168.1.0/24 for active hosts using ICMP

```sh
x ip iter  192.168.1.0/24 | x ip map -
```

## Usage

```sh
x ip map
```

# x ip tps

Discover port using tcp request in parallel

## Examples

Scan localhost for open ports in the range of 1-10000, equivalent to 'x ip tps'

```sh
x ip tps
```

Scan localhost for open ports in the range of 1-65535, equivalent to 'x ip tps'

```sh
x ip tps -a
```

Scan bing.com for open ports in the range of 1-10000

```sh
x ip tps bing.com
```

Scan localhost for open ports in the range of 10000-20000

```sh
x ip tps 127.0.0.1 10000-20000
```

Scan the local host for odd open ports in the range of 1-10000, open ports in the range of 30000-40000, and the port 55555.

```sh
x ip tps 127.0.0.1 1-10000:2 30000-40000 55555
```

## Usage

```sh
x ip tps|tcp-portscan [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `-a` | Scan all ports (1-65535) |
| `-c` | max concurrency, default is 10000; this is just the max concurrency, the actual concurrency will increase according to network conditions |
| `-t`, `--timeout` | timeout, default is 0.5s for non-internal network addresses, and 0.1s for internal network addresses |
| `-r`, `--retry` | retry times, default is 0 times |

# x jq (1): Interactive JSON Data Exploration Tool

## 1. Introduction: Challenges and Solutions for JSON Data Processing

In modern software development, JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) has become the de facto standard for data exchange. However, directly processing large amounts of JSON data can be very tedious, especially in command-line environments. `jq` is a powerful command-line JSON processing tool that allows you to query, transform, and filter JSON data using a functional programming-style DSL (Domain-Specific Language).

Although `jq` is powerful, its imperative syntax and complex expressions may have a learning curve for beginners. To address this, the website [jqplay.org](https://jqplay.org) and the [jqp](https://x-cmd.com/install/jqp) command-line solution provide interactive ways to explore jq.

::: tip
x-cmd provides a more powerful interactive JSON exploration solution
The `x jq r` in this article is an interactive JSON data exploration tool provided by x-cmd, built on `fzf`, offering a more intuitive and efficient JSON data processing experience.
:::

## 2. Core Features and Advantages of `x jq r`

The core goal of `x jq r` is to make JSON data exploration simpler, faster, and more efficient. It achieves this through the following key features:

:::: ul
:::li Interactive exploration
Skip the edit-run loop: type or change `jq` expressions in `x jq r` and see output immediately—faster learning and debugging.
:::
:::li YAML preview
JSON is universal but not always easy to scan. `x jq r` renders results as YAML via `yq`; nested data is often quicker to read.
:::
:::li Dependency management
You do not need to pre-install `jq`, `yq`, or `fzf`. `x-cmd` provisions them on demand and keeps the footprint small.
:::
:::li Fuzzy search and filtering
`fzf` helps you jump to fields or values inside JSON without tedious manual filtering.
:::
::::

## 3. Workflow of `x jq r`: Exploring JSON Data Step by Step

The workflow of `x jq r` is very simple and intuitive:

1. **Data Input:** Pass JSON data to the `x jq r` command through a pipe.

   ```bash
   x docker image ls --json | x jq r
   ```

   This command passes the JSON output of the `x docker image ls` command as input to `x jq r`.

2. **Expression Input:** `x jq r` launches the `fzf` interface. In the interface, you can input `jq` expressions.

3. **Real-time Preview:** As you input `jq` expressions, `x jq r` executes them in real time. Valid expressions are shown as YAML in `fzf`; invalid ones surface error hints. This feedback helps you understand expressions and fix mistakes quickly.

4. **Exit and Output:** Press `Enter` to exit `fzf`. The final `jq` expression is printed to the terminal so you can reuse it in other commands or scripts.

## 4. Example Demonstration: From Docker Image List to Specific Attribute Extraction

Let's demonstrate the use of `x jq r` with a concrete example:

### 4.1. Get Docker Image List

First, use the `x docker image ls --json` command to get the JSON list of Docker images.

```bash
x docker image ls --json
```

This command outputs a JSON array containing information about all Docker images.

### 4.2. Explore Data with `x jq r`

Pass the JSON data to `x jq r` through a pipe:

```bash
x docker image ls --json | x jq r
```

This will launch the `fzf` interface and display the JSON data of Docker images.

### 4.3. Explore JSON Structure

:::: ul
:::li `.` (root)
Enter `.` in `fzf` to view the full JSON document and grasp the top-level shape.
:::
:::li `.[]` (array items)
Enter `.[]` to iterate array elements; the UI walks them one by one.
:::
::::

### 4.4. Extract Specific Attributes

:::: ul
:::li `.[] | .RepoTags` (pipe)
`.` reads fields; `|` chains steps. This expression lists `RepoTags` for each image.
:::
:::li `.[] | .RepoTags[0]` (index)
Take index `0` from `RepoTags` to show the first tag per image.
:::
::::

### 4.5. Real-time Preview and Adjustment

During the process of inputting `jq` expressions, `x jq r` displays results in real-time, allowing you to immediately see the effect of the expressions. If the results don't meet expectations, you can modify the expressions at any time until you get the correct results.

## 5. Summary of Advantages: Why Choose `x jq r`?

:::: ul
:::li Easy to start
Interactive feedback lowers the `jq` learning curve for newcomers.
:::
:::li Faster debugging
See results as you type so JSON issues surface without extra command churn.
:::
:::li No manual installs
`x-cmd` pulls in `jq` / `yq` / `fzf` as needed instead of you wiring versions by hand.
:::
:::li YAML is easier to scan
Nested structures are often quicker to read in YAML than raw JSON alone.
:::
::::

## 6. Extended Reading: Other Interactive Tools in the x-cmd Ecosystem

`x-cmd` also provides similar `fzf`-based interactive exploration tools for `yq`, `find`, `rg`, and other commands. These tools follow the same design philosophy: simplify command-line work and improve the experience. Examples:

- **`x yq r`:** Interactive YAML exploration, similar in spirit to `x jq r`, for YAML data.
- **`x find r`:** Interactive file search, built on `find` and `fzf`.
- **`x rg r`:** Interactive code search, built on `ripgrep` and `fzf`.

## 7. Extension: x-cmd Automatically Installs Required jq, yq, fzf Dependencies on Demand

:::: ul
:::li Prefer local binaries
If `jq`, `yq`, and `fzf` are already installed, `x jq` uses them first.
:::
:::li Fallback: x-cmd pkg
When binaries are missing, `x-cmd` downloads builds from its managed pkg channel, then runs them.
:::
:::li Default: no system-wide install
Outside environments like Termux, `x-cmd` avoids dropping tools into system paths or mutating global env by default. Pin a install with `x env use jq`, or pick a recipe via `x i jq`.
:::
:::li Since v0.6.0: system package managers
You can opt into on-demand installs via the OS package manager (Termux, iSH, container Linux, Homebrew, etc.). That path needs permission to install software.
:::
::::

::: warning
**Permission Note:** Using system package manager installation mode requires the current user to have direct permission to install software.
:::

# x kev - Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Query Tool

## Introduction

The `x kev` module is a command-line tool for querying the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. This tool provides two main functions: listing all KEV vulnerabilities and listing the top N KEV vulnerabilities.

## Usage

The `x kev` module supports the following subcommands:

### `ls` Command

List all vulnerabilities in the KEV catalog.

```bash
x kev ls
```

This command will output all vulnerability information in the KEV catalog.

### `top` Command

List the top N vulnerabilities in the KEV catalog.

```bash
x kev top <number>
```

Where `<number>` is the number of vulnerabilities to list. For example, to list the top 100 vulnerabilities, use:

```bash
x kev top 100
```

This command will output information about the top N vulnerabilities in the KEV catalog.

## Usage Examples

Here are some usage examples of the `x kev` module:

::::ul
:::li List all KEV vulnerabilities
```bash
x kev ls
```
This command will list all vulnerabilities in the KEV catalog.
:::

:::li List the top 100 KEV vulnerabilities
```bash
x kev top 100
```
This command will list the top 100 most impactful vulnerabilities in the KEV catalog.
:::
::::

::: tip
The KEV catalog comes from CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and contains information about vulnerabilities that have been confirmed to be exploited in the wild.
:::

## More Information

Please visit our homepage [https://x-cmd.com](https://x-cmd.com) for more information.

# x keyring backend

Switch or query the OS backend (keychain / secret_service / kwallet / windows / null)


::: tip
Priority: env &gt; marker file &gt; OS autodetect (Darwin = keychain, Linux = secret_service, Windows = local Credential Manager).
:::

::: tip
`windows` backend: stores in Windows Credential Manager (`x keyring backend set windows`); first call has ~1s cold start, fine for low-frequency access.
:::

::: tip
`null` = disable keyring; useful for CI / sandbox.
:::


## Examples

List available backends

```sh
x keyring backend ls
```

Show the active backend

```sh
x keyring backend get
```

Pin to secret_service

```sh
x keyring backend set secret_service
```

Pin to Windows Credential Manager

```sh
x keyring backend set windows
```

Disable the keychain entirely (refuses all ops)

```sh
x keyring backend set null
```

## Usage

```sh
x keyring backend
```

# x keyring cget_

script-friendly cget — iCloud Keychain get into a variable; for byte-exact round-trip inside scripts


::: tip
Difference from `cget`: writes to a shell variable instead of stdout — no trailing-newline side-effect from `$()`.
:::


## Usage

```sh
x keyring cget_ [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | service name |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--ns`, `--namespace` | namespace name (default x-cmd-keyring, shared across Apple devices) |

# x keyring cls

iCloud Keychain list (macOS-only)


::: tip
Parses `security dump-keychain` output (default search list includes iCloud), filters same as `ls`. Current namespace by default; `-a` lists all.
:::


## Usage

```sh
x keyring cls [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | optional service filter |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--ns`, `--namespace` | namespace name (default x-cmd-keyring, shared across Apple devices) |
| `-a`, `--all` | list every namespace |

# x keyring get_

script-friendly get — writes to a variable; for byte-exact round-trip inside scripts


::: tip
Difference from `get`: writes to a shell variable instead of stdout — no trailing-newline side-effect from `$()`, useful when the value must round-trip byte-exact or be reprocessed.
:::


## Examples

# x keyring ls

List entries (current UID by default); output is service&lt;TAB&gt;namespace


::: tip
Backend determines enumeration: keychain parses `security dump-keychain` (real genp list); KWallet uses `kwalletcli5 -l`; SecretService has no global list — only `secret-tool search service <svc>`. On Linux, `-a` (list all namespaces) often returns empty; that's by design.
:::


## Examples

List current UID's entries

```sh
x keyring ls
```

Filter by service

```sh
x keyring ls github
```

Show entries under a specific namespace

```sh
x keyring ls --ns alice
```

List every namespace (escape UID isolation)

```sh
x keyring ls -a
```

## Usage

```sh
x keyring ls [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | optional service filter |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--ns`, `--namespace` | namespace name (default x-cmd-&lt;UID&gt;) |
| `-a`, `--all` | List every namespace (escape UID isolation) |

# x keyring set

Write a password to the keychain; namespace defaults to x-cmd-&lt;UID&gt;. Pipe the password via stdin (or tty silent prompt)


::: tip
Positional order: service first, optional password second. The namespace is no longer positional — it goes through `--ns`.
:::


## Examples

Silent tty prompt for the password

```sh
x keyring set github alice
```

Pipe via stdin in a script (prefer printf, not echo)

```sh
printf '%s' "$pw" | x keyring set github alice
```

Override the default namespace so deploy-bot has its own slot

```sh
x keyring set --ns deploy-bot github alice
```

## Usage

```sh
x keyring set [FLAGS] <#1> <#2>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | service name |
| `#2` | password (omit to read from stdin / tty prompt) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--ns`, `--namespace` | namespace name (default x-cmd-&lt;UID&gt;) |

---
url: /mod/keyring/unlock.md
---
# x keyring unlock

Optional, macOS real unlock; other OS no-op + note (daemon-managed)


::: tip
macOS-only: other OS keychains are unlocked by daemon / login session; no CLI unlock. Linux secret_service / kwallet auto-unlock on user login; Windows CM auto-unlocks on user logon. To force re-unlock, logoff and back in.
:::


## Examples

macOS prompts for password; other OS no-op + note

```sh
x keyring unlock
```

macOS script: pipe password once to unlock

```sh
x keyring unlock <<<"$KEYCHAIN_PW"
```

## Usage

```sh
x keyring unlock
```

# Faster Than Claude Code, Domestic AI Programming Assistant Kimi Code

Using Claude Code or Cursor with unstable connections and frequent timeouts?

Today, here's a better option accessible directly in China with stronger Chinese understanding and superior terminal operation — **Kimi CLI**.

## What is Kimi CLI?

Kimi CLI is a terminal AI programming agent launched by Moonshot AI.

| Feature | Claude Code | Cursor | Kimi CLI |
|---------|-------------|--------|----------|
| Network | VPN required | VPN required | **China-accessible** |
| Chinese | Average | Average | **Stronger** |
| Terminal | Limited | None | **Full control** |

## Installation

One command:

```sh
x kimi
```

Auto-installs on first run. To upgrade:

```sh
x kimi --upgrade
```

## Core Advantages

### 1. China-Accessible, No VPN Needed

Claude Code and Cursor both require stable VPN connections. Kimi CLI works directly in China with faster, more stable responses.

### 2. Stronger Chinese Understanding

As a domestic AI, Kimi understands Chinese instructions more accurately:

```
帮我写一个批量重命名图片的脚本，按拍摄日期重命名
```

It understands Chinese context like "拍摄日期" (shooting date) better than Claude.

### 3. True Terminal Native

Press `Ctrl-X` to switch to Shell command mode, and AI executes any terminal command for you:

```
帮我创建一个 React 项目并启动开发服务器
```

Kimi will sequentially execute `npx create-react-app`, `npm install`, `npm start` — all in one go.

### 4. ACP Protocol Support

Native Agent Client Protocol support, seamlessly integrated with Zed, JetBrains and other editors:

```json
{
  "agent_servers": {
    "Kimi Code CLI": {
      "command": "kimi",
      "args": ["acp"],
      "env": {}
    }
  }
}
```

## Comparison Experience

### Scenario: Fix Errors

**Cursor**: Open editor → Wait for indexing → Right-click AI Chat → Paste error → 30s+

**Kimi CLI**: "帮我看看这个报错 TypeError: Cannot read property 'map' of undefined", result in 3 seconds.

### Scenario: Write Scripts

Kimi has better understanding of Chinese instructions and can handle complex requirements.

## When to Use Kimi CLI

- Unstable connections, slow responses
- Many Chinese instruction understanding needs
- Pure terminal operation scenarios
- Want faster response speed

## Summary

- Install: `x kimi`
- Upgrade: `x kimi --upgrade`
- Website: https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-cli

Found it useful? Like and share～

# x last - View User Login/Logout and System Reboot Records

The `x last` command is used to view recent user login and logout records, as well as system reboot records. It supports multiple output formats (JSON, CSV) and views (tree view), making it convenient for users to quickly view and analyze login/logout information.

## Quick Start

Here are some common `x last` command examples:

::::ul
:::li View recent user login and logout records
```bash
x last
```
:::

:::li View in CSV format
```bash
x last --csv
```
:::

:::li View in JSON format
```bash
x last --json
```
:::

:::li View system reboot records
```bash
x last --reboot
```
:::

:::li Group by reboot, display in tree view
```bash
x last --tree
```
:::
::::

## Output Formats and Views

The `x last` command supports the following output formats and views:

::::ul
:::li Default Format
Displays user login and logout times, usernames, and other information in an easy-to-read table format
:::

:::li JSON Format (`--json`)
Outputs data in JSON format for easy program processing and analysis
:::

:::li CSV Format (`--csv`)
Outputs data in CSV format for easy import into spreadsheet software
:::

:::li Tree View (`--tree`)
Groups user login and logout records by system reboot and displays them in a tree structure, clearly showing login activities within each reboot cycle
:::
::::

## Using with Other Commands

The `x last` command can be combined with other `x-cmd` commands. For example, you can combine it with `x grep` to filter login records for specific users.

::: tip
Combining with `x grep` allows you to quickly locate specific users' login history
:::

## More Information

The `x last` command provides rich functionality to help users better understand system login activities. You can visit [https://x-cmd.com](https://x-cmd.com) for more information.

# x line arg1

Process each line from stdin as $1 to a shell function, one line at a time.

## Examples

Add "item" prefix to each line (outputs "item 1", "item 2", etc.).

```sh
seq 5 | x line arg1 'echo item $1'
```

Process each line and show the value of $1.

```sh
printf "%s\n" a b c | x line arg1 'echo got $1'
```

## Usage

```sh
x line arg1
```

url: /mod/line/args.md

# x line args

Group lines from stdin into batches of n lines, process each batch with a shell function.

## Examples

Group every 2 lines, output "group 1 2", "group 3 4", "group 5 6".

```sh
seq 6 | x line args -n 2 'echo group $1 $2'
```

Group every 3 lines, output "batch 1 2 3", "batch 4 5 6", "batch 7 8 9".

```sh
seq 9 | x line args -n 3 'echo batch $1 $2 $3'
```

## Usage

```sh
x line args
```

# x line duo

Find and print duplicate lines from stdin, preserving the order of their second appearance. Supports `-f field` to check a specific field and `-s separator` for custom field separator.

## Examples

Process two lists (1,2,3 and 5,4,3), print duplicates (3) at 2nd occurrence.

```sh
{ seq 1 3; seq 5 -1 3; } | x line duo
```

Show commands appearing more than once in /bin and /usr/bin.

```sh
{ ls /bin /usr/bin; } | x line duo
```

## Usage

```sh
x line duo
```

# x line join

Join all lines from stdin with a specified separator. Supports `--noblank` to skip empty lines, and optional `begin`/`end` to wrap each element.


::: tip
Scripting: `join_`
:::


## Examples

Join lines with a comma and space.

```sh
echo -e "a\nb\nc" | x line join ", "
```

Join lines with a pipe separator.

```sh
seq 3 | x line join " | "
```

Join lines, skipping blank lines.

```sh
echo -e "a\n\nb" | x line join --noblank ", "
```

## Usage

```sh
x line join
```

# x line uni

Deduplicate lines from stdin, output only the first occurrence of each. Using a set for O(1) lookup, faster than `sort | uniq`.

## Examples

Deduplicate two number lists (1, 2, 3 and 3, 2, 1), output unique sequence 1, 2, 3.

```sh
{ seq 1 3; seq 3 1; } | x line uni
```

Show all commands in /bin and /usr/bin, each command listed only once.

```sh
{ ls /bin /usr/bin; } | x line uni
```

## Usage

```sh
x line uni
```

# x llmf chat

Chat mode for multi-turn conversation via OpenAI-compatible API

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x llmf chat request](#x-llmf-chat-request) | Send chat request |


### x llmf chat request

Send chat request


- **Usage**:

```sh
x llmf chat request [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#n>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | The parameter content will be concatenated with spaces and sent to AI as a question |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--temperature`, `-t` |  | Control the diversity of model generated results, with a value greater than or equal to 0, when the temperature is higher, the model will be more random |
| `--seed` |  | Control the reproducibility of the job. Passing in the same seed and job parameters should produce the same results, but may differ in rare cases. If a seed is not specified, one will be generated for you. |
| `--maxtoken` |  | Control the maximum token length of the model response |
| `--jina` |  | Through jina reader, send the webpage content as context to AI |
| `--ddgo` |  | Send ddgo search content as context to AI |
| `--tldr` |  | Send tldr content as context to AI |
| `--eval` |  | Send the execution command results as context to AI |
| `-e` |  | Send the variable value as context to AI |
| `--file`, `-f` |  | Send file content as context to AI |
| `--kv` |  | Send key-value pairs as context to AI |
| `--session` |  | Specify session value |
| `--minion` |  | Specify minion file |
| `--history`, `-n` |  | Specify the number of history as context |
| `--model` |  | Specify AI model |
| `-p`, `--pipe` |  | Specify to get pipe content |
| `--tool`, `--allowed-tools` |  | Comma-separated list of tool names to allow (e.g. "writefile,writefile,shcmd") |
| `--provider` |  | Specify AI provider |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `-P`, `--nopipe` | Specify not to get pipe content |
| `-c` | Confirm before sending the request content to AI |
| `--edit` | Edit the request content in the terminal |
| `--question` | Request content |
| `--reasoning` | Show AI's reasoning process |
| `--no-reasoning` | Do not show AI's reasoning process, default on |
| `--stream` | Use streaming output, default on |
| `--no-stream` | Do not use streaming output |
| `--require-question` | Disallow empty request content |
| `--start-with-repl` | Start in REPL mode before sending the request |
| `--end-with-repl` | Start in REPL mode after sending the request (default behavior in interactive mode) |
| `--start-without-repl` | Start without REPL mode before sending the request |
| `--end-without-repl` | End without REPL mode after sending the request |
| `--without-repl` | Do not start REPL mode |

# x llmf cli

Command line interface mode for quick one-off text generation

## Examples

Example: quick text generation via CLI

```sh
x llmf cli -p 'Write a story about llamafile'
```

## Usage

```sh
x llmf cli [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-m`, `--model` &lt;FPATH&gt; |  | Specify model file path (GGUF format) |
| `--mmproj` &lt;FPATH&gt; |  | Specify multimodal projection model path (LLaVA vision model) |
| `-p`, `--prompt` &lt;STRING&gt; |  | Set prompt for text generation |
| `-t`, `--temp` &lt;N&gt; |  | Set generation temperature (randomness level) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--stdin` | Read content from stdin and append to prompt |
| `-`, `--edit` | Use interactive editor to edit prompt |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x llmf cli --](#x-llmf-cli) | Pass native llamafile CLI arguments |


### x llmf cli --

Pass native llamafile CLI arguments


- **Usage**:

```sh
x llmf cli -- <#n>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | Additional arguments for llamafile --cli |

# x llmf serve

Start API server mode with OpenAI-compatible HTTP interface

## Examples

Example: start API server

```sh
x llmf serve -m llava/v1.5-7b/q4_k.gguf --nobrowser
```

## Usage

```sh
x llmf serve [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] [SUB_COMMAND]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-m`, `--model` &lt;FPATH&gt; |  | Specify model file path (GGUF format) |
| `--mmproj` &lt;FPATH&gt; |  | Specify multimodal projection model path (LLaVA vision model, GGUF format) |
| `-p`, `--port` &lt;PORT&gt; |  | Set server listen port |
| `--host` &lt;IPADDR&gt; |  | Set server listen address |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--nobrowser` | Do not auto-open browser on startup |


## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x llmf serve --](#x-llmf-serve) | Pass native llamafile server arguments |
| [x llmf serve getembedding](#x-llmf-serve-getembedding) | Generate text embeddings, requires bge model series |


### x llmf serve --

Pass native llamafile server arguments


- **Usage**:

```sh
x llmf serve -- <#n>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | Additional arguments for llamafile --server |


### x llmf serve getembedding

Generate text embeddings, requires bge model series


- **Usage**:

```sh
x llmf serve getembedding [OPTIONS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Text string to generate embedding for |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `-f`, `--file` &lt;FPATH&gt; |  | Read text content from file |

# x ls - View Directory or Archive Contents

## View Current Directory Contents

`x ls` provides an interactive app that helps users quickly view contents of the current directory or a specific path, especially suitable for scenarios where you need to frequently view directory contents during debugging.

```sh
x ls
x ls ~/.x-cmd.root
```

![x ls (1)](/image/mod/ls.1_1.webp)

![x ls (2)](/image/mod/ls.1_2.webp)

In the interactive app:
- Users can quickly switch between different directories using keyboard shortcuts and view files and their basic information.
- After selecting a file or directory and pressing Enter, a next-step quick operation menu will be provided, such as changing directories, deleting files, etc.

## View Contents of PATH Directories

In certain scenarios, you may need to view directories introduced by the PATH environment variable in your system to analyze environment variable configuration or troubleshoot whether commands are executing correctly.

Run the following command to provide an interactive app for viewing directories and their contents introduced by the PATH environment variable in your system.

```sh
x ls :path
```

![x ls :path](/image/mod/ls.1_3.webp)

## View Archive Contents

`x ls` also provides a function to quickly list archive file structures without extraction, for scenarios where you need to check archive contents or confirm whether compressed files are valid.

```sh
x ls :/path/<archive-name>.zip
x ls :/path/<archive-name>.tar.gz
x ls :/Users/xcmd/Download/x-cmd.zip
```

![x ls :tar](/image/mod/ls.1_4.webp)

::: tip
Supports viewing common archive formats such as .zip, .tar.gz
:::

---
[More] To learn more about the ls module, please visit x-cmd official website - x-cmd.com/mod/ls

---
url: /mod/ls/cookbook-2.md
---

# x ls (2) - View System Information

## View Process Information

`x ls :ps` provides an interactive APP that helps users quickly view all running processes in the current system and their basic information (such as process ID, memory usage, etc.). It is suitable for users who need to frequently check and control processes.

```sh
x ls :ps
```

![x ls :ps 1](/image/mod/ls.2_1.webp)

![x ls :ps 2](/image/mod/ls.2_2.webp)

- In the interactive APP:
   - Users can use keyboard shortcuts to browse different processes and view the detailed information of each process.
   - After selecting a process and pressing Enter, a shortcut operation menu will be provided for the next step, such as viewing detailed information, ending the process, etc.

## View CPU Information

`x ls :cpu` can quickly view the CPU configuration and status information of the current system, including the processor model, number of cores, number of threads, etc.

```sh
x ls :cpu
```

![x ls :cpu](/image/mod/ls.2_3.webp)

## View Virtual Memory Information

`x ls :mem` can display the virtual memory usage of the current system, including total memory, used memory, free memory, and other indicators.

```sh
x ls :mem
```

![x ls :mem](/image/mod/ls.2_4.webp)

---
[More] If you want to learn more about the ls module, please visit the x-cmd official website - x-cmd.com/mod/ls

# x mac alias

Set an alias for the `x mac` command

## Examples

Enable the alias feature, set it to mcli, and use mcli instead of x mac in the future

```sh
x mac alias enable mcli
```

Enable the alias feature, if no parameter is provided, it defaults to m, and you can use m instead of x mac in the future

```sh
x mac alias enable
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x mac alias status](#x-mac-alias-status) | Check the current alias status of the `x mac` command |
| [x mac alias enable](#x-mac-alias-enable) | Set and enable an alias for the `x mac` command |
| [x mac alias disable](#x-mac-alias-disable) | Disable the set alias |


### x mac alias status

Check the current alias status of the `x mac` command


- **Usage**:

```sh
x mac alias status
```

### x mac alias enable

Set and enable an alias for the `x mac` command


- **Usage**:

```sh
x mac alias enable <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | alias |


### x mac alias disable

Disable the set alias


- **Usage**:

```sh
x mac alias disable
```

# x mac appid

List all applications installed in the /Applications directory, along with their respective App ID.

## Examples

# x mac - macOS Command Line Assistant

Still struggling with tedious macOS command line operations? x mac is here! Like your exclusive command-line Swiss Army knife, it's powerful yet simple to use, and will completely change the way you interact with your terminal! Say goodbye to boring commands and embrace an efficient, convenient operation experience!

## Touch ID sudo: Say Goodbye to Password Hassles

Never type lengthy sudo passwords over and over again! x mac supports using Touch ID to authorize sudo commands—just a light touch to get administrator privileges, secure and fast, instantly making you a macOS master!

```bash
x mac tidsudo enable  # Enable Touch ID sudo
```

## Custom Shortcuts: Your Personal Command Shorthand

Tired of typing those long commands? x mac allows you to create custom shortcut commands. For example, set "m" as the abbreviation for x mac, then you can access all functions by simply typing "m"! You can set any abbreviation you like according to your preferences, making your command line operations more personalized and efficient.

```bash
x mac alias enable m  # Set "m" as abbreviation for x mac
# Or customize abbreviation:
x mac alias enable mymac  # Set "mymac" as abbreviation for x mac
```

## More Practical Features at a Glance

x mac's functionality goes far beyond sudo authorization and command abbreviations. It also includes a series of powerful features to help you efficiently manage your macOS system, making your Mac run smoother and more secure!

x mac provides a powerful set of macOS command line tools covering system management, network settings, device information, and more. It not only simplifies your daily operations but also improves your work efficiency and security. Experience x mac now, start your efficient macOS command line journey, and feel unprecedented convenience and smoothness!

# Sandbox Isolation for ClaudeCode / OpenClaw - x-cmd Sandbox Guide

When you run AI programming assistants like ClaudeCode or OpenClaw on your Mac, they execute various commands—user-provided scripts, third-party tools, and AI-generated code. Sandbox isolation is essential to prevent **AI executing erroneous commands** (like `rm -rf /`) and **malicious scripts stealing data** (SSH keys, cloud credentials).

`x mac sb` wraps macOS's native `sandbox-exec` to provide rule sets and fine-grained permission control, allowing AI programming assistants to run commands following the **principle of least privilege**.

## Quick Start

### Block Access to Sensitive Directories

```bash
# Block claude from accessing SSH keys, Library, etc.
x mac sb -9 -d "$HOME/.ssh" -d "$HOME/Library" claude
```

### Prevent AI from Deleting Repository History

```bash
# Prevent claude from writing to ~/project/.git to avoid accidental repository history deletion
x mac sb -9 -d w:~/project/.git claude
```

### Run Scripts with Minimal Privileges

```bash
# Only allow reading ~/project directory
x mac sb -0 -a r:~/project -a x:/bin/bash bash ~/project/script.sh

# Disable network access
x mac sb -9 --no-net curl --head https://x-cmd.com
```

## Why Sandbox?

AI programming assistants face two major risks:

1. **AI hallucination or being poisoned**: Executing erroneous commands like `rm -rf /`, or being manipulated by prompt injections
2. **Malicious scripts**: Secretly uploading user data, reading SSH keys, or cloud credentials

x mac sb establishes a security boundary through the sandbox-exec mechanism, containing any issues within the smallest possible scope.

## Case Scenarios

### Case 1: Block Access to Sensitive Directories

**Scenario**: When ClaudeCode executes tasks, it might attempt to access your SSH keys, cloud credentials, and other sensitive data.

**Solution**: Block access to sensitive directories

```bash
x mac sb -9 -d "$HOME/.ssh" -d "$HOME/.aws" -d "$HOME/.kube" claude
```

This allows ClaudeCode to read and write project files normally, but prevents access to SSH keys and cloud credentials.

### Case 2: Block Deletion of Important Files

**Scenario**: You ask ClaudeCode to clean up the project, and the AI mistakenly prepares to delete the `.git` directory.

**Solution**: Block deletion of specific directories

```bash
x mac sb -9 -d w:~/project/.git claude
```

Now even if the AI executes `rm -rf .git`, it will fail, and you won't lose your version history.

## FAQ

### Q: Will completely blocking network access affect normal usage when running ClaudeCode?

Yes, it will. ClaudeCode needs network connections to communicate with its backend. If network access is completely disabled, the AI won't be able to function.

It is recommended to use **denylist mode**: use `-9` to allow everything by default, then only block sensitive directories:

```bash
x mac sb -9 -d "$HOME/.ssh" -d "$HOME/.aws" claude
```

### Q: How to prevent AI from executing destructive write operations?

Use `-d w:directory` to block writing to specific directories. For example, only allow reading in the project directory and block writing:

```bash
x mac sb -9 -d w:~/project claude
```

### Q: What is the difference between rule set -9 and -0?

- `-9`: Allow everything by default, use `-d` to deny individually (denylist mode, suitable for most scenarios)
- `-0`: Deny everything by default, use `-a` to allow individually (allowlist mode, for high security requirements)

### Q: Can rule sets and permission options be used together?

Yes. Rule sets provide base permissions, and permission options adjust on top of that. For example:

```bash
x mac sb -3 -a ~ bash -c 'ls ~'
```

Rule set `-3` provides base permissions, and `-a ~` additionally grants access to the home directory.

### Q: How to view the generated sandbox config for debugging?

Use `--dryrun` to only print the config without executing, or `--pp` to print the full policy:

```bash
x mac sb --dryrun -9 -d "$HOME/.ssh" claude
```

# x mac note

Command Line Interface for Apple Notes


::: tip
If you encounter permission issues when running for the first time, go to [System Settings] &gt; [Privacy & Security] &gt; [Automation] and grant your terminal app (e.g., Terminal, iTerm, x, Alfred) permission to access the Notes app.


- **Usage**:

```sh
x mac note rm_folder <#1> <#2>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | Folder name |
| `#2` | Child folder name |

# x mac re

A CLI for managing Apple Reminders


::: tip
If you encounter permission issues when running for the first time, go to [System Settings] &gt; [Privacy & Security] &gt; [Automation] and grant your terminal app (e.g., Terminal, iTerm, x, Alfred) permission to access the Reminders app.
:::


## Examples

Add a reminder titled "Buy milk" at 6:00 PM on June 25, 2025

```sh
x mac re add "Buy milk" "2025-06-25" "18:00"
```

Mark the reminder titled "Buy milk" as completed

```sh
x mac re comp "Buy milk"
```

Update the reminder "Buy milk" to "Buy milk,egg" and change the time to 7:00 PM on June 25, 2025

```sh
x mac re update "Buy milk" "Buy milk,egg" "2025-06-25 19:00"
```

List all reminders

```sh
x mac re ls
```

Retrieve the detailed information for the reminder named "Buy milk"

```sh
x mac re get "Buy milk"
```

Remove the reminder titled "Buy milk"

| [x mac re update](#x-mac-re-update) | Update a reminder's title or time |
| [x mac re get](#x-mac-re-get) | Get detailed information of a specific reminder |

# x mac sandbox

Sandbox, a wrapper for macOS sandbox-exec; users can now use `-0|-1|-3|-5|-9` to set basic permissions and add/remove permissions.

## Examples

Open claudecode, deny access to: $HOME/.bitcoin, $HOME/.ssh, $HOME/Library

```sh
x mac sb -9 -d "$HOME/.bitcoin" -d "$HOME/.ssh" -d "$HOME/Library"  claude
```

Ruleset 9 allows all permissions by default. To stop curl from Internet you need to specify --no-net

```sh
x mac sb -9 --no-net curl --head https://x-cmd.com || echo "Successfully stop curl from Internet"
```

Ruleset 0 deny all permissions by default. To Run the command like /bin/echo, you need to specify --init and execute permission for file /bin/echo

```sh
x mac sb -0 --init -a x:/bin/echo /bin/echo hi
```

Ruleset 1 provides default permissions for to access system bin folders and run basic command like echo

```sh
x mac sb -1 /bin/echo hi
```

Ruleset 3 provides default permissions for running the non-interactive command line tool like ls

```sh
x mac sb -3 bash -c 'ls ~' || echo "Failed to run ls because premission of home directory is not granted"
```

Ruleset 3 provides default permissions for running the non-interactive command line tool like ls, but user still need to grant permission for the target directory

```sh
x mac sb -3 -a ~ bash -c 'ls ~'
```

Ruleset 5 provides default permissions for running the interactive CLI app like bash

```sh
x mac sb -5 bash
```

Ruleset 5 provides default permissions for running the terminal app like `x-cmd ls`

```sh
x mac sb -5 x-cmd ls
```

Deny write access to /tmp. The command `touch /tmp/test.txt` should fail.

```sh
x mac sb -0 -d w:/tmp touch /tmp/test.txt && echo "Failed to create file" || echo "Successfully denied write access"
```

Allow read access to a specific file `/etc/hosts`. The command `cat /etc/hosts` should succeed.

```sh
x mac sb -0 -a r:/etc/hosts cat /etc/hosts
```

Deny all filesystem access to `/tmp`. The command `ls /tmp` should fail.

```sh
x mac sb -0 -d /tmp ls /tmp
```

## Usage

```sh
x mac sandbox|sb [OPTIONS] [FLAGS]
```

## Options

| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--wd`, `--workdir` |  | Allow access to the specified working directory |
| `--wf`, `--workfile` |  | Allow access to the specified working file |
| `--trace` |  | Print debug information to the specified file |
| `-c`, `--code` |  | Add custom sandbox rule code |
| `-q` |  | Quick add sandbox rule code (short form) |
| `-a` |  | Allow operations on a file or path. Format: `[rwx]:path`. `r` read, `w` write, `x` execute. `p` file or subdirectory (default). For example: `r:/path/to/file` (read file), `w:/path/to/dir` (write directory), `x:/bin/bash` (execute), `d:/tmp` (directory and subdirectories), `f:/etc/hosts` (specific file) |
| `-d` |  | Deny operations on a file or path. Format same as -a |
| `-F` |  | Deny filesystem access to the specified path (x-denyfs) |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--dryrun` | Only print the generated sandbox profile, do not execute the command |
| `--pp`, `--print-policy` | Print the generated sandbox policy |
| `-9` | Allow all operations by default (allow default), users can reduce permissions to prevent accidental mistakes or protect privacy information leakage; users can use this to build a security sandbox with a blacklist approach |
| `-1` | Use ruleset 1 (x-ruleset-1), provides permissions to access system bin folders and run basic commands |
| `-3` | Use ruleset 3 (x-ruleset-3), provides permissions for running non-interactive command line tools |
| `-5` | Use ruleset 5 (x-ruleset-5), provides permissions for running interactive CLI applications |
| `-8` | Use ruleset 8 (x-ruleset-8), provides permissions for pasteboard access |
| `--init` | Allow initialization operations (x-init) |
| `--all` | Allow all filesystem access (x-allow-rwx "/") |
| `--allrx` | Allow read and execute permissions (x-allow-allrx) |
| `--tty` | Allow TTY access (x-allow-tty) |
| `--no-tty` | Deny TTY access (x-deny-tty) |
| `--homebin` | Allow access to the user's home bin directory |
| `--sysbin` | Allow access to the system bin directory |
| `--home` | Allow access to the user's home directory |
| `--no-home` | Deny access to the user's home directory |
| `--pwd` | Allow access to the current working directory |
| `--no-pwd` | Deny access to the current working directory |
| `--ws` | Allow access to the workspace directory (the most recent directory with .x-cmd) |
| `--no-ws` | Deny access to the workspace directory (the most recent directory with .x-cmd) |
| `--fork` | Allow process forking (x-allow-fork) |
| `--no-fork` | Deny process forking (x-deny-fork) |
| `--net` | Allow network access (x-allow-net) |
| `--no-net` | Deny network access (x-deny-net) |
| `--e` | Allow file existence check (x-allow-file-existence-check) |
| `--no-e` | Deny file existence check (x-deny-file-existence-check) |
| `--ioctl` | Allow ioctl operations (x-allow-ioctl) |
| `--no-ioctl` | Deny ioctl operations (x-deny-ioctl) |
| `--pb` | Allow pasteboard access (x-allow-pb) |
| `--no-pb` | Deny pasteboard access (x-deny-pb) |
| `--root` | Allow root filesystem access (x-allow-rwx "/") |
| `--no-root` | Deny root filesystem access (x-denyfs "/") |

Entering sleep mode

:::

```sh

```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--screen`, `-s` | Just put the display to sleep |
| `--machine` | The entire system went to sleep, with the CPU, display, and hard drive all ceasing activity. |

# x man - Enhanced man Command

The `x man` command is an enhancement to the standard `man` command, providing a more convenient man page query and usage experience, including fuzzy search using `fzf`, command explanation using `mankier`, and direct access to tldr pages.

## Quick Start

```sh
x man ls          # View ls manual
x man git         # View git manual
```

## Basic Usage

The basic usage of the `x man` command is as follows:

```bash
x man [OPTION] [keyword]
```

Or use a more concise syntax:

```bash
x man :[keyword]
```

Where `keyword` is the command or keyword you want to look up.

## Main Features

### 1. Fuzzy Search with fzf

`x man` uses `fzf` by default to provide an interactive man page list, making it easy to quickly find target documentation. Experience it directly by running `x man` without any parameters:

```bash
x man
```

<!-- ![x man fzf](/image/mod/xman_fzf.png)  *(Replace with actual screenshot)* -->
*(Please replace `/image/mod/xman_fzf.png` with the actual screenshot file path)*

### 2. Direct Access to tldr Pages

Use the `:` prefix to quickly look up tldr pages:

```bash
x man :ssh
```

This will directly display the tldr page for the `ssh` command, providing concise and clear command usage instructions.

### 3. Explain Commands with mankier

Use the `--explain` or `-e` option to get more detailed command explanations using `mankier`:

```bash
x man -e ssh
```

This will use `mankier` to explain the `ssh` command, providing easier-to-understand descriptions.

### 4. Search man Pages by Keyword

Use the `-k` option to search man pages by keyword:

```bash
x man -k disk
```

This will use an interactive UI to list all man pages containing the keyword "disk".

## Advanced Usage

### Custom Configuration (Future Feature, Prospective Only)

Future versions may support custom configurations, such as specifying `fzf` themes or other personalization settings.

## Summary

The `x man` command greatly improves the efficiency of finding and using man pages by integrating tools like `fzf` and `mankier`. Whether quickly looking up command documentation or deeply understanding command usage, `x man` provides convenient solutions.
Please visit [https://x-cmd.com/mod/man](https://x-cmd.com/mod/man) for more information.

---
url: /mod/mankier/cookbook-1.md
---

# x mankier - ManKier Manual Page Search and Browse Tool

`x mankier` is a command-line tool for searching and browsing manual pages on ManKier. ManKier provides a large number of Unix command manual pages, and `x mankier` allows you to conveniently access and use this information.

## Explain Commands

Use the `explain` or `e` command to explain a shell command:

```bash
x mankier explain ls -l
```

This will return an explanation of the `ls -l` command.

## Search Manual Pages

Use the `query` or `q` command to search manual pages:

```bash
x mankier query grep
```

This will search all manual pages containing "grep". You can use `-j`, `-c`, `-y` parameters to output results in JSON, CSV, and YAML formats respectively. The `--app` parameter will display results in an interactive interface.

```bash
x mankier query -j grep
x mankier query -c grep
x mankier query -y grep
x mankier query --app grep
```

## Get Manual Page Details

Use the `page` command to get detailed information about a specific manual page:

```bash
x mankier page grep.1
```

This will return the manual page content for the `grep` command. Similarly, `-j` and `-y` parameters can control the output format.

```bash
x mankier page -j grep.1
x mankier page -y grep.1
```

## Get Manual Page Section Content

Use the `section` command to get content from a specific section of a manual page:

```bash
x mankier section grep.1 NAME
```

This will return the content of the "NAME" section in the `grep` command manual page. `--json` and `--txt` parameters control the output format.

## Get Manual Page Reference Information

Use the `ref` command to get all links pointing to and from a specified manual page:

```bash
x mankier ref grep.1
```

This will return all link information related to the `grep.1` manual page. The `-j` parameter can control the output format.

## Search Using DuckDuckGo

Use the `ddgo` or `:` command combined with DuckDuckGo to search for information on the ManKier website:

```bash
x mankier : awk
```

This will use DuckDuckGo to search for "awk" related information on the ManKier website.

::: tip
ManKier provides rich Unix command manual pages and is an excellent resource for learning Linux/Unix commands
:::

## More Information

Please visit [https://x-cmd.com/mod/mankier](https://x-cmd.com/mod/mankier) for more information.

# x mirror docker

setting the docker mirror

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x mirror docker pull](#x-mirror-docker-pull) | Provide a method to download images from the image source without modifying the Docker Daemon. |
| [x mirror docker set](#x-mirror-docker-set) | Setting the default mirror for pull image |
| [x mirror docker unset](#x-mirror-docker-unset) | Unset mirror |
| [x mirror docker get](#x-mirror-docker-get) | Get the currently set default mirror |


### x mirror docker pull

Provide a method to download images from the image source without modifying the Docker Daemon.



::: info Principle: First, download the image from a mirror site, then modify the tag (for example, download codeberg.org/x-cmd/alpine:latest, then change it to alpine:latest).
If you need to modify the Docker proxy and image source, you can use `x docker daemon proxy` or `x docker daemon mirror`.
:::


- **Examples**:

Pull the image kali-rolling:latest from the codeberg.org/x-cmd

```sh
x docker mirror pull -m codeberg.org/x-cmd kali-rolling:latest
```

Set the docker mirror to https://docker.m.daocloud.io

```sh
x docker daemon mirror set https://docker.m.daocloud.io
```

Set "docker.m.daocloud.io" as the default mirror for `x docker mirror pull`

```sh
x docker mirror set "docker.m.daocloud.io"
```

- **Usage**:

```sh
x mirror docker pull [OPTIONS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | image path |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--mirror`, `-m` |  | mirror url |


### x mirror docker set

Setting the default mirror for pull image


- **Usage**:

```sh
x mirror docker set
```

### x mirror docker unset

Unset mirror


- **Usage**:

```sh
x mirror docker unset
```

### x mirror docker get

Get the currently set default mirror


- **Usage**:

```sh
x mirror docker get
```

# x mistral chat

chat with mistral

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x mistral chat request](#x-mistral-chat-request) | send a request |


### x mistral chat request

send a request


- **Usage**:

```sh
x mistral chat request [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#n>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | The parameter content will be concatenated with spaces and sent to AI as a question |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--temperature`, `-t` |  | Control the diversity of model generated results, with a value greater than or equal to 0, when the temperature is higher, the model will be more random |
| `--seed` |  | Control the reproducibility of the job. Passing in the same seed and job parameters should produce the same results, but may differ in rare cases. If a seed is not specified, one will be generated for you. |
| `--maxtoken` |  | Control the maximum token length of the model response |
| `--jina` |  | Through jina reader, send the webpage content as context to AI |
| `--ddgo` |  | Send ddgo search content as context to AI |
| `--tldr` |  | Send tldr content as context to AI |
| `--eval` |  | Send the execution command results as context to AI |
| `-e` |  | Send the variable value as context to AI |
| `--file`, `-f` |  | Send file content as context to AI |
| `--kv` |  | Send key-value pairs as context to AI |
| `--session` |  | Specify session value |
| `--minion` |  | Specify minion file |
| `--history`, `-n` |  | Specify the number of history as context |
| `--model` |  | Specify AI model |
| `-p`, `--pipe` |  | Specify to get pipe content |
| `--tool`, `--allowed-tools` |  | Comma-separated list of tool names to allow (e.g. "writefile,writefile,shcmd") |
| `--provider` |  | Specify AI provider |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `-P`, `--nopipe` | Specify not to get pipe content |
| `-c` | Confirm before sending the request content to AI |
| `--edit` | Edit the request content in the terminal |
| `--question` | Request content |
| `--reasoning` | Show AI's reasoning process |
| `--no-reasoning` | Do not show AI's reasoning process, default on |
| `--stream` | Use streaming output, default on |
| `--no-stream` | Do not use streaming output |
| `--require-question` | Disallow empty request content |
| `--start-with-repl` | Start in REPL mode before sending the request |
| `--end-with-repl` | Start in REPL mode after sending the request (default behavior in interactive mode) |
| `--start-without-repl` | Start without REPL mode before sending the request |
| `--end-without-repl` | End without REPL mode after sending the request |
| `--without-repl` | Do not start REPL mode |

# x neo fetch

Display system information (default command)

## Usage

```sh
x neo fetch [FLAGS]
```

## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--mini` | Mini mode - show minimal information |
| `--std` | Standard mode - show standard information |
| `--all` | All mode - show all available information |
| `--llm` | LLM mode - plain text output suitable for AI |
| `--ui` | UI mode - side-by-side logo and info display |
| `--logo` | Specify logo name |
| `--no-logo` | Disable logo display |
| `--color` | Enable color output |
| `--no-color` | Disable color output |
| `--title` | Show title (user@host) |
| `--os` | Show operating system |
| `--host` | Show host information |
| `--kernel` | Show kernel version |
| `--uptime` | Show system uptime |
| `--pkgs` | Show package count |
| `--shell` | Show shell information |
| `--resolution` | Show screen resolution |
| `--de` | Show desktop environment |
| `--wm` | Show window manager |
| `--wmtheme` | Show window manager theme |
| `--theme` | Show GTK theme |
| `--icons` | Show icon theme |
| `--terminal` | Show terminal information |
| `--terminalfont` | Show terminal font |
| `--cpu` | Show CPU information |
| `--gpu` | Show GPU information |
| `--memory` | Show memory usage |
| `--info` | Custom info format string |
| `--indent` | Set logo indentation |

# x nets view

Display detailed information for a specified table, supporting interactive selection or direct table name specification

## Examples

Start interactive mode, select the table to view

```sh
x nets view
```

View information for the 'internet' table (TCP/UDP connections)

```sh
x nets view internet
```

Output 'route' table information in TSV format

```sh
x nets view --tsv route
```

## Usage

```sh
x nets view|v [FLAGS] <#1>
```

## Arguments

| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | table name |


## Flags

| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `--tsv` | Output in TSV format |
| `--csv` | Output in CSV format |

# Not just notifications — let AI Agents proactively alert you

Your build has been running for hours, you switched to another window and forgot to check back. An AI Agent has been grinding away in the background for minutes, and you have no idea if it's done — one `x notify` command solves all of this.

`x notify` is a cross-platform desktop notification tool that works on macOS, Linux, and Windows / WSL. It auto-detects your system and calls the corresponding native notification backend (osascript / notify-send / PowerShell), popping up a system alert in any scenario.

But its real value goes beyond that — **letting AI Agents proactively notify you when tasks complete** — that's what `x notify` is really about.

## Quick Start

### Send a basic notification

Just pass the notification content. The title defaults to `X-CMD Notify`:

```bash
x notify "build finished"
```

### Customize the notification title

Use `--title` (or `-t`) to set a title that makes your notification instantly recognizable:

```bash
x notify --title "Build" "build finished"
```

### Use a custom icon

On Linux and Windows, you can specify an icon path with `--icon` (or `-i`):

```bash
x notify --icon /usr/share/icons/Adwaita/symbolic/status/dialog-warning.svg "task done"
```

## Let AI Agents Send Notifications

When an AI Agent runs a long task, you can't just stare at the terminal the whole time. The Agent finishes silently — no feedback loop — unless you proactively ask. `x notify` fills this gap: let the Agent pop a system notification when it's done, visible no matter which window you're in.

Any AI Agent with shell execution capability (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, etc.) can call `x notify` directly — no extra configuration needed.

### OpenClaw

Add a notification call at the end of an OpenClaw skill definition to get automatic alerts when tasks finish:

```text
After completing all steps, run the following command to send a notification:
x notify --title "OpenClaw" "Task {task_name} completed"
```

### Claude Code

Claude Code has shell tool access — just tell it in conversation:

```text
Generate this week's project report, and use x notify to alert me when done
```

Claude Code will automatically run `x notify --title "X-CMD Notify" "Weekly report generated"` at the end of the task.

For more automation, you can write hook rules in `CLAUDE.md` so Claude Code sends notifications by default after every long task. You can also embed notification logic directly in `/skill` definitions.

## FAQ

### Q: Why does `--icon` not work on macOS?

macOS `osascript display notification` does not support custom icon parameters. `--icon` is silently ignored on macOS. This flag only takes effect on Linux (notify-send) and Windows (PowerShell).

### Q: `notify-send` not found on Linux?

`notify-send` is part of the `libnotify` package. Install it per your distribution:

- Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt install libnotify-bin`
- Fedora: `sudo dnf install libnotify`
- Arch: `sudo pacman -S libnotify`

### Q: How do I make AI Agents (OpenClaw / Claude Code) send notifications?

Write `x notify` commands directly into the Agent's prompt or skill definition. When the Agent has shell tool access, it will automatically invoke the notification. Typical usage:

```bash
# Chained approach
x claude -p "long task" && x notify --title "Agent" "done"

# Inline approach (written in prompt)
After completing the task, run x notify --title "Agent Task" "Task completed"
```

### Q: What about special characters in messages (quotes, backslashes)?

Don't worry about it. `x notify` automatically escapes quotes and backslashes in `msg` and `title` to adapt to each platform's notification interface. Just pass the raw content — no manual handling needed.

### Q: Does it work under Windows WSL?

Yes. `x notify` sends native Windows notifications via PowerShell under WSL — works out of the box with no extra configuration.

# x ohmyposh - Beautify Your Terminal

## Interactive Preview of Terminal Themes

`x ohmyposh` is an enhanced module designed for [oh-my-posh](https://ohmyposh.dev). Just execute the following command to open an interactive app to preview multiple terminal themes.

```sh
x ohmyposh
```

![x ohmyposh](/image/mod/ohmyposh.1_1.webp)

::: tip
In the interactive app, the left side shows theme names and the right side shows theme effect styles. After the user selects and presses Enter, they can choose to use the specified terminal theme
:::

## View Currently Used Theme

The following command can view the currently used terminal theme:
```sh
x ohmyposh current
```

![x ohmyposh current](/image/mod/ohmyposh.1_2.webp)

## Set Theme

The `x ohmyposh` module has `120+` built-in terminal themes. You can use the `x ohmyposh ls` command to view all available themes.

If you want to change the terminal theme, you can use the `x ohmyposh use` command to apply a new theme in the global environment:

```sh
x ohmyposh use montys
x ohmyposh use half-life
```

## Use Different Themes in Different Environments

`x ohmyposh` supports specifying different terminal themes for different environments, making it convenient for users to distinguish between environments.

```sh
# Set to use half-life theme in VSCode terminal environment
x ohmyposh use --vscode half-life

# Set to use blueish theme in Windows Terminal environment
x ohmyposh use --windows blueish
```

You can also set different themes for different Shell environments.
```sh
# Set to use 'montys' theme in PowerShell environment
x ohmyposh use --shell powershell montys

# Set to use 'half-life' theme in Fish Shell environment
x ohmyposh use --shell fish half-life
```

## Customize Terminal Theme

The `x ohmyposh` module supports user-customized terminal themes. Users can create their own terminal themes and use the `x ohmyposh use` command to apply custom themes.

```sh
x ohmyposh use /path/to/my-theme.json
```

::: info
x ohmyposh supports JSON format custom theme files
:::

---
[More] To learn more about the ohmyposh module, please visit x-cmd official website - x-cmd.com/mod/ohmyposh

# x ollama chat

chat with model

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x ollama chat request](#x-ollama-chat-request) | send a request |


### x ollama chat request

send a request


- **Usage**:

```sh
x ollama chat request [OPTIONS] [FLAGS] <#n>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#n` | The parameter content will be concatenated with spaces and sent to AI as a question |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--temperature`, `-t` |  | Control the diversity of model generated results, with a value greater than or equal to 0, when the temperature is higher, the model will be more random |
| `--seed` |  | Control the reproducibility of the job. Passing in the same seed and job parameters should produce the same results, but may differ in rare cases. If a seed is not specified, one will be generated for you. |
| `--maxtoken` |  | Control the maximum token length of the model response |
| `--jina` |  | Through jina reader, send the webpage content as context to AI |
| `--ddgo` |  | Send ddgo search content as context to AI |
| `--tldr` |  | Send tldr content as context to AI |
| `--eval` |  | Send the execution command results as context to AI |
| `-e` |  | Send the variable value as context to AI |
| `--file`, `-f` |  | Send file content as context to AI |
| `--kv` |  | Send key-value pairs as context to AI |
| `--session` |  | Specify session value |
| `--minion` |  | Specify minion file |
| `--history`, `-n` |  | Specify the number of history as context |
| `--model` |  | Specify AI model |
| `-p`, `--pipe` |  | Specify to get pipe content |
| `--tool`, `--allowed-tools` |  | Comma-separated list of tool names to allow (e.g. "writefile,writefile,shcmd") |
| `--provider` |  | Specify AI provider |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `-P`, `--nopipe` | Specify not to get pipe content |
| `-c` | Confirm before sending the request content to AI |
| `--edit` | Edit the request content in the terminal |
| `--question` | Request content |
| `--reasoning` | Show AI's reasoning process |
| `--no-reasoning` | Do not show AI's reasoning process, default on |
| `--stream` | Use streaming output, default on |
| `--no-stream` | Do not use streaming output |
| `--require-question` | Disallow empty request content |
| `--start-with-repl` | Start in REPL mode before sending the request |
| `--end-with-repl` | Start in REPL mode after sending the request (default behavior in interactive mode) |
| `--start-without-repl` | Start without REPL mode before sending the request |
| `--end-without-repl` | End without REPL mode after sending the request |
| `--without-repl` | Do not start REPL mode |

# x ollama - Local Large Language Model Runtime Tool

Want to run large language models locally? Ollama makes it easy! `x ollama` wraps Ollama, providing a convenient local AI experience.

## Quick Start

```sh
x ollama                # Start conversation
x ollama chat llama2   # Chat with llama2
```

## Core Features

### Model Management

```sh
x ollama list           # List downloaded models
x ollama pull llama2   # Download model
x ollama rm llama2     # Delete model
```

### Model Running

```sh
x ollama run llama2    # Run model
x ollama chat          # Chat mode
x ollama generate      # Generation mode
```

### Quick Operations

```sh
x ollama <model> "question" # Quick Q&A
```

## Supported Models

*   Llama 2
*   Mistral
*   Code Llama
*   Orca
*   Vicuna

::: tip
First-time use requires downloading models, which takes longer. Once downloaded, subsequent use will be very fast!
:::

## Use Cases

*   Local AI experience
*   Privacy-sensitive scenarios (data stays local)
*   Offline use
*   Development testing

# x openai --cfg

Manage configuration items such as API key, default proxy, and more


::: info
- apikey: Set the OpenAI API key
- model: Set the OpenAI model
- maxtoken: Set the maximum tokens for GPT (optional)
- proxy: Set the network proxy for API requests
:::


## Examples

Set the default model to gpt-5.1.

```sh
x openai --cfg model="gpt-5.1"
```

Print the current configuration of the openai module.

```sh
x openai --cfg cat
```

```sh
x openai --cfg [SUB_COMMAND] <#n>
```

# x openai audio

Convert speech to text and text to speech

## Examples

Text to speech

```sh
x openai audio generate --input "hello x-cmd" --model tts-1 --voice alloy
```

Recognize speech and translate to English using the whisper-1 model

```sh
x openai audio translate --model whisper-1 test.mp3
```

## Sub Commands

| Name | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| [x openai audio generate](#x-openai-audio-generate) | Text to speech |
| [x openai audio transcribe](#x-openai-audio-transcribe) | Transcribes audio into the input language |
| [x openai audio translate](#x-openai-audio-translate) | Translates audio into English |


### x openai audio generate

Text to speech


- **Usage**:

```sh
x openai audio generate [OPTIONS]
```

- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--input` |  | The text to generate audio for |
| `--model` |  | One of the available TTS models |
| `--voice` |  | The voice to use when generating the audio |
| `--response_format` |  | The format to audio in |
| `--speed` |  | The speed of the generated audio |
| `--output_path` |  | The path to the resulting audio file |


### x openai audio transcribe

Transcribes audio into the input language


- **Usage**:

```sh
x openai audio transcribe [OPTIONS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | The audio file path to transcribes |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--model` |  | ID of the model to use, Only whisper-1 is currently available |
| `--language` |  | The language of the input audio |
| `--prompt` |  | An optional text to guide the model style or continue a previous audio segment |
| `--response_format` |  | The format of the transcript output |
| `--temperature` |  | The sampling temperature, between 0 and 1 |


### x openai audio translate

Translates audio into English


- **Usage**:

```sh
x openai audio translate [OPTIONS] <#1>
```

- **Arguments**:


| Argument | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `#1` | The audio file path to translate |


- **Options**:


| Name, Shorthand | Default | Description |
| ------- | ------- | ------- |
| `--model` |  | ID of the model to use, Only whisper-1 is currently available |
| `--prompt` |  | An optional text to guide the model style or continue a previous audio segment |
| `--response_format` |  | The format of the transcript output |
| `--temperature` |  | The sampling temperature, between 0 and 1 |

| `--maxtoken` |  | Control the maximum token length of the model response |
| `--jina` |  | Through jina reader, send the webpage content as context to AI |
| `--ddgo` |  | Send ddgo search content as context to AI |
| `--tldr` |  | Send tldr content as context to AI |
| `--eval` |  | Send the execution command results as context to AI |
| `-e` |  | Send the variable value as context to AI |
| `--file`, `-f` |  | Send file content as context to AI |
| `--kv` |  | Send key-value pairs as context to AI |
| `--session` |  | Specify session value |
| `--minion` |  | Specify minion file |
| `--history`, `-n` |  | Specify the number of history as context |
| `--model` |  | Specify AI model |
| `-p`, `--pipe` |  | Specify to get pipe content |
| `--tool`, `--allowed-tools` |  | Comma-separated list of tool names to allow (e.g. "writefile,writefile,shcmd") |
| `--provider` |  | Specify AI provider |


- **Flags**:


| Name, Shorthand | Description |
| ------- | ------- |
| `-P`, `--nopipe` | Specify not to get pipe content |
| `-c` | Confirm before sending the request content to AI |
| `--edit` | Edit the request content in the terminal |
| `--question` | Request content |
| `--reasoning` | Show AI's reasoning process |
| `--no-reasoning` | Do not show AI's reasoning process, default on |
| `--stream` | Use streaming output, default on |
| `--no-stream` | Do not use streaming output |
| `--require-question` | Disallow empty request content |
| `--start-with-repl` | Start in REPL mode before sending the request |
| `--end-with-repl` | Start in REPL mode after sending the request (default behavior in interactive mode) |
| `--start-without-repl` | Start without REPL mode before sending the request |
| `--end-without-repl` | End without REPL mode after sending the request |
| `--without-repl` | Do not start REPL mode |

# Quick Install openclaw

::: danger
⚠️ Security Notice
OpenClaw (formerly known as Clawdbot) and its agent-related features may carry certain risks. To prevent agent runaway or continuous operation, X-CMD provides a "last resort" tool [`x gram`](https://x-cmd.com/mod/gram).

This tool serves as an "emergency brake" and can perform the following actions:
- Force circuit breaker: Immediately terminate all related agent processes
- Data preservation: Archive the agent's memory data
- Complete cleanup: Clear the original runtime directory to eliminate the risk of automatic recovery

Related reading: [[0201] Don't use clawdbot openclaw on root! x-cmd releases 0.7.15, one command to kill all running Agents](https://x-cmd.com/blog/260201)
:::

## Quick Preview

```bash
# If you haven't installed x-cmd, run this command
eval "$(curl https://get.x-cmd.com)"

# If you're on macOS but don't have brew, you can install brew first
x install brew

# Install openclaw and the latest versions of commands and environments required for common skills
x openclaw --install
```

## Detailed Explanation

### If you haven't installed x-cmd, just open your terminal:

x-cmd is a one-stop command-line toolkit with powerful features for both human users and AI. It also simplifies the installation methods for many tools.

```bash
eval "$(curl https://get.x-cmd.com)"
```

::: tip
If you still don't know how to install, please refer to https://x-cmd.com/start
:::

Note that you may need a newer version of x-cmd to have the openclaw module, please run:

```bash
x upgrade beta
```

### Install clawdbot/openclaw

To better use clawdbot/openclaw, we created the openclaw module. Users can install and use it with one click:

```bash
x openclaw --install
```

![openclaw-install](/image/mod/openclaw.1_1.webp)

::: warning
This command installs not only openclaw but also common command tools required to run openclaw, such as communication tools, etc. Additionally, if you're on macOS, it will call brew to install macOS-specific tools
:::

If you don't have brew, you can run `x i brew` to quickly install brew:

![install-brew](/image/mod/openclaw.1_2.webp)

## Next Step -- Configuration

::: info
Don't worry, this is also simple, it just requires more patience
:::
